13 July

Business of the House
THURSDAY, 13 JULY 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Mr SPEAKER: Does the Prime Minister desire to take any formal or other business
before proceeding to the Order of the Day set down?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Yes, down to and including reports of
select committees. It is also proposed to take the Order of the Day for the local Bill.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): A point of order, Mr Speaker.
The second class of estimates on today's Order Paper for consideration during the
Committee stage of the Appropriation Bill is Accident Compensation. The paper conveying
answers to questions asked in the Public Expenditure Committee yesterday has not yet come
to hand. Vote Agriculture and Fisheries is also included for consideration today, although
admittedly it is the last on the list. However, the full estimate has not yet been discussed in
the committee to which it was sent. I bring to the attention of the House the undue pressure
that is being placed upon it. In many cases the matters for consideration are based on reports
that are made available on Tuesday and discussions that take place in committees on
Wednesday. The business is brought back to the House on Thursday, without members
having had the opportunity to consider answers to questions or even properly to consider the
reports that have been presented. I draw attention to those two estimates which are set down
as the business of the House for today.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): There is nothing unusual in having
reports tabled on Tuesday, considered by the Public Expenditure Committee or other
committees on Wednesday, and debated on Thursday. That has been happening for as long
as I have been in the House and, I imagine, for a great deal longer. I think that is normal
with the supplementary estimates every year, and with other estimates as well.
These matters, properly and traditionally, are discussed between the Whips. I was
informed last night that the Senior Opposition Whip had agreed that what we had set down
for today was adequate for a day's business. Indeed, only a week or two ago, for the first
day's consideration of the estimates, I set down 2 days' work for a normal year, and the
Opposition complained that there was not enough business for 1 day. By the end of the
evening, however, we had not got half way through it. It is becoming a habit of the
Opposition to make these spurious complaints.
The answers to the questions the Deputy Leader of the Opposition referred to were on
the Minister's desk this morning, and I am informed that if they are not in the hands of
Opposition members it is merely a matter of transmission. Certainly they will be in their
hands long before they have to debate them. If they were asked yesterday, it is obvious that
members could not expect to receive them before this morning, and the Minister informs me
that they are on the way. Any estimate that has not been passed by the appropriate
committee, of course, cannot be debated; so that question does not arise.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Well, it is on the Order Paper.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The Deputy Leader of the Opposition has been in the
House for a year or two now, and surely he knows that an estimate cannot be debated in the
Committee of Supply unless it has been passed by the appropriate committee.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: I realise that perfectly.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Well, why does he raise it as a spurious point of order?
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui): Mr Speaker—
Mr SPEAKER: Procedural matters are probably best dealt with by the Whips, but if
they are to be brought up in the House-and there is nothing to stop the leaders of the
parties from raising matters relating to the business, although I repeat that it is probably
better for them to be dealt with by the Whips without taking up the time of the House-I do
not think we want to engage in a point of order discussion on them. Strictly speaking, the
matter is not a point of order, and it is not one on which I can adjudicate. However, if the
member for Wanganui has information that could be helpful to the House without
prolonging the discussion unduly, I am prepared to hear him.

## p. 1748 (#10) ############################################

13 July
Business of the House
Mr MARSHALL: I acknowledge the point made by the Prime Minister, that there was
an agreement between the Whips about the amount of business, but I think we ought to keep
in mind one major point made by the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, which is that, if
papers are requested, it would be helpful to the Opposition to have them as soon as they are
available to the Minister, as the Prime Minister indicated they are. The point has been made,
quite rightly, that having a report published one day, sending it to a committee the next day,
and debating it in the House on the third day is proceeding with undue haste in the view of
many of us. If we are to work under that system-and we have no control over it-it would
help the Opposition greatly if the papers requested in the Public Expenditure Committee
and in other committees were made available rather earlier than they have been so far this
year. It is very difficult for us to prepare for debate if those papers arrive just an hour or two
before the debate.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Naturally, we shall do that to the greatest
possible extent, but members will realise that some questions asked in the committee require
research in the department. It is not new for this to happen. In previous years, under
successive Governments, we have been under similar pressure in debating legislation that
has had to be passed immediately.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Estimates have been put to one side when questions have not been
answered.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Members will appreciate that this is an election year, and I
guess members on both sides hope that they will not be sitting on into November with an
election at the end of that month, if that is the time it does occur. I should have thought that
members would be able to accept a situation that is not novel. It has often happened before
under successive Governments, and without this constant criticism. We shall get the material
to members as quickly as possible, but they must realise that, if an estimate was taken
yesterday and it is to be debated today, the earliest they are likely to get answers to their
questions is about midday today. I am informed that the particular item to which the
Opposition does not have answers will be available shortly.
I make the same offer that I made on an earlier occasion. Should the debate happen to
come up this afternoon we can, if the Opposition wishes, postpone it until this evening, but I
recall that, when I made that offer earlier, the matter came up in the evening because we did
not reach it earlier, and I guess that it will be much the same today.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I have just received the
material from the Accident Compensation Commission in answer to the questions put in the
Public Expenditure Committee, but the questions I asked have not been answered. The six
questions quite properly asked by the member for Lyttelton have been answered, as have
those asked by the member for Petone, and that is all. I have a record of my questions, but
there is no reference to them. That is the problem we are up against. We are asked to debate
issues before we have answers to the questions put in the Public Expenditure Committee.
What is the point in having a Public Expenditure Committee hearing if we do not receive
answers to our questions?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I am very sorry for the honourable
member if he asked a question in the Public Expenditure Committee and does not have it
answered in writing. I suggest that he ask the question again when the Minister is in the
chair. The Minister cannot be held responsible for questions asked by the member in the
Public Expenditure Committee which somehow the Accident Compensation Commission
has not answered. The Minister was not there. Would the Junior Opposition Whip contain
himself for a moment.
Mr SPEAKER: Order!
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Yes, if he will put his handkerchief in front of his mouth,
that might stop him. As members know, questions asked in the committee are taken down
by an official of the Accident Compensation Commission who is there for that purpose. He
takes the questions away, and answers them in writing. If he did not understand the
question, missed it, or failed to answer it, there is little that can be done about it now.
Mr Marshall: All the conventions are going.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: What would the honourable member know about
conventions? He has only been here 5 minutes.
Mr SPEAKER: I think this discussion has gone about as far as it needs to. Already we
have spent about 10 minutes discussing a matter that will be dealt with in the Committee of
the Whole. If members wish to take up their time in this way, I suppose they are entitled to

Business of the House
do so, but it should be done briefly. It is not a matter that can be resolved at this stage.
Procedures exist for dealing with these matters outside the Chamber. The convention is
there for the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, or their representatives, to
undertake this procedure. If we are to have a discussion on this matter, it should be
conducted properly without the type of interjection we have been having, which could lead
to disorder.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): In the meantime, the chairman of the
Public Expenditure Committee, and the Senior Government Whip, who has rung the
chairman of the Accident Compensation Commission, tell me that no written answers were
required to the questions put by the Deputy Leader of the Opposition. Both the chairman of
the Accident Compensation Commission, who apparently appeared before the committee,
and the chairman of the Public Expenditure Committee, have independently and separately
stated that the Deputy Leader of the Opposition asked no questions that called for a written
answer, so we shall have to leave it for debate in the Committee of Supply.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I accept the Prime Minister's
assurance that he does not know what he is talking about. He was not there. I asked a
specific question, which was-
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I think the honourable member is now anticipating that the
House will go into Committee. We do not need to have a discussion on the details. At the
moment we are having a discussion, not entirely out of order, on the business of the House.
That is all we are concerned with just now.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: In the Public Expenditure Committee I asked the specific
question, "How many cases have been waiting for 2 years or more for a decision?"
Mr Talbot: And the honourable member got a verbal answer.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: No, I did not get a verbal answer. As part of a general discussion
on the work of the Accident Compensation Commission I made it quite clear that I wanted
to know how many cases had been waiting that long. I still do not have the answer.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): The position is becoming quite ludicrous.
Normally, this would be an exchange of views on the business of the House, but we are
getting into a debate on whether or not a member got an answer to a question he put in the
Public Expenditure Committee. The chairman of that committee says that the honourable
member received a verbal answer that there were 50 000 such cases. Obviously, the
chairman of the Accident Compensation Commission, having given that verbal answer, did
not believe he was called upon to give it again in writing. It is as simple as that. We are
supposed to be talking about procedure, not whether 50 000 is the right answer, or whether
it should have been given in writing or verbally. We will have time for that later in the
evening, if the honourable member is still here.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): If the answer is 50 000-
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I should like the honourable member to throw some light on the
procedures of the House and not to go into details of what occurred in the select committee.
What occurred in the committee is confidential at this stage to members of that committee
and should not be reported until the House goes into the Committee of the Whole. As I
understand it, the select committee is not open to members of the news media, and therefore
the information is confidential at this stage.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: You should make that point to the Prime Minister.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I am sorry if I appeared to make that remark to the Deputy
Leader of the Opposition. It applies to any member who has spoken so far on this matter.
My recollection is that the detail of what happened in the select committee and the question
asked was raised first by the honourable member himself.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: That is quite true.
Mr SPEAKER: So, I am prepared to have a very short explanation from the honourable
member. Then we should leave it at that because I would not like this to go any further.
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): Mr Speaker-
Mr SPEAKER: I can see that the Junior Government Whip is anxious to enter the fray,
too, but I think it would be better if he were to throw more light on this in the Committee of
the Whole House.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: He is the chairman of the committee.
Mr SPEAKER: At this stage he should not get into the debate. The Chairman of
Committees will be chairing the debate on the estimates. I do not have that pleasure.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I am quite happy to submit to

you or to anyone else the notes I took. The Prime Minister's reference was not an answer to

NOTICES OF MOTION-PROCEDURE
Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay): A point of order, Mr Speaker. Could I draw your attention
to Standing Order 107 relating to debates on private members' notices of motion? I am
concerned-as I expect my colleagues on my left are-about the loss of private members'
rights and the procedures that are followed, apparently without the authority of the Standing
Orders, but by convention. I refer to the assumption of the right to decide on the order of
priority in which notices of motion appear on the Order Paper. The present convention is
that this should be left exclusively to the two party Whips, but the Standing Order does not
say this will be so-nor does it say it shall be otherwise. I accept that, but believe that the
Standing Order is badly drafted. It does not state who shall advise the Clerk by noon on
Tuesday which motion will be debated, and it does not say either that the Whips shall have
this power.
The Standing Order states that the notices of motion shall be alternated, which should
mean: (1) National; (2) Labour; (3) Social Credit; (4) Independent National; and (5) Labour
Island Bay. That is not happening. The arrangements made by the Whips, and the
assumptions on which they are based are exercised under the authority of the Chair, so I ask
you to review the desirability of continuing these assumptions in the light of private
members' rights.
Mr SPEAKER: I am grateful to the member for Island Bay for having drawn this matter
to my attention yesterday, so that I was able to research it. I considered the matter at the
beginning of the session and invited the Whips from either side to take it under their wings,
as it were, and to try to come to some arrangement that was satisfactory to the Leader of the
Social Credit Political League as well as to the independent members.
In 1974, when only two parties were in the House and there were no independent
members, the Standing Orders Committee discussed the procedures for private members'
notices of motion. Its recommendations are incorporated in the group of Standing Orders
from 99 to 107. Standing Order 107 provides for the Clerk to be notified of the notices to be
debated, and for him to arrange them on the Order Paper in the order selected, alternating
those selected. Although the Standing Order does not specify who is empowered to select
the notices of motion and notify the Clerk, in practice this has been done by the Whips.
The words "alternating those selected" suggest that the notices of motion fall into two
groups; otherwise they could not be alternated. Therefore, they should represent those
selected by the Government on the one hand and the Opposition on the other. Although the
office of Whip is not defined in the Standing Orders nor in any statute, the Whips do exist-I
am pleased to say-in practice and in remuneration, and can be seen to exercise the function
that has tacitly fallen to their lot under that Standing Order. I do not know who else could do
it.
I can find nothing in the Standing Orders that should make me upset the present
arrangement whereby the Government and the Opposition Whips determine what private
members' notices of motion shall be debated, and which members from either side should
speak in the debate. Under the Standing Orders, members wanting to take part in these
debates must arrange it with the Whips. I think it would be proper for the Whips to make
reasonable provision for independent members and members of the smaller parties to take
part. However, these members should bear in mind that over the last 4 years an average of
26 motions have been debated each year, which is about one-third of a motion for each
member other than Ministers. A back-bencher may hope to move about one private motion
each Parliament and to speak to perhaps two others. If my mathematics are accurate, I


## p. 1751 (#13) ############################################

13 July
Notices of Motion-Procedure
1751
suggest that it would be more than fair if independent members and those from the smaller
parties were able to move one private motion and speak to one or perhaps two others each
session.
I reiterate that as the Standing Orders-imperfect though they are on this matter at the
moment-are written, and as they have been interpreted in practice, in my opinion it is still
over to the Government and the Opposition Whips to work with the Clerk in deciding what
notices will come up for debate, and which members will debate them. The independent
members and the Leader of the Social Credit Political League should work in with the
Whips. There is a lot of good will between the Whips, of which I have certainly been aware. I
cannot help the member for Island Bay more than that.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): The report of the 1974 Standing Orders Committee goes further
than the Standing Orders, and suggests that each week the Government and the Opposition
should select the notices of motion to be debated. I acknowledge your arithmetic, and
confirm that the arrangement you mentioned has been discussed already by the Whips on
both sides, and that we can see no difficulty in following that arrangement for the minor
parties.
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui): I should like to assure the member for Island Bay, as I
have already assured the member for Rangitikei, that if representations are made we would
be happy to negotiate with him. I am surprised that the member for Island Bay did not
realise that, and I am surprised also that he has just discovered that provision, which has
applied for 4 years. In fairness to the Whips I should say that we have our own
representatives to consider, and that it would be unreasonable to expect Whips to make
concessions for independent members beyond those made for their own members. I assure
the member for Island Bay and other independent members that we would be happy to
discuss arrangements for the nomination of notices of motion, but I do not guarantee that
their requests will be met.

3. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central), on behalf of Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori),

the resolution of the Fiji Parliament. The text has been conveyed to the New Zealand
Government by the High Commissioner for Fiji in Wellington, and the questions raised by
the resolution are now the subject of discussions between the Fiji and New Zealand
Governments.
Mr Prebble: Does the Government consider that the language test is justified, in view of
the ill feeling it has caused?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I am not aware of ill feeling. That is too emotive an
expression. I am aware of the cogent reasons and arguments put forward by the High
Commissioner for Fiji, and accordingly I have asked the Department of Foreign Affairs to
refer the submissions back to the interdepartmental committee on overseas students, which
made the decision. I have asked the department to do that, and I shall then consult the high
commissioner.
Mr Prebble: Is the Minister confident that, following on representations made by the

be referred back to the committee. I will take it from there when I hear from the committee.

designed by the New Zealand Council for Educational Research and are supported by the
interdepartmental committee on overseas students. The High Commissioner for Fiji has
admitted that the tests are properly applied to students from the Asian regions and other
areas. He has put forward submissions about Fiji being included. Until the submissions have
been studied by the committee I am not able to comment. The appropriate professional body
has made the decision on the basis of the results of the study.

RNZAF-Women Aircrew Trainees
6. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Defence: Does the RNZAF accept
applications from women for entry to train as pilots or aircrew?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence): Women are not accepted for training
as pilots or aircrew, but all other branches and trades of the RNZAF are open to them.
Mr Rogers: Can the Minister give the reasons why women are not trained as pilots?
Hon. ALLAN McCREADY: I can give three or four reasons. Women would not be
employed in combat trades or combat areas; servicewomen would not be required to do
work that was extremely demanding physically or performed under arduous conditions; and
certain employment requiring lengthy and expensive training would not be available to
servicewomen until the low retention rate has been improved. Many first-quality young men
are volunteering to become pilots, and until that supply fails the department will retain its
present policy.
Mr Prebble: Is the Minister aware that women are now flying as commercial pilots and
that much of the flying done in the Air Force is similar to commercial flying, and, if so, why
are women being discriminated against?
Hon. ALLAN McCREADY: Perhaps a 747 would not go into combat.

ISO Containers-Subsidies and Deliveries
8. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: What

New Zealand Shipping Corporation, and how many have been delivered in each year against
the contract?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): For the year ended
31 March last year the contribution from the Government was for 20 containers at a cost of
$53,000. For the year ended 31 March this year the Government's contribution was for 910
containers at a cost of $3,113,000. It is expected that all the remaining 170 containers will be
delivered and paid for by October this year. The estimate of the Government's contribution
for these is $1,134,000. The total contribution from the Government for the 1100 containers
will therefore be about $4.3 million. As a direct result of obtaining the Shipping
Corporation's contract the firm has been successful in securing contracts for the supply of
containers to the United States of America and Western Germany.
Richard Walls: Referring to the latter part of the Minister's answer, what was the value

amounts to approximately $6 million.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Does the Minister agree with the original decision to place the order
with this Dunedin firm?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: My information is that in July 1974 the
Government, of which the honourable member for Mt. Albert was a member, agreed to the
Shipping Corporation ordering a container vessel for the New Zealand-European trade.
Following this decision the corporation accepted a tender from a British firm for 850 general
purpose containers and 1100 insulated containers. The Government subsequently required
the corporation to purchase remaining containers from New Zealand manufacturers. The
decision was taken by the National Government in January 1976, resulting from these
payouts.
Waitangi State Forest
9. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Forests: Are there any plans for a
replanting programme in the Waitangi State Forest on the West Coast using rimu or other
native species?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Yes, there are plans to replant those areas of
Waitangi State Forest that are not naturally regenerating satisfactorily to rimu forest after
logging. Twenty-five thousand rimu seedlings have been lined out in the Totara Flat nursery
in preparation for planting trials on the West Coast commencing next year. Sufficient rimu
and kahikatea seed has been sown in the Totara Flat nursery this year to allow 250 000
seedlings to be grown for future plantings at Waitangi and other indigenous State forests. As
it requires some 4 years to produce sturdy seedlings for planting, use will be made of wildings
collected from dense rimu regeneration for enrichment planting over the next 3 or 4 years.

Drug Seizures
11. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Customs: Has a different system of measuring
seizures of drugs been introduced since 1 April 1977, and has that changed method been
adopted in calculating the figures set out on page 17 of the annual report of the Customs
Department?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I can confirm that a new system of
measuring seized quantities of drugs has been introduced since 1 April 1977 and has been
used to calculate the figures shown in the 1978 annual report of the Customs Department.
The Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 came into force on 1 June 1977 and introduced new provisions
relating to the evidence of analysis of controlled drugs in court proceedings. Consequent
upon the introduction of these new provisions the basis of measuring the amount of drugs
seized by my department was changed. Formerly, the figure quoted was the bulk weight of
the seized substance, including its controlled drug content. However, the procedure now
adopted is to publish only the net quantity of controlled drugs seized following analysis of the
bulk substance by the DSIR. I should stress that whatever method of measurement is used to
record seizures of controlled drugs it would be quite wrong to interpret a single statistical
table as evidencing the relative success or failure of my department's overall anti-drug
activities.
Mr Brill: Can the Minister then confirm that the member for Sydenham was quite
incorrect in informing the House last week that it was a lie that the system had been changed
in the current year's report?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The method of computation has been changed. The member
for Sydenham can be assured that the change is permanent, and next year will be more
clearly drawn to the attention of readers of the Customs Department's annual report.
Mr Kirk: Could the Minister inform the member for Kapiti that there was no
discrimination in the report when stating the difference in the systems?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Yes.

Fish-Processing Facilities-Chartered Vessels

experimental purposes will be carried out on board the vessels. The Sealord Products
proposal provides for 50 percent of the catch to be further processed on shore in New
Zealand for export. The New Zealand Economic Zone Exports Ltd. and Wanganui Trawlers
(Wholesale) Ltd. will also process fish ashore, but to a lesser extent. All projects are
experimental and are designed to permit each company to assess the economics of operating
with freezer-type trawlers in New Zealand waters for processing here and marketing the
catch as New Zealand-processed products internationally.

Hon. J. B. BOLGER: There will be opportunities on all ventures for some New Zealand
involvement in the crewing of the vessel.

NELSON CITY FORESTRY EMPOWERING BILL
Introduction
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson): I. move, That leave be given to introduce the Nelson City
Forestry Empowering Bill. This is a local Bill of nine clauses. The purpose of the Bill is to
empower the Nelson City Council to acquire land for afforestation purposes or other
purpose incidental thereto; to empower the council to carry on the business of forestry on
any land vested in it whether within or without the city of Nelson and not being land held for
any particular purpose other than forestry, waterworks, water collection, water supply, and
water conservation; to empower the council to cut and sell timber from any of its plantations;
to empower the council to use and develop any land for the carrying on of farming
operations incidental to the management of forestry land, or recreational purposes
consistent with the use of forest land; to empower the council to carry on industry related to
forestry; to empower the council to prepare working plans for forestry; to empower the
council to grant permits to take forest produce from forestry land; to empower the council to
raise special loans for any of the purposes set out in the Bill; to empower the council to
exercise any of the powers contained in the Bill on land known as Waahi Taakaro,
notwithstanding any restrictions, reservations, designations, or statutory enactment or rule
of law to the contrary; and to provide that the council shall always have been deemed to have
any of the powers set out in the Bill.
The Bill is necessary because the Municipal Corporations Act of 1954 does not permit


## p. 1760 (#22) ############################################

1760
13 July
Nelson City Forestry Empowering Bill
local bodies to benefit from commercial plantations. The Bill specifically mentions the area
of Waahi Taakaro. The Nelson City Council wishes to continue its tree planting on the steep
gorse-covered slopes of Waahi Taakaro. Seventy percent of the area proposed to be planted
in pines is covered by gorse. It is intended to establish a net area of 328 ha with commercial
exotic species at Waahi Taakaro within the next four years, with a total yield, it is hoped, of
215 800 m³ between the year 2005 and the year 2012.
In 1971 the Nelson City Council acquired 1731 acres from Maitai Farms Ltd., primarily
as a recreational area for the citizens of Nelson. Some areas at Waahi Taakaro lend
themselves to intensive recreational use, particularly areas of near-flat topography, close to
the road on both sides of the Maitai River. However, other areas are more remote, very
steep, and do not really lend themselves to recreational use. If they were to be put to that
purpose they would need a lot of development and roading in order to release any
recreational potential. The council intends to plant and use for afforestation less than half
the area purchased by it in 1971. It is felt that the dual use of afforestation and recreation will
bring about the best and most reasonable management of the area. The council's plan of
commercial afforestation on some of the area will, it is felt, provide a back-drop to the
country now covered with gorse, which is at present only marginal farm land with
unattractive pockets of indigenous scrub. The forestry development management plan aims
to provide future income to assist with long-term recreational development in the city of
Nelson, and to increase and complement the recreational potential of Waahi Taakaro where
it is compatible with sound forestry management practices.
The Friends of the Maitai, a community group interested in protecting the well-being of
the Maitai Valley, are opposed to the Bill and are circulating a petition opposing it. They do
not want any commercial afforestation on Waahi Taakaro. Their views have been listened to
by the Nelson City Council, and will continue to be heard; already several modifications
have been made to the planting programme because of their representations. Most Nelson
city councillors support the Bill. The silent majority of Nelsonians also supports the Bill, and
as member for Nelson I, too, firmly support it. Sensible planting will be a responsible
management move, and in time will mean a great deal to the ratepayers and the people of
Nelson.
Motion agreed to.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

BAY OF ISLANDS COUNTY EMPOWERING (COMMUNITY CENTRES)
AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. The only
community centre now operating under the Act is the Maromaku Community Centre,
involving 48 householders in the Bay of Islands County. The centre's funds are raised by
levies, which are used for the maintenance and upgrading of facilities in the community
centre complex, comprising a hall-used by the people of the district for general meetings,
church, bowls, badminton, and so on-tennis courts, and the domain.
The funds are now insufficient to provide reasonable maintenance of the facilities. Cost
increases have also precluded the provision of any improvements to the centre's facilities.
When it is realised that a large part of the complex is made of wood, it can be appreciated
that a considerable amount of maintenance and general improvement is required. A public
meeting of the community last year was attended by 21 of the total number of 48
householders, and it was decided unanimously to raise the levy on each householder to $10 a
year. The people of the area are to be commended for realising that they must contribute
more money if they want to maintain their community centre.
Bill read a second time.

Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) said that the number of 2-year-old claims

Compensation Commission paid the State Insurance Office for services rendered.

Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei) said that New Zealand's accident compensation concept
was one of the most enlightened in the world, with the commission guaranteeing that
anyone, irrespective of the cause of injury, including considerations of fault, would be
compensated while injured as well as for any permanent injury-a great change from the old
fault law. However, an anomaly existed in that a victim of an accident was entitled to
compensation well above that received by a person suffering similar disabilities and
disadvantages arising from illness. As an enlightened society, New Zealanders should fully
support a widening of the principle of compensation to include the latter class of victim.
The commission had on 23 June expressed justifiable doubt about whether it could
continue to meet in the long term even claims based exclusively on accident risk. It would be
difficult to continue compensation at present rates because of the growing problem of the
Government sustaining social services at present levels when the national cake, or the
resource base to fund or support the level of social welfare implied under accident
compensation was shrinking during falling productivity. Nevertheless, within present
resource levels, adjustments could be made to secure the removal, at least to some extent, of
anomalies that had arisen in compensation being extended to accident victims and not
sickness victims. Rates had been struck on victim risk, with no liability attached to the cause
of the disability. That principle might have to be compromised in the short term to fund
accident compensation further to give a fair deal to sickness victims, a step towards receiving
equality of benefit with accident victims.
Was there not a case for returning to some element of fault liability? A drunken driver
could knock someone down and the commission and everyone else on victim risk paid for
injuries caused by that drunken driver, who, within the terms of the Act, bore no liability or
financial responsibility for his irresponsible actions. The same principle applied to a burglar
or criminal falling through a skylight and badly injuring himself. In certain areas funding
could be assisted by placing liability on the person causing the injury. Fines would not be the
answer. An added and effective deterrent would be for the drunken driver to be made
responsible for his actions by being forced to contribute to some degree to the injuries he had
caused, and to that end the Government should consider allowing the courts to require
compensation or restitution to be paid by that person within the limits of his capacity to pay.

the Government had sought to base its case was not getting that salary at the time of the
comparison. A fair comparison would be a single taxpayer on the average wage in 1975 and a
single taxpaper on the average wage in 1978.
The challenge to the Government was quite simple: $100 would be paid to any charity if
an average taxpayer paying $1,425 in 1975 under the Labour Government and an average
taxpayer paying $598 in 1978 could be produced. Like had to be compared with like, and that
was the end of the argument.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister) said he had been misrepresented. He had
not said that the taxpayer in the case he had cited would pay $598 in tax. He had said the tax
would be under $400.
Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora) said that a person on $6,000 under the M and F and single-
income family rebate codes would pay under $400 in tax-in fact $338.50 for the year ending
31 March 1980-compared with $1,420 in 1975. A taxpayer on $4,000 would have paid $670
tax for the year ended 31 March 1975, so that, if a taxpayer's income was $2,000 more for the
year ended 31 March 1980, his tax of $338.50 would be substantially less than it would have
been under the Labour Government. In its first year in office, the Labour Government had
collected 33.5 percent more tax than had been collected the year before.
The member for Auckland Central had accused temporary workers in the Inland
Revenue Department of disclosing confidential information. Those workers would be
covered by the Inland Revenue Department Act and the Official Secrets Act, and breaches
of those Acts were criminal offences. Any person who knew that another person had broken
a law that carried criminal sanctions had a duty to report such a breach. Had the member for
Auckland Central reported those breaches to the Inland Revenue Department. The
member's comments about cheques clearly showed that he did not understand the
procedures of a legal firm.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department) said
that the department had always had temporary staff, who all took an oath. Temporary staff
were vetted to the extent that 216 had been taken on to the permanent staff. Allegations
were not evidence, and he would wait for a letter from the member for Auckland Central
giving evidence of the incidents he had described.
Tax reform in the recent Budget had been concentrated on the average taxpayer, and
1 400 000 taxpayers would benefit. Wage tax reconciliations were continuing figures that
were picked up each year. They could not be broken down to give a particular change for the
current year, but it was estimated that, out of 150 000 employers, 10 percent might have
outstanding payments at any one time.
He agreed that the Inland Revenue Department was in some ways a commercial
enterprise. It had to maximise revenue in terms of the law. The department was constantly
considering ways to improve its methods. The twin principles of taxation of equity and
efficiency demanded that. The department regarded itself as a business. It was fair that it
should pick up all taxation that accrued, and it was efficient of it to do so. If the department
could improve its methods it would generate more income. It was not necessary to wring the
last penny out of people who could not pay their tax. He was impressed with the
department's attitude to people who had difficulty in paying their taxes. The normal
procedure was to impose a 10 percent penalty. About $600,000 a year was written off in bad
debts, but in relative terms that was a small amount. The department did a good job in
maintaining the tax take from citizens, both in equity and in efficiency of administration.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) said that the Government would collect an all-
time record tax take in 1978-79. Tax as a percentage of the national income had risen to a
record level. Land and income tax had increased by $120 per head for the ordinary taxpayer.
The principles that were generally applied for taxation were equity and the ability to pay.
The Government had slammed the low-income people with a tax increase. That was the
Government's tax reform.
Some national superannuitants were confused about the tax imposed on their pensions,
which had formerly been non-taxable. The Public Expenditure Committee had established

ths National Party.
The National Party's election policy had been to abolish the property speculation tax to
assist speculators and property dealers. Was it intended to honour that promise? Did the

Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department) said

under discussion, except by the indulgence of the House, for personal explanations."

With regard to the member's reference to my earlier ruling about the constitutional
right of members to give notices in the House censuring me, a Minister, the Government,
the Opposition, or any member, the right is there and I shall protect it. The right is to be
used in a way in which it should be used, for that purpose and not as an incidental tagging on
of a reference to something that has already been dealt with by the House. If a member
wants to censure me for a ruling I have given, then he must refer to something that has
already occurred in the House. He is perfectly right in those circumstances. If a member

he wants to censure anyone. I ruled his notice out on the ground that it contained words that

FARM OWNERSHIP SAVINGS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation): I move, That the Farm Ownership Savings Amendment Bill be introduced.
There are two types of farm ownership savings bank accounts. In the ordinary account the


## p. 1781 (#43) ############################################

14 July
1781
Farm Ownership Savings Amendment Bill
depositor may save up to $3,000 a year, to a maximum of $30,250 The depositor will receive
a grant of from 25 percent to 50 percent of the total eligible savings, depending on the length
of time the account has been open. In special accounts the depositor may save up to $4,000 a
year, to a maximum of $50,000. Each year the depositor will receive a rebate of 45c for each
eligible dollar saved, and when the tax payable is less than $1,800 the rebate will equal the
tax. To qualify for the benefits the accounts must have been open for a minimum of 3 years
when the depositor goes sharefarming, and for 5 years when the depositor is purchasing a
first farm. Under the present scheme depositors must have acquired substantial practical
farming experience from the time of opening the account. The benefits under the scheme are
not available to depositors or their spouses who have had a substantial interest in farming
either solely, jointly, or in common with any other person in New Zealand or elsewhere.
The Bill proposes to enlarge the criteria for eligibility set out in the Act. It will allow a
wife to have a farm ownership savings account and to be eligible for benefits on the savings,
subject to these being used for farm purchase, and provided her husband is also a depositor
and meets the criteria of the scheme. The provision will bring the farm ownership savings
scheme into line with the home ownership savings scheme, under which both husband and
wife can save and receive benefits towards the purchase of their first home, provided that in
the case of the farm ownership savings scheme one of them is actively involved in farming.
The Bill will also allow a depositor who elects to withdraw initial savings for an approved
sharefarming proposition to continue to save for farm ownership. The benefits and the
savings withdrawn to finance the sharefarming venture would be deductible from the
maximum amount available for farm purchase and allow a sharefarmer, who has received
benefits for this purpose and who subsequently purchases a farm, to retain those benefits. I
propose to move that the Bill go to the Lands and Agriculture Committee to consider
whether further refinements could improve it.
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central): The Opposition does not propose to
discuss the Bill at this stage. I am pleased that it will go to a select committee. Members will
then have the opportunity to study its ramifications and ask questions. I have no intention of
holding the House up now.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation): I move, That the Farm Ownership Savings Amendment Bill be referred to the
Lands and Agriculture Committee, and that the proceedings of the committee during the
hearing of evidence be open to accredited representatives of the news media.

NEW ZEALAND REGISTER OF OSTEOPATHS INCORPORATED BILL
Introduction
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That the New Zealand Register of
Osteopaths Incorporated Bill be introduced. The Bill, of two substantive clauses, has been
promoted at the request of the New Zealand Register of Osteopaths. Its purpose is to make
it an offence for any person who is not a member of the New Zealand Register of Osteopaths
Incorporated to use any description that is calculated to imply that he is such a member. It
does not mean that a person cannot call himself an osteopath, but it does mean that he
cannot state or imply that he is a member of the New Zealand Register of Osteopaths.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): I am pleased that the Bill has been introduced by the Minister. I
hope it passes speedily through the House.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): If it is proposed to provide a penalty for persons who
misrepresent that they are members of an incorporated society, which this legislation does,
why was the matter not dealt with by an amendment to the Incorporated Societies Act?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): It has been my experience that, whatever one
tries to do in this life, there will always be somebody without responsibility who says that
there is a better way, and asks why it was not used. The legislation has been prepared in this
way because the osteopaths requested it.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

CUSTOMS ORDER CONFIRMATION BILL
Introduction
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That the Customs Order
Confirmation Bill be introduced. This is a very minor measure to confirm in terms of section
131 of the Customs Act 1966 all Orders in Council made under sections 124, 124A and 125A of
the Act on or after 1 July of the previous session but before 1 July during the present session
and laid before Parliament in accordance with the Regulations Act 1936. Section 131 of the
Customs Act provides that, unless these orders are expressly validated by Act of Parliament
and passed during this session, they will expire at the close of the session.
Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central): As this is a purely procedural measure required
by section 131 of the Customs Act 1966, the Opposition has no argument with it.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
QUESTIONS ORAL
Vocational Training-Young Maoris
1. Mr WETERE (Western Maori), on behalf of Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori), to
the Minister of Maori Affairs: Can he indicate the areas in which vocational training
expansion is proposed by his department and in which manual skills training for urban Maori
youngsters is to be introduced, and give the number who will receive training annually in
each of the two groups?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): This year 9 new courses providing
training for 146 young people were mounted in south Auckland and Taranaki. In Manukau
these included ladies' hairdressing, general merchandising, coach and body building,
secretarial and typing, and meat retailing; and, in New Plymouth, painting and decorating,
fitting and turning, fitting and welding, and joinery. Proposals are at present being discussed
and arrangements negotiated for the setting up of courses in basic skills in provincial towns
such as Whangarei, Tauranga, Rotorua, Gisborne, Napier, Palmerston North, Wanganui,
and Nelson for 150 Maori and Pacific Island school leavers. These will be for agriculture,
office work, welding, building maintenance, etc. Further proposals are under way to give
trade training to another 80 young people in horticulture, secretarial work, catering, fishing,
and engineering. At present there are no firm proposals for the giving of either trade training
or other vocational training to Maori and Polynesian youth from the main metropolitan
areas, although some discussion is taking place on the matter.
Mr Wetere: Is it correct that in his answer to the last part of the question the Minister
said no provision would be made for urban Maori youngsters?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: At present there are no firm proposals for giving either trade
training or other vocational training to Maori and Polynesian youth from the main
metropolitan areas. The member will be aware that a trial scheme at the Otara technical
college is experimenting with training urban Maoris as well as other young people. That
experiment has broken away from bringing the urban child into the city to be trained.
Mr Rogers: How many people are involved in this training scheme at present?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: I do not have the figure with me. However, as I pointed out in
my original answer, provision is being made for 146 extra.

Drugs-Customs Surveillance
4. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Customs: Is there evidence that a
number of illicit narcotics shipments destined for the New Zealand market have left the
country on the ship in which they arrived solely because of tight surveillance on the part of
the New Zealand Customs Department?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): Containment in Customs anti-narcotic
work is one arm of the total activity. There have been Customs operations in which narcotics
have been discovered on board ships and in which there has been evidence that quantities
undetected left New Zealand on the vessels that brought the goods here. An example is the
vessel Straat Fraser, which in the latter half of 1976 was the subject of long-term surveillance
in its period on the New Zealand coast. In this period, rummages of the vessel revealed
quantities of both cannabis and heroin and there was every indication that further quantities
were present on the vessel. Subsequent intelligence revealed this to have been so and that
the narcotics had returned from whence they came. In cases of this nature information is, of
course, rather shadowy, and it is detailed evaluation of the evidence that produces the
indication I have given. I have quoted only one specific instance, but this is a sufficient
indication of the success of the Customs procedures-procedures that will benefit greatly
from the additional resources that have been made available for the department's
enforcement activity.
Mr Wellington: In that case, would it be fair to regard drug seizure figures as a reliable
indicator of the effectiveness of Government activity?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: This is an indication of why we must regard seizure figures as a
fallible guide.

Questions-Oral
Christchurch Gas Company-Coal Requirements
5. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Is the Christchurch Gas
Company obtaining all the coal it requires, and, if not, what steps are being taken to meet its
requirements in quantities and type of coal?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): Yes, the company is obtaining all the coal it
requires.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Can the Minister confirm that the type of coal required by the
Christchurch Gas Company is not available?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The Christchurch Gas Company is being supplied by the State coal
mines with all the coal it requires in both the high-swelling Liverpool and Denniston type
and medium-swelling Strongman categories. The question was probably directed at the fact
that in the high-swelling category the company wants all Liverpool coal, whereas it is being
supplied with 75 percent Liverpool with the balance from Denniston.
Hon. F. M. Colman: As the company is receiving only 75 percent of its requirements of
Liverpool coal, will the Minister take steps to ensure that it receives all its requirements of
that coal?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: That is impossible.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Why?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: It is not possible to do better than this from Liverpool's present
output. In anticipation of the Christchurch Gas Company ceasing to use coal for gas making
within the next few years, the State coal mines have been operating a non-replacement rule
for labour at the Liverpool and Strongman mines at Greymouth. This was to get the size of
the work force down to a level at which the effects of losing such a large coal customer could
be handled without having to make miners redundant. This level has now been reached and
the State is replacing men who leave from those two mines. This means that for the
immediate future the output from the Liverpool mine will remain at about its present level,
and the Christchurch Gas Company can expect to continue to draw 75 percent of its high-
swelling coal requirements from this source.
Irrigation Scheme, Clyde
6. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) to the Minister of Works and Development: What
progress is being made with investigation of potential irrigation schemes associated with D63
Dam at Clyde?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): Following the
Government's authorisation in March 1977 of $500,000 expenditure over 5 years for

progress has been made. Aerial photographs and contour maps of the area have been
produced as a matter of urgency. A report has been prepared on the state of the Earnscleugh

and land holders of the area to discuss the options in the report, and there is a good level of
support for improved irrigation development, using the resources offered by the proposed
Clyde dam.

irrigation investigations will be available to meet the continuing cost over the 5 years?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: I can give the honourable member that assurance. This was a sum
especially put aside from the Ministry of Works and Development's vote, and it has no
bearing on the $8.2 million that is put aside this year in the main vote for investigation and
construction of irrigation schemes.

Wanganui Technical Institute or Community College
9. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: In view of his comments
in the letter to the Wanganui Boys College Board of Governors dated 18 May 1978 that
"whether and when establishment" of a technical institute or community college occurs is "a
matter for the Government to decide", has the Government not yet decided as a matter of
principle to establish a technical institute or community college in the Wanganui region?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The Government, in approving last year
the establishment of new community colleges in Northland and Rotorua for 1978, adopted a
general policy for the development of community colleges. The establishment of any
community college will depend both on whether it meets the usual criterion of minimum load
and on the priority that it can be accorded among other proposals for educational
development. A senior technical division at Wanganui Boys College is providing tertiary
training, and building planning for a community college is proceeding. However, no date has
yet been determined for the establishment of a community college as an independent
institution.
Mr Marshall: I take it that the Minister's answer is that there will eventually be one of
these institutions. Has the Minister any tentative idea of how long it will take to establish
either a community college or a technical institute in the region?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It is my belief that to establish a true community college there
must be more than just a tertiary institution in a city. Therefore I believe we have taken the
first positive steps towards the establishment of a community college by the establishment of
the senior technical division. To that we should very soon add some activities outside the city
of Wanganui-and as the member knows, I have plans for those. Within a relatively short
time we can look forward to the establishment of a community college in Wanganui, but the
final decision as to timing has not been made. The buildings, which are going ahead, will
obviously be the nucleus for a community college.

Farm Incomes-Government Support
10. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) to the Minister of Agriculture: To ensure farm income
sufficiency, what will the National Government's contribution be to (1) direct price support,
(2) on-farm cost support, (3) off-farm cost support?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): There can be no one rigid formula to
determine either the total amount of Government assistance required by the agricultural
sector over time, or the relative amounts comprising the three types of support quoted.
Obviously the assistance provided will fluctuate in accordance with many factors, including,
among others, the strength of market prices for our primary commodities, the exchange rate,
the cost of processing and distribution, and the cost of farm inputs. The Government is
committed to maintaining the viability of our main export industry, and takes appropriate
action to this end as required.
Mr Bruce Barclay: If the Minister is unable to give the answers to parts (1), (2), and (3),
does that mean he has given away the concept of income sufficiency?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: No; obviously the whole thing is based on income sufficiency. I
cannot give specific figures, because we do not know how many lambs will be born this year,
or how many will be processed. Therefore we have no idea what the final average price for
lamb will be, and we are unable to estimate at this stage whether the Government will have
to give price support. We do not know how much fertiliser will be used.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Guaranteed income sufficiency!
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Yes that we have, and that we have carried out.
Mr Falloon: Has the Government put itself in a much better position than any other
Government to be able to ascertain farm income sufficiency by establishing the agricultural
review committee?
Mr SPEAKER: That is beyond the scope of the question, which is related to farm
income sufficiency and what the Government's contribution will be.
Mr Rogers: The Minister did not have an answer to the question, so therefore he has
said that the Government has no policy on agriculture-
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I called the member to ask a supplementary question, not to
make a speech.
Mr Rogers: Can the farmers expect handouts this year, because it is election year, and
can they expect to get no assistance whatever in the next 2 years?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: The farmers can expect to get the assistance they need to
maintain income sufficiency. I remind the member that in 1975, which was an election year,
the Labour Government gave the farmers a handout of $50 million because they needed
assistance.

11. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What cuts have there
been in the quantity of gas coal supplied to the works at Dunedin, Oamaru, and Invercargill,

cuts in the quantity of coal supplied to these 3 gas undertakings. There was 1 week in May
when supplies of Liverpool coal to Oamaru, Dunedin, and Invercargill were reduced by 1
railway wagon each-that is, of 10 to 12 tonnes-to ease a temporary shortage of Liverpool
coal at the Christchurch gasworks. With that sole exception, Oamaru and Invercargill have
received all the coal they ordered from the State coal mines. In the case of Dunedin, it would
like to get 80 tonnes of Liverpool coal a week, but is being supplied with only 60 tonnes. That
is better than the position last year, when it drew an average of 53 tonnes of Liverpool coal a
week.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Can the Minister give an assurance that the gas companies named
will continue to get the type of coal they want from the State coal mines?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The State coal mines are conscious of the need to make certain types
of coal available to manufactured gas undertakings, and the department is doing all it can to
ensure that these supplies are received. My inquiries show that the State coal mines have
measured up to the needs of the gas undertakings.

Social Welfare Benefit Payments
15. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Social Welfare: What discussions
took place between the respective Governments on the change in the payment system of
benefits to British pensioners resident in New Zealand, and what efforts were made to
simplify the procedure for the 15 000 elderly people affected by these changes?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The payment system for United
Kingdom pensions is, of course, entirely a matter for the United Kingdom authorities. The
head of the overseas branch of the United Kingdom Department of Health and Social
Security visited New Zealand in late 1977 for preliminary discussions regarding the
expressed intention to pay pensions direct from the United Kingdom. Following his return to
the United Kingdom, the New Zealand authorities were informed that it had been decided
to introduce the direct payment system. Accordingly, in August 1978 the United Kingdom
authorities will commence direct payments by bank draft of all British national insurance
pensions in force in New Zealand. This will bring the payment system for New Zealand into
line with that operating for United Kingdom pensions in all other countries. The
Department of Social Welfare, on behalf of the United Kingdom authorities, has written to
each pensioner involved explaining the new method of payment. An invitation to pensioners
who are having difficulties with the new system of payment to contact their local Department
of Social Welfare office has been extended through the news media.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Can the Minister give an indication of the interim arrangements
being made by his department for the changeover period, to ensure that no hardship is
experienced by British pensioners resident in New Zealand during the adjustment period?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The Department has sent out two letters. One has been sent to
pensioners who are receiving only the British pension, and another letter has been sent to
United Kingdom residents who are living in New Zealand and who receive national
superannuation. In addition, the Director-General of Social Welfare made the comment,
through the news media, that if anybody had problems with the new system of payment or
found that it meant they were short of money because of the changeover they should contact
their local office of the Department of Social Welfare. I give an assurance that no one will
suffer. Anyone who has any difficulties should contact the local office of the Department of
Social Welfare and we will see that they are well looked after.
Mr Falloon: Has the Minister any idea whether the discussions included comparisons
between the levels of national superannuation paid in New Zealand and in Great Britain?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, I can tell the honourable member that New Zealand
national superannuation is considerably more than the British pension. The pension from
Britain will be posted in the form of a bank draft and paid into a bank account, and the net
difference will be made up by a payment from the national superannuation fund here.
Mr Prebble: And no one will be worse off?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: No, no one will be worse off.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that, in terms of New Zealand currency, the
payment of the British pension will vary from time to time because of changes in the
exchange rate; and, in respect of those British pensioners who are also entitled to a payment
from the Department of Social Welfare in New Zealand, how often does the department
propose to make adjustments to the New Zealand payment because of any variation in the
exchange rate?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The sterling rate received in New Zealand will be deducted from
the net rate of national superannuation, and the difference will be paid to the United
Kingdom pensioners; so they will receive exactly the same net amount as the national
superannuitants, which, as I stated previously, is a higher rate than is paid in Britain.
Mr Prebble: I ask the Minister to elucidate his answer. I understood him to say that the
sterling rate of the benefit would be taken as the base, and that it would be made up to the
rate of the New Zealand pension. As the sterling rate changes from day to day and as the
Department of Social Welfare will have no way of knowing the date the pension was paid
into the beneficiary's bank account, how can it be made up to the New Zealand pension;
and, when making it up, will the Department of Social Welfare take into account the fact
that all British beneficiaries, under the new scheme, will have to pay an exchange penalty for
changing sterling into New Zealand currency?


## p. 1789 (#51) ############################################

14 July
1789
Questions-Oral
Hon. H. J. WALKER: No, there will be no penalties. The department in Britain will
advise how much is paid to the British resident living in New Zealand, and the Department
of Social Welfare here will merely deduct the pension received from Britain at the current
rate of exchange.
Mr Prebble: On the date it is put into the bank account or on the date it is paid by the
Department of Social Welfare?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: On the date it is received.
Mr Prebble: How do you know that?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: That is what was decided between the British Government and
the Department of Social Welfare in New Zealand. Beneficiaries are not particularly
interested in what the member for Auckland Central has to say, because he always appears
to be confused, but I emphasise to beneficiaries that they will not be worse off as a result of
the changeover. In fact, they will be substantially better off, because national super-

AUCKLAND WAR MEMORIAL MUSEUM MAINTENANCE BILL
Introduction
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I move, That leave be given to introduce the
Auckland War Memorial Museum Maintenance Bill. The purpose of the Bill is to
consolidate and bring up to date existing legislation governing the management of the
museum's affairs, and, in particular, the basis upon which local authorities contribute
towards the cost of maintaining the museum, and the distribution of local authority
representation on the council. The Bill would not in any way interfere with the internal
workings of the Auckland Institute and Museum Trust Board, which is the lessee from the
Auckland City Council of the land on which the building stands and in which the building
itself is vested by statute, nor in the affairs of the incorporated society known as the
Auckland Institute and Museum.
By far the greatest proportion of funds needed to maintain the museum, to administer


## p. 1791 (#53) ############################################

14 July
1791
Auckland War Memorial Museum Maintenance Bill
it, and to pay salaries, etc., is derived from contributions made by local authorities in the
area commonly known as the Auckland Province. It was from this area that contributions
were received from members of the public for the construction of the original museum
building after the first world war, and for extensions to it after the second world war, and the
museum stands to commemorate the services of those men and women of the Province of
Auckland who served and who fell in the various wars in which this country has been
involved since 1914. The Bill proposes that every local authority in this area shall contribute
to a greater or lesser degree, to the cost of maintaining the museum, that their contributions
will be by way of levy upon them by the museum council, and that the local authorities in
their turn shall have the option of meeting the levy either out of general revenue or by way of
a special rate. The Bill includes the formula on which the levy will be apportioned amongst
the various contributing local authorities.
The Bill makes substantial changes in the present system of local authority
representation on the council of the museum. These changes are intended to provide a wider
spread than exists at present, having regard to shifts in population and to changes in local
authority districts since the present maintenance legislation was enacted in 1963. An
important provision in the Bill, which does not appear in the present legislation, is that the
levy proposed for each year shall require the prior approval of a special committee of the
museum council, on which representatives of the contributing local authorities will be in a
majority.
There are a number of incidental additions and amendments to the existing legislation
but, primarily, the Bill is concerned with the apportionment of levies, and the spread of
representation on the museum council by persons appointed or elected to it by contributing
local authorities. The Bill has been promoted by the council of the Auckland War Memorial
Museum with a view to consolidating and bringing up to date the existing legislation
governing the management of the museum's affairs, and, in particular, the basis upon which
local authorities contribute towards the cost of maintaining the museum and the distribution
of local authority representation on the council. The Bill would not in any way interfere with
the institute's board.
The first schedule to the Bill lists all the local authorities in this area, and it is proposed
that each shall contribute each year to the total amount required to staff and maintain the
museum, and to support the numerous activities it undertakes for the benefit of the general
public. The museum could not survive without those contributions, and it is, and always has
been, a basic principle that the museum, as a war memorial, shall be open to the public free
of an admission charge. Specific reference is made to this principle in clause 5(2) of the Bill.
Individual contributions to the total amount of the levy required to finance the museum
in any one year are calculated on the following formulas: (a) the capital value of rateable
property in the district of each contributing authority is fixed by the Valuer-General as at 31
March preceding the year for which the levy is to be made, and the Government Statistician
calculates its population as at the same date; the financial year begins on 1 April; (b) the
capital value of a contributing authority and its population are then adjusted by multiplying
each by the differential factor appearing in the first schedule; (c) following upon the existing
legislation, the metropolitan areas have all been given a differential factor of 1, as in the
present legislation, and the outer areas making up the balance of the Auckland regional
district have been given a common factor of 0.6; (d) Great Barrier Island County Council
and Waiheke County Council have been given differentials of 0.2 and 0.4 respectively; (e)
the factor for local authorities in group 4 has been arrived at by taking into account the
distance that the office of each is away from the Central Post Office at Auckland, and its
purpose is intended to reduce the basis of the levy the further a contributing authority is from
the centre of Auckland. They have first been given a differential factor of 0.4, and this has
been reduced by 0.0015 per km, depending upon the distance that the authority's office is by
road from the Central Post Office. The minimum differential factor is 0.05, regardless of
distance; (f) the notional capital value and notional population that result from the use of the
differential factor form the basis of the levy; (g) the total amount of the levy cannot exceed in
any year 1/225c in the dollar on that notional capital value plus 2.5c per person of the
notional population of the district; (h) however, if a contributing authority in groups 2, 3, or
4 in the first schedule shall establish a museum in its district that employs professional staff,
at a salary, at present, of not less than $9,134 per annum, the levy is to be reduced by 25
percent for one such person so employed, by 50 percent for two, and by 75 percent for three
or more. This provision has been introduced to avoid the situation where a local authority


## p. 1792 (#54) ############################################

1792
14 July
Auckland War Memorial Museum Maintenance Bill
might be called upon to help finance the Auckland War Memorial Museum whilst at the
same time it had an obligation to its local museum.
The salary figure is tied to what is considered to be the appropriate Government scale,
and this is described in the Bill. Provision is made for the differential factor to be adjusted
for ensuing years. There is also a provision to enable boundaries to be adjusted and the
Local Government Commission would have a wide discretion to review the effect of this
provision if there was a change in local body amalgamations. The area subject to the levy is
fixed and cannot be extended.
Changes will be made in the personnel of the museum council. At present it consists of
16 persons elected by members of the Auckland Institute and Museum Society, and 13
appointed by contributing local authorities. Of those 13, 4 are members of the Auckland
City Council and are appointed by it. The remainder are elected by fixed groups of
contributing authorities from nominees who must be members of their own councils. This
was laid down in the 1963 Act. It is now proposed that there shall be a total of 14
contributing members on the museum council. Of these, three will be Auckland City
councillors appointed by that council, two appointed by the Manukau City Council, one by
the Takapuna City Council, and one by the Waitemata City Council. The local authorities
mentioned in paragraph (b) in group 1 of the first schedule would elect two persons, who
would be drawn from the members of those councils. The local authorities mentioned in
paragraph (c) of group 1 would similarly elect two persons from the members of those
councils. The local authorities mentioned in groups 2 and 3 would together elect one such
person, and the local authorities mentioned in paragraph (a) in group 4 and in paragraph (b)
in group 4 would separately elect one each. These provisions have been inserted to ensure
the widest possible spread of representation. However, in the event that this basis of
representation may become unbalanced, the Executive could make any necessary changes
by way of Order in Council. Contributing authority representatives would hold office for 3
years, corresponding with the time of local body elections.
The remaining provisions of the Bill are basically machinery in nature and do not
warrant specific mention. The Bill has been brought forward by the local authority in
response to a statement made by the Local Bills Committee 3 years ago, when it was pointed
out that the legislation governing the management of the museum should be updated.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): The Bill has my full support,
but, as Minister of Local Government, I must advise the House that I have been told by
many local authorities, particularly the Hamilton City Council and borough and county
councils in the Waikato area, that they have certain objections to their fee being mandatory.
Mr H. N. Austin: So has Northland.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: It is the same in the Northland area, from where I have also
received objections. I have told the local authorities that the Bill will be referred to the Local
Bills Committee, when they will have an opportunity to make representations. Therefore, I
believe the Bill should be introduced and referred to the Local Bills Committee so that
objections can be considered at that level.
Motion agreed to.

RURAL INTERMEDIATE CREDIT AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. D. MacINTRYE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. This Bill removes an anomaly
between the interest rate charged by the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation to its stock
loan borrowers, mainly sharemilkers, and the rate that the rural intermediate credit
associations can charge. The Bill also effects some minor administrative changes. The
original Act was passed in 1927, and 50 associations were set up. That number has now
dwindled, and only four remain at Hamilton, Hauraki, Matamata, and Morrinsville.
Almost exclusively they are used by dairy farmer sharemilkers. The terms and conditions of
the loans include interest, working on the same basis as the Rural Bank. The present limits
were set in the 1974 legislation which set up the Rural Bank.
Section 24(2) states that the Minister shall, from time to time, set rates of interest and
make adequate provision to cover the costs of administration. The Rural Bank shall allow a 1


## p. 1793 (#55) ############################################

14 July
1793
Rural Intermediate Credit Amendment Bill
percent margin to cover managerial expenses. For the initial purchase of stock the Rural
Bank's current rate of interest is 7½ percent for a normal term of 5 years, rebated to 6 percent
for the first 3 years. Subclause (1) of clause 2 of the Bill enables the Rural Bank to fix the
maximum rate of interest that associations can charge when on-lending. The rate will be
fixed at the same level as the rate charged by the Rural Bank for the same type of loan-at
present, a maximum of 7 percent. Subclause (2) of clause 2 validates loans made by
associations after 21 July 1977 at interest rates up to 71 percent. However, in most cases the
actual rate charged will have been 6 percent, because interest is normally rebated to this
figure for the first 3 years on that type of loan. The allowable limit for associations is at
present 7 percent, but will be amended by the preceding subclause (1).
Clause 3 transfers the provision relating to the terms and conditions on which loans may
be granted from the Finance Act 1932-33 (No. 2) to the principal Act. This will enable the
repeal of the Finance Act 1932-33 (No. 2). Clause 4 extends to 28 days the time for
regulations to be laid before the House.
