NOXIOUS PLANTS BILL
Second Reading
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill consolidates and amends the Noxious Weeds Act 1950 and its
amendments, and includes as a separate part a consolidation of the Nassella Tussock Act
1946 and its amendments. The Bill gives effect to the report of the Committee of Inquiry on
Noxious Weeds Administration, chaired by Mr Jack Fitzharris, presented in September
1973. The committee was set up in 1972 to review the state of noxious weeds control. It
travelled extensively and received submissions from more than 140 organisations before
recommending wide-ranging changes in the administration of noxious weeds control.
The report, known as the Fitzharris report, has been widely accepted as a blueprint for
change in the control of noxious weeds. Because of the extent and significance of the
proposals, and the desirability of combining all noxious weeds legislation, it was decided to
introduce a new Noxious Plants Bill. The main provisions of the Bill are: (a) the
establishment of a 10-member Noxious Plants Council comprising an independent chairman,
a Department of Lands and Survey representative, a New Zealand Forest Service
representative, a Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries representative, two Counties
Association nominees, one Municipal Association nominee, two Federated Farmers
nominees, and one commercial and technical group representative. The council's functions
will be to initiate and promote policy on noxious plants administration, to decide which
noxious plants should be classified as class A or class B, and to recommend to the Minister of
Agriculture forms and procedures for financial assistance; (b) eight regional co-ordinating
committees will be established, each to cover a region of the Ministry of Agriculture and
Fisheries. The chairman will be the ministry's regional advisory officer, with representatives
from the Department of Lands and Survey, the district noxious plants authority, each
province of Federated Farmers, and co-opted members ensuring the spread and balance of
membership, and Maori landholder representation in regions containing a large area of
Maori land; (c) territorial local government will remain responsible for noxious plants
control and administration. District noxious plants authorities, comprising either one county
or municipality, or a number, will be formed to employ full time trained noxious plants
officers; (d) the Crown is to be bound by the new Act, making land-holding departments
responsible for financing their own control programmes in co-ordination with one another
and the Noxious Plants Council; (e) noxious plants will be classified A or B. On the
recommendation of the Noxious Plants Council, the Government will cover the cost of class
A eradication, and, if considered warranted, will assist in the control and subsequent follow
up of class B noxious plants; (f) the two Nassella Tussock Boards are retained as constituted
by the present provisions in Part II of the Bill.
The proposed Noxious Plants Council will ensure the active involvement of parties most
directly concerned with noxious plants control, and a planned approach at both national and
local level. The council will be expected to initiate research programmes and action for early
control of aquatic weeds, in particular, which under the present legislation have been
uncontrolled. Classifying noxious plants into class A and class B is desirable because of the


## p. 1794 (#56) ############################################

1794
14 July
Noxious Plants Bill
differing control or eradication requirements of various species. Few terrestrial and aquatic
plants would fulfil the proposed criteria for class A. Government assistance here would be
for immediate eradication, with the follow-up work left to the owner-occupier. Class B
would involve a greater number of noxious plants, the types varying according to the region.
The principal physical and financial inputs here would come from the owner-occupier on a
planned district or regional basis, with some Government assistance if the regional co-
ordinating committees and the Noxious Plants Council considered it was warranted. The Bill
was referred to a select committee, which heard 20 of the 63 written submissions received.
The work put into many submissions impressed the committee, and, after lengthy.
deliberations, a large number of amendments have been made, most of which are of an
administrative nature.
I shall now briefly outline the clauses of the Bill. Clauses 1 to 4 cover the short title and
the commencement date of the Act, the binding of the Crown, the general purpose of the
Bill, and an interpretation section defining words used in the Bill. Clause 5 establishes the
Noxious Plants Council. Clauses 6 to 15 are administrative clauses relating to the council,
and also provide for the inter-departmental committee on nassella tussock to continue as an
advisory committee of the council.
Clauses 16 and 17 set out the functions and powers of the council, and the broad
functions of initiating and promoting a policy of noxious plants administration. This includes
the consideration of declarations of class A and class B noxious plants, Government
assistance for control and eradication of noxious plants, the encouragement of research, the
promotion of training noxious plants officers, and the requirement for a report within 3 years
on when the Nassella Tussock Board should be dissolved. The council is also empowered to
prohibit or restrict for up to 12 months, by notice in the New Zealand Gazette, the
movement of any specified articles containing noxious plants, and to inspect animals and
agricultural machinery to ensure they are not contaminated.
Clauses 18 and 19 set out the procedures for declaring weeds to be class A or class B.
Class A weeds will be declared by Order in Council with the approval of the Minister of
Finance, and class B weeds will be declared by the council. Clauses 20 and 21 concern the
delegation of council powers. Clauses 22 to 28 establish the eight regional co-ordinating
committees, and define their membership, administration, and functions. Membership of
these committees, which many submissions thought was unsatisfactory has been amended to
give committees the power-with the approval of the Noxious Plants Council-to co-opt
members to maintain a geographic balance, and to ensure that the interests of Maori
landholders are protected.
Clauses 29 to 34 provide for the establishment of district noxious plants authorities,
their management committees, functions, subsidies for their administration, the raising of
rates, and for the Crown to act if a district authority defaults. Clauses 35 to 37 set out the
requirements in preparing district and regional programmes-the basis for all the work
carried out under the Act. Clauses 38 to 40 give district authorities powers to undertake
work and to recover the cost if an occupier is in default. Clauses 41 to 45 require district
authorities to appoint full-time noxious plants officers trained to the council's requirements,
and for half, or such other proportion as the Minister determines, of their salary and
expenses to be paid by the Government.
A new clause included by the select committee allows, in certain circumstances, ministry
officers to be appointed as noxious plants officers. Clauses 46 to 55 are general provisions
covering such activities as emergency actions in respect of class A aquatic plants, the
certification of seeds, responsibility for noxious plant control on roadsides, issue of notices,
appeals, regulations, offences, and penalties. Clause 47A prohibits growing, sowing, or
selling noxious plants, but allows the council to approve exceptions for scientific and other
purposes. Of all the general provisions, clause 48, concerning the responsibility for noxious
plant control on roadsides, has caused the most concern. The committee finally agreed to
amend the Bill to remove the responsibility from the owner of the road and place it with the
adjoining occupier, as provided in the Noxious Weeds Act 1950. Provision is also made for
the owners of roads-counties, municipalities, and the National Roads Board-by
agreement, to take over control of roadsides when they consider that this is desirable.
Clauses 56 to 118 provide for the continuation of the Marlborough and North Canterbury
Nassella Tussock Boards, which were established under the Nassella Tussock Act 1946.
Thus, the boards are empowered to continue their valuable planned control work on nassella
tussock while the council investigates how best they can be co-ordinated with the new


## p. 1795 (#57) ############################################

14 July
1795
Noxious Plants Bill
administrative structure. Clauses 119 and 120, and the schedules, relate to repeals and
revocations, as well as transitional provisions. The select committee has recommended the
inclusion of a new clause 119A, which covers consequential amendments to other Acts.
I consider that the Bill, as amended by the select committee, will provide an effective
framework for the administration of noxious plants control and eradication. It actively
involves and concerns the Crown, local authorities, and occupiers, and with its methods of
education, involvement, and co-operation, should help to foster the change of attitude
envisaged in the Fitzharris report. I take the opportunity to congratulate Mr Fitzharris, not
only on his report, but on the way he chaired the interim committee that brought the Bill to
the House.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Bill is of a bipartisan nature, and the Opposition
fully supports it, and endorses what the Minister has said about Mr Fitzharris, who helped to
compile the report. I congratulate him, and all those associated with him during the
hearings. The Minister pointed out that the Bill is a consolidation of the principal Act, and
will bring about a better understanding of the noxious plants problem. The Bill establishes
the Noxious Plants Council, and regional co-ordinating bodies and district authorities have
been included. The committee gave careful consideration to the definition of Maori land
originally drafted into the Bill. The amendment confines the definition of Maori land to
unoccupied Maori land. A report from the Department of Maori Affairs clearly states that
other Maori land could be taken account of by local authorities. We commend the Bill to the
House.

DANGEROUS GOODS AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. As I said when I introduced the Bill, its principal purpose is to facilitate the
implementation of the Government's decision to transfer the administration of the
Dangerous Goods Act from the Department of Internal Affairs to the Department of
Labour. The transfer will consolidate in the Department of Labour the industrial safety
inspection responsibilities currently undertaken by the dangerous goods inspectors of the
Department of Internal Affairs. It will involve the transfer from one department to the
other-but not necessarily from their present locations-of some 19 personnel in
Wellington, Auckland, Rotorua, Napier, Christchurch, and Dunedin.
Because of the wider district office network of the Department of Labour, the coverage
of advisory and inspection work will be intensified, but local authorities will continue to
exercise their responsibility for dangerous goods. The work of a dangerous goods inspector
has become increasingly complex in recent years, and it is essential that the inspectorate
should be placed in an environment where it has adequate back-up facilities, and where the
work of the inspectors can be fully integrated with that of factory inspection. The change
will, to some extent, widen the traditional responsibility of the Department of Labour
beyond the industrial safety sphere into the sphere of public safety, such as the responsibility
for the control, from the safety point of view, of petrol stations, and the labelling and
transportation of a wide variety of hazardous substances.
I am hopeful that, after the change, steps will be taken to implement a training scheme
which has been devised by my department for dangerous goods inspectors employed by both
local government and the department. The time has passed when we can afford to have part-
time and partly qualified inspectors employed on this vital inspection work. Plans have been
prepared to ensure that the inspector of the future will be fully trained, and employed full
time. This may well entail grouping local authorities, or, in some instances, working through
regional and united councils established by the Local Government Act. The move which this
Bill permits is good, and it will be of undoubted benefit to the public, to the Administration,
and to the Government's officers.
The Bill also provides the means of controlling the type of pump to be used for
refuelling tanks in motor vehicles operated by liquefied petroleum gas. A number of vehicles
use this fuel in Auckland, and already one type of pump has been submitted to the chief
inspector for approval. LPG is an extremely hazardous substance, and, because of its high
density, it is essential that effective safety conditions should apply to the premises from


## p. 1796 (#58) ############################################

1796
14 July
Dangerous Goods Amendment Bill
which it is dispensed. The authority which the Bill gives to the chief inspector to approve
pumps used for dispensing LPG is similar to that which he already has for petrol pumps.
There is no question of control being applied to a situation-mentioned by the member for
Porirua during the introduction of the Bill-where a person refuels a tank by decanting LPG
from a cylinder. The Bill is a simple measure.
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): The Opposition has no serious objection to the Bill, which is,
to some extent, in tandem with the next Bill on the Order Paper. It is a logical development
that the Department of Labour-which supervises the Factories Act and all sorts of tasks
associated with industry-should also supervise dangerous goods. I should like answers to
one or two questions about the operation of the Bill. If the supervision of the handling of
dangerous goods is to be taken from the Department of Internal Affairs and handed to the
Department of Labour, it will impose extra duties on that department, and will involve extra
finance. In the Dangerous Goods Amendment Bill there is no clause-as there is in the
following Bill-that provides for money not spent by the Department of Internal Affairs to
be transferred in future to the Department of Labour. Will the Department of Labour have
sufficient staff to deal with the extra duties involved in the supervision of dangerous goods?
The department has its hands full dealing with New Zealand's massive unemployment
problem. New tasks will be transferred to the Department of Labour from the Department
of Internal Affairs, and we want an assurance from the Minister that the Department of
Labour will get additional staff to deal with those new tasks. We want an assurance that
Department of Labour staff will not be taken away from their task of finding employment for
the unemployed; that more safety officers will be recruited by the department; and that more
finance will be provided.
The Minister understands the tremendous problems involved in handling dangerous
goods. What steps will the Department of Labour take to organise the supervision of
dangerous goods entering the' ports? In recent years there have been endless problems
because of bad labelling of dangerous goods coming over the wharves. Often the labels are
indistinct, or the goods are misnamed, and it is dangerous to handle containers of hazardous
materials. Inadequately labelled goods need the greatest supervision, and penalties should
be imposed on those who bring these goods into New Zealand. This has been accentuated by
the incident at a Spanish camping ground this week when, according to press reports, butane
gas exploded killing hundreds of people.
It is important that dangerous goods should be correctly labelled, whether they are
handled on a wharf or in a factory. It is essential that we take a firm approach to ensure that
labels correctly emphasise the hazards of what is within a container. The Opposition is
concerned that the Department of Labour should be given the extra staff, so that people
dealing with unemployment and the labelling of dangerous goods are not taken away from
their jobs. With assurances on those two matters, I hope the Bill will pass without
opposition.
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I shall try to answer the points raised by the
member for Grey Lynn. The technical staff will be transferred to the Department of Labour.
No staff will be allocated additional duties. The officers will be transferred from the
Department of Internal Affairs to the Department of Labour. The transfers will not interfere
with the functioning of the Department of Labour. The transfer of unspent money is a
machinery matter. It will automatically be transferred from the Department of Internal
Affairs to the Department of Labour. No other legislation is necessary to effect the transfer
because the vote is not separated into two items. By implication, the member for Grey Lynn
did not refer to legislation, but to regulation, when he spoke about goods coming over the
wharves. The Minister would be the first to concede delay in promulgating the dangerous
goods regulations. That is something we have attempted to avoid. Only this morning there

Second Reading
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. Like the Dangerous Goods Amendment Bill, this Bill facilitates the transfer of
industrial safety functions from the Department of Internal Affairs to the Department of
Labour. In this instance it is the supervision and control of explosives that is involved. This is
a function that is the sole responsibility of the Government. There is no local authority
involvement whatsoever.
The traditional role of the Department of Labour will be widened to some extent,
because inspectors of explosives throughout the country are also involved in the control and
sale of fireworks, and with the highly hazardous task of dealing with improvised explosive
devices, deteriorating explosives, and so on. There are very few of us who really understand
and appreciate the dangers that these officers meet uncomplainingly and treat as part and
parcel of their day-to-day work. They are a small body of dedicated men who play an
essential and unsung role and I raise my hat to them. I take this opportunity to record how I
appreciate what they have done and express my regret at losing direct contact with them.
They are dedicated men, and it has been a pleasure to work with them.
The Bill also makes a minor amendment to the principal Act to enable consignments of
display fireworks to be handled at a wharf. In the main, these consist of signal flares and
similar devices. Generally they come in small consignments that do not involve any greater
hazard than other substances that can already be transported across the wharves. Like its
accompanying measure, the Dangerous Goods Amendment Bill, this Bill is a simple one.

commodity that is dangerous shall be correct and give sufficient warning to all people
handling it.

QE II Arts Council of New Zealand Amendment Bill (No. 2)
QUEEN ELIZABETH THE SECOND ARTS COUNCIL OF NEW

AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Second Reading
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. When I introduced the Bill last November, I explained that its principal purpose
was to provide for the establishment of a Council for Traditional Maori and Polynesian Arts.
The Bill was introduced to fulfil the Government's undertaking to encourage the practice
and appreciation of Maori and other Polynesian arts. In my speech on the introduction I
agreed that there were likely to be some differing views about the new council, and I felt that
all these views had to be taken into consideration. Therefore, I suggested that the Bill be
referred to the Maori Affairs Committee so that interested people and organisations would
have an opportunity to express their views.
The number of submissions received was not great, but each was relevant, and several
constructive proposals were put forward. The nature of the proposals and suggestions
showed the great significance of cultural matters in the everyday life of Maori and Pacific
peoples, and the importance they place upon them. Cultural activities are the main means by
which any group of people expresses the values of its own identity, and, consequently are of
particular importance to any minority ethnic group. As a result of the proposals it received,
the committee has recommended several changes to the draft Bill, and I must say that I agree
with all of them.
When the Bill was introduced last year, I proposed that the council be called the Council
for Traditional Maori and Polynesian Arts. At that time, however, I expressed the view that
the use of the word "traditional" might be one matter that the committee should consider. I
foresaw one of the main points that emerged in submissions to the committee, namely that it
is very difficult to differentiate between the traditional and the modern in these arts.
3069 All art forms undergo a process of continuous evolution, and Maori and South
Pacific arts are no different from others. As a result, there is no clear-cut demarcation
between traditional and modern expression. Many modern artists derive inspiration and
ideas from traditional forms, and although the modern artist might differ in interpretation
from his predecessor, nevertheless the work of a contemporary artist inevitably draws upon
what has gone before. He draws upon the past for his inspiration.
Mr Hunt: Colin McCahon.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Exactly. However, the feature that is particularly strong within a
culture that places great value on the achievements of its ancestors brings me to the point
that I do not know of any people, with the possible exception of the Mexicans, that places
such importance on its past as does the Maori.
Mr Prebble: What about the Japanese?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Possibly one could include the Japanese, but in a slightly different
manner, in my opinion. Can the works of artists such as Sandy Adsett, Para Matchitt, or
Peter Sharples be described as traditional or modern? Similarly, should writers who write
modern verse or prose in traditional Maori language be described as traditional or modern? I
could give more examples of these problems of definition, but I hope I have made my point.
The committee has therefore recommended that the word "traditional" be dropped, and
that the new council support all forms of cultural expression of the Maori and Pacific Islands
peoples.
When I introduced the Bill I knew that the use of the term "Polynesian" in the title of
the council would be open to debate. Strictly, "Polynesian" includes the Maori race within
its interpretation, and excludes other ethnic groups from the Pacific Islands who reside in
New Zealand. There are small numbers of Melanesian and Micronesian peoples here. For
these reasons, the committee has recommended that the title be changed from Maori and
Polynesian to Maori and South Pacific to include all the peoples from the South Pacific
residing in New Zealand. This way, no one Pacific group is excluded from the operations of
the new council. I do not think anyone can now feel that provision is not made for his
interests.
The other major issue on which submissions were received was the membership of the
new council. The Bill as introduced provided for considerable consultation about the
appointment of council members. It required me to consult with the Minister of Maori
Affairs and to consider any other nominations submitted by any person or organisation. The


## p. 1801 (#63) ############################################

14 July
1801
QE II Arts Council of New Zealand Amendment Bill (No. 2)
Bill as reported back by the committee still requires me to consult with the Minister of Maori
Affairs, but goes a little further and specifically requires me to have regard to his views and
to consider any nominations submitted by him. This change will help to make it clear that I
would certainly pay strong heed to any suggestions made by the Minister of Maori Affairs,
and I am sure that any future Minister for the Arts would do the same. This will, I am sure,
dispel any doubts that any Maori group might have.
The provision that I may consider nominations submitted by other people and
organisations remains. I hope that organisations and individuals who are interested in Maori
and South Pacific arts will take advantage of the opportunity. In fact, I now invite them to
send their nominations in to me.
I believe that the Bill, as introduced, contained an implicit understanding that a
majority of the council members would be Maoris, or people from the Pacific. That is
certainly what I had in mind when I introduced the Bill. I said at that time that the council is
for Maori and Pacific people, and their policies and their ideas are needed to make it work.
However, some witnesses expressed their concern that this may not be the case. Certainly,
the way the Bill was worded it would have been possible, however unlikely, for the Council
for Maori and South Pacific Arts to have consisted entirely of Europeans. This would have
been quite absurd, of course, and certainly was not intended. I do not want the council to be
something imposed by Parliament, or to be seen as something alien.
The new council, if it is to work as I am sure everyone in the House wishes it to, must be
representative of the people whose cultures it is to serve. Responsibility for promoting the
development of Maori and South Pacific cultures in New Zealand must be placed firmly in
the hands of the people concerned.
I am happy that the Bill as reported back makes special provision for their membership
of the council. It requires the chairman to be either a Maori or from the South Pacific. Of the
eight other members, at least four must be Maori and at least two must be of a South Pacific
race. This will ensure that the majority of members on the council will be either of the Maori
or South Pacific races, and that the council will not only be for them but it will be of them. It
will also ensure that the council will be composed of people who have an intimate knowledge
and experience of their cultures. It will be on the basis of this expertise that the policies of
the council will be developed, and I do not think that anyone could object to that idea.
Those are the main changes the committee recommended be made to the Bill, and, as I
said earlier, I whole-heartedly support them. I explained when I introduced the Bill that the
Council for Maori and South Pacific Arts would be included within the structure of the
Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council. I believe it is most important that the development of all
our arts proceed in close association, so that the maximum opportunity for co-operation and
co-ordination can be created. To ensure this, the chairman of the Council for Maori and
South Pacific Arts will be, ex officio, a member of the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council and
will certainly be brought in to take part in all discussions on the arts scene in New Zealand.
I hope that, through the sharing and mingling of ideas and experiences, greater mutual
understanding of our various cultures can take place. I am struck by the fact that during the
last decade or so, many of the most exciting things that have happened in New Zealand have
been at the interface between Maori and pakeha cultures. We can think of the way that Witi
Ihimaera has drawn on his Maori background to add to our perception not only of Maori life
and culture but also of what the novel or the short story can do.
Mr Wetere: That's Witi.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Yes, Witi, who is now in our High Commission office in
Canberra. We can think of the excitement that one of Para Matchitt's or Cliff Whiting's
murals creates, as they draw upon Maori forms but express them through the use of modern
materials. We can see how a pakeha painter like Gordon Walters has used the koru motif to
produce abstract paintings of great elegance, or how Jenny McLeod drew upon Maori
mythology to produce her music dramas like "Earth and Sky". So the list could go on; but
those examples, I think, are sufficient to let us know that it is likely that distinctively New
Zealand cultural expressions are emerging from the intertwining of the different strands that
make up our cultural heritage. As these are spun and woven I am sure the fabric they create
will be both vibrant and strong.
Under its present Act, the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council is charged to "encourage,
promote, and develop the practice and appreciation of the arts in New Zealand, including
Maori and Pacific Island arts". I am sure that some of the credit for what has happened in
recent years can be given to the council. It has, in fact, supported both the conservation and


## p. 1802 (#64) ############################################

1802
QE II Arts Council of New Zealand Amendment Bill (No. 2) 14 July
the development of Maori and South Pacific arts for several years, and it is interesting to
note that two of the very rare honours it has bestowed by way of fellowships have been
awarded to artists of Maori descent, Rangimarie Hetet, working in traditional weaving, and
Ralph Hotere, a painter working in a contemporary idiom but sometimes, at least, showing

Other fellowships have been awarded to Bruce Mason, a playwright who has

Omai-have added so much to our understanding of the Maori people.
I referred in passing to Witi Ihimaera. Until he was posted to Australia a few months
ago, to help look after our interests in the High Commission in Canberra, he was a member
of the arts council. His influence on it was profound. He played a very important part in
developing the thinking about the setting up of this new council, and I should like to pay
tribute to him for the work he did in this regard as well as for the contribution he made to the
work of the council.
Returning now to the Bill, although it has achieved a lot, I am sure the arts council
would be the first to agree that the establishment of the new council will provide it with much
more knowledge and experience to help it to achieve much more in the future. I also believe
that in the past many Maori and Pacific people have been reluctant to approach the Queen
Elizabeth II Arts Council for assistance. To many people, not only Maoris and Pacific
Islanders, the arts council must seem to be a remote entity, perhaps not interested in the
cultural expression of ordinary people. Nothing could be further from the truth. It is true
that the arts council is principally interested in supporting professional standards, and that its
programmes are geared towards that end. Its grants to individuals, for example, cover the
fields of music, theatre, dance, visual arts, film and video, and Maori and Pacific arts. Within
those fields, applicants may apply for assistance with vocational training, major projects,
overseas study, and so forth. Any one of any race-and I want to make it clear that any one
of any race-may apply to the arts council for assistance from any of the programmes if it is
appropriate.
On the other hand, the regional arts councils and the Council for Maori and South
Pacific Arts will be involved more with the encouragement of participation in the arts. The
regional arts councils now have funds to provide assistance to local arts groups and
community arts councils, so that they can encourage such groups to provide greater
participation. The Council for Maori and South Pacific Arts will play a similar role by
encouraging people to become active in cultural activities in their own areas. It is hoped that
not only Maori and Pacific people will become involved in Maori and Pacific art forms, but
that other people will develop an interest in those areas.
I am convinced that this policy will lead to greater participation in all art forms,
whatever their ethnic origin, by all groups of people, whatever their race. I believe that this
will lead to a greater understanding of our cultural differences, and that as a result,
understanding, tolerance, and a sense of unity in diversity will develop.
However, the Council for Maori and South Pacific Arts must not be viewed simply as a
source for handouts. The Bill provides it with a number of important functions, and indeed
its grant-making responsibilities come some way down the list. The council will be required
to assist and advise the Queen Elizabeth Arts Council and the three regional arts councils
and community arts councils. Where necessary, it will also be required to co-operate with the
arts council in carrying out its functions relating to the practice and appreciation of Maori
and South Pacific arts in New Zealand, and also to co-operate with educational and
broadcasting organisations in the promotion and development of the arts. It may also carry
out activities to promote and support Maori and Pacific arts on behalf of the arts council.
Its role, then, is not just to distribute funds to various individuals or groups; it is much
more than that. It will carry out a wide range of other functions to support Maori and South
Pacific arts and to ensure their encouragement, promotion, and development. As a result, I
am sure that those arts will flourish even more and that New Zealand will become a better
place for us all.
May I now refer to some of the existing Maori organisations involved in the
development of Maori arts and crafts. Probably few members in the House have not visited
the Maori Arts and Crafts Institute at Whakarewarewa and seen the splendid work being
done under the leadership of Mr Kuru Waaka. The Maori Purposes Fund Board has a

14 July QE II Arts Council of New Zealand Amendment Bill (No. 2)
1803
distinguished history of helping to nurture Maori culture. The New Zealand Maori Council,
the Maori Women's Welfare League, and, more recently, the Maori Artists and Writers
Association, and the various Maori culture clubs up and down the country have all played a
valuable role in helping to preserve and develop Maori culture. Each of these bodies has
been, in a sense, a whaka huia within which the cultural treasures of the past have been kept.
The new council will in no way cut across what they are doing. I hope the member

its establishment a criticism of what they have achieved. Instead, it will provide a link

nominations for membership of the council that they might let me have.
A very serious deficiency in the present pattern of support for the arts in New Zealand
has been the lack of support from the Government for the arts of the Pacific Islands,
although, for several years, the Polynesian Festival Committee of the Maori Purposes Fund

The cultures of the Islands of the South Pacific have been uprooted from their own
environment and replanted in our very different soil. As yet these plants have not become
very big or deeply rooted. That they will is beyond doubt, and that they can grow and thrive
sheltered by the great totara of Maoritanga is a matter which gives rise to real pride.
It was a matter of great joy to me, and I believe a great cause for pride in our nation,

gave evidence questioned in any way the appropriateness of their playing this role with the
Maori people. I consider that, when enacted, this Bill will, by setting up the Council for
Maori and Pacific Arts, achieve something of deep and abiding value in the development of
our multicultural society. Because of this, I believe that, though it is a small Bill of only 15
clauses, it will be one of the more important measures which Parliament will enact this year.
I shall refer just briefly to two matters which are covered by the Bill other than the
establishment of the new council. The first amends the present provision that the chairman
and other members of the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council are appointed for 3 years.
Because there can be circumstances when someone who would be an ideal member of the
council would not be available for the whole term, it is proposed to amend this section of the
Act to provide simply that members will be appointed for terms not exceeding 3 years. The
second provides local authorities with an option-at their discretion-to make a grant to
community arts council for administrative services rather than providing those services
themselves, as at present. I assure the House that this proposition is acceptable to everybody
concerned.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Opposition strongly supports the Bill. I shall not

Hon. D. A. Highet: And that is very much appreciated.

know where something that is called "traditional" starts or finishes. Maori members said
that they did not know where the cutoff period should be. We were not sure whether it was

The word "Polynesian" was discussed at great length. Most people know that Maoris

the Melanesians, and Micronesians, and so we had to define it as "South Pacific" arts. That

changes are indicative of a living growing culture. They have contributed to a situation where
the range of cultural and artistic forms utilised by Maori people is broader and richer today
than at any previous time."
It is the recognition of this living, growing culture, this richer, broader range of artistic
endeavour, that has made the establishment of the new council for Maori and South Pacific
arts so important and so necessary. Maori art has been through difficult and trying times.
Very few areas of New Zealand escaped the early effects of European occupation, the Maori
wars, and the decline last century in the Maori population. In the first quarter of this
century, Maori art remained in a state of decline. Morale and health were at a low ebb, and
many people believed that many aspects of Maori culture, including the visual arts, would
disappear altogether. At that time, with the active support of Sir Apirana Ngata, the
Government established a national school of Maori arts at Rotorua in 1930. To illustrate the
school's successes I have only to refer to the many fine works of Pene and John Taiapa. After
the second world war many young Maori students, having passed through the primary and
secondary levels of the New Zealand education system, were beginning to be exposed to
European art teaching.
Mr Wetere: This is history.
Dr SHEARER: Yes, a little of your own history that you should know. Consequently, by
the 1950s many Maori artists were starting to modify traditional styles, experiment with new
ideas and media, and add their own expression to their work.

It was important to me, and my response was immediate, I suppose, because of my
distinctive responsibility as one who is part Maori. There are many facets to being a Maori.
One is the capacity to respond uniquely to occurrences in the environment, and indeed in the
universe. Another is the capacity to perceive, through a somewhat different vision and
perspective, that every colour has life and is more graphic, and that the forest sounds and
choruses of nature are music. This is indicated in the work by Cliff Whiting. There is so much
that is spiritual in a world observed through Maori perspective, a spirituality distinct from
that of organised church religion. The distinction is clearly post-European.
I bore all this in mind when suggesting the amendment, because the true awareness of a
cultural difference often eludes even the most well intentioned. I appreciate that because it
undoubtedly occurs in the reverse. I appeal to the House to acknowledge that such unique
niceties are of benefit and well worth savouring as an asset to our total culture. They are
unique perceptions, and because they are provided for in the Bill it has the full support of the
Opposition, particularly those of us who represent specifically Maori electorates.
This uniqueness should be a visual norm rather than an exception. Consequently, I
believe that buildings such as the New Zealand Parliament, our overseas missions, and more
of our public buildings could very well be graced by the work of such unique artists as Sandy
Adsett, Para Matchitt, Graham Ford, Fred Graham, Cliff Whiting, and their ilk. They are
unique, like the Maori language. New Zealand does not recognise this. I should like to see
the day when this uniqueness is recognised by making the language and these art forms
available to all children.
The Bill has not come too soon, and I congratulate the Minister on the concept behind
it. I know that Witi Ihimaera, who is now in Canberra, was very much involved. I

is based on the European culture, but for too long the Maori people have not been able to

honourable member has a Maori culture background-heritage, language, and so on-but
she also has a New Zealand background, heritage, and culture. For my part, I have a
European background and culture, but also a New Zealand background and culture. The
point I am making is that the "New Zealandness" is the contribution from both European
and Maori cultures.
Increasingly over the last few years a further mainstream from the South Pacific has
been introduced. The setting up of the Maori and South Pacific Council envisaged in the Bill
recognises that to preserve our "New Zealandness"-if I can call it that we need to
preserve and strengthen the contributing factors making up our own uniqueness. Anyone
who travels around the world will know that a New Zealander can be easily recognised. For

14 July QE II Arts Council of New Zealand Amendment Bill (No. 2)
1811
example, a New Zealander can be recognised in a London bus simply because of his accent.
It is quite strange that too often when in New Zealand we tend to ignore the
contribution of the Maori people, but when we travel overseas what do we take with us? Is it
not a bagful of plastic tikis made in Hong Kong, or a record or two of Inia te Wiata, or
someone else? We are very proud to produce them, but when we come back to New Zealand-
we tend to push them aside. In the time that lies ahead there will develop in this country-
not only in the forms I have mentioned such as language and the more obvious art forms such
as carving-a truly New Zealand - orientated culture based on other art forms. Already we
have true New Zealand painters, authors, and poets, and if you look very closely you will see
that they all have this uniqueness.
I congratulate the committee on the changes it has made to the Bill. In removing the
word "traditional" from the Bill, the committee has recognised that we are not concerned
merely with traditional art. We do, of course, recognise that traditional art is one of the
contributing factors, but the committee has shown that it recognises also that there is a
moving and modern Maori and Pacific Island art.
I also applaud the change of name. In Auckland there is a Pacific Islands Education
Resources Council, and the name is "Pacific Islands" not "Polynesian". We should, in the
future, change the name of the Polynesian Education Foundation to allow for a similar
recognition of the wider nature of the foundation than is envisaged in the word
"Polynesian". In setting up this council we have come of age in another way-by recognising
the need for the development of the two cultures. I have appreciated greatly the opportunity
to study the Maori language. It has opened my eyes. I am not suggesting that everybody in
this country should learn the Maori language, but it teaches us to appreciate the differences
between ourselves and the other peoples who form this country. We all gain a lot from
studying each other's language, and I am sure that as the Pacific Islanders become more and
more members of New Zealand society they will do the same.

Transport Amendment Bill (No. 2)
TUESDAY, 18 JULY 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Introduction
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That the Transport
Amendment Bill (No. 2) be introduced. The Bill corrects an anomaly in the 1974 amendment
to the Transport Act 1962. I shall explain briefly how the anomaly came about. Before 1974,
harbour ferry service licensing in Auckland was the preserve of the Auckland Harbour Ferry
Service District Licensing Authority. In 1971 the Government decided that passenger service
licensing in the district of a regional authority should be dealt with by one authority, the
regional transport licensing authority. In 1974, the then Government decided that harbour
ferry licensing should be dealt with by the regional transport licensing authority instead of by
a separate harbour ferry service authority. Auckland was the only area concerned.
Therefore, in 1974, the jurisdiction of the regional transport licensing authority in Auckland
was extended to cover harbour ferry services. This was achieved by an amendment to section
120A of the Transport Act 1962.
The jurisdiction of the authority was deemed to be over all harbour ferry services that
are, or are intended to be, operated within the district of the regional authority. In Auckland
the district of the regional authority is defined in the Auckland Regional Authority Act 1963
as comprising the areas of a number of cities and boroughs, and a town. However, the
territories of the local bodies making up the area of the ARA all end at high-water mark.
That is the anomaly in the 1974 amendment. It appears that the authority does not have due
jurisdiction over areas of sea and over services within the harbour. The Government of the
day had clearly intended that the regional transport licensing authority should have that
jurisdiction.
The Auckland Regional Transport Licensing Authority has been acting in good faith in
considering harbour ferry services to be within its jurisdiction. That, after all, was the aim of
the 1974 amendment. The additional amendment I am proposing to section 120A of the
Transport Act will correct the error and validate the decisions of the regional transport
licensing authority that have already been made. I do not believe that this matter should
prove to be contentious, since it is designed purely to give effect to the intention of
Parliament that the 1974 amendment should give regional transport licensing authorities the
job of harbour ferry service licensing in regional districts.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I do not suggest that the
Opposition will oppose the Bill, but I wonder how often Parliament's time has to be taken up
by this sort of pointless amendment. Ferries sail between wharves, which, under any man's
definition, are above the high-water mark. The fact that the wharves are attached to the
bottom of the sea does not mean that they are below the high-water mark. The earlier
interpretation was quite clear-if the termini were within the regional area, that gave the
responsibility for licensing the services to the regional authority. Now some bright lawyer
says that, because the ferries sail on the harbour, which is outside the regional area, we have
to have the amendment. The ferries cannot operate if they cannot tie up. Why do we need
the amendment?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): The Government has been
advised that it is necessary for Parliament to validate what it did in 1974. The honourable
gentleman was a member of the Government of the day. There was an anomaly in the matter
of jurisdiction, which we want to correct.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): What does the Bill mean when it refers to termini that are
within, or in the close vicinity of, the boundaries? What criteria has he established for
determining what constitutes a close vicinity? Who wants this legislation? Is it a particular
transport group that has run into difficulties? Is it a particular competitive operator? Is it a
company that has on its board a former Minister of the Government? Who is stirring for this
legislation?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): The honourable member would

know that better than I do, because it comes from within his own profession. The validity of

Antarctic Treaty-Fish Exploitation
6. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What changes
does he foresee in the Antarctic Treaty to provide for supervision of the exploitation of the
stock of fish and krill in the region?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): The
Antarctic Treaty countries decided at the ninth consultative meeting in London last year
on the establishment of a regime to control the fishing of living marine resources in
Antarctic waters before the end of 1978. This will not involve any changes in the Antarctic
Treaty. A special meeting of treaty countries was held in Canberra in March of this year,
and a draft convention was drawn up; it will be a new agreement that makes provision for
the establishment of a commission on Antarctic marine living resources. The commission
would be supported by a scientific committee and would be responsible for setting
conservation standards. The special meeting in Canberra did not complete the draft
convention and the meeting was resumed in Buenos Aires on 17 July-yesterday for a
further 2-week sesson.
Mr W. R. Austin: In view of the extraordinary amount of protein in the region, will New
Zealand play a major part in the harvesting of the resource?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: New Zealand is vitally interested in that resource,
and in the other countries that are fishing, which will have a place in the organisation to be
established.
Hon. M. Rata: What are the attitudes of the delegates who represent New Zealand at
the treaty discussions?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The delegates are acting in New Zealand's interests,
and will consider the other countries interested in the resources. New Zealand believes that
other countries should be actively involved in fishing the resources.
Mr Isbey: Did the original meeting in Australia encourage the exploitation and mass
slaughter of whales in the Antarctic?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Last week I answered a series of questions on
whales. New Zealand has taken a positive attitude to reducing the kill, and it has considered
the standard of living of the Eskimos. New Zealand considers that they should have limited
access to the whales.

Antarctic Treaty-Mineral Resources
15. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What proposals, if
any, are being considered by the Antarctic Treaty powers to control the exploration and
development of mineral resources in the Antarctic region?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): The Antarctic
Treaty powers, at their most recent consultative meeting held in London in September 1977,
agreed to the following principles: first, that they would continue to play an active and
responsible role in dealing with this issue; secondly, that the protection of the unique
Antarctic environment and its dependent ecosystems should be a basic consideration;
thirdly, that the interests of all mankind in Antarctica should not be prejudiced; and,
fourthly, that the principles embodied in the Antarctic Treaty should be included in the
future regime for mineral resources. This subject will be on the agenda for the tenth
consultative meeting to be held in Washington later next year, and will also be the subject of
a preparatory meeting that will focus on the legal and political aspects. In the interim, it was
agreed that States would refrain from all exploration and exploitation of mineral resources.
Mr W. R. Austin: Has the Minister any information to suggest that the exploitation of
some of these minerals might be imminent?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have no such information at this stage.
Hon. M. Rata: What specific policy direction, if any, has the Government given to its
delegation in respect of this meeting and the proposed meeting in Washington?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The policy of the New Zealand Government, and of
the other Government concerned with this, is that it does not exclude projects relating to
scientific research, but it does exclude commercial exploitation. The Government is opposed
to that, but it does support scientific research.

Industrial Accidents-News Media Reports
17. Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora) to the Minister of Labour: How many reports on
industrial accidents has the department published, and does it have difficulty in getting
adequate coverage in the media?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): As a general rule, details of industrial
accidents are not published in the news media. This is because most industrial safety
legislation administered by my department contains provisions that prohibit publishing of
specific information obtained by inspectors in the course of their work. One exception to this
is the Agricultural Workers Act 1977, which authorises the publishing of information on
agricultural accidents with my consent. My department has for some time published general
summaries of serious and fatal accidents in the Labour and Employment Gazette, and this has
proved to be very successful and will continue. I personally strongly support the publication
of accident details as part of a prevention programme, and, as industrial legislation is
reviewed, amendments will be included to facilitate the controlled release of accident details
to the news media, including trade journals. Where publication is possible, few difficulties
are experienced by the department in getting adequate media coverage.
Mr Isbey: Would the number of man-days lost because of work accidents be greater
than the number lost because of industrial disputes? The media appears to publicise the man-
days lost in industrial disputes, but not the far greater number of man-days lost in industrial
accidents.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: That is barely related to the original question. What the member
for Rangiora was asking about, and what I tried to answer, was the publication of the details
of how individual accidents had happened, in the belief that experience and education are
the best teachers. I should like the Department of Labour to emulate the Inspector of Air
Accidents, and the reports he publishes. That has nothing to do with the number of days lost
by accidents vis-a-vis strikes. It is purely a method of trying to prevent further accidents.

Infant Mortality Figures
21. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East),
to the Minister of Health: Could he outline the latest available figures of infant mortality in
New Zealand; and how do these compare with the rates over the previous 5 years?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I am pleased to say that there is an improvement
in the latest available mortality rates for infants-that is, children under 12 months of age.
For the year 1971 the rate per 1000 live births was 16.6; for 1972, 15.6; for 1973, 16.2; for
1974, 15.6; for 1975, 16; and for 1976, 14. To improve the rate further, the Department of
Health is at present involved in a national study of the social and medical factors associated
with each post-neonatal death in an attempt to elicit the cause of death so that appropriate
remedial preventive action can be taken.
Richard Walls: The Minister confined his answer to children under the age of 12
months. Are figures available for children aged from 1 to 5 years?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes. In health terms, when we speak of infants we mean children up
to the age of 12 months. Many people think of older children as infants. There has been an
improvement in older children too. The mortality rate for children between the ages of 1 and
5 is based on deaths per 100 000 of population. The figure for 1965 was 106.6, for 1973 it was
96.1, and for 1976 it was 75.2. I might say that 40 percent of these deaths in New Zealand are
from accidents, drowning, and poisoning. They are not health related. If we take out
accidents, drownings, and poisoning, New Zealand rates fairly highly.
HOSPITALS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Hospitals
Amendment Bill. This is a Bill of four clauses that does not involve an appropriation. It
provides that hospitals and other institutions are not to be closed or restricted without the
consent of the Minister, upon recommendation of the regional or territorial authority given
after full opportunity has been provided for public submissions and objections to the
territorial or regional local authority concerned. It provides for advance warning of the
intentions of hospital boards to be given in respect of any proposed closure or change of use,
and also requires hospital boards to state publicly the reasons for any proposed closure or
restriction, and to say what may be substituted and to give dates. It gives local authorities as
well as individuals a right of objection. In doing so, it assists them considerably to fulfil their
planning functions.
The Bill's objective is to eliminate problems such as those that have arisen over the St.
Helens Hospital in Wellington, and provides for greater public supervision of hospital board
actions, and thus a greater community participation and involvement in democracy. The
problem of St. Helens prompted the Bill, which, if adopted, would apply nationwide. When
there is a problem, little good is ever served by simply identifying it and bemoaning the fact
that no one can solve it. It is up to us to solve the problem, if there is one, and not to bewail
the fact that there is a problem. I have not spent time on public meetings or tours of
inspection over the issue, but have devoted what time I could to finding an answer to this
specific problem.
The Bill, with whatever imperfections it may have at this stage, is an answer not simply
to the problem of St. Helens, but to similar problems wherever they may be in New Zealand.
St. Helens is in some ways unique. It is a hospital for women, run by women. Its function is
to minister, not to sickness, but to health, to birth, and to life. The decision to close it and
transfer its function elsewhere, apparently to ensure adequate availability of material for use
in training men in obstetrics, overlooks this philosophy, this view of the functions of St.
Helens that have in the past proved so beneficial to mothers in many walks of life.
The decision also overlooks the fundamental philosophy that hospitals should be for the
use of people, not people for the use of hospitals; and there are some justifiable public
misgivings on this count. Councillor Helen Ritchie, the Labour candidate for Ohariu, said
that doctors have expressed concern to her about access to their patients in the new block


## p. 1822 (#84) ############################################

1822
18 July
Hospitals Amendment Bill
that is proposed. She quoted a child psychologist as saying, "In an era when many are
wanting more natural births, we have now witnessed a decision which relegates birth and
women to an automated factory process." Those who made submissions in 1977 were
assured that no final decision would be taken without prior consultation.
Clause 3 makes the Bill retrospective to the date of the last triennial elections of the
Wellington Hospital Board so far as St. Helens Hospital is concerned. Because of various
happenings since the election of the board, which were not made very obvious beforehand,
there would be retrospective effects back to 8 October 1977, so that, no matter how far the
moves have gone to close St. Helens Hospital, to change its health services, the Wellington
Hospital Board would have to comply with the provisions of the Bill if it was enacted.
Recent history has shown several controversies in various parts of New Zealand that
have demonstrated insensitivity, and perhaps indifference, by hospital boards to the wishes
of the people. The situation shows the need for people to take part in the decision making on
the future of public hospitals and other public health institutions, and in particular on any
proposal to close, restrict, or change their use.
The Bill would not remove any hospital board rights. It would simply require hospital
boards to justify their decisions against possible public objections. The costs involved in the
public hearings and other matters provided for in the Bill would be paid by the regional
authority or the territorial authority. The hospital board would not stand the expense, so
there would be no indirect appropriation. The benefit to the local authority would lie in its
greater supervisory role in hospital planning in relation to a neighbourhood or a community.
A further relevant matter on this aspect is that those parts of the Bill that refer to the
Minister and to the Hospitals Advisory Council are merely a re-enactment of what is already
in section 55 of the principal Act, but would be taken out and re-enacted with the additional
provisions proposed in the Bill.
The substance of the Bill is to provide a new dimension to the present provisions under
which a hospital board is not permitted to close any institution under its control, or to restrict
the forms of care, treatment, or relief in or from any institution under its control. Before the
Hospitals Advisory Council would come into the matter, the authority must first make an
appropriate recommendation. The Bill would provide a system for people to take part in the
decision making, so that the public, organisations and various authorities would have the
option of making submissions and objections to a regional authority, or, when there is none,
to a territorial authority so that the submissions and objections could be considered, the
board given the opportunity to state its case, and a recommendation made to the Minister.
An affirmative recommendation in favour of the closure or restriction of an institution would
be necessary before the Minister could give his consent.
The immediate effect of passing the Bill would be nationwide availability of popular
participation in the making of decisions affecting those involved. Some people say that
illness is New Zealand's largest industry. It is certain that a great deal of public money has
gone into hospitals and health institutions, and will go into them in the future. It is equally
certain that the public has a right to have a voice in its destiny, and when some hospital board
wants to close an institution or to change the system of care in an institution the people will
know.
I hope that the Government will give me the courtesy of permitting the Bill to go to a
select committee, as it did so willingly with the private member's Bill of the member for Grey
Lynn, which dealt with an equally important topic. The Bill does not involve an
appropriation. It would assist the Minister in the fulfilment of his functions. It involves the
public in decision making that affects it centrally.
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I think everybody in the House, and certainly
everybody in Wellington, knows the position about St. Helens Hospital, because the hospital
board's deliberations, both at the committee and at the board stage, were open to the press,
and were well reported. People had the opportunity to comment and to express their points
of view in public and in private. This matter has been under consideration for a long time.
The member for Kapiti, who is a former member of the Wellington Hospital Board, made
deep and considered representations to the board and to me about the matter, and the
member for Wellington Central has made representations to ensure that the matter is
properly considered by those concerned.
I have also received representations from Mr Nathan, the National Party candidate for
Island Bay, who is very concerned that the right action be taken. We share his concern. We
are interested in the right action being taken, but we must at the same time have some


## p. 1823 (#85) ############################################

18 July
1823
Hospitals Amendment Bill
confidence in the hospital board, which in due course will make a recommendation to the
Minister. The hospital board has the oversight of the area from which its members are
elected, and is responsible for making sure that the essential requirements of the people in
that area are met in the proper way.
The Wellington Hospital Board, not the Wellington City Council, controls St. Helens
Hospital. I understand that the member for Island Bay, who has brought the Bill forward,
has had some experience on the Wellington City Council, and it may be as a result that he
has completely misunderstood and misjudged the situation. The geographical local authority
does not have any experience in or knowledge of the hospital board's administration, and the
members of the council are not elected to do that type of work. The hospital board has
boundaries that are completely different from those of the Hutt County Council, the Hutt
City Council, and the Wellington City Council, and the hospital board makes the decisions
affecting hospitals within its area.
A recent decision of the hospital board was to keep open a maternity hospital in Upper
Hutt. Other decisions of the hospital board affecting the work on and progress with the
building and opening of the Kenepuru Hospital show that the board is concerned that the
needs of the people should be met. Everybody knows the member for Island Bay who has
promoted the Bill knows, and every member in the House knows that plans for the
Wellington Hospital Board's new obstetrical and gynaecological block were made when the
birth rate was very much higher than it is now. Apparently the hospital board has made a
decision, but it has not yet made a recommendation or a case to me. However, from what I
have read in the press, it appears that the hospital board has found that it has overplanned
and has too much capacity, and that it has made a decision, but that decision has not been
communicated to me. At least the suggestion has been made that, as the hospital board has
overprovided, St. Helens should be closed.
I was interested to read in the press that Miss Joy Motley, the principal nurse at St.
Helens Hospital and the President of the Nurses Association-a nurse of considerable
experience and good judgment-made this statement: "I am very sad, but I have to agree
that the board's decision to close St. Helens is the right one."
If the hospital board has decided to close St. Helens and communicates that decision to
me, it will be following a great deal of public discussion on the matter. The Wellington
Hospital Board has had many public representations made to it. I do not know whether the
member for Island Bay is aware of this, but, in case he does not know, I can advise him that,
after any decision made by the hospital board, the matter would be referred to the Hospitals
Advisory Council and considered again. That council will probably follow its normal
procedure, and send a subcommittee to look at the situation on the spot-and the
subcommittee would discuss the proposal with the public if it considered that was necessary.
Last year, when it was proposed to close a maternity hospital at Hunterville, the
Hospitals Advisory Council sent a subcommittee to Hunterville. The recommendation made
by that subcommittee was that the hospital should not be closed; and, although the hospital
board had recommended that it should be, it was not closed. The Hospitals Advisory
Council also sent a subcommittee to Fairlie, and, as it recommended, the hospital in Fairlie
was closed.
I emphasise that if the Wellington Hospital Board recommends that St. Helens Hospital
be closed, and does so bearing in mind all the public discussion there has been on the
proposal, the Hospitals Advisory Council will then consider the recommendation. If the
council considers that there has been insufficient public discussion and that further meetings
should be held, it will arrange for them. Members of the House will have further
opportunities to ask the Minister about the matter if they want to do so. The Minister will
later face the responsibility of accepting or not accepting the advice of the Hospitals
Advisory Council, and at that time the Minister can have such consultations, public or
otherwise, as he thinks necessary. Therefore, it is ridiculous to suggest that some regional
planning council representing geographically bodies that do not elect hospital boards, whose
boundaries do not coincide with the hospital board's boundaries, and which has no
knowledge or expertise whatsoever in the matter, should make decisions on the closing of
hospitals. I think the member for Island Bay is perhaps trifling with the House in bringing
forward the Bill and suggesting that it should go to a select committee.
Mr Hunt: You haven't even read the Bill.
Hon. T. F. GILL: I have read the Bill carefully, and my departmental officers have also
read it. I have received comments from them expressing, roughly, the view that I am giving.

development of obstetric hospitals in isolation from normal base hospital facilities. The lack
of instant anaesthetics, blood grouping, and biochemical services is critical."
Because of the lack of facilities and because specialist staff are not readily available, St.
Helens Hospital does not admit emergencies or cases at risk-that is, when pregnancy is less
than 35 weeks or when there are other reasons for suspecting that there could be problems
with the new-born child. Caesarean sections can be carried out at the hospital, but, once
again, the majority of such cases are dealt with at Wellington Hospital. A decision by a
hospital board to close a hospital is not made lightly, and I am sure no one would suggest
otherwise, particularly in this instance.
The honourable member may be ignoring the Minister's point that, at this stage, the
board has not made a recommendation-although I have no doubt that one is forthcoming-
and also that the Hospitals Advisory Council must give its recommendation. In most cases-
and in this one, I certainly hope-it will set up a subcommittee to hear the views of members
of the public. It will go to the site, interview people, and hear the views of those concerned,
including nurses and medical officers. Having made a decision, it will pass its
recommendation on to the Minister. Sufficient precedents have been established to allow for
the dissemination of such views, and I sincerely hope that those precedents will be followed
when the council's recommendation is received by the Minister of Health.
I am advised that the Hospitals Advisory Council has permitted deputations to make
representations directly to the council itself. Again, that could be useful. Some time ago a
subcommittee travelled to Hunterville to investigate a recommendation that the maternity
hospital there should remain open. One also travelled to Fairlie to investigate a
recommendation that the hospitial there should be closed. That obviously shows that the
subcommittee, rightly and properly, will seek local opinion.
The Bill provides that the regional planning authority should have the power to hear
objections on a decision to close a hospital. It would be quite wrong for such an authority to
intervene in an area that is a statutory responsibility of an elected hospital board. Sufficient
avenues are available to the public to have views heard. That is very important, because
people should have the opportunity to convey their views. At present there are only five
regional planning authorities in the country, and in the absence of regional planning
authorities it would be over to the territorial local bodies to make the recommendation. The
position of Miss Motley, President of the Nurses Association and principal nurse at the
maternity hospital, has already been referred to. In her report she said that the new unit
should not be a combination of St. Helens and ward 11. It should be a new hospital.
Mr SPEAKER: I am sorry to interrupt the honourable member, but his time is
exhausted.
Dr WALL (Porirua): This is a timely Bill, and draws attention to the fact that our
medical services are increasingly being dominated by technical decisions, and that less and
less attention is being paid to the obvious social uses and some of the social responsibilities of
those medical services. A review of some of the absurd things that have been done in the
name of technical efficiency in the past 20 years, particularly under the previous National
Government, will, I think, put the matter in context.
Members are probably not aware that, with the exception of the administration of
anaesthetics or the prescribing of drugs, the only surgical or medical procedure that any


## p. 1827 (#89) ############################################

18 July
1827
Hospitals Amendment Bill
member of the public cannot legally carry out-providing he does it successfully-is the
delivery of a baby. In other words, any member of the public, without any medical
qualification, can carry out-provided he does it successfully-brain, heart, lung, or any
complicated surgery he choses to; but he may not deliver a baby except in an emergency.
That is how absurd things have become; the law allows us to do vastly difficult technical
things, but it is illegal for someone with no medical qualifications to carry out a simple
physiological process such as the delivery of a baby. It makes one wonder how the human
race has survived.
This has developed over the past 20 years. It is an example of technocrats telling the
members of the public that they know best; and there is an element of this in the present
organisation of our maternity services. I am concerned that the imposition of professional
unit control over our maternity services-such few as are left and appear to be necessary
with our declining rate of fertility-will further divorce the conduct of what is essentially a
physiological process from the ordinary medical scene where it has been carried on
successfully for so long. I do not doubt that acute or rapidly developing emergencies arise,
and that provision must be made for them, but it is very different to suggest that the facilities
that allow a woman to be delivered, in an ordinary case, by the doctor of her choice under
conditions in which we are prepared to provide practical aid, should be subverted to the
technical needs of a highly sophisticated professorial unit with all the educational
requirements of future practitioners tied into the requirements of the patient and the child as
well as members of the public; yet that is what I see coming about.
I do not deny that there is a need to provide adequate teaching services, which can best
be done, and must continue to remain, under the disciplined control of a teaching unit.
However, provision must be made for general practitioners, many of whom have vast
experience in this field, to continue to handle ordinary deliveries for the ordinary patient in
surroundings that are attractive to the doctors and the patients. Those amenities are being
diminished, although not intentionally, and although the technocrats may say that provision
is being made for more beds, the atmosphere of the institution changes because it is
dominated by the teaching requirements of the professorial unit. That cannot be avoided.
In the past few years the trend has been to take medical services back to the community.
I have some reservations about that, because of the technical complexity of some of the
services, but despite my reservations it is a valid and timely move. The very technical
requirements of maternity work have been given as the reason maternity hospitals have
closed all over the country. Such hospitals could have evolved to become the nucleus of a
community health service.
It is for this reason that I support the introduction of the Bill, which I hope will go
before a select committee so that the conflicting interests of technical people in the medical
profession and the ordinary man in the street may be balanced, because they certainly need
to be. We must remedy the situation in which every facet of the delivery of medical care has
been dominated by people with technical qualifications, and also those with a particular
affluent, educated outlook. The educated affluent seem to ask what the best way would be in
which to treat these poor ignorant people from the lower classes, and what would be
suitable, appropriate, and sufficient care for these people. That outlook stinks, but I see this
happening increasingly under the influence of the academics, the administrators, and the
technocrats in the medical profession.
More people should be prepared to speak up and say that they want their own doctor to
look after them at a price they can afford, because he will be concerned about their
treatment. I know there are men who want to do this, and I know also that the situation,
which this Act sets out to remedy, will destroy the position for those on lower incomes. The
people on higher incomes will be able to enjoy good social medicine.
I hope that the Bill will be referred to a committee, and that the needs of the people,
particularly in my electorate, will be considered, because there will be an efficient voice
speaking for the people and demanding that the needs of the community are considered
along with the technical requirements of the health service. In many districts the grass-roots
medical services are inadequate and are being provided in a way that suits the people who
deliver the services, while the people for whom the service is provided are becoming fodder
for the medical machine.
Mr BRILL (Kapiti): I support the spirit of the Bill, or, perhaps more correctly, the

Island Bay has taken an interest in the effect of the hospital on residents in the Newtown

area, and he has followed up his concern by bringing in a Bill that is intended to achieve a

However, I find it difficult to agree that the Bill itself has any real relationship to the

My second major reservation, which is fatal to the Bill, is about the proposal that the

People in my electorate have little enough faith in the Regional Planning Authority when it
carries out its planning functions, and they would have some concern if its functions were to
extend to health planning. The expertise of the Regional Planning Authority-if any is to be
discerned at all-is in land use and the allocation of resources throughout its region.
The question that will be asked about the closure of St. Helens in favour of the obstetric
and gynaecological unit is whether one of the wards in the O. and G. unit could be otherwise
used. That question could not be considered in any helpful way by the Regional Planning

to consider such matters, will be able to cross-question the hospital board more effectively
than could members of Parliament or the Regional Planning Authority. The committee,
