hoops when considering whether this alternative, which was favoured by the hospital board
last year, is still feasible.
I do not believe that there is any prospect of the Regional Planning Authority saving St.
Helens. If that is the purpose of the Bill, then it will not achieve its objective. I recommend
the member to pin his faith to the Hospitals Advisory Council, which, I have been told by the
Minister, will be directly concerned with the degree of public consultation that precedes any
decision to close a hospital. It will consider the amount of public consultation in the
Wellington area about St. Helens.
It will find that there was a great deal of public consultation, not in 1978, but in 1977,
when scores of submissions were received, time was allowed for written submissions to be
submitted, hearing dates were set, and open hearings were held. The consequence of that
properly constituted series of consultations was a decision that St. Helens would not be
closed. It was decided that it would remain open, at least until 1981, when the effect of
opening the Kenepuru general hospital could be considered. That was decided almost
unanimously by the hospital board after it had found, by consultation, that the public was
almost unanimous in condemning the closure of St. Helens. We can ask what the board
members themselves thought public opinion was.
Last year was an election year, and members took a vote around the table as to whether
they would close St. Helens, and they decided, with remarkable unanimity, that it would be
a bad idea to close the hospital. This is not an election year, and they have decided it is a
good idea to close St. Helens. I suggest that is a reasonable measure of board opinion, from
which we can conclude that the board knows perfectly well that the public of Wellington is
opposed to the closure of St. Helens. When board members were obliged to face their
electorates last year, they passed a resolution to the effect that the hospital would stay open.
Even the new Labour member of the hospital board-the sole representative of the
Labour Party on the board-campaigned vigorously to have St. Helens remain open, but this
year she was not present at either meeting that discussed the matter, and she is the only
member of the hospital board who has not voted on the question. Every other member of the
board has, but the new Labour member, who is also the Labour candidate for Kapiti, has not
yet voted aye or nay.
Why have all those board members changed their minds? The reason given was that the
Department of Health had sought from the board a report on the possible duplication of
plant in St. Helens and the O. and G. block. I take leave to doubt whether there will be very
much use in the new hospital of plant from St. Helens. Those of us who toured the O. and G.
block only a week or so ago were impressed by the lavish standard of construction. Clearly
no expense has been spared, clearly the new block is a magnificant amenity, and clearly, it


## p. 1829 (#91) ############################################

18 July
1829
Hospitals Amendment Bill
will not be cluttered up with second-hand machinery and plant pulled out of the walls of St.

We have had no figures, but I suggest that it would be very surprising if more than about
$50,000 were saved after allowing for the cost of transferring the plant from one place to the
other. We have to put that in context-the cost of the new O. and G. block is over $14
million. The suggestion that is now made by the hospital board is that it is necessary to close
St. Helens because there may be a saving of, I suggest, about $50,000. We have not had any
figure from the board as to the actual savings, and we probably will not know it until the
equipment is moved.
The hospital board has not told the public what it will do with St. Helens. It has, in
effect, suggested that the hospital should be closed in order to scavenge a few spare parts to
use in the new O. and G. block, but it has not made any decision as to what it will do with
what is a comparatively new-12-year old fully-functioning maternity hospital. That seems
to me to be a curious sort of decision. First it decides to close the hospital, then it will decide
what to do with it.
Despite what is being said by the hospital board and the newspaper reports about the
meeting of Labour Party candidates, I do not believe that the block can possibly duplicate
the advantages of St. Helens. In the first place, it is in the middle of a hospital campus, amid
sickness and disease, and, as has been pointed out by the member for Island Bay, maternity
cases are concerned with life and living, and birth, appropriately set aside from an
atmosphere of sickness. Secondly, the O. and G. block stands in the middle of a concrete
jungle. It is a towering 13-storey monolith, and will never compare with the bungalow-type
suburban atmosphere of St. Helens, which is found so restful by the mothers who have their
children there. Thirdly, fewer than half of the mothers-in fact, little more than a third-will
have the right to a single room in the new block. In St. Helens, every mother has that right.
If there are to be cubicles for four mothers, all of whom will have the right to have their
babies with them, what consideration will be given to the woman who does not want to have,
and should not have during the immediate post-natal period, the noise and upset of three
other babies in the room during the night? That is common enough around the country, but
St. Helens has achieved a new high in nursing care, where every mother can have her own
room, and, if she chooses, can have her baby with her. It seems to me that it is a backward
step to close St. Helens-a declaration that the standard of nursing care there is too high,
and, therefore, it should be closed. Regretfully, I do not believe that the Bill will achieve its
objective of keeping the hospital open.

QUEEN ELIZABETH THE SECOND ARTS COUNCIL OF NEW ZEALAND
AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 14 July 1978
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): I support the Bill. Although I was absent when it was
last debated, I heard part of the debate. I was happy to hear the remarks of the Minister in
charge of the Bill and the Minister of Education. I thank the member for Auckland Central
for his kind remarks. The opportunity to discuss in some depth internal relationships
between various ethnic groups in New Zealand is regretfully rare, but the Bill has afforded
the House a welcome opportunity to examine the issue impartially. The purpose of the Bill
has been adequately explained, and its introduction should not be regarded as a lack of
confidence in statutory authorities charged with the responsibility of promoting various
traditions, customs, and practices, but as a recognition of those traditions and customs. The
committee heard little argument about traditions and modern art.
The new council must take every possible opportunity to acquaint the Pacific island
community in New Zealand with its functions and powers, and how it can help promote their
traditions and customs. The absence of submissions by various Pacific island groups within
New Zealand does not necessarily mean that they were neither interested nor unable to
submit opinions. It is absolutely essential to acquaint people at the grass-roots level with the
existence of the council. Maori groups also must be fully consulted.


## p. 1834 (#96) ############################################

1834
QE II Arts Council of New Zealand Amendment Bill (No. 2) 18 July
The creation of the council may avoid an academic and snobbish attitude towards
traditions and the encouragement of art. The other day I received a copy of Koru, published
by the New Zealand Maori Writers and Artists Incorporated, which gives modern expression
to the work and stories of their forebears. Probably that is the kind of work the new council
will encourage. The member for Auckland Central reminded the House that Maori
traditions and customs are alive today. The daily needs of cultural enrichment must be met,
and should be a council responsibility. The Government has approved a grant of $50,000
towards the work of the council, but it should increase the percentage of the total
appropriation from the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council. More finance is needed, not only
to maintain the council's work, but also in recognition of the importance of culture.
Hon. D. A. Highet: It doesn't mean that is all they will get.
Hon. M. RATA: I am glad to have the Minister's assurance that it does not necessarily
mean that that is all they will get, but the $50,000 approved by the Government will be useful
in initiating the important work of the new council. At this stage I consider it appropriate to
pay tribute to the New Zealand Maori Arts and Crafts Institute and the Maori Purposes
Fund Board-to name only two-and to those voluntary groups which are not statutory
boards but which have carried out a useful function in the past. It is hoped and envisaged
that in future the council created by the Bill before us will carry out that role, and give
greater impetus to the promotion of New Zealand's traditional arts.
I return to the needs of the South Pacific island communities within New Zealand.
Various groups from Western Samoa, the Cook Islands, Fiji, Niue, Tonga, and one or two
other islands will be encouraged to establish their own distinctive identities, and to follow
their pursuits and interests in their own way. I hope every encouragement possible will be
given to them. As I said earlier, the council must be mindful to give high priority to that task.
Indeed, it would do well to pursue that first, before becoming involved in other major policy
decisions. Members of the council should consult all island groups early about the council's
existence to ensure that they realise that the council will encourage them to pursue their
cultural interests. I firmly believe that the new council will prove a very welcome addition to
existing institutions and organisations.
Finally, neither the Bill nor the House can add a great deal of substance to the traditions
of any people; that task rests entirely in the hands of the people concerned. All the Bill aims
to do is to provide support wherever possible to ensure that people of different ethnic
backgrounds are encouraged to pursue their cultural heritages. I emphasise that no one, and
certainly no statutory authority, can do for people what they must do for themselves. Much
will depend on the value they themselves place upon their own arts and cultures. I wish the
council every success with its new responsibilities, and I trust that it will win the confidence
of all the people it is being set up to assist.
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): It is a pleasure to follow the member
for Northern Maori in the debate. He has shown clearly his support for the Bill. I agree
entirely that there is a great need for us to be able to co-ordinate, bring forth, and help the
South Pacific island communities to flower. Becauss of their smallness, and the fact that they
are not unified, they have not yet been able to get together as much as we would wish. The
member knows that the concept of the Polynesian Maori is a catalyst to bring them together.
I found the committee hearings on the Bill very interesting. We agreed on the need for
substantive amendments to the Bill, and we found that the department was prepared to
accept the proposed amendments.
I congratulate the Minister for the Arts on sending the Bill to the Maori Affairs
Committee. There is a need for a council such as that proposed, and for the legislation we
are considering. Originally the idea was to support the establishment of a Maori Art Council,
but after considering the matter further it was decided that it would be better to graft the
council to the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council, if for no other reason than to improve that
council.

Board, the New Zealand Maori Council, the New Zealand Maori Women's Welfare League,
and the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council. All gave very interesting evidence. They
congratulated the Minister on having introduced legislation that gives a new dimension to
the arts. As the member for Northern Maori said, the funds already allocated are just the

SPEAKER'S RULING-NOTICE OF MOTION
Mr SPEAKER: Before I call for notices of motion, perhaps I should rule on the matter
that was raised with me by the Prime Minister on Friday of last week. Honourable members
will recall that there had been some discussion on the notice of motion put down by the
honourable member for Christchurch Central, which now appears on the Order Paper.
The Prime Minister asked me to give a considered ruling on whether it is a proper
procedure for notices of motion to be based on suspicion and on rumour. As he said, ". . .
that could lead to a wild allegation becoming publicly the subject of a notice of motion, and
being given wide publicity, even though there is not a 'skerrick' of truth in it." He went on to
say, "I believe it is wrong for a member to take suspicion and rumour and make allegations
in the House by way of notice of motion, which inevitably will be given publicity, because
some people will believe the allegations." It is well known that if mud is thrown, some sticks.
It is also well known that those who persistently throw mud build a reputation for themselves
that is likely, eventually, to engulf them. So I have borne that in mind in coming to my
conclusion.
Standing Order 103 gives the. basic rules on the admissibility of notices of motion. It
consists of three paragraphs, two of which are relevant to the present question. Paragraph
(a) provides that notices of motion shall not contain any unbecoming or offensive expression
or any expression or words which would not be permitted in debate. The first question is,
therefore, whether words invoking suspicion and rumour are unacceptable on those
grounds. Words that are unbecoming or offensive in themselves would be ruled out on that
ground, but if the words themselves are acceptable, should the inference of suspicion or
rumour be a ground for ruling them out of order? Speaker's ruling 53/5 is helpful on this
point, when it states that the use of ambiguous words capable of conveying a sinister as well
as an innocent meaning should be avoided. More recent rulings have been along the lines
that words tending to lead to disorder should not be used. I think, personally, that that is
probably the best guide. That guide can be applied to the literal meaning, having regard to
the context, and also to the question of taste.
Paragraph (b) of Standing Order 103 provides that notices of motion shall not contain
any statement of facts or name of any person unless they are strictly necessary to render the
notice intelligible and can be authenticated. The questions raised by this paragraph are
whether the statements are strictly necessary, and whether they can be authenticated. If
suspicions and rumours are included in a notice of motion, they must be identified and
authenticated as such. If the words used give rise to a clear inference of improper conduct by
a member or a group of members, they are out of order, and should not be used in debate or


## p. 1837 (#99) ############################################

19 July
Speaker's Ruling-Notice of Motion
1837
included in a notice of motion, except for the purpose of bringing a charge against the
members concerned.
Speakers' rulings 78/1, 78/2 and 81/2 make it clear that if a charge is to be brought
against one member by another member it must be done by a substantive motion, which can
be dealt with in a proper constitutional way-that is, by reference to a committee or by
debate in the House. I would add to those provisions something that I regard as very
important-namely, that any charge or notice of censure against a member must relate to his
conduct as a member. I would exclude activities or conduct that are irrelevant to his status as
a member. Charges against him in his private capacity should be brought in the courts.
The right of free speech in the House, the right to criticise anybody, including the
Government, a Minister, or a member for his stewardship, is fundamental. It flows from the
principle of the accountability of the Government, and of individual members for that
matter, to Parliament. I have a duty to protect members from improper words or
imputations incidental to the motion before the House-that is, matters that are irrelevant. I
informed members at the beginning of the session that that was what I proposed to do. If
there is a rumour abroad, it may be false, but its existence is a fact, and it might be wise to
have it debated in the House on a proper motion, to let its truth or falsity be exposed. That,
one could reasonably assume, lay behind the Prime Minister's request on Friday to have the
notice of motion by the member for Wigram put down for debate.
Every right is balanced by a duty. The right to free speech must be matched by the duty
of the member to exericse that right with responsibility, cognisant of the effects on those
referred to in the rumour, and on Parliament itself. Words or statements that cannot be
authenticated may not be included in a question or a motion, but that does not prevent a
member from exercising his right to ask a question seeking confirmation or otherwise of a
report or rumour; nor his right, by motion, to inquire into the stewardship of Ministers or
members in their official capacity. I would expect all members to use those rights
responsibly.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I ask, with due
respect, if all members could have a copy of that very important ruling?
Mr SPEAKER: I would be very happy to do that. I had intended to circulate it to the
leaders of the parties. However, if honourable members would also like a copy I am quite
happy to arrange that.

Social Welfare Benefits
11. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Social Welfare: Has he read the New

"The honourable member has taken the statement out of context. Since the present

Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: The report, a copy of which I have here, is not a direct

Armed Services Technicians-Shortage
13. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill), on behalf of Squadron Leader DRAYTON (St.
Albans), to the Minister of Defence: Has he seen the article in the Auckland Star of 8 July in
which a Department of Defence spokesman is reported as saying that a shortage of middle-
ranking technicians is partially responsible for the grounding of a large proportion of Air
Force Iroquois helicopters, and what is he doing to keep this expensive equipment working
by replacing the skilled NCOs who have left the force during the past year?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of Defence replies: "I
have seen the article in question. The grounding of Iroquois helicopters was not attributable
to a shortage of technical staff. Structural cracks were found in the underfloor beams of four
aircraft, and these were grounded for a period. All are now back in service. Because of some
shortages of middle-level technicians, inspection and repairs took longer than would
otherwise have been the case. The training programme for technical trades has been
streamlined over the last 2 years. Delays between initial military training and specialist
courses have been reduced to a minimum. More intensive technical courses have resulted in
an increase in output of trained technicians. Also, pay levels will shortly be improved for
skill and experience, but it will be some time before the shortfall is made up. At the present
rate of recruiting it is expected that the shortages will be overcome in the next 2 or 3 years".

expected to have good chances of success.

Kaitaia Airport
16. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru), on behalf of Hon. R. L. BAILEY
(Heretaunga), to the Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services: What was the
estimated cost in 1975 of upgrading and resealing the Kaitaia runway, and what is the
estimated cost today?
Hon. C. C. A. MCLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services):
The estimated cost of reconstructing the runway at Kaitaia in 1975 was $532,000. Under that
authority, base course metal costing $210,000 has been purchased and stockpiled on the site.
The present-day cost of completing the project is assessed by the Ministry of Works and
Development at $450,000.
Mr Lange: Are the present-day assessments of costs made on the basis of the work being
done now, or when the ministry has the mind to do the work, and, if that is so, what later
date is it on which the costs are based?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I understand that provision is made in the estimates for
the work to be done, but a specific approval would still be needed at the time. On the
question of the present-day costs, I got them from the Ministry of Transport.
Mr Hunt: Can the Minister confirm that the additional cost is already more than
$100,000?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: From the figures, that is correct, but I remind the
honourable member that engineering costs alone have risen at the rate of 1.15 percent a
month.
Mr Lange: When did the Minister first undertake to provide for this reconstruction, and
how much has the cost escalated since the promise was made by the National Government?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I have given no promise to reconstruct the runway.
Mr Lange: You bought the metal.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: Yes, but I have given no undertaking. I repeat that it is
provided for in the estimates, but a special approval will still be needed when the time comes
for the work to be done.
Mr H. N. Austin: Can the Minister confirm that the metal is not deteriorating even
though it is left in the open until such time as the Government can do the work?
Hon. C. C. A. MCLACHLAN: I do not think the metal would deteriorate, but I remind
the House that these questions go to the very core of the matter. On becoming the
Government we had to get the priorities right. It is a misrepresentation to say that I
promised the reconstruction of the runway.
Hon. M. Rata: Will the amount of $450,000 be sufficient to upgrade the Kaitaia

Hon. C. C. A. MCLACHLAN: I should have thought that a former Minister would know
the answer to that question. That is today's figure. It will depend on escalation of costs, and
that is a major problem. I was asked for today's price, and I have given it.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: When does the Minister propose to call tenders for the work to be
completed, or has he adopted some other method of having the job done?
Mr SPEAKER: That is getting beyond the original question.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: Provision is made in the estimates for this work to be
done. It still has to be approved when the Government decides that it should be done, and
then it will proceed.

Misuse of Drugs Act
21. Mr McLAY (Birkenhead) to the Minister of Health: Is he aware of a decision
delivered in the Christchurch Supreme Court on 12 July 1978 by Mr Justice Casey dismissing
an appeal against conviction by a student charged with possession of a drug for supply; does
this decision indicate any problem with the provisions of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, and
is any urgent amendment necessitated by the decision?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have seen the newspaper report of the case
referred to by the honourable member. The Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 does not, as the
reported statements of the judge indicate, contain any offence of possession of a class C drug
such as cannabis for the purpose of supply to a person of 18 years or over. There are offences
under the Act of simple possession or of possession for purposes of sale, which should be
adequate to deal with similar situations. However, care must be exercised in the preparation
of prosecutions for offences under this legislation to ensure that persons are appropriately
charged.
Mr McLay: Does the newspaper report indicate that any further offence needs to be
created under the Misuse of Drugs Act to deal with the particular situation that arose in that
case?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No, not to deal with that particular situation. However, the
Government is concerned about the misuse of drugs, and the member for Birkenhead is
chairman of a subcommittee that has been considering the problem. We are concerned about
the supply of hard drugs. The Act may be inadequate at present, and we may need to
introduce some more severe penalties.
Mr Lange: Can the Minister indicate to the House and to the member for Birkenhead
whether the person acquitted in the Supreme Court at Christchurch could have been
convicted on a charge of simply possessing the material?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I do not want to be critical of the action taken. I thought I had made it
clear in my answer to the original question that great care must be exercised in the
preparation of prosecutions for offences. I also said that there is an offence of being in simple
possession or of possession for the purposes of sale. I should have thought that would be a
clear indication to the member of the offence for simple possession.

1. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Maori Affairs: How
many statutory boards, committees, tribunals councils, etc., within the jurisdiction

are the names of those which have since been established?

statutory boards and committees were in existence when the present Government
assumed office: Maori Land Board-7 district Maori land advisory committees;
Maori Purposes Fund Board-Maori Soldiers Trust Committee; 11 district Maori
trust boards. All of these statutory boards and committees are still in existence
and no new ones have since been established, except that members were appointed
to the Waitangi Tribunal under the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975.

Peat Shortage
3. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Energy: Has he seen
the article in the New Zealand Herald of 13 May 1978 entitled "Clamp on
peat mining slated", and, if so, is the Government going to take any steps to ensure
that North Island horticultural nurseries will have a ready supply of peat at a
reasonable price?
Answer
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: I have read the article in the
New Zealand Herald, which refers to the difficulty being experienced by N.Z. Peat
Ltd. in obtaining access to peat deposits on the Hauraki Plains and the effect
this may have on supplies of peat to North Island nurserymen. There are two main
suppliers of horticultural peat in the North Island. They are Hauraki Peat Ltd.
and N.Z. Peat Ltd., both of which obtain their supplies from coal-mining leases
that they hold in the Waitangaruru-Pouarua area of the Hauraki Plains. The
area held by N.Z. Peat Ltd. will soon be worked out, and the company has applied
for a lease over a new area. The area concerned is a sensitive one from the point
of view of flood control, and several organisations-the Hauraki Catchment Board
and regional water board, the Ministry of Works and Development, and the
Department of Lands and Survey-have interests in the use that is made of it.

that an area where peat mining may be permitted has now been defined and that
a new application for a coal-mining lease will soon be made.

Linton Coal Mine, Ohai
12. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: (a) What is
the estimated life of the Linton mine at Ohai, and to what stage are plans advanced
to replace this mine; (b) what machinery is required for the replacement mine,
and when will this be ordered; (c) to what extent have coal reserves in the region
been proven?
Answer
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: Extraction work in the Linton
mine is scheduled to be completed at the end of 1978. The opencast area, from
the face of which the replacement mine will be established, has been stripped
and the 25 000 tonnes of coal made available is currently being won. The initial
mine development will be done using the Alpine miner and new conveyor equip-
ment at present at Ohai. Equipment to mechanise the mine fully will be purchased
over the next 21 months. The main items of equipment to be purchased are face
machines, shuttle cars, and additional conveyor belting. The new mine is situated
in a syncline between Nos. 6 and 12 opencasts. The distance between the faces
of these opencasts is 22 chains. Over the area, 12 surface bore holes have been
put down and have penetrated the seam to be worked.
(30/6/78)
Speared Fish Sales
13. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Fisheries: Is it his intention

the sale of speared fish caught in amateur fishing competitions. However, it will

an amendment to the Fisheries Act 1908 has been passed.

Housing Loans Interest Rates-Trustee Savings Banks
16. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) to the Minister of Finance: What
were the interest rates charged by each of the trustee savings banks for housing
loans at (a) 1 December 1975, (b) 1 June 1978?
Answer
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The range of
interest rates charged by trustee savings banks for housing loans as at 1 December
1975 and 1 June 1978 is: 1 December 1975, 6 to 9 percent; 1 June 1978, 8.5 to
12 percent. At each date the upper limit was generally applicable only to larger
mortgages, although this situation varied between individual banks. The rates
are those applicable on mortgages for owner-occupied houses and do not neces-
sarily include rates charged on other types of housing mortgages, e.g., on flats
for investment purposes. Any comparison between individual banks is not mean-
ingful, because of the different criteria laid down for different types of lending.
(30/6/78)

Napier-Taihape Road Upgrading
20. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) to the Minister of Works and Development:
(a) Has he read the article in the Hawke's Bay Herald-Tribune of 21 June 1978
headed "Pulp plan in trouble" in which the. Director of Roading refers to the
Napier-Taihape road as "extremely substandard" and probably unsafe for bringing
pulp from the Karioi mill. to the port of Napier; (b) can he say what
steps he is taking to have the road upgraded, how much will be expended, and
when this work will start; and (c) will he give the expenditure on the road in
question, giving details, in each of the March years 1975, 1976, 1977, and 1978?
Answer
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: I have
read the article referred to by the honourable member. The Napier-Taihape
road is a county road under the control of the Rangitikei and Hawke's Bay
County Councils, and responsibility for maintenance and upgrading rests with
these local authorities. Arrangements are being made for a joint inspection of
the road to be carried out on behalf of the National Roads Board by engineers
of the Ministry of Works and Development in conjunction with the two counties
concerned. It is up to the counties to make provision in their roading programmes
for any work considered necessary, and to apply for funds to the National Roads
Board through the district roads councils concerned. This has yet to be done, and
I am unable to give any indication of the counties' proposals at this stage. The
following table shows the total expenditure on the road in question for the years
ended 31 March, 1975, 1976, 1977, and 1978:

Special Votes-Criteria
22. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Justice: In what circumstances is
a person recorded on the incorrect parliamentary roll entitled to register a special
vote under section 99 (c) of the Electoral Act?
Answer
Hon DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: The Chief Electoral
Officer advises that under section 99 (c) of the Electoral Act an elector who was
registered for a particular district in 1975 and has not changed his address from
that district may vote as a special voter in 1978 for the electorate in which that
address is now situated, even though he may have been incorrectly enrolled in
another electorate. By virtue of section 99 (d) the same is true if he has applied
for registration between the time of the 1975 election and writ day for the 1978
election. In either event his special vote will be counted.
(5/7/78)

Questions and Replies
West Taupo Forests Management
31. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) to the Minister of Forests: In view of his
reply to question 16 on 15 June that he intended to release a decision on the
future management of west Taupo forests in 3 months; and in view of his reply
to question 18 on 20 June that a decision would be made in 2 months, can he
tell the House what the date of the release will be?
Answer
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: Both statements were indica-
tive rather than definitive. At the closing of the seminar held at Taupo in March
to consider New Zealand Forest Service management proposals for State forests
of the Rangitoto and Hauhungaroa Ranges in the central North Island, I invited
delegates, together with any interested organisations or individuals not present
at the seminar, to submit their views to me on the future management of these
forests by 31 May. These submissions have now been analysed and I have had
preliminary discussions with Forest Service officers on the analysis. The Forest
Service is at present preparing a paper on the major issues, and when these have
been fully considered by the Government decisions on the future management of
the west Taupo forests will be announced. A date for such an announcement has
not been decided and it is not particularly relevant whether it is 2 or 3 months
away. What is important is that the matter is being given urgent attention and
careful consideration by the Government, as it affects the future lives of many
New Zealanders and the communities they live in.
(5/7/78)

TV2 Coverage, West Coast
34. Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast) to the Minister of Broadcasting: Has
he seen the report entitled "No action in TV2 is deplored" in the Greymouth
Evening Star of 19 June, which says in part that the TV2 Action Group deplored
"the lack of interest shown by the Minister of Broadcasting in not replying to
correspondence, and further delays could effectively promote a change in
policy of negotiations into an undesirable situation of recommending the with-
holding of TV licence fees throughout the whole of the West Coast", and does
he propose any action to prevent this?
Answer
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: The report
referred to by the honourable member deals with a matter that has been the
subject of a number of representations over a period on behalf of West Coast
viewers. A detailed reply explaining the whole situation was forwarded to the
TV2 Action Group on 15 May, and I am aware that a further detailed reply is
pending to a later letter received. As has already been conveyed to the group,
the payment of a licence fee is required by law for the operation of a television
receiver, and has never been equated to the quality or extent of the service
available. If it was so equated, apart from the massive cost and complexity in
establishing fees and administering their collection, less revenue would be available,
and the net effect would be to slow up coverage, particularly in areas where there
are greater technical difficulties and lower population.
(5/7/78)

couple with three children, in cases where the breadwinner earned $95 or less by way
of ordinary-time weekly earnings, and $20 extra weekly from overtime, bonuses,
secondary employment, (i) qualified for family benefit capitalisation of up to $2,000,
(ii) qualified for a Housing Corporation loan of $22,800 at 3 percent interest to
build a house, with weekly repayments of $21.09; (b) can he indicate the cost of
the average building proposition financed by the Housing Corporation as at 1 June
1975; (c) what is the proportion of the average building proposition a Housing
Corporation loan of $22,800 and maximum family benefit capitalisation amounted
to at that time; (d) could he indicate the cost of the average building proposition
financed by the Housing Corporation as at (i) 31 December 1977, (ii) 1 June 1978;
(e) at each date, could he give details of the assistance the Housing Corporation
was able to offer to assist the breadwinner of a family, including two children, if

sources, (iii) $160 weekly from all sources; and (f) under "details" in (e) could he
give (i) the maximum loans for which each of these breadwinners was eligible, (ii)
the interest on loans, (iii) weekly repayments, (iv) maximum family benefit
capitalisations for which these breadwinners were eligible, and (v) the proportions
of building costs as at 31 December 1977 and 1 June 1978 respectively that
maximum Housing Corporation assistance was equal to?

Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: (a) (i) No. (ii) No.
$15,300 (being standard average loan $13,000, low-income supplement $2,000,
and general reserve fund $300). No section loan is included. Interest would be at
51 percent, and weekly repayments $20.14. (b) $24,342. (c) 93.6 percent, but as
shown in (a) (ii) above $22,800 was not the maximum loan advanced by the
corporation. (d) (i) $29,732. (ii) Not available yet, but for May 1978, $31,799.
(e) 31 December 1977: (i) $140 p.w.-standard average loan $13,000 plus $3,000
low-income supplement, 8 percent rebated to 6.5 percent interest reviewable 3-
yearly. (ii) $150 p.w. standard average loan $13,000 plus $3,000 low-income

Maori Land Development Encouragement
40. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) to the Minister of Maori Affairs: In view
of the Budget statement on land development encouragement loans given on pages
19 and 20, can he advise how multiple-owned Maori land corporations, and 438
trusts, take advantage of such incentives in order to bring such pockets of land
into production?
Answer
Hon. DUNCAN MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs) replied: The land
development encouragement loan scheme is to be administered by the Rural
Banking and Finance Corporation, which will accept applications from 1 August
1978. Maori incorporations and trusts interested in the scheme should lodge
applications with the nearest office of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation.
The Department of Maori Affairs will render assistance, upon request or where
necessary, in dealing with such applications, particularly if the applicant is already
a mortgagee of that department or of the Maori Trustee.

Judicature Act-Proposed Amendment
43. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Justice: Does he
intend amending the Judicature Act this year as recommended in the report of the
Public and Administrative Law Reform Committee on standing in administrative
law?
Answer
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: The report of the
Public and Administrative Law Reform Committee on standing has been released
only in the last 2 months. In accordance with the Government's policy in these
matters, interested parties will be given the opportunity to peruse the report and
to make their views known to the Government before a decision is taken on its
implementation. It is not intended to have a Judicature Amendment Bill this
session.

Houses Taken under Public Works Act-"Home for Home" Concept
45. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Works and Develop-
ment: Has the review committee looking into the compensation criteria for homes
taken under the Public Works Act reported yet, and, if so, does the Government
intend to introduce legislation this year providing for a home for a home?
Answer
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: The Public
Works Act review committee has completed its work, and the formal report was
released to the public during March of this year. The Government policy that
compensation should be based on the principle of a home (or a farm) for a home
(or a farm) of equal standard was introduced in 1976. The review committee has
accepted that the new provisions are adequate for those situations in which replace-
ment homes (or farms) must be provided.

Da Locomotives-Financing Arrangements
47. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Railways: What are
the arrangements entered into in rebuilding the Da locomotives overseas for: (a) the
amount of the loan or credit arrangement; (b) the number of locomotives involved;
(c) the term of the loan or credit arrangement; (d) the interest rate; (e) the total
amount repayable?
Answer
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: The total number
of Da locomotives being rebuilt in Australia is 54. The amount of credit arranged
for this project totals A$15,583,496 repayable at an interest rate of 8 percent.
The first 35 Da locomotives required a loan of A$9,278,496. Repayments on this
loan will commence on 1 January 1979 and end on 31 December 1983. The amount
repayable will total A$11,818,500. The second batch of 19 locomotives required
A$6,305,000, and repayments totalling A$8,006,037 are expected to begin on 1
September 1980 and to cease at 31 August 1985.

Housing Corporation Lending Criteria
48. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Housing: (a) Can he
confirm that under Housing Corporation lending criteria in force as at 1 June
1975 a young couple with no children, in cases in which the breadwinner earned
$80 or less weekly from ordinary-time weekly earnings, together with $20 weekly
from other than ordinary time wages, was eligible for Housing Corporation loans
totalling $20,800, at 3 percent interest, with repayments of $28.15 weekly; (b)
what was the cost of the average building proposition, including section costs,
financed by the Housing Corporation at that time and what proportion of this
cost was a loan of $20,800 equal to; (c) could he indicate the cost of the average
building proposition financed by the Housing Corporation as at (i) 31 December
1977, (ii) 1 June 1978; (d) at each of these dates could he indicate details of the
assistance the Housing Corporation was able to offer a young couple if the bread-
winner earned (i) $120 from all sources weekly and his wife did not work, (ii)
$140 weekly from all sources and his wife did not work; and (e) would he give
in each case under "details" (i) the maximum loan for which the breadwinner
was eligible, (ii) interest on loans, (iii) weekly repayments, (iv) the proportion
of building costs as at 31 December 1977 and 1 June 1978 that maximum assistance
in each case was equal to?
Answer
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: (a) No, I cannot
confirm that. Such a couple as the honourable member describes could have
qualified for a 3 percent interest rebate, but the maximum loan assistance would
have been $16,000 ($14,000 standard average loan, Auckland or Wellington, plus
a $2,000 low-income supplement). By including the general reserve fund contri-
bution, $320, plus the $400 for mortgage repayment insurance, the weekly
repayments based on a total loan of $16,720 with interest at 3 percent over a
30-year loan term would have been $16.34. This excludes, however, any loan
provided to freehold sections. (b) At 1 June 1975 the average cost of a building
proposition financed by the Housing Corporation was: building $18,265, land
$6,077, a total of $24,342. A loan of $16,000 (net) represented 65.73 percent of that
cost. (c) The cost of the average building proposition financed by the Housing
Corporation at: (i) 31 December 1977 was building $21,922, land $7,810, a total
of $29,732; (ii) 1 May 1978 (figures at 1 June 1978 not available) building
$23,546, land $8,253, a total of $31,799. (d) and (e) Details of assistance the
Housing Corporation could offer a young couple: (i) if the breadwinner earned
$120 gross weekly and his wife did not work:

(6/7/78)
Auckland Education Board-Administrative Autonomy
54. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Education: Does he intend to
grant the Auckland Education Board autonomy to administer its own funds "in
order that the needs of its schools, which differ in some respects from those in
other parts of the country, may be recognised", as recommended in the annual
report of the Auckland Education Board?
Answer
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The Auckland Educa-
tion Board already has a certain amount of autonomy in administering its basic
equipment funds. The basic equipment scheme for primary and intermediate
schools that was introduced in 1972 makes provision for all schools to receive a
basic entitlement of supplies and equipment at full cost to the Government.
Grants are made annually to the various education boards for furnishing and
equipping schools, and last year the Auckland Education Board received approxi-
mately $1.4 million. The board has complete autonomy as to how some of these
grants are apportioned to schools. It is inherent in the scheme that very large
schools, those with high proportions of infant classes, and schools with a high
proportion of pupils with language difficulties and other special problems, may
receive additional items of equipment on the recommendation of the district
senior inspector.
(6/7/78)

Housing Corporation Loans Criteria
63. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Housing: Further to
the question asked by me on 20 June and answered on 27 June, can he indicate
why changes to the definition of "income" introduced in the 2 March 1976 mini-
Budget measures, which are part of the criteria affecting eligibility for family
benefit capitalisation, were not included in the original answer; and can he list
each of the changes that were made in the definition of income used to determine
both family benefit capitalisation and hence eligibility for low-income supplements
at that time?
Answer
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: My reply of 27 June
1978 outlined changes to the basic income limit for family benefit capitalisation
since 1 January 1976. I confirm that in March 1976 additional changes were made
to the eligibility criteria not related to the basic income limit. At that time the
definition of income for the purposes of capitalisation and low-income supplements
was amended. Since that time such income has been defined as the breadwinner's
total income based on current taxable earnings including overtime, secondary
employment and allowances, or the average over the past 12 months, whichever
is the higher.

Farm Workers' Employment Scheme-Training
70. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Labour:
Is any form of training given, or encouraged, for workers employed on farms under
the Government's farm workers' employment scheme?
Answer
Hon. D. S. THOMSON (Acting Minister of Labour) replied: The farm employ-
ment scheme is designed to create jobs for persons who would otherwise be
unemployed. The extent to which structured training is provided under this
scheme is dependent upon the employer, and the nature of the work provided.
The aims and objectives of this scheme include the promotion of developmental
activities on farms, and, as a consequence, most workers engaged under the scheme
will be able to improve their work experience, skills, and aptitudes.

Housing Corporation Loans to buy Sections
72. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Housing: (a) What
assistance to purchase sections is the Housing Corporation able to offer to people
wishing to build homes at present; (b) can he give details of the terms of assistance
in force for section purchase, to include: (i) maximum amounts available, (ii) loan
terms, (iii) interest rates, (iv) criteria for eligibility, and (v) whether the loans
apply only to sections sold by the Housing Corporation; (c) can he indicate for how
long loans under the above terms have been available?
Answer
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: Loan assistance for
the purchase of private sections terminated in October 1975. Purchase of Crown
and HCNZ sections under long-term agreements with varying deposits (minimum
10 percent) can leave the balance of the purchase price outstanding and there is
no upper limit. Should the purchaser of a Crown or HCNZ section subsequently
receive a building loan from the Housing Corporation, the balance of the purchase
price outstanding at that time may be included in the mortgage given, and
repayment adjusted to a new term of up to 30 years. HCNZ sections suitable for
modest to low-cost housing are offered by way of ballot and preference is given
to landless applicants intending to build within 12 months. The interest rate
payable on these sections is 81 percent. High-priced sections (i.e., over $10,000)
less suited to modest low-cost housing, are often offered by ballot with preference
given to landless applicants. The interest rate payable on these sections is 10
10
percent.

Arapawa Island-Scenic Reserve
80. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) to the Minister of Lands: Can he confirm that
the scenic reserve on Arapawa Island is in fact unfenced, and thus that domestic
stock can gain access, and will he confirm also that damage to the reserve occurred
through uncontrolled burning of scrub?
Answer
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: The Arapawa Island scenic
reserve is unfenced at present. Fencing of the 18.9 km boundary is being considered,
but any fencing programme could be undertaken only in conjunction with adjoining
owners. Because of the very steep terrain of the island, and the short life of fencing


## p. 1885 (#147) ###########################################

19 July
1885
Questions and Replies
wire in the exposed climatic conditions on the island, fencing will be a very
expensive undertaking, and careful consideration is necessary before any decision
is made to fence the reserve. Domestic stock have access to the reserve, but as this
stock graze only the open grassed areas and do not browse the bush they are not
preventing regeneration of the bush to any marked degree. As far as I am aware,
no damage has occurred to the reserve through uncontrolled burning of scrub. There
were a number of burn-offs on private land last summer, one of which did get out
of control, but this was on the western side of the island and some distance from
the scenic reserve.

81. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier)) to the Minister of Railways: In the negotiations
for the railing of pulp from the Karioi mill near Ohakune to New Plymouth, was
any price set for the Railways to cart pulp to Napier, and if so, what was the
difference between carting it by rail to Napier and New Plymouth?
Answer
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: The Railway rates
quoted to the principals of the Karioi pulp mill project are, for competitive reasons,

quoted to New Plymouth was slightly cheaper than the rate quoted to Napier.

frozen, along with all other Railway charges, since November 1971.

Pysiotherapists-Group Rate Benefit
84. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: Is he aware that at
the present time physiotherapists working for the Federation of New Zealand
Parents Centres (Inc.), as far as obstetric treatments are concerned, are paid
40c per class member with a maximum of 15 in a class, and that it is many
years since an increase was last granted, and, if so, when will this group receive
an increase in payment?
Answer
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: The rates of physiotherapy
benefit, including the group rate, were increased with the effect from 1 July 1974.
The group rate cannot be considered in isolation from that applying to individual
patients. At this stage there is no proposal to increase this benefit. In accordance
with this Government's policy statement, however, all health benefits have been
kept under review and I should comment that the immunisation, maternity,
specialist, and laboratory services benefits have all been increased, as has the general
medical services benefit for children. The radiological benefit is also to be increased
from 1 October 1978. I should remark also that, as with most other health benefits,
the physiotherapy benefit is only part of the physiotherapists' remuneration. They
are also entitled to charge patient fees in addition to the benefit.

Arapawa Island Goats Shot-Hydatids Risk
87. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) to the Minister of Forests: Is it correct that
carcasses of goats shot by cullers on Arapawa Island are simply being left to rot,
and, if so, does this contravene the Hydatids Act, and can he give an assurance
that this does not constitute a risk of hydatids to other domestic animals on the
island?
Answer
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: In the initial few days of
the feral goat reduction campaign on Arapawa Island the carcasses of goats shot
on farm land were not disposed of. The carcasses of goats shot on farm land and
on the margin of the forest reserve are now being disposed of in accordance with
the arrangement the Forest Service has with the National Hydatids Council.
Disposal of carcasses previously shot is also being undertaken. The arrangement
the Forest Service has with the National Hydatids Council is that when goats
are destroyed in forested or mountainous country where there is no contact with
domestic stock or dogs the disposal of carcasses is both impracticable and unneces-
sary. In the reverse situation, and on farm lands in particular, goat carcasses are
disposed of as a matter of course. The omission to do so during the initial work
on Arapawa Island was an oversight that has since been rectified.

Aviation Agreement-New Zealand-Fiji
93. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) to the Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteoro-
logical Services: What are the terms of the aviation agreement between Fiji
and New Zealand regarding points of departure for Air Pacific from Fiji, and what
is the demand for intermediate stops to or from New Zealand?
Answer
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological
Services) replied: The air transport agreement signed by the Governments of Fiji
and New Zealand is a public document. It grants Air Pacific the right to operate
between Fiji and Auckland via the following intermediate points: Tonga, New
Hebrides, New Caledonia, and Norfolk Island, and provides that one intermediate
point must be used on all services. Rights are also granted for services via various
intermediate points to Niue, Rarotonga to Tahiti, and beyond to Chile. The
demand or otherwise for intermediate stops to or from New Zealand depends very
much upon the marketing efforts of the carrier operating the route. Renegotiation
of the agreement is expected to get under way later this year.

respectively are at present irrigated?
Answer

The implementation of irrigation proposals is dependent on landowner support and

Fish Farming Failures
98. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Fisheries: Has he seen the
article in the Nelson Evening Mail of 10 June 1978, in which the dangers of trout
farming are outlined; and, with reference to the fact that eel-farming attempts are
failing, could he confirm that disease and economic factors were responsible, and
outline the nature of the diseases?
Answer
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: I have seen the article
referred to by the honourable member. Disease and economic factors did contribute
to the failure of the first eel-farming attempts but these were not the only ones that
were responsible. Biologically the diseases are of two groups, bacterial and protozoan,
but fungal diseases, which are secondary diseases, also occurred. The most persistent
disease of the lot is one called "white spot", a protozoan disease. It is mainly a
problem with small eels and it can be difficult to control unless diagnosed early.
However, this disease is found frequently in aquarium fish and fish in the wild
throughout the world. Currently research work on eel farming is being carried out at
the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries research farm at Te Kaha.
(30/6/78)
Housing Corporation Mortgage Repayments
99. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Housing: Has he read
the section on repayment conditions in the 1976 Housing Corporation's loan survey,
which indicates that more than one-third of Housing Corporation clients were
committing 30 percent or more of the head of household's gross income to mortgage
repayments, and can he (i) confirm that no increase was made in the basic Housing
Corporation loan until February 1978, despite the high repayments many corporation
clients were being forced to make, and (ii) can he give more recent figures to indicate
what proportion of Housing Corporation clients are committing more than 30 percent
of their gross income in mortgage repayments?
Answer
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: Yes, I have read the
statement referred to. The honourable member is now aware that almost 60 percent
of borrowers paying more than 30 percent were two-income families. Consequently,
repayments as a proportion of family income were considerably less. In reply to (i) I
confirm that no alteration was made in the basic loan by the Labour Government
between July 1974 and November 1975 and the National Government until February
1978. The National Government did, however, introduce last year a single-income
family supplement. (ii) The proportion of Housing Corporation mortgages
committed to mortgage payments exceeding 30 percent of head of household's gross
income in 1977 was 31.5 percent. Details are not yet available for the 1978 year.

Plastic Road-Marking Paint
114. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga), on behalf of Mr PREBBLE (Auckland
Central), to the Minister of Works and Development: In view of the criticism of
plastic paint and the danger of that to motor cyclists, what action is his department
taking to find an alternative form of road marking?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The paint used for
pavement marking is either chlorinated rubber, or alkoid based. Plastic paints are not
used for road marking, because they wear rapidly. The slippery nature of road-
marking paint when placed on smooth surfaces is recognised, and for this reason the
area of paint applied is kept to the minimum necessary for traffic guidance. In urban
areas where the risk of manoeuvring or braking on pavement marking is greatest
alternative materials such as pre-cut sheeting with higher skid resistance, and
thermoplastic materials, are being increasingly used. Because of the high cost of these
materials their use is limited to higher risk areas such as pedestrian crossings, limit
lines, and lane arrows. Pavement-marking materials used in New Zealand are similar
to those used in other countries. Overseas developments are continually monitored
and adapted in this country after evaluation, and if appropriate.

IMF Restrictions-Foreign Exchange
117. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Finance: Is the undertaking
regarding "restrictions on current international payments" given to the International
Monetary Fund by the Minister of Finance on 16 October 1974, and reaffirmed on
three subsequent occasions, still in full force and effect; and does that undertaking
relate to impediments to the purchase by New Zealanders of foreign exchange?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The undertakings given by
the previous Minister of Finance were made during a series of purchases of foreign
exchange under the International Monetary Fund's oil facility. I released the texts of
those undertakings in February 1976, and reaffirmed them the following month, when
we made a fifth and final purchase. They are still in effect and will remain so for as
long as these purchases, which amount to NZ$288 million, are outstanding. The
undertaking is to refrain from imposing restrictions on our current international
payments that are inconsistent with our obligations under the fund's articles of
agreement, without prior consultation with the fund. Article VIII prohibits the
introduction of discriminatory currency arrangements or multiple currency practices
without the approval of the fund. The imposition of a tax on foreign exchange clearly
falls within the scope of this article. I cannot predict what attitude the fund would
take to such a tax, but an adverse judgment could lead to a request to repay our oil
facility drawings.

Union Ballots
121. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) to
the Minister of Labour: Can he justify the legality of the ballot of the New Zealand
Freezing and Related Industries Clerical Officers Industrial Union of Workers on
compulsory unionism, for which some non-members received voting papers, some
members did not receive a voting paper, and others received two?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): After issuing a notice to the
Registrar of Industrial Unions requiring a ballot, my direct involvement in the
exercise ceases and the legality of the manner in which the ballot is conducted rests
entirely with the registrar, who has answered the criticism. In compiling the roll of
persons eligible to vote he adopted the list of names of persons supplied to him and
certified as correct by the secretary of the union. Union membership is not a pre-
requisite in deciding whether a person is eligible to vote, and it is simply a question of
whether the person is bound by the unqualified preference clause in the award. This
could explain why some non-members received voting papers and some members did
not. I understand that a small number of persons received more than one ballot paper
because their names were duplicated in the list of persons supplied by the union.
Because of the check system employed by the registrar when the ballot has closed, the
returning officer will ensure that only one vote per person is counted.

Foreign Exchange Remittances, Pacific Islands

and what proportion of this figure is estimated to arise from personal, as opposed to
business, payments?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): Total foreign exchange
remittances through the banking system to the Pacific Islands in the year ended
March 1978 amounted to $90 million. Of this total, remittances for imports were
$28.7 million, and capital remittances were $4 million. Total payments in the
invisibles category amounted to $57.5 million, of which travel remittances accounted
for $28.7 million- largely the expenses of New Zealand tourists visiting the Islands.

temporary residents leaving New Zealand, and legacies-amounted to $7.3 million.
These remittances are for the following countries: Fiji, Tonga, Western Samoa, Niue,
Nauru, Tahiti and other French Pacific Islands, New Hebrides, and other smaller
islands in the general area of the South Pacific.

provide out-of-season employment for workers under the temporary employment
scheme. During 1977, in anticipation of higher levels of unemployment in 1978,
approval was given for the Forest Service to overexpend its vote. The total approval

Foreign Exchange Charges and GATT
150. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Customs: Does the General
Agreement on Tariffs and Trade contain any provision for retaliation by other
contracting parties in the event of the New Zealand Government adopting fees or
charges on foreign exchange?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): Article XXIII of the General
Agreement on Tariffs and Trade specifically provides for retaliatory action if a
contracting party should consider that any benefit accruing to it directly or indirectly
under the agreement is being nullified or impaired, either as the result of the failure of
another contracting party to carry out its obligations under the agreement, or by the
application by another contracting party of any measure, whether or not it conflicts
with the provisions of the agreement. In the event of the New Zealand Government
imposing fees or charges on foreign exchange it would be open to any other
contracting party to base its justification for taking retaliatory action on this
provision.

Freezing Works Strikes, Southland
160. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) to the Minister of Agriculture: What was the
estimated loss in terms of overseas earnings caused by the Southland Freezing Works
strikes during 1975, 1976, and 1977?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The Minister of Agriculture replies:
"It is not possible to provide the sort of estimate that the honourable member seeks.
This is because regionally-based industrial action in the meat industry does not
simply translate into lost overseas earnings. It may be possible for buyers to arrange
for stock to be slaughtered at other works, or the effect may simply be to delay the kill.
Losses can, however, occur when shipping programmes are disrupted or when the
effect is to bunch shipments at ports of destination, leading to an oversupply situation
and lower prices. Furthermore, if stock has to be removed from the works or held in a
situation where the animals lose condition, or if farmers avoid stocking their
properties to an optimum level solely to provide additional feed for stock for slaughter
through strike periods, then the loss is obviously significant."

Income Tax-Opposition Proposals
162. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Finance: Has he seen the report in
the Dominion of 7 June 1978 in which the Deputy Leader of the Opposition describes
the proposed income tax steps espoused by the Opposition, and, if so, can he state
whether his department has calculated the revenue cost of those proposals as against
(a) the tax tables adopted by the last Labour Government in 1975, and (b) the tax
tables described in the 1978 Budget?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): No, I have not seen the
Dominion report; I got someone to look it up for me. The income tax steps outlined by
the Deputy Leader of the Opposition were somewhat imprecise, but he indicated that
they would cost about $600 million a year comparied with the existing rate structure.
It is not possible to calculate the revenue effects without fuller details, but as far as is
possible to gauge from the information given in the article it appears that $600 million
would be an underestimate. Using the same assumptions underlying the
Government's Budget forecast, Labour's alternative rate structure would cost about
$700 million. However, a $100 million error is not unusual for the people on the other
side of the House. The present rate structure is based on the tax rates introduced by
the Labour Government in 1975, and incorporates a 5 percent reduction from
February 1978 costing $200 million a year. Therefore, Labour's alternative system
would currently yield about $900 million a year less than the tax rates introduced in
1975. By comparison, the Government's new rate structure, which will take effect in
October, will yield about $500 million a year less than the Labour Government's 1975
rates. It appears, therefore, that in current annual terms Labour's tax rates could
reduce income tax by $400 million more than the Government's new rate structure.
Of course, this would not represent an overall tax cut, as the Opposition proposes to

of the family tax rebates introduced by the present Government, which reduce annual.

Accident Compensation Act
163. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: Has he read the article
in the Evening Post of 29 June 1978, which states: "An anomaly in the Accident
Compensation Act is highlighted in a Supreme Court judgment released today"-
dealing with the fact that a self-employed person who suffered a heart attack during
his work was not covered, but an employee in the same position was-and, if so, will
he take the recommendation of the judge that it "is a matter for the Legislature"?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Labour): The provision in the
Accident Compensation Act giving cover in respect of heart attacks applies only to
employees, and even that is subject to certain qualifications. The self-employed are
not covered for heart attacks unless the attack is a consequence of an injury or
accident. This is not considered to be an anomaly. The distinction was deliberately
made when a partial definition of the phrase "personal injury by accident" was
introduced by the amending Act of 1974. There is a variety of reasons for this
distinction, which would take too long to give at this time. The Accident
Compensation Commission would, on request, gladly give a statement on those
reasons. In the Supreme Court judgment referred to, the judge made no
recommendation for change, nor did his judgment use the word "anomaly". As a
matter of interest, I have asked the commission for a report on the case, but am
advised in the meantime that the commission sees no reason for recommending any
change in the Act.

Nuclear Testing Ban
169. Mr HUNT (New Lynn), on behalf of Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central)
to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What steps have been taken to implement the
blue manifesto promise to "campaign against all nuclear testing and the proliferation
of nuclear weapons"?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The Acting Minister of Foreign
Affairs replies: "New Zealand has been in the forefront of efforts at the United
Nations calling for a comprehensive test ban treaty that would put an end to all
nuclear weapons testing. In July 1977, New Zealand submitted written comments to
the Disarmament Committee in Geneva (known as the CCD) on the various
problems associated with the conclusion of a comprehensive test ban. At the last two
sessions of the United Nations General Assembly we negotiated and introduced the
resolution on the subject. New Zealand was also active at the special session on
disarmament, once again stressing the need for urgency and the obligation of the
negotiating nuclear weapon States to achieve a treaty that will command the widest
possible adherence. We have also called for universal adherence to the non-
proliferation treaty in order to halt the spread of nuclear weapons. In his statement to
the special sesson, the Minister of Foreign Affairs suggested that consultative
machinery dealing with proliferation issues should be established along the lines of
the nuclear suppliers group, but including both exporters and importers of nuclear
materials."

encourage joint problem-solving by the parties themselves. Disputes are better solved

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Labour): It is debatable how far

this. I agree with the general principle that disputes should be resolved as close to
their point of origin as possible. Many are, but the member well knows that it is not
always possible to effect a reconciliation at that level.

overdraft or a loan from a lending institution, when in fact within the terms of the
offer the true interest rate charged on credit advanced is of the order of 45 percent?
Mr ALLEN (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and
Industry: The Minister of Trade and Industry replies: "A bank loan or a loan from a
lending institution would need to be at interest rates of less than 10 percent per
annum calculated on monthly rests to be cheaper, over a 2-year period, than the
Farmers Trading Company's offer. As money is not generally available at 10 percent
interest, I see nothing offensive in the company's offer. Consequently, no action is
necessary".

Minister would take steps to inform clubs immediately of what he sees as the legal
position?
Hon. ALLAN McCREADY (Minister of Police): No prosecutions have been
brought against any club under the new Act relating to the selling of quick-fire raffles.

brought without prior referral to the legal section at Police headquarters. I should
emphasise that in no way have the police been searching for any such case on which
to prosecute, but have simply given advice in response to queries from sports clubs
and hotels. The member will be well aware that it is for the police to decide whether
or not a particular prosecution would be brought. However, the police have a
discretion in these matters, and I have been advised by the commissioner that, in any
decisions made, considerable weight will be given to the fact that differing
interpretations exist, and, in particular, the fact that the law will shortly be clarified
in favour of such raffles.

Environmental Impact Reporting Procedures

What changes have been made in the environmental impact reporting procedures
over the past 2 years?
own
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment): The changes that I
announced on 16 June last are, first, that the departments will now carry out their
environmental evaluations, and public input will be required. The
Commissioner for the Environment has the responsibility to examine and to report on

licensing authorities, and tribunals within the procedures for the submission of a
Crown case.

at the Huntly Power Station. There is no one particular reason for this delay. It is the
result of an accumulation of many minor delays that have occurred during the 4

delay to the first unit to a minimum.

Venison and 1080 Poison
191. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen the
article in the Marlborough Express of 24 June 1978 in which it is reported that a
helicopter has been seen lifting game from an area where 1080 had been laid; can he
advise whether deer carcasses from 1080-poisoned areas are identifiable; and, further,
what guarantee can be given that venison exported to Europe has not come from a
1080-poisoned area?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The Minister of Health
replies: "I have seen the report referred to. The Minister of Health has no
responsibility as to the quality of venison exported to Europe, but the following
comments may be of interest to the honourable member. It is not usually possible to
identify the carcasses of deer that have eaten 1080 baits, but sometimes the contents
of their stomachs might be dyed green from the dye added to the 1080-treated carrots.
No guarantee can be given that exported vanison will not contain 1080, but the law
requires all persons who lay 1080 baits to advertise in the local press well in advance
of the time that poison will be laid specifying the areas in which they propose to lay
poison. As far as the Department of Health is aware, no work has been done with deer
in particular, but other animals, including sheep, have been fed 1080 and their meat
fed to dogs, which are particularly sensitive to 1080. The results have shown that
there is unlikely to be any hazard from eating meat from animals poisoned with 1080.
No one is known ever to have been poisoned by eating venison taken from an area
treated with 1080."

Home Insulation-Inflammable Paper
194. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Energy: Can he confirm that a
Pakuranga factory manufacturing macerated paper insulation that has been installed
in the ceilings of thousands of homes throughout New Zealand with the
encouragement of the Government was recently gutted by a fire in which the
insulation material burned quite readily; and, if so, can he justify the continued
Government support for the use of chopped-up paper as an insulant since its claims of
being fire retardant are clearly suspect?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): There was a fire on 16 June 1978 at a
Pakuranga factory that manufactured macerated paper insulation. To produce this
material, waste paper is given a fire-retardant treatment. While the untreated paper
at the factory burned quite readily, the treated material did not burn even though the
jute sacks in which it was stored caught fire. The insulation material produced by the
factory is regularly checked by inspectors of the Standards Association of New
Zealand. Prior to the fire, it was last checked on 22 May and found to be completely
satisfactory. I am satisfied that there is no basis for the member's conclusion that the
fire-retardant properties of this material are suspect, and that there is no cause for
alarm amongst the many thousands who have installed it.

private agencies is due for completion this month. The Government will be using this
report to help advance and co-ordinate matters relating to noise pollution.

Venison and 1080 Poison
197. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Agriculture: Has he seen
the article in the Marlborough Express of 24 June 1978-and I now find the Minister
has read it-in which it is reported that a helicopter has been seen lifting game from
an area where 1080 poison had been laid; can he indicate how this practice might
affect export of venison if European countries were aware of it; and how does the
Government propose to control indiscriminate shooting by commercial operators?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I am aware of the article in
the Marlborough Express of 24 June 1978 reporting the lifting of game from an area
where 1080 poison had been laid. The New Zealand Forest Service investigated the
matter and established that, while it appeared that the helicopter concerned had
flown out of the Black Birch catchment where 1080 poison had been laid, it was
actually on its way from the Jordan Station in Awatere Valley delivering chamois
carcasses to a truck in Taylor Pass Road. This information was subsequently
published in the Marlborough Express of 27 June 1978-and I hope the questioner has
read that newspaper also. Regarding the possibility of deer carcasses being exported
to European markets, stringent requirements related to controls of poisoning
operations and procurement of game are strictly enforced by the New Zealand Forest
Service and by my ministry to prevent the possibility of such occurrences.

France, Germany, and the EEC commission, in addition to talks with similar visitors
from Japan, the United States, Canada, and Australia. We have found such
exchanges of considerable value, because they give us a clearer idea of other donor
countries' aid policies and aid administrative procedures. We have found that these
European and other administrators wanted to draw on New Zealand's substantial
and detailed experience of the Pacific countries' needs. In a number of cases we have
arranged for the visitors to meet also representatives of Pacific countries in
Wellington to talk about their countries' specific needs.

Economy-Fall in Production
222. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Finance: Has he read the
article in the Evening Post of 29 June quoting the New Zealand Institute of Economic
Research comment on the economy: "The most obvious effects are reduced
production, a high rate of unemployment, and surplus capacity in industry.
Production is estimated to have fallen by 1 percent during the year to March 1978
and it is still falling", and, if so, what urgent action is he taking to reverse the trend?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): Yes, I have read the article.
Government economic policy since October 1977 has been directed towards
stimulating domestic activity and reducing the rate of unemployment, while
continuing to limit inflation. The measures recently announced in this year's Budget
give considerable impetus to this policy. In this regard I would refer the member to
pages 5 to 12 of the Financial Statement, which was read in the House on 1 June 1978.
There is already evidence of an upturn in expenditure and production, and, indeed, of
productivity. The volume of retail trade increased by about 2 percent in the March
quarter of this year after taking account of seasonal factors. The measures introduced
over the last 12 months will lead to a sustained improvement in production, and
eventually in employment.
