West Taupo Wildlife Reserve
234. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Forests: Is it correct
that the proposed wildlife reserve in the west Taupo area is 3 300 ha, and is it the only
totally unlogged virgin native forest left in the North Island?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): It is assumed that this question
relates to the wildlife sanctuary proposed for the north Pureora State Forest by the
Native Forests Action Council, which incorporates approximately 3 400 ha of virgin
native forest. In fact, the Forest Service proposals for reserves in the west Taupo State
Forests, largely confirming the scientific co-ordinating committee's own proposals,
cover some 25 600 ha of mostly virgin native forest. However, these areas are far from
being the only totally unlogged virgin forest left in the North Island. On all land
tenures there are about 2 000 000 ha of unlogged forest, comprising both protection
forest and other categories, including that contained in national parks and reserves.
In State forests, unlogged forest extends over about 840 000 ha, including at least
200 000 ha of lowland forest that may be zoned and managed for purposes other than
soil and water conservation.
(11/7/78)
Honey Marketing Authority-Interest Rates
235. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of
Finance: Why is it proposed that the Government should charge up to 9 percent
interest on advances to the Honey Marketing Authority when 1 percent is charged on
advances to the New Zealand Dairy Board?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): By a long-standing
arrangement, interest has been charged on advances to the Honey Marketing
Authority as follows: 1 percent on advances up to $180,000, and 5.5 percent on
advances in excess of that. The upper limit on the overdraft was increased from
$380,000 to $700,000 in 1977. Because stocks of honey on hand are larger than usual,
the level of overdraft accommodation has had to be temporarily raised above the limit
of $700,000. Interest at 9 percent is being charged only on advances to the authority
in excess of $700,000. It would therefore be inappropriate to compare this rate with
the rates charged to the Dairy Board.
Police Resignations
236. Mr. SCHULTZ (Coromandel), on behalf of Miss DEWE (Lyttelton), to
the Minister of Police: In view of the comments in the report of the New Zealand
Police for the year ended 31 March 1978 about the decrease in the number of
resignations, which are now at their lowest level since 1974, can he give reasons for
the substantial decline?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): There are several reasons why
the number of resignations has gone down. One is that morale in the Police is at a
very high level, and that has been brought about by a considerably improved salary
scale dating from October 1976 and improvements generally in working conditions.
Aside from salary increases, two innovations that have been particularly beneficial
are the introduction of a special allowance payable to policemen in sole-charge
positions as recompense for the extensive intrusion into the lives of their families, and
a vehicle programme approved by the Government, which will provide a police car at
rural police stations, thus enabling the family car to be used for normal family
purposes.

Housing Corporation Standards-House Foundations
243. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Housing: Can he confirm as
correct that the Housing Corporation requires older homes to have continuing
concrete foundations or concrete piles to qualify for loans, while Housing Corporation
homes on new subdivisions are allowed wooden piles, and how long is this double
standard to apply, thereby adding a financial burden to home seekers seeking to buy
older homes?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: It is not now correct that the Housing Corporation
requires older homes to have continuous concrete foundations or concrete piles to
qualify for loans, and I deny the suggestion that the corporation is operating a double
standard. In some cases the corporation may require renewal of wooden piles where
decay has occurred. Because of the difficulty of replacement under an existing house,
repiling is often easier by using concrete piles. There is no technical reason, however,
why wooden piles treated to commodity specification C2B as defined by the Timber
Preservation Authority cannot be used where this is practicable. In some areas,
continuous concrete foundations for new houses are required because the soil is of
inadequate capacity to carry roof loads. However, the corporation would not decline
a loan on an existing house without continuous foundations if the piles had performed
satisfactorily.

will presumably, like any other member, retain any damages he recovers.

dried Pinus radiata replace native timbers in finishing uses?

member is referring to Mr Leay's address, "It's time to think", given to the second
Colenso seminar held in Auckland in November last year. Mr Leay, in the context of
a wide-ranging speech concerned more with the future than the past, was seeking to
stress that, as a community, we tended to squander too large a proportion of our
resources. It was in reference to this point that he felt Governments were usually the
worst offenders. It is not possible, of course, to see "Government" as a single
industry. The activities of central government cover a multitude of areas. If one looks
at Government trading departments it is true that, on average, their profitability is
less than average profitability in the private sector. There are many reasons for this,
not all related to efficiency. The Government is at present looking at the financial
objectives of trading departments with a view to improving efficiency, and, in this
respect much progress has been made by this Government since December 1975.

State House Rentals
254. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) to the Minister of Housing: What is the present
formula used to assess State house rentals?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): The present formula used to
assess State house rentals is one-sixth of family income up to $100 per week; thereafter
it increases to 30c in the dollar for a weekly income between $101 and $140 and it
increases to 40c in the dollar for income exceeding $140 a week. The rent is reviewed
annually and may not be increased by $10 a week in any one year and may not exceed
the fair or market rent for the particular property.

Cyprus-Turkish Occupation
258. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Is the
New Zealand Government continuing to condemn the internationally declared
illegality of the continuing mainland Turkish occupation of nearly half of the territory
of our Commonwealth brother country of Cyprus, and will the Government consider
sanctions against Turkey?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): At the
Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in London in June 1977, and at the
thirty-second session of the United Nations General Assembly last year, the New
Zealand Government supported resolutions calling for the withdrawal of all foreign
troops from Cyprus. The Government deplores the armed division of Cyprus. It
supports the Government of Cyprus under President Kyprianou, but does not
recognise the Turkish Federated State of Cyprus. The possibility of sanctions being
imposed on Turkey by the international community to wrest concessions from Turkey
on Cyprus has not been formally proposed. If and when it is, the Government will
have to consider the matter in the light of the position at the time, and in view of the
likely prospects of any such actions achieving the goals they seek.

Air New Zealand Association of Employees-Ballot
259. Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei) to the Minister of Labour: Will he assist the

since the management of Air New Zealand has instructed the editor of Air New
Zealand Staff News not to publish a paid advertisement regarding a ballot proposal?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): It is not entirely clear what sort of
assistance it is intended I make available to the Air New Zealand Association of
Employees with respect to its intention to conduct a ballot of its Air New Zealand
staff on the question of forming an industry-based union. No ministerial approval is
required for the association to conduct a ballot of this nature. The question here is one
of union coverage. Several unions now have separate coverage for Air New Zealand
staff. In order to form an industry-based. union those unions having coverage at
present would need to be persuaded to forfeit their coverage. This would be a matter
for discussion between the unions concerned and the association. While a favourable
ballot result on the question of the formation of an industry-based union would have
no status under the law, it would certainly add weight to the association's position in
discussions with the unions concerned.

19 July
universities, even when they had the New Zealand School Certificate or University
Entrance qualifications, and were there any discussions with the Fijian education
authorities about this?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): It has been found over the
years that communication skills necessary for success by overseas students in New
Zealand's schools and universities were not really assessed by passing School
Certificate subjects or the University Entrance examination. On the other hand, the
achievement test for overseas students-sometimes called LATOS-was specifically
designed by the New Zealand Council of Educational Research to test the adequacy
of foreign students in the kind of language skills necessary to cope with tuition in this
country. The test was extended to Fijian students last year to bring them into line
with all other overseas students. The Fijian education authorities were aware that
tests were being held, and co-operated in their administration. However, I have been
informed that the matter is at present under review.
(12/7/78)
Whale Catch
261. MARILYN WARING (Raglan), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton
East), to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Could he indicate whether the New
Zealand delegation to the International Whaling Commission conference pressed for
a reduction in the total catch for the coming whaling season?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): The
New Zealand delegation to the thirtieth annual meeting of the International Whaling
Commission was instructed to oppose a return to the indiscriminate hunting of past
years and support moves to allow whale populations that have suffered from
overexploitation to recover. The Government believes that the surest way to
implement both instructions lies in strict adherence to the recommendations of the
scientific committee of the IWC, an impartial group of whale scientists drawn from all
member countries of the commission. With the support of the New Zealand
delegation, the scientific committee's recommendations on quotas for all except the
Northern Hemisphere sperm whales were approved. A special session of the
committee will reconsider quotas for sperm whales in December.

262. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori), on
behalf of Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori), to the Minister of Maori Affairs: Is he
aware of the call by Dr Rangi Walker, President of the Auckland District Maori
Council, to New Zealand employers to provide more young Maori people with better
job and employment opportunities, and, if so, what steps is he proposing or has he
initiated to encourage this?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): I am aware of Dr Walker's
call. Specialist officers have been appointed in my department in Auckland and
Wellington to meet employers, firms, and organisations-including Government
departments and commercial companies-and encourage the employment of young
Maori people. They also try to direct appropriate applicants to such positions and, at
the same time, channel others into increased educational opportunities and
employment where vocational training is available, outside the trade training
schemes run by the department. Other community officers of the department,
although unable to specialise, carry out the same role in co-operation with their other
duties and, in particular, encourage and co-ordinate the efforts of the Maori
communities towards the same end.

to the honourable member to furnish details for further inquiries should he so desire.

Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): For the purpose of discussing Ministers' replies to
questions, I move, That the House do now adjourn. I propose to refer to a number of
questions asked about the railways and specifically to question 208, which stands in my name
and in which I asked the Minister of Railways some questions about the state of the
passenger cars on the surburban railway services around Wellington. I referred in particular
to the unsafe wheel conditions of a number of the wagons used in the Wellington area. In its
manifesto the Government promised to co-ordinate rail and transport services, but in fact it
has had a very sorry record in the past 2 1/2 years. One finds a desperate situation in the
suburban rail services, and particularly in the passenger services that are still called "prestige
services" throughout New Zealand.
I return to the condition of stock wheels. Reference has been made previously to the
backlog of work for the wheel lathe situated at the Wellington branch locomotive depot and
the fact that it would take 6 months, working 7 days a week for 24 hours each day, to catch
up with the work required to be done. I refer again to that fact, and to what I term "the red
light report" that the Minister received through the General Manager of Railways about the
desperate situation facing surburban passenger rail services and national passenger rail
services. Why is that report being kept secret? Why is it not being acted upon?
The Government is failing to meet the needs of rail users. Passenger and goods services
are being allowed to run down very badly. Several newspapers have given prominence to the
problem, and many people are concerned that the Government is taking no action.
Newspaper editors have commented on the seriousness of the situation, but the Minister
cannot bring himself to confess the truth publicly. The Railway Tradesmen's Association
featured an editorial in its July publication headed "Stop Waffling, Minister". The editorial
was given a great deal of prominence, and I repeat its call: not only should the Minister stop
waffling, but so should his colleagues. I cannot emphasise enough that the situation in the
New Zealand railways today is very serious. Indeed, everyone, apart from Government
members, seems to be aware of that. When the Minister does make a statement, it is usually
wrong. He often contradicts himself, and he contradicts his departmental officers. I shall
give one classic example.
In a Christchurch Press article on the run-down condition of stock published on 30 June
the Minister was quoted as saying that the level of maintenance on both long-distance and
suburban trains was lower than he liked, "but this is a long-standing problem arising from a
shortage of skilled men". However, the Addington branch secretary of the National Union
of Railwaymen, Mr Mader, writing to Mr Goodfellow, General Secretary of the National
Union of Railwaymen, said on 6 July 1978: "The department has a policy of staff ceilings,
and at present tradesmen who retire are not being replaced. Here at Addington we have
tradesmen who have been engaged since Christmas, and are employed on semi-skilled and
labouring work on the understanding that when a tradesman vacancy occurs they will be
transferred." That has not happened, in spite of the fact that tradesmen have retired. How
can the Minister justify his statement about the shortage of skilled tradesmen and the fact
that the level of maintenance work is lower than he would like? The fact remains that he, the
Government, and the department are all victims of the sinking-lid policy, to the extent that
the Railways Department does not now have the tradesmen. The railway tradesmen
themselves verify that fact, and the branch secretary of the National Union of Railwaymen
has told his national secretary that the Minister does not know what he is talking about.
During that time the suburban railways stock has been running down-and it has now
reached the stage where last Friday at Wellington the breakdown of one unit meant that
passengers were taken in the guard's van of a following unit, thanks to the good-heartedness
of a guard who will probably be rapped on the knuckles for disobeying Railways regulations.
The situation is deplorable and cannot be allowed to continue after the Government
promised co-ordination and improvement in transport.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): Never have I heard so much
eyewash and politicking by a member who was the Minister of Transport in a Government

Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori): I want to address
myself to question 47 and to questions 55 to 57. This Government has cut out 477 rail
services, of which 400 were in my electorate. Members opposite cannot blame that on the
Labour Party. Of that number, 221 are in the North Island and 256 are in the South Island.
They include such services as Wellington to New Plymouth, Dunedin to Alexandra,
Dunedin to Palmerston, Wellington to Napier, Wellington to Napier and Gisborne,
Christchurch to Picton, and Wellington to Woodville.
This Government is supervising the decline of the public transport system, and nowhere
is this decline more evident than in the New Zealand railways. If the network of the public
transport system is destroyed, it will simply place increasing pressure on private motor
vehicles. The cost of servicing private motorcars is one of New Zealand's greatest economic
and conservation problems, and it will almost certainly get worse. There is a conflict of
policies that is typical of the counter-productive courses followed by this Government in its
ignorance.
The cry of this Goverment is, "Leave it to the market. Market forces will solve it." By
leaving the determination of New Zealand's future transport system to the mercy of the
market-place this Government has again fallen back on discredited and outdated policies.
Clearly the question should be turned around. A wise Government would ask, how can we
ensure that the public transport system does not disintegrate? It should then address itself to
the solution that guarantees an answer to that question.
Our system of private motor vehicles for transport is little short of ridiculous compared
to what happens in other countries. Let us consider the number of makes of cars that we
have in relation to the population. We have over 150 makes of motorcars. In this remarkable
set of circumstances we have an excellent example of the result of the dominance of market
forces. Because New Zealand's trade was virtually an extension of Britain's, the real
vulnerability to which New Zealand's trade is exposed has never been fully appreciated. It
has been hidden by the relationship with Britain. However, now that this umbilical cord has
been weakened, and must become progressively weaker it is obvious to everyone who
studies the problem that it is a result of the myopic vision of past planners, particularly
because of the dominance of the market place on decisions. Therefore, the real question that
the Government must ask itself is, surely, what can it do about it?
There is absolutely no doubt that the last thing to do should be to preside over the
collapse of the public transport system; yet that is the direction which has been clearly
signposted by this National Government's transport policies. On the one hand we have had a
clear call, that has been evident to some since 1973, for less dependence on petrol because of
its cost in terms of overseas funds. On the other hand, if the public transport system
collapsed then it would force on to private motor vehicles those who can afford them. Those
who cannot afford them would be forced on to rail services, which have, however, been cut.
That is counter-productive, and clearly shows the inconsistency and conflict in the policies
being followed by the Government. For energy conservation there is one policy, and for
public transport there is another.
I repeat that in the North Island 941 services that were operating when this Government
took over have been cut to 720. In the South Island there were 608 railway services when the
Government took over, and that figure has been cut to 352. The Government should serve
the people, and that will require public transport for those who cannot afford private
transport.

can get $20,000 at 8.5 percent, and then they can borrow at 5 percent from the Post Office;
they may be able to afford to capitalise the family benefit and get $3,000 there. But there is
still a gap; they still have to afford that $40 and $50 a week to service their first and second
mortgages, and then they are minus capitalisation. In the meantime they would still have had
to save another $2,000 or $3,000 just to build their house and buy the section. If they can get
that far under this Government, they are expected, I presume, to live on bare boards. It is
not a matter of choice; it is that more people are being driven in that direction.
The Minister of Housing must know that there is ample evidence that many more young
people, and some not so young, would prefer to have a new house. We can justify greater
numbers of new houses than are being built now, and again I refer to the Housing
Commission's report. But the major constraint is that deposit gap and the lack of quality
finance spread over a reasonable period and not at a crippling rate of interest. So here we
find another major difference between the two parties. Yes, the National Government, late
in the piece, may have come to realise at least one of the follies of its ways. Low-start
mortgages may very well help a few people, and I sincerely hope they do. They will not help
many, because of the rate of interest. The Government, through the Housing Corporation,
slapped 3 percent on the rate of interest. That will be rectified under the next Labour
Administration.

The motion completely outlines the success of the Government's policy of giving
exports the priorities they need-the opposite of the Labour Government's policy, which
gave imports that priority, doubled them in the years 1972 to 1975, and nearly bankrupted
New Zealand in the process. Compared to the Labour Government's witless policy of
"spend, borrow, and hope", the Government's export programme is a roaring success, and
the people know it; but, compared to Labour's "go broke" policy, anything would be a
roaring success. Quoting the exact figures, received today in the overseas exchange
transactions issued by the Reserve Bank, the value of exports from New Zealand in the years
since 1975, the years of this National Government, have more than doubled, from $1,633
million to $3,392 million. Agricultural exports have doubled, manufacturing exports have
doubled, forestry exports have doubled, and miscellaneous exports have doubled, which
adds up to give this increase of more than twice in the 2 years that the Government has been
in office.

The agreement with Japan on trade and access to that country for our products is a basic
facet of the economic restructuring being undertaken in New Zealand. Since the formal
trade agreement of 1958 we have been trying to get better access for our products to Japan.
The recent agreement entered into with Japan's Minister of Agriculture, Mr Nakagawa,
marked a significant breakthrough, a high point in terms of an understanding between the
two countries. In the course of that accord, agreement was reached on 12 specific points, but
I shall deal with only the principal point; the very significant and substantial concession by
Japan that trade and fish are inextricably tied together. Previously, Japan had always said,
"We will talk about the two separately; we will not talk about trade at the same time as we
are negotiating on fish". Japan always wanted to negotiate the fish deal first. Now, because
of the agreement entered into in Wellington, the Japanese have agreed that trade access to
Japan for New Zealand will be, and will continuously remain, part of the fishing
negotiations. Every year, when the fishing agreement relating to New Zealand's 200-mile
economic zone comes up for renegotiation, we shall have the opportunity of putting forward
arguments to test the sincerity of Japan's assurances on access for our beef and dairy
products. In my view, that is the most significant part of the breakthrough. It is a complete
reversal of Japan's previous approach. In future, Japan will negotiate trade and fishing rights
concurrently.

Australia and New Zealand on NAFTA was the best ever established. Apparently members
opposite have a short memory-or are they completely out of touch with the Minister of
Trade and Industry and the Deputy Prime Minister?
About mid-April 1978 the annual review of NAFTA was concluded, and the total
improvement in the agreement from New Zealand's point of view was the addition of eight
minor commodities to schedule A. A newspaper report on the free schedule section said,
"There appears to be no prospects of any substantial advance for at least another year". The
eight items added to schedule A were: fire engines, golf bags, floor tiles, cast iron pipe
fittings, travellers' cheques, roof tiles, climber winches, and foam used by florists. What a
magnificent achievement. I was not surprised to find that travellers' cheques had been added
to the list. In view of the travel tax imposed by the Government, New Zealanders would not
be creating much demand for them. They would have more impact in Australia.
Only a few months ago, a review of NAFTA was undertaken by the Deputy Prime
Minister, who is also the Minister of Overseas Trade-the Minister of Trade and Industry,
and the Australian Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Trade and Resources, and Minister
of Commerce. The mountain laboured and brought forth a mouse, the eight minor items I
have mentioned. On the debit side for New Zealand, restrictions on trade with Australia
have been placed on manufacturers and exporters. The decline in the clothing trade with
Australia is a matter of major concern to New Zealand manufacturers. Hardly a town or a
city in New Zealand has not witnessed the closing of a major clothing industry, with the
consequent loss of thousands of job opportunities. The member for Kapiti and his colleagues
are out of touch with what is taking place in relation to NAFTA.

Sitting suspended from 5.30 p.m. to 7.30 р.т.
ELECTORAL AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Second Reading
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. As I explained during the introduction, the purpose of the Bill is to place on the
Government the responsibility of enrolment for parliamentary elections. This is necessary
for three reasons. The first is the need to overcome the present emergency that has arisen
over enrolments for this year's general election. As members know, there is widespread
public concern about the state of the rolls-the irregularities, errors, omissions, and other
mistakes. The second reason is that the present system of enrolment does not secure
maximum enrolment, and the third reason is the need to ensure that what has happened on
this occasion will never again happen in this country.
There can be no real objection to the changes proposed in the Bill, because their
purpose is to strengthen our democratic parliamentary system, and no Government com-
mitted to the concept and ideal of a democratic parliamentary system can logically
oppose them. The way in which democratic parliamentary systems are under attack
throughout the world is another reason why democratic governments everywhere should
take every opportunity to strengthen their electoral laws and ensure that they are effective.
Yet, when the Bill was introduced it was opposed by the National Government, which claims
to support the democratic parliamentary concept.
When opposing the Bill the Minister of Justice, who is in charge of the Electoral Office,
alleged that the irregularities had been caused by the provisions of the Electoral Act passed
by the former Labour Government. However, that claim is nonsense. The confusion is the
result of the maladministration of the Government and the Minister of Justice's
maladministration of the portfolio. After all, the Government has been in office for almost 3


## p. 1954 (#216) ###########################################

1954
19 July
Electoral Amendment Bill (No. 2)
years, and if there is anything wrong with the electoral system it has had all that time to put
the matter right. In 1976 and 1977 the Government passed amendments to the Electoral Act.
If there had been anything wrong with the law as the Government has alleged-why did it
not change the law while making those other amendments? It could have taken the
opportunity to make any changes that were desirable. Everyone knows that the Government
did not make those changes because the problems were due to the Government's
maladministration of the Act, and not to any defects in the law.
For some time the Government has been aware of public concern about irregularities
and mistakes in the rolls, including the omission and duplication of names, and the retention
of names of people who have died. In addition there has been the failure, following the
boundary changes, to transfer persons to their new electoral rolls and the placing of names
on the wrong rolls. Even the Minister of Justice, when replying to a question gave
information that he subsequently had to admit, was wrong. He could not give accurate
information to members of Parliament on a matter concerning the electoral system. The
problem is not a defect in the law, but a defect in the administration, and that is a matter that
comes within the competence of the Government.
The proposal in the Bill does not create a precedent. It merely brings New Zealand law
into line with the law as it exists in Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom. In
Australia, the system is simple enough. It provides for electors to enrol as they do here, but
it also provides for the Electoral Office to employ canvassers to check up on and enrol
residents. Those canvassers go from door to door in much the same way as the census
enumerators do in New Zealand, and they record on a schedule the names and addresses of
residents eligible to enrol. Those schedules are checked by the Electoral Office, and if it is
found that people who are entitled to be on the roll, are not on it, the Electoral Office takes
the initiative and advises those people of the fact and sends them an enrolment card. The
matter is followed up.
Another reason it is essential that our rolls be correct and that there be confidence in
them is a constitutional one. Our electoral system and the enrolment system on which it is
based must be and should be seen to be accurate and above reproach. A prerequisite to the
right to vote on election day is that a person be on the roll. The right to vote every 3 years
and to change the Government if desired is the only real and effective constitutional
safeguard we have in New Zealand. Hence, confidence in our enrolment system is absolutely
vital to parliamentary democracy in this country.
New Zealand lacks adequate formal constitutional safeguards. It is the only country
without an effective written constitution and a second chamber. There is in effect, very little
left of the 1852 Constitution Act, and in the main we rely on the ancient laws, precedents,
and conventions of the United Kingdom. As I have said, there is very little effective modern
legislation that is available to us as a country, and for that reason we rely heavily and
constitutionally on our electoral system. If doubt were ever cast on our electoral system it
would undermine confidence in the fundamental basis of our democratic process. So, for
that reason it is essential that the Government and Parliament take every possible step to
strengthen the system by ensuring that people who are entitled to vote are on the roll.
Why can we not follow the precedents of the Commonwealth countries to which I
alluded? Any Government wanting to ensure the maximum exercise of franchise-which is
what democratic government is all about-should take every step to ensure that that is
possible. We should do so especially after our experience this year with the present
enrolment system. Everybody concerned with the future of our democratic system is
concerned about the state of the rolls. The proposals in the Bill would enable the
Government, even at this late stage, to supplement present procedures to ensure that every
person entitled to vote at this election is enrolled and can exercise that right. I hope the
Government will change its mind and its attitude towards the electoral system.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The only good thing about the second
reading of the Bill is that it will give every member who speaks in the debate the opportunity
to encourage people to play their part, as the law provides, and make sure that they are on
the correct roll. I shall make that point over and over again, because democracy is preserved
by a partnership between the Crown and the people. The Crown provides the machinery for
the production of the rolls that are necessary when we poll our votes on election day, and
people must exercise their duty in response to the right granted by the Crown and enrol
themselves once they are qualified to vote.
The rest of the Bill is not only worthless, but it is dangerous, because, if it were passed,

Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori): The Bill aims to
retrieve democracy before it eludes not all New Zealanders but some New Zealanders.
Unless the present law is amended, the unsophisticated will be denied democracy at the next

present system, including the Government's 1977 legislation, must be changed. I cannot be
more emphatic than that.
The legislation introduced by the Government last year demonstrated electorate elitism
and amounted to a bureaucratic gerrymander. Gerrymandering is, in essence, fiddling with
the electoral system to gain political advantage. In fiddling with the franchise of the total
electorate the Government is trying to gain political advantage. Without the changes
proposed in the Bill this elitist gerrymander will remain, and will effectively disfranchise
more than 75 500 New Zealanders. The Government's attitude to the issue of enrolment and
voting is a procedural gerrymander. National Party strategists obviously believe that the
Government will gain political advantage by disqualifying from voting people who miss out
on enrolling. The strategists believe that the people in this category tend not to be National
Party supporters. At the last election about 75 500 votes were disallowed. About 12 000 of
those were Maori votes, most of which would have supported the Labour Party. Most
observers would agree with the National Party strategists and, therefore, it is transparently
obvious that this is a procedural gerrymander.
Will the National Government deny that that is the real reason for its decision? I want
none of its waffle about responsibility. To put it another way, can the National Government
prove that that is not the real reason for its decision? Government speakers have not
answered the fundamental question: why, if we are a democracy, should a person who casts a
vote on election day, and who is eligible in all other respects, not have that vote counted?
The fact that everybody with the franchise should be encouraged to vote is fundamental to
democracy. This issue, more than any other, shows clearly the difference between National
Party philosophy and Labour Party philosophy. The Labour Party believes that everybody
should be encouraged to vote, and that where procedures are found to be a prohibiting
factor they should be adapted to ensure that the maximum number of people participate in
the vote. Obviously, the National Government believes that in order to have a vote
everybody must go through a procedure which must inevitably eliminate some-as I have
said, 75 500 at the last election. It is another unnecessary obstacle course guaranteed to
eliminate the less sophisticated.
Why should this be? Why should this elitist practice exist in this egalitarian country?
Why should somebody who makes the effort to vote on election day, and who satisfies the
normal qualifications, be denied a vote? Why should such vast numbers of New Zealanders

Mr COOPER (Otago Central): To debate the Bill effectively, one has to understand

It is interesting to note that when the Labour Party was the Government in 1975 it was
pleased with the legislation on the statute book. But the Labour Government was suddenly
annihilated at the 1975 election, and because of that the Electoral Act has turned sour. Now
the member for Wigram, with a dose of pre-election jitters and the heeby-jeebies, has

difficulties, and that it would be hard to put the 92 electorates on to the main rolls and the

that to exercise his or her democratic rights in local government and central government
elections it is sometimes necessary to use a pen, or to walk down to the local post office and
get in touch with the electorate officer to make sure that his name is on the roll.
Fortunately, although the member for Southern Maori denigrated those who work so
hard to prepare the rolls, the main rolls and the supplementary rolls have been properly
managed by people with substantially more logic and common sense than Opposition
members have shown tonight. Labour would expect dozens and possibly hundreds of people

who is not, and then saying, "Don't worry; if you turn up on polling day, they will give you a
vote." Labour members are treating New Zealanders almost with contempt about their
democratic rights.
The great problem, as instanced tonight by the member for Southern Maori, is that
Labour members know quite well that in 1978 intelligent people will make certain they are
on the main roll. If they are not, they will get on the supplementary roll-and they will vote
National. There is no doubt about that at all. Opposition members know they represent
many people who are less intelligent, who will not take much trouble to get on the rolls, and
Labour members are frightened that those people will not be able to vote. I should like to
know whether the Labour Party is contemplating compulsory voting if it becomes the
Government.
As a candidate in one central government election and four local government elections,
I took the trouble to make absolutely certain that every person, regardless of the way they
intended to vote, was on the roll. I have seen many people associated with political parties
and others who believe in democracy going out of their way on every possible occasion to
make certain that their friends, associates, acquaintances, and others who are not on the roll
are told to enrol. There is an extensive advertising campaign on radio and television, and in
the newspapers. The Government is making certain that everybody eligible will vote in the
1978 election; and the Government believes in democratic voting procedures.
The Bill is a farce. It is weak. It shows the shallowness of the Labour Opposition. I
cannot understand why this private member's Bill was not sponsored by the Leader of the
Opposition. It will not resolve anything. I expect it will be heavily defeated, but if the
Labour Government ever contemplated such a Bill, it would turn election into a circus-a
farce. The panic within polling booths would be opposed to normal democratic procedure. I
urge Opposition members to think seriously about the consequences of changing existing
procedures, and I urge them to stop making vicious attacks on those in the bureaucracy who
have served us so well under the Electoral Act.

should not be agreed to, because the police believe the Bill to be effective now. The member

how the Bill should be amended to ensure it would be effective in cutting out vice in massage

of a legitimate business, that is pure socialism, and is another reason for the motion being
negatived.
Our Standing Orders make no provision for four readings of a Bill. If a matter of
substance and of considerable public interest suddenly arises between the Committee stage
and the third reading, it can be appropriate for the House to send a Bill back to a select
committee so that new material can be incorporated into the legislation. I have had
experience of that myself when an obvious need has come up. I think the Judicature Act last
year was one such example. The indication was quite clear that new rules from the Supreme
Court rules committee should be written in, and we took that method of doing so, as
provided for in the Standing Orders.

that he can get a little more speaking time for himself on a matter the Opposition has
unanimously supported, and perhaps get himself another headline. There is no merit in his
proposal, and I intend to vote against it.

have involved the Government in any change in policy, unless its policy is to encourage the
ownership of these institutions by the criminal element; as I do not really believe that that is

the proposals.
I am at a loss to understand why the Minister was not prepared to accept them,

being imposed upon him to draw up regulations. All that we asked was that he amend the

out so that privacy arrangements were not so tight as to allow clandestine prostitution.
There was no compulsion on the Minister to do anything such as ordering the police to
inspect premises for that purpose. There was no compulsion on him to write regulations. All
we proposed was that he should not close the door, so that if it became desirable to provide
for this in a few months' time he would not have to say, "I would like to do this, but
Parliament did not give me the power." Parliament has tried to give him the power. The
Minister cannot say later that his inability to deal with the matter in a simple,
straightforward, practical way can be laid at the door of anyone but himself.
It would have been quite simple. He would merely have had to include the power to
make regulations. If he found, as he claims to find now, that the Bill did provide for proper
control, that it had totally eliminated prostitution and drug trafficking from these
institutions, and that the certificate of approval that they had been given was one that the
Government was proud to give, then my proposal would have been unnecessary. However,
if in a few months' time prostitution is flourishing in institutions that have the stamp of
Government approval, the responsibility for having made the decision will be this Minister's.
If the criminal element is able to control and promote the development of prostitution
and trafficking in drugs, and is able to accumulate wealth from a most undesirable
occupation-the exploitation of young inexperienced girls-people will be able to say that it
is being done in Government-approved institutions. The Minister will not be able to absolve
himself from responsibility, becaue he has refused to take the steps suggested by the
Opposition.
The chairman of the select committee said that Opposition members had not divided the

because of a misunderstanding, reported to the House that the decision on this matter was
unanimous, it does not alter the fact that second and possibly third wiser counsels have
influenced the Opposition's attitude. The point has been discussed further, and the
Opposition believes that the legislation as it now stands is useless, and that the proposals it
put forward should be reconsidered and incorporated in the Bill. If that were done the

It is unfortunate that the Minister has decided not to take advantage of the opportunity
presented to him by the Opposition, and will not accept the assistance offered by the
Opposition to deal with what everyone has agreed is a difficult problem. If he had accepted
the assistance offered, people would be able to say that Parliament was unanimous in what it
wanted to do, and had done its best. The Minister cannot say that now. All he can say is that
the Government, with its majority, has overruled other opinion, and has decided that the
Government-no matter what the future may hold-knows best. I hope it does.

Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill.
Because this is an interrupted speech, I shall recap certain points. I clearly spelt out the
Opposition's major objection to the Bill. The Government should produce evidence that the
takeover-and it is a takeover, not a merger-is desirable for New Zealand aviation, both
domestically and internationally. It is just not good enough to ask for the support of
Parliament without adequate information being given, but that is what is being done. We are
being asked to approve a blank cheque, to approve the Bill, when the relevant information is

19 July
1969
New Zealand National Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill
held by only a few. It is not good enough for the Government to say that it has carried out an

It is not good enough to say that in the longer term there will be a profit of $10 million a
year, when, in fact, in the shorter term of perhaps 3 years the cost will be $1.4 million a
year-the figure mentioned in the report I saw. The longer-term profit estimated in that
report is $7 million, but there is no substantive evidence; yet the Minister, the Prime
Minister, and others, have gone around the country saying that a profit of up to $10 million a
year will result from the merger of the two airlines. As pointed out in the feasibility study,
and as mentioned publicly, every possible advantage from a merger-in the short term,
anyway-could be achieved by accepting the suggestion put forward by NAC to form a New
Zealand Airlines Commission, but keeping the domestic and international services separate.
It is obvious that the committee did not give serious consideration to that positive
constructive suggestion. The decision had been made. The problem of how to pad and
package it for public consumption was left to the committee. In its submissions NAC stated
at some length that it believed the domestic air services would best be served by an
organisation dedicated to that purpose. It also suggested that the airlines commission, if
established, might see an advantage in merging the domestic and international activities if
common aircraft and routes were involved. An airlines commission would have the power to
draw those operating functions together in part or in whole.
I wrote those words down from the report, and have repeated them to indicate that
positive constructive suggestions were put to the committee investigating the possibility of a
merger. If the committee gave serious consideration to those words it did not state so
publicly. That statement, and many others in the report, should be made public. The
Minister and the Government have an obligation to publicise the report before asking
Parliament to support the dissolution of NAC and its merger with Air New Zealand. The
study pointed out all the advantages; there were no disadvantages. The alternative showed
the advantages, if in fact they were such. The public has been told nothing about the report,
but these and other alternatives were put forward to the committee by NAC.
The Opposition demands to know how Parliament can oversee the affairs of a limited
liability company, especially when it refuses to use the office of the Auditor-General. In his
report to the House the Auditor-General pointed out the advantages of his office auditing
the operations of NAC, a public corporation, the records of which came under his scrutiny.
Air New Zealand does not submit its records; that practice will continue. How can a limited
liability company be accountable to Parliament? Will there be any accountability to
Parliament? The Minister and members opposite must answer these questions.
The people are concerned about the internal provincial services and their maintenance
under the merged airlines. When introducing the Bill the Minister made reference to his 13-
page, well-padded, thickly-worded statement. The final paragraph reads: "On the basis of
the evidence put to the Government, no diminution of levels of service to the domestic or the
international traveller or of standards of service to any particular centre within or beyond
New Zealand is foreseen as a result of the merger." Why could the Minister not have
answered the Airline Pilots Association when it asked him for a positive assurance that
Friendship services would not be replaced by third-level airlines? He could not answer the
question, but replied: "I can give no such assurances. You know that these services depend
on traffic, load factor, and the availability of aircraft. If such services were not paying for
themselves the community would have to pay."
The New Zealand National Airways Act and the rules under which NAC operated
ensured the continuation of desirable public services even if they were not paying. The
Opposition wants the Minister or the next Government speaker to give an assurance to the
people in the provincial regions that there will be no danger of their services not being
maintained even though they have been taken over by Air New Zealand. The Minister
knows that some of the services do not pay, and on 24 May the Acting Minister pointed out
that some of them were not economic. The uneconomic services are Auckland-Tauranga-

Wanganui-Wellington, Palmerston North-Wellington, Rotorua-Palmerston North,

Normally, when a takeover takes place, an enterprise that is financially strong gobbles
up a competitor that is not. We have all heard rumours about Air New Zealand's financial
position and NAC's financial buoyancy. In this instance, instead of a powerful financially
buoyant enterprise taking over a smaller competitor, a financially embarrassed airline has

proposal would have been referred to the Commerce Commission for examination, but in
this instance it was not. The Government has condoned the takeover and has told people
nothing about it.

believe in the principle of confidentiality it should be applied to all circumstances. The editor
of the Aviation Digest was not comfortable about the takeover, and criticised it as a most
undemocratic and ruthless action. Those are my words. The Minister of Transport knows
what the report contains, and should have accepted the responsibility of telling the House
and the country.
The Bill, which comes to the House months after the takeover, does nothing but legalise
an illegality, and, to remove the slur of legalising an illegality, the Minister should make the
report public. If this were done, we, as representatives of the people and protectors of public
enterprise, would know that the action taken could be justified. If we do not know what it
means and are being asked to accept mythical figures, we have nothing to back up the

Hive Levy Bill
THURSDAY, 20 JULY 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
HIVE LEVY BILL
Introduction
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Hive Levy
Bill be introduced. Let me make it quite clear at the start that the Bill is supported by the
industry. The only change made to the existing situation is that the collecting agency for the
levy will be the National Beekeepers Association rather than the Honey Marketing
Authority. The Bill provides for a compulsory levy on all beekeepers with 50 or more hives
at a rate per hive fixed by the Minister of Agriculture following joint recommendations from
the New Zealand Beekeepers Association and the Honey Marketing Authority. The levy is
to be collected by the National Beekeepers Association and used to help fund the
association's operations and the non-trading functions of the New Zealand Honey Marketing
Authority.
The present compulsory levy of 15c a hive on all beekeepers with 50 or more hives is
collected by the Honey Marketing Authority pursuant to the Honey Marketing Authority
Regulations 1975. Approximately three-quarters of the levy is paid to the association to fund
its operations, and one-quarter is retained by the authority to fund its general industry and
promotional functions as distinct from its trading operations. The reason for the change is
that the association is the main recipient of the funds collected and the industry considers it
should collect the levy.
Doubts were expressed by the parliamentary counsel in 1975 when the hive levy was
first introduced into the Honey Marketing Authority regulations. It was considered that the
regulations under the Primary Products Marketing Act 1953 relating to the marketing of
honey were not the most suitable means of imposing a levy for funding the association. As I
intimated earlier, there has been full consultation with the National Beekeepers Association
and the Honey Marketing Authority, both of which are happy with the present Bill. The
industry conference held in July 1977 also expressed its full support for the Bill.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): Does the shifting of this levy to
the National Beekeepers Association have anything to do with the Government's hope to
run the Beehive after the election? Is the fixing of the levy on all those who keep more than
50 hives an indication of the maximum size of the majority the Government can hope for this
year? It looks as if giving the levy to the National Beekeepers Association is a little like 10
bob each way; cut your liability if you do not have the membership, and pay it to yourself if
you have.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): Can the Minister explain the meaning of clause 15, and why it is
in the Bill? Why are we legislating for an event that has not happened-apparently in the
pious hope that it will and then, in clause 15, seemingly destroying the whole impact of the
legislation?
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central): Although the Minister said the Bill had
nothing to do with the marketing transactions of the Honey Marketing Authority, in answer
to a question I asked the other day the Government admitted that the interest rate to be
charged to the Honey Marketing Authority was to be increased from the present 1 percent
and 5 percent to 9 or 9.5 percent on more than $1 million. I pointed out at the time that this
was unusual for producer boards. Can the Minister give me an unequivocal assurance that
none of the levy will be used to help pay the high interest rate being charged by the National
Government for the Honey Marketing Authority overdraft? The increased interest rate has
been troubling many beekeepers. I should be very concerned if the money derived from
provisions in the Bill went towards that.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): I did not hear the Minister say whether the Bill would
be referred to a select committee. As the Bill is important, can the Minister indicate whether
he intends to refer it to a committee?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): As the Bill has the full
support of the industry I do not think it is necessary to refer it to a select committee.


## p. 1978 (#240) ###########################################

1978

Hive Levy Bill
Members on this side of the House are not worried about getting into the Beehive after
November, because they are confident that the public will not elect the drones on the other
side. If the member for Christchurch Central had read the Bill even briefly he would have
seen that no mention is made of interest rates.
The member for Mangere spoke about clause 15, which is headed "Transitional
provisions". I am at a loss to understand what information the honourable member was
seeking. The clause simply states that if the Minister has not received recommendations from
the two bodies concerned by 16 November this year, the levy payable will be the same as at
present, namely, 15c for each hive. The clause provides for the authority and the association
to recommend jointly before 16 November a different levy rate for the coming year.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I want to take up the matter of clause 15, because I,
too, have read clause 3, which states that, subject to the Act, every beekeeper shall pay an
annual levy to the association. The clause also provides for the fixing of the levy. Up to that
point the Bill appears to be quite clear.
The Minister has assured the House that the Bill has the full support of the two
organisations involved. However, clause 15 appears to contain a threat to them, in that if
they do not play ball with the Government a 15c levy on each hive will be imposed. Have the
organisations indicated what they consider the return will be? Will it be about 15c a hive, or
is the Government levying 15c, sure in the knowledge that it will not get agreement from the
organisations? Was the figure of 15c proposed by the two bodies? If so, what is the reason for
the clause? If the organisations fail to make a recommendation this year, they might not be
able to agree next year. What will happen then? Will there be another amendment to the
Bill? Before we agree to the Bill, which is not to be referred to a committee, we should have
a further explanation from the Minister.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): The Government does not
operate with threats. That might be the Labour Party's approach, but it is not ours. The
present hive levy is 15c a hive, and, to cover the possibility that the association and the
Honey Marketing Authority do not make a further recommendation before 16 November,
clause 15 makes provision for that levy of 15c a hive to continue. That is fairly simple and
straightforward, and the clause makes it clear.
Clause 3(2) relates to the continuing situation and states: "On or before the 30th day of
November in each year the Minister shall, after receiving the joint recommendations of the
Association and the Authority, fix by notice in the Gazette the rate at which the levy is to be
paid in the next succeeding year." There is nothing very complex about that.
Clause 3(3) states: "If, in any year, a joint recommendation under subsection (2) of this
section is not made to the Minister by the 16th day of November, the rate for the next
succeeding year shall be the same as that last fixed under this section." That is also very
simple. If they want to vary the rate, the two bodies have to make an application to the
Minister. If they do not make such an application, the rate remains the same. I can assure
you there is no threat. The 15c is the amount of the levy that is now levied under the Honey
Marketing Regulations.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I asked the Minister what he expected the rate to be
after the Bill comes into force. Perhaps I should have asked that question of the Minister
whose name appears on the Bill-the Minister of Agriculture.
Mr Lange: One's the worker, and one's the drone.
Mr PREBBLE: One is a worker, and one is a drone-ha, ha. If the Minister who is
purporting to introduce the Bill does not know the answer to the question, perhaps the
Minister of Agriculture, who is in the Chamber and whose name appears on the Bill, can tell
me what the levy is expected to be. Perhaps he can also explain to the House the unusual
situation whereby a Bill is being introduced in his name while he sits there and lets someone
else do the talking. Who is the queen bee in agriculture?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): If the member for Auckland
Central knew anything about the organisation and the administration of the Agriculture
portfolio, he would know that it is my responsibility, as the Associate Minister of
Agriculture, to look after that aspect of agriculture. The question the honourable member
asked again anticipates what the two organisations might recommend to the Minister. It is
not my responsibility, when introducing legislation, to anticipate what two bodies might
recommend to the Minister by the thirtieth day of November. If they do not make a
recommendation, the current levy of 15c a hive will be paid. If the industry agrees to an
alternative recommendation and makes that known to the Minister in due time, that will be

Ferguson Road Intermediate School
1. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Education: Is he aware of the

Hubodometers
5. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Transport: Why are traffic
officers issuing offence notices to transport operators for failure to have hubodometers
fitted, when in some cases they have been ordered for over 3 months and are not yet
available?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): When a traffic offence notice is
issued, the operator is invited to make an explanation on the reason why a hubodometer is
not fitted. The explanation is then referred to an investigating officer of the Ministry of
Works and Development, who advises the chief traffic officer of the validity of the claim. If it
is found that the hubodometer is on order but has not been received by the operator, no
further action is taken on the matter.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Would it not be satisfactory for the operator of a vehicle to carry
a certificate in his truck to the effect that the hubodometer has been ordered? Would that
not satisfy a traffic officer?

scrapped. The components are sorted into ferrous and non-ferrous material, with the ferrous
material being used in the department's foundries, and the non-ferrous being sold to best

Department of Labour increased by 6.6 percent. In 1975 the Labour Government saw fit to
pay beneficiaries 53 percent of the average wage. As from 31 August next, the National
Government will be paying 80 percent of the average wage. Beneficiaries will always be well
looked after under a National Government.

Beef Quotas-Japan
20. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: Can he confirm that the

percentage of these quotas has decreased?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade): Allocations for Japan's beef
imports are made every 6 months. Although the total current allocation, for April to
September 1978, shows an increase over the allocation for the corresponding period in
1977-48 000 tonnes, in comparison with 40 000 tonnes-it is less than the total allocation
for October 1977 to March 1978 of 52 500 tonnes. New Zealand's exports of beef to Japan
for these 6-monthly periods have been as follows: 794 tonnes for April to September 1977, or
1.98 percent of total imports, and 3278 tonnes for October 1977 to March 1978, or 6.24
percent of total imports. For the current 6-monthly period, New Zealand's share in the two
tenders called so far has been 6.03 percent and 5.36 percent.
Mr Isbey: Will the percentage of New Zealand's beef exports to Japan improve as a
result of the recent trade agreement with Japan?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Obviously that will depend on the process of tendering. As I
have already indicated to the honourable member, New Zealand's proportion of beef
exports has gone up, but this depends on tenders being called. The first tender for the
present period called for 6627 tonnes, and New Zealand is supplying 399.5 tonnes, or 6.03
percent. The second tender called was for 5500 tonnes, of which New Zealand will supply
295 tonnes, or 5.54 pereent. Some tenders call for corn-fed beef and others for grass-fed
beef.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Is it correct that Australian percentages have increased at a higher
rate than New Zealand's?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: I do not have those figures with me, but I am sure I can get
them for the honourable member.
Mr Isbey: Will the tendering position for New Zealand beef exports to Japan improve as
a result of the recent trade agreement?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The obvious reply to the honourable member is that tenders
will be called, and New Zealand exporters will submit tenders. On the price offered the
tenders will either be confirmed or not. New Zealand is not, and never has been, in the
position of giving beef away. Exporters supply the best market they can find.
Mr Isbey: Is the Minister now stating that, because of the tendering position, no trade

Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Perhaps I should put my answer in words of one syllable for

Land Purchase Bill
committee in that behalf. The honourable member for Hobson has assured us that he has

member for Hobson is authorised to bring the report back to the House.
Mr H. N. AUSTIN: In presenting the report I should like to add the following
comments. The Land Purchase Bill was introduced towards the end of the 1977 session of
Parliament. After a number of submissions had been heard, the Bill was held over at the
request of Federated Farmers, pending further consideration of the purchase of farm land by
forestry companies. In its second submission, however, Federated Farmers stated that
although it was somewhat divided it remained united in its opposition to the undue
aggregation of rural land. There was some opposition to the Bill, but the weight of evidence
generally was very much in favour of its proceeding. There was particular support from the
Federation of Young Farmers Clubs, which has a membership of over 6000. The New
Zealand Sharemilkers Association made submissions independently of Federated Farmers,
and submissions from the New Zealand Farm Workers Assocation were also received.
After careful consideration the committee recommended that the Bill be allowed to
proceed as amended. The first major change was the amendment of the long title by adding
the words "to control the acquisition of farm land for forestry purposes" after the words
"farm land". There was substantial support for that change. In clause 1 the date has been
changed from July 1978 to January 1979. That was necessary because the Bill has been held
over for several months pending further consideration. Part I is amended to read, "Control
of sales and leases of farm land to prevent undue aggregation of farm land and to control the
acquisition of farm land for forestry purposes".
1070
In clause 3 the committee has inserted the words "or forestry company" after the words
"farming company". That type of amendment appears frequently throughout the Bill. In
clause 3 the term "4 hectares" has been amended to read "5 hectares". This has been done
to include the 10-acre blocks that are not included in the term "4 hectares". Clause 4
contains quite a number of amendments, including the insertion of the words "or forestry
company" after the words "farming company".
Clause 12 has been redrafted and divided into two parts to define more clearly the legal
descriptions proposed in that portion of the Bill. One significant change in clause 12 is the
addition of the words "whether individual or family units" to the expression "to ensure and
preserve the diversification of the ownership of farm land". Clause 19 relates to the purchase
of land by foreign interests, and reference to the British Nationality and New Zealand
Citizenship Act 1948 has been removed. That should more properly be dealt with in clause
22 by the Land Valuation Tribunal under its legislation and amendments in 1968 and 1969.
Finally, clause 30, which deals with offences, has been amended to increase the penalties for
individuals from $200 to $1,000, and for companies from $1,000 to $5,000.
Overall, the amendments have resulted in a much more satisfactory Bill. Perhaps not
everyone will agree with them, and I should say at this stage that the Opposition has some
reservations which no doubt it will comment on later. I believe that the amended Bill will be
endorsed by many, particularly by young farmers and sharemilkers who seek continuing
opportunities to purchase their first farm.
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central): In the main I support the Land
Purchase Bill, as reported back, but I draw attention to one or two matters. The Land
Purchase Bill is, in essence, a pick-up of the Labour Government's 1975 legislation that was
introduced and referred for recess study. However, because it wanted to score a political
point, the National Government decided to change the name of the legislation and introduce
its own Bill. Nevertheless, the principle is the same, the purpose of the Bill being to
overcome the undue aggregation of land, and to stop the process that has gone on for a
number of years through the formation of 10-man companies to acquire land. They buy as
much land for their purposes as they desire.
Initially, representatives of Federated Farmers supported the Bill when they gave
evidence before Christmas. After Christmas, for reasons that nobody is quite sure about, Mr
Wright, the President of Federated Farmers, stated in evidence that Federated Farmers was
opposed to the Bill. One of the reasons was that forestry companies were not tied in, but we
had evidence from people interested in forestry who said that they were tied in, and that
when buying land in the past they had always been required to go through these procedures.
However, the committee in its wisdom decided to tighten up the procedure, and that
provision is now in clause 12.
We were told that the New Zealand Farm Workers Association, the New Zealand


## p. 1989 (#251) ###########################################

20 July
1989
Land Purchase Bill
Federation of Young Farmers Clubs, and the New Zealand Sharemilkers Association were
very keen that the Bill should proceed, because they want as much land as possible to be
made available to young people who want to go farming. I asked the Minister a question in
the House about this, because an article in the Wairarapa Times-Age had stated that a group
of Wairarapa farmers had started a nationwide campaign to kill the Bill, which was about to
be introduced. No doubt the Minister was under some pressure to have the Bill postponed,
and to prevent it from being proceeded with. Representatives of Federated Farmers told the
select committee that they were opposed to the Bill's proceeding. Indeed, from 22 March
until the week before last the select committee did not discuss the Bill. However, I am
pleased that the National Government eventually overcame opposition and saw fit to
proceed with it.
As the member for Hobson has said, the Opposition has some reservations about the
Bill, but I shall not discuss them in detail this afternoon. I must point out that Part II is a
complete lift-out from the old Bill which tidied up the position in relation to overseas
ownership of New Zealand land. By not amending the Bill in any way the Government is
llowing overseas interests to purchase land in New Zealand. I think particularly of Cecil
Peak, which an overseas interest was able to acquire despite the objections raised by the
Department of Lands and Survey. A provision was incorporated in the 1975 Bill to prevent
this from happening again. I understand that such a provision is not included in Part II of this
Bill, and the Opposition will have more to say about that during the second reading debate
and the Committee stage.
Mr N. P. H. Jones: Are you going to oppose the Bill?
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY: The member for Invercargill has obviously just woken up,

those in Part II.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The member for Christchurch Central said that
the Government had taken over a Bill to amend the Land Settlement Promotion and Land
Acquisition Act, which was introduced in the dying hours of the Labour Government. The
Bill was examined over the recess and found to be wanting in some of its provisions. The Bill
being reported back protects New Zealand ownership of New Zealand farm land and off-
shore islands. It aims at preventing the undue aggregation of farm land and at ensuring that,
as far as possible, our farm land is owned by the people who work it. Great emphasis is
placed on the family unit.
At the select committee the exclusion of forestry from the Bill's provisions was
criticised. That has been included. The provisions of clause 12 have been extended to give
greater discretion to the Land Valuation Tribunal. Basically, the Bill takes up the intentions
of the Land Settlement Promotion and Land Acquisition Act 1952, which were thwarted by
the 10-man company loophole. That loophole has been removed, and greater discretion has
been given to the Land Valuation Court in making decisions relating to the undue
aggregation of farm land.
The Opposition has expressed some reservations about the provisions on the purchase
by overseas interests of land on islands. Contrary to what the member for Christchurch
Central said, this clause has been amended. The amendment aims at removing the need for
the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Lands jointly to authorise the purchase by an
overseas resident of a residential section on Waiheke Island, which really is no more and no
less than a suburb of Auckland. This exclusion by Order in Council is limited to an area of up
to 4000 m², so the provision refers to residential sections only.
The member for Christchurch Central said the Government had taken over a Bill from
the Labour Government, but he overlooked the fact that Part I of the original Act, which
gave the State the power compulsorily to acquire farm land for settlement purposes, has
been removed. If the Crown wants to purchase farm land for settlement purposes it should
do so by free negotiation. I appreciate the general support the Opposition has given to the
main provisions of the Bill.

Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department) said
that the allegation that temporary staff in the department were guilty of irresponsible
misbehaviour was unfair and unsubstantiated. No evidence had been produced to support
the claim. It had been said that temporary staff had looked up their neighbours' tax returns
to see how much the person had earned. The district commissioner in Auckland had not
been told about that behaviour. He expected that a member who had links with the local
department would have drawn the matter to the district commissioner's attention, because it
warranted administrative concern. Nothing had been said to the commissioner in
Wellington. He was satisfied that the charges were unsubstantiated and that they should be
withdrawn. He had asked the member for Auckland Central to give him any evidence, but in
the past week none had been received. Who was irresponsible: the people charged-who
could not answer the charges-or the member who made the allegation?
The temporary staff members, like the permanent staff members, had gone through a
selection procedure. They had made a declaration of secrecy before the district
commissioner or the deputy commissioner. The employee was required to state that he had
read the declaration. In some cases the declaration had been read to the employee to ensure
that it was fully understood and accepted as a basis for employment.
He wanted the public to have confidence in the department, its procedures, and its
employees. He had had many dealings with the department and had found that the officers
were aware that confidentiality and secrecy were required. The department's relationship
with the public was dependent upon that. As Minister, he had been told that he could not
receive certain information. The commissioner and his successors would want to retain the
public's confidence in the department. About 200 temporary employees had been recruited
to the permanent staff. That meant that the permanent staff had not found that the
temporary staff were lacking in the qualities required to serve in the department. In the
course of a person's duties a neighbour's file could pass across his desk, but that would be by
chance. The commissioner had assured him that the permanent staff would check, and if a
temporary staff member had made a special effort to cut across his normal line of work he
would be checked by his supervisor. He would expect that in normal administrative practice.
