Notices of Motion-Admissibility
Mr SPEAKER: When the Standing Orders Committee considered the notices of motion
procedures in 1974, it was finally agreed that Mr Speaker should be given the responsibility
for vetting notices of motion to see whether they contained matters that infringed the
Standing Orders relating to notices of motion, mainly Standing Order 103, which states:
"Notices of motion shall not contain any unbecoming or offensive expression or any
expression or words which would not be permitted in debate; contain any statement of facts
or name of any person unless they are strictly necessary to render the notice intelligible and
can be authenticated; anticipate discussion of an order of the day." I was on that committee,
I made it quite clear to the committee that in my opinion it was making a nonsense and a
mockery of the procedures of Parliament. However, I was overruled by Parliament. The
recommendation of the Standing Orders Committee was accepted, and as Speaker I have to
abide by that rule.
If the House wants to change the procedures in the way suggested by the Senior
Opposition Whip, I am happy to accept some sort of direction from it on the matter, but my
view is that lodging notices of motion is very much a personal matter for the individual
member. I have always believed that, by handing the responsibility to the Speaker to vet
these notices, some of the responsibility is taken from honourable members. I know of no
honourable member who is incapable of accepting full responsibility for his actions as a
human being and as a member. I ask the Senior Opposition Whip to ponder that thought. If
the House directs me to change the procedures that I adopt, I shall do so; obviously I must. I
believe that the type of notice that is lodged by members is very much in their own hands. It
is their Parliament, not only mine. I do not consider I can accede to the request of the
honourable member, because what he is asking me to do is beyond the scope of the Standing
Orders, and I am bound by the Standing Orders unless the House directs otherwise.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori): I give notice that
next sitting day I shall move, That this House applauds the courage and tenacity of Mrs Beth
Furmage in challenging and defeating the Government's inhumane policy of unnecessarily
prying into the intimate personal lives of social welfare beneficiaries under the pretext of
preventing the abuse of the benefit, and recommends to the Government that the Minister of
Social Welfare be stripped of his portfolio.
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I
invite you to study that notice of motion closely. In my view, it is full of inaccuracies and
does not outline the case as it was presented to the court and ruled on by a judge of the
Supreme Court.
Mr SPEAKER: I have had a look at the notice of motion, and in my opinion it does not
infringe any of the provisions of Standing Order 103. It does not contain any unbecoming or
offensive expression, and so far as I know it does not contain any statement of fact that
cannot be authenticated. If the Minister has information that is not available to me, we are
back in the position of my having to authenticate the veracity or otherwise and the reliability
of statements, quoted in a notice of motion, that are attributable to a newspaper, for
example. All I have to do is to make sure that the words quoted in the notice of motion are
the same as the words in the newspaper. I cannot chase around to see whether the newspaper
reports are accurate or inaccurate; that is a matter for debate later. The only way that I can
see to clear up this matter is to have it debated, so that the Minister has the opportunity of
clarifying the position. Alternatively, we could adopt the procedure followed by the member
for Auckland Central. Those are the only possible ways, as far as I can see, in which the
Minister can clear up any misunderstandings in the notice of motion, because as it stands at
the moment it does not, in my opinion, infringe the Standing Order.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I should like you to look at one
specific part of the notice of motion to which I take objection. I think the reference to the
Government's policy should be authenticated by the honourable member. If she wants to use
such words in the way she has, then I think she should be asked to establish the source of the
comment.
Mr SPEAKER: I looked at the word "inhumane" very carefully. I suppose that, as
being an unbecoming or offensive expression when it is related to the Government's policy,
it is borderline, but whether it is accurate can properly be decided by debate. Again, I think
honourable members should ponder very seriously the insertion in their notices of motion of
words to which offence can be taken. What is the objective of the notice of motion? Is it to
be offensive, or is it to draw attention to a deficiency in the Government's policy, or
something like that? If it is the latter, I urge honourable members to remove from their

QUESTIONS ORAL
Marsden Point Oil Refinery
1. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Energy: In view of his statement
as reported in the Evening Post of 11 July that "financial and processing arrangements have
been finalised" for the expansion of the Marsden Point oil refinery, what effect will the
arrangements have on the cost of locally refined products?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The financial and processing arrangements
referred to by the honourable member establish the bases on which the refinery expansion is
to be designed and operated. They also set out the criteria for calculating the refiner's fee in
the future. The finalisation of these arrangements was a pre-requisite for undertaking
detailed feasibility studies into the processing options. As I stated in answer to a question in
the House last year, the rationale for the expansion of the Marsden Point refinery is that it
will be cheaper for New Zealand to import whole crudes and refine them locally instead of
continuing to import petroleum products. This benefit will accrue even though the refiner's
fee will have to be increased to recoup the costs of the expansion.
Hon. W. W. Freer: When will the officials finalise with the company the new basis for
the refining fee?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I understand that the question could well be resolved next year.
There are three options. Perhaps I could refer the honourable member to an extract from the
annual report of the former Ministry of Energy Resources, which was available in the House
recently and which states: "Agreement was reached with the Refining Co. Ltd. on the
financial arrangements which are to apply to the refinery expansion and the basis for
reaching a decision on the processing route to be used. The company's consultants are now
undertaking a feasibility study which will determine which of the three processing options
will best meet New Zealand's demand for petroleum. Provision has been made for the
ministry, along with the Government's technical advisers, to participate in this evaluation
process". My inquiries lead me to believe it could well be into next year before the choice
among the options is finally determined.

Electoral Forms-Labour Party Distribution
6. Mr BIRCH (Franklin) to the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the circular letter sent
out to schools in Canterbury by the Labour Party's regional office enclosing enrolment
forms, is the circular correct, and is it part of his department's electoral policy in that it
indicates that inquiries should be directed to the Labour Party's regional office in
Christchurch?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The circular letter has been brought to
my attention. It has been circulated without the approval or consent of my department. It is
not part of my department's policy.
Mr Birch: Is it a desirable practice for a third party to come in between an elector filling
in an electoral form and the Post Office at which that form should be lodged?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: It is not uncommon for party political canvassers to assist
with the registration of electors. Electoral officers endeavour to check electoral enrolment
cards, if that is possible, to ensure correctness, but it should be noted that there is a claim in
the circular put out by the New Zealand Labour Party Canterbury regional council that the
form displayed is a completed form. In fact it is incomplete, as the signature of the applicant
is not shown. This could be misleading for newly qualified electors seeking enrolment. My
department does not and cannot accept any responsibility for circulars issued by party
political canvassers.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Do I take it from the Minister's answer that although it is not part
of the electoral officer's work as such, to do this, the Minister has no objection to political
parties assisting with the work of getting a clean roll?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No, providing the work is done responsibly and accurately,
and people have confidence in those canvassers. The great danger is that there could be a
temptation for irregularities if people do not have confidence in those who offer them cards.
If the law is to be discharged there is an obligation on every citizen to get on the register.
Those cards have not only to be completed but to go through a third party- in this instance
the Canterbury regional office of the Labour Party-and thence to the electoral officer, and
until the electoral officer has the cards that obligation cannot be discharged.
Mr Comber: Does the procedure outlined by the Minister allow for the possibility that,
a person having completed an enrolment form but being of a different party political
persuasion, the form might not finally find its way to the electoral office?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I have just recognised that possibility in my previous answer,
when I said that canvassers must act responsibly and see that any cards completed by people
they call on get through to the electoral officer. I recognise that there is the danger of
irregularities. I cannot cite any knowledge of any, but I can only hope that canvassers act

Housing Policy
7. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Housing: Did he make the statement
quoted in a propaganda leaflet issued in support of the National Party candidate for
Papatoetoe, which reads: "We are no longer out to build thousands of low-cost homes, but
fewer better-quality homes", and if so, is it correct?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I have not seen the pamphlet referred

quoted, nor the context in which it was made. I do not deny, however, that I could well have

30 years as the housing shortages of the post World War II period have been replaced by a

thousands of low-cost homes, but fewer better-quality, and perhaps even larger, homes.

Hawke's Bay Hospital-Patient Care
9. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen a statement in the

matter?
Hon. T. F. GILL. (Minister of Health): As stated in my reply to an earlier question from
the honourable member, it is a matter for the Hawke's Bay Hospital Board to decide its
priorities and allocate funds to meet its nursing staff and other operating requirements.
Although the board's two intensive care units have a low average bed occupancy rate, there
are times when the units are under pressure and a full quota of nursing staff is required. I am
confident that the board is fully competent to manage its affairs in such a way that essential
services, such as intensive care units, are staffed to the required level. For this reason, I do
not intend to ask the Department of Health to investigate the board's management as
suggested by the honourable member.
Mr Hunt: What must happen before the Department of Health will investigate the
board's management?
Hon. T. F. GILL: It would take more than a newspaper statement that the standard of
nursing for some Hawke's Bay patients could be reduced, and the Government needs more
than that sort of statement before it would interfere with the proper responsibilities of the
elected representatives of hospital boards.

cause of the difficulties experienced, especially at weekends?
Mr SPEAKER: I do not think that is related to the question, although it may be
germane to the present position.

drunken driving throws pressures on intensive care units, requiring staff levels to be high. I
cannot answer specifically on the Hawke's Bay Hospital Board's position, but, as a general
observation, I can say that the incidence of weekend drunken driving means that staff
numbers in intensive care units must be maintained at a level to cope with peaks which would
be quite unnecessary without that load.
Mr Christie: Can I take it from the Minister's previous reply, when he said he would not
take notice of a newspaper report, that he is doubting the credibility of Miss Ryan, the chief
nursing sister?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Can the honourable member not remember for at least 2 minutes
what I said? I did not say that I would not take notice of a newspaper report. I said I would
not take action to investigate a hospital board on the basis of a statement in a newspaper that
nursing services could be affected.

Broadlands Geothermal Power Project
14. Mr LA VARIS (Taupo) to the Minister of Energy: Is the present time-scale for
implementation of the Broadlands geothermal power project still valid, and, if not, what are
the new dates being set for completion of the first and second stages?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): In 1977 the Power Planning Committee
recommended a commissioning date of October 1983 for the first of three 50 MW units at
Broadlands geothermal power station. The second and third units were to follow at 6-
monthly intervals. Although the Power Planning Committee has not yet formally revised this
programme, it is already clear that some changes will be necessary. The present intention is
to develop Broadlands in two stages. The first stage in commissioning relates to a
development of 80 to 100 MW, and the final stage, to bring the output up to a nominal 150
MW, would follow about 5 years behind the first stage, or when adequate field experience
had been obtained. The likely commissioning date for the first unit of stage 1 is about
October 1984—that is, about a year later than shown for the first unit in last year's
programme.

Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The Clutha Valley
Commission, in its interim report in March 1974, gave comparative estimates of $300 million
for proposal F and $320 million for proposal H. Those estimates were based on 1973
construction costs. Comparative estimates quoted at various times since that date have
remained basically the same, apart from adjustments made to reflect the escalating costs of
construction and the increasing price of purchasing the installed plant from overseas. The
latest updating of the estimate was made in September 1977 in the Crown's submission to the
Otago Catchment Board seeking a water right for the Clyde Dam. At that time the
comparative estimates were $732 million against $797 million, and were based on early 1977
construction costs. Over the period 1973 to 1977 the difference in cost between the two
alternatives therefore increased from $20 million to $65 million.

would have been the site for the second dam in the H proposal has shown up difficulties that
were not known before.

NEW ZEALAND COUNCIL FOR POSTGRADUATE MEDICAL EDUCATION BILL
Introduction
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That the New Zealand Council for
Postgraduate Medical Education Bill be introduced. This is a very important Bill, which will
have a wide-reaching effect on the health services of New Zealand. It will create a council for
postgraduate medical education in New Zealand. The council has become feasible because
New Zealand has come of age in specialist medical education.
Until about 10 or 15 years ago most New Zealand medical graduates looked particularly
to the United Kingdom for their specialist medical education. Specialist Australasian
colleges did exist, but their qualifications tended to be considered as secondary to the British
qualifications. As a result of the growth of knowledge, skill, and teaching facilities the New
Zealand medical graduate can now gain his postgraduate education in New Zealand.
Certainly this will need supplementing by overseas super-speciality experience, but the
important thing is that the New Zealand graduate will not only be trained in New Zealand,
but will also continue to serve the needs of New Zealand patients. Formerly, after
postgraduate training overseas there was a regrettable tendency for some of New Zealand's
finest graduates to stay overseas after obtaining their qualifications. This wastage will be
substantially lessened. It is important to emphasise that postgraduate education does not
apply merely to the established major specialties in medicine, but also takes account of the
growing specialty of family medicine. The major endeavour up to now has been to ensure
that future general practitioners have the opportunity to take properly structured
postgraduate education to enable them to practise their important medical specialty to the
best possible degree. The Government's emphasis on community health will succeed only if,
within the team of health workers, the medical leader has received appropriate training to
enable him or her to fill that role.
Apart from the question of vocational education, the Bill enables due regard to be taken
of continuing education. So fast are medical knowledge and techniques developing that the
half-life of medical knowledge grows shorter and shorter. That means that in all aspects of
medical practice there is a growing need for continuing education.
I must pay tribute to the Postgraduate Medical Society, which arose in various parts of
New Zealand to meet as best it could the needs of doctors in the regions. Further, the
Federation of Postgraduate Medical Societies has played a very important role in co-
ordinating and developing courses of training throughout New Zealand, including some of
the peripheral provincial centres. That work will go on, but will be greatly strengthened by
the development of the council envisaged in the Bill. Education will be developed to meet
the needs of doctors in all aspects of medical practice.
These needs require research to ensure that the programmes developed are
appropriate. The council, through the regional organisations proposed, will ensure that
doctors throughout the country-not only in the metropolitan and large provincial centres-
can obtain assistance to ensure that their knowledge is maintained. Not all the education will
be by way of formal lectures; much will depend on small group discussions with appropriate
resource people and the publication of appropriate educational material by the department,
the medical and clinical schools, and the regional postgraduate officer.
The council has founded a major development in the family medicine training
programme. This will be enlarged to take account of the known need for better trained
family doctors. The medical curriculum has become so burdened by the broad range of
material included that there is a need for vocational and continuing education in every aspect
of medicine. The Bill owes its genesis to a discerning request from the medical profession
about 7 years ago to study co-ordination and support for postgraduate medical education


## p. 2023 (#285) ###########################################

21 July
N.Z. Council for Postgraduate Medical Education Bill
2023
The New Zealand Council of Postgraduate Education has been doing good work, but has
now reached a stage where the provisions in the Bill are necessary to enable its work to be
fully developed.
Members will notice that provisions in the Bill ensure that the council will have
appropriate links with the medical and clinical schools, the University Grants Committee,
the Department of Health, the practising profession, and the specialist colleges. The Bill will
ensure that postgraduate medical education, both vocational and continuing, will be placed
on a sound footing to encourage co-operative development, to avoid overlap, and to ensure
that no section of the profession is denied the benefit of postgraduate medical education.
Turning now to the contents of the Bill, clause 3 establishes the New Zealand Council
for Postgraduate Medical Education as a body corporate, which will consist of 17 people. It
will include the Director-General of Health, the chairman of the Medical Council of New
Zealand, and the chairman of the New Zealand Postgraduate Medical Federation
Incorporated. Four of the 17 members will have responsibility for postgraduate medical
education at the Otago and Auckland Medical Schools and the Wellington and Christchurch
Clinical Schools. As provided for in clause 12, the same four people will serve as regional
directors of the southern, northern, Wellington, and Canterbury regions. Clause 12 enables
the council to appoint registered medical practitioners as employees of the council to be the
directors of the Waikato and central regions; and, by virtue of their office, these two regional
directors will be members of the council.
Clause 3 provides for eight of the general council members to be appointed by the
Governor-General on the advice of the Minister of Health: three medical practitioners to be
nominated by the College Liaison Committee, three medical practitioners to be nominated
by the New Zealand Medical Association, one person who is a member of the University
Grants Committee, and one person who is not a medical practitioner. One of the three
nominees of the College Liaison Committee will need to be a member of the New Zealand
College of General Practitioners. One of the three New Zealand Medical Association's
nominees will need to be a member of the New Zealand Resident Medical Officers
Association.
Clause 4 provides for a 2-year term of appointment for council members other than ex-
officio members. Appointed members may also be reappointed, but are restricted from
holding office continuously for more than three terms. Clause 6 provides for members of the
council to elect a chairman and a deputy chairman annually from among their members.
The functions of the council are set out in clause 19. They may be summarised as being
to advise the Minister of Health on postgraduate medical education and to promote and
support the furtherance of postgraduate medical education. Clause 9 enables a three-
member national executive committee to be established consisting of the chairman of the
council and two other members elected by the council.
Clause 13 establishes regional executive committees consisting of the regional director
in each case, and five others to be nominated by the college liaison committee, professional
bodies, and hospital boards in each region. Clause 11 divides New Zealand, for the purposes
of the Bill, into six regions-Northern, Waikato, Central, Wellington, Canterbury, and
Southern. The first schedule to the Bill specifies the hospital districts which will make up
each region. Clause 12 provides for a director for each region. The powers of the council may
be delegated-as provided for in clause 21-to members, officers, or committees of the
councils. The power to spend money or to deal with the property of the council may be
delegated only to the national executive committee or a regional executive committee.
Clauses 23 to 32 spell out various financial provisions relative to the council. Clause 33
requires the council to report annually to the Minister. Contrary to the wording in the Bill as
it now stands, the intention is that the council report as soon as practicable after 31 March
each year. In the draft of the Bill held by members the date is given as 30 June. However,
this was thought to be too late, especially as finances are being appropriated and will be open
for discussion during each year's estimates. Clause 34 requires the council's annual report to
be tabled in Parliament. The Bill gives statutory recognition to the New Zealand Council for
Postgraduate Medical Education, and delineates its functions, powers, responsibilities, and
organisational structures. The Bill is not contentious, and the council is in agreement with its
provisions.

Dr WALL (Porirua): I wonder if the Minister could tell us a bit more about the Bill,

"I'm in the boat Jack, let's keep all the rest out"? That has happened repeatedly among
professional and para-professional bodies. I can think of one such body recently formed-
the Australasian Society of Psychiatrists. One has only to look at the convulsive
manoeuvrings over the years of the Australasian College of Surgeons in its requirements for
membership, which varied from an impossibly strict examination-which it found no one
was bothering to take up-to opening membership to everyone who was a fellow of a United
Kingdom college. That complete and total reversal of policy occurred in the space of a very
few years.
Will the Minister give statutory power to such bodies which have been unable to pursue
a consistent course in selecting their members, quite apart from ensuring that their members'
standards were in any way consistent? What powers will such bodies have? Does the
Minister want a statutory body set up just to spend some public money? In the past a
statutory constitution has not been a necessary prerequisite for a body to spend public
money.
If the Minister is setting up a statutory body with powers to dictate on postgraduate
medical education, will this militate against people going overseas for postgraduate
qualifications-in many ways an extremely desirable practice? If so, it will most certainly
produce academic and professional in-breeding in New Zealand which will not be in the
long-term interest of the profession.
The Minister made great play about the half-life of medical knowledge becoming
shorter as the years go by. This was certainly so, and appeared to be endlessly progressive
from about the early 1940s to the 1970s. However, as the Minister must surely be aware if he
peruses medical publications and professional journals, we are getting to the stage of
diminishing returns in the extension of medical knowledge, as we are in so many other areas.
So that argument is not nearly as appropriate now as it was. One has only to look at the rate
of introduction of new drugs-of which the Minister must be aware as he has to decide which
should be on the free list-to see that that is slowing down, although other factors, including
testing requirements, should be taken into account. However, it does indicate that the main
argument put up by the Minister for the diminishing half-life of medical knowledge is
becoming increasingly obsolete.
To go back to my original reservation, I see no problem about encouraging
postgraduate education. I am entirely in favour of it, but I have grave reservations about
establishing an increasingly closed shop. I could give numerous examples of how this has
worked against the advancement of medical practice in New Zealand. One has only to think
of the treatment of alcoholism, which has become a closed shop. Although psychiatry is still
regarded as the appropriate speciality, it was decided overseas some years ago, notably in
Canada, that psychiatry was an inappropriate speciality for the control of an addictive
disease.
In setting up a body with the statutory authority to advise him, what safeguards has the
Minister provided for the public to ensure that innovative procedures in medicine will not be
crippled by the controlling influence of this body on people who will conduct more advanced
medical practice within New Zealand? Its aims and objectives are good, but I do fear the
extent of the power that is being put in the hands of a relatively small number of people
whose background is limited to academic spheres.

allegation that the industrial court might not have known its mind about the effect of the
general wage order. In rounding off its decision the court says, in paragraph 43: "This order
will operate only in respect of prescribed minimum rates of remuneration. There will be no
legal compulsion upon any employer to increase the rate of remuneration of a worker if that
worker is already receiving a rate in excess of the nominal minimum rate prescribed in the
relevant award or collective agreement after that minimum rate has been increased by the
amount specified in this order." So let us dispose of that element straight away. It is quite
clear that the judge knew what he was doing; and I have no doubt that a judge as
experienced as Judge Jamieson was aware of all the current law and took it all into account.
Mr Prebble: Are you saying the judge is lying?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The judge set out his opinion in his judgment, and the
member for Auckland Central, who is a lawyer, should understand that. This Bill proposed
by the member for Roskill, who happens also to be the president of the Labour Party, is
misnamed. It should be called the "Labour Party Abject Surrender Bill". The principle it
abandons has been central to stabilisation measures taken by all Governments during the
past 7 years, including those taken by the member for Roskill when he was Minister of
Labour in 1974 and 1975. I refer to the 12-months' rule-an agreed and essential element of
stabilisation. That 12-months' rule has been in effect since March 1971, when the first wage
stabilisation legislation was introduced in the form of the Stabilisation of Remuneration Act,
and it has continued to apply in all subsequent wage stabilisation measures. I recall that in
1970, when the Rt. Hon. J. R. Marshall asked the Employers Federation and the Federation
of Labour to get together to try to stop the wildly escalating wage rates, it was the only
matter on which the employers and the Federation of Labour could agree. It was enshrined
in the law in March 1971 and it has been in the law ever since, but the Labour Party
proposes, abysmally, to abandon it.
The Bill is a "Labour Party Abject Surrender Bill" in the sense that it is merely a cease-
fire surrender bill, and not a negotiated peace settlement Bill. If it provided for negotiation
there might be something to be said for it; there might be an argument in its favour. Its
essence is an abject surrender in the long struggle against inflation, and it is typical of Labour
Party legislation. The importance of the 12-months' rule is well known to the Labour Party,
and particularly to the member for Roskill. That was shown not only by his reference to it
during the second reading of the General Wage Orders Bill last year, but by the fact that it is
set out in the regulations made by the Labour Government in 1974. It is significant that the
essential safeguard against inflation is to be abandoned by the Bill.
Regulation 6 of the 1974 regulations is headed, "Rates of remuneration to be fixed for
at least 12 months". It states, "(1) Subject to this regulation, no instrument made after the
commencement of this regulation shall fix any rate of remuneration unless that rate is to
continue in force for a period of at least 12 months from the date of the coming into force of
the rate of remuneration fixed by the instrument"-and so on. Another one stated that
instruments could be increased in a certain manner set out in regulation 16(H). Regulation
6(4) was revoked in the General Wage Orders Act last year, as the member for Roskill
knows, and as the court knew.
Mr Prebble: No, it didn't.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: It did indeed. It knew, and it is impertinent for a lawyer
member of the House, the member for Auckland Central, to reflect on the court's
competence in that way. The Labour Opposition has always been against the criteria set out
in the General Wage Orders Act. Section 6 of the Act, which the Government deliberately
amended last year, states that the court shall give paramount importance to the promotion of
the economic stability of New Zealand.

The Government will support the Arbitration Court. Wage and income restraint, and

management. It is agreed that we have a strong Bench, and that the court can fulfil a major
social and economic function. For about 100 years the Arbitration Court played a vital role.
We all know the problems caused in the last 10 years when there was no court to sustain
economic management.

NEW ZEALAND NATIONAL AIRWAYS CORPORATION DISSOLUTION BILL
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 19 July 1978
Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North): Perhaps this is a good opportunity to recount a
little of the debate we heard a couple of nights ago, so that we can arrive at some semblance
of order. The lady member for Lyttelton presented a very full and complete address, and
thoroughly discounted the arguments put forward by the member for Timaru. We had also
to listen to the member for Grey Lynn, who may have given us an entertaining message, but
it was totally uninformed. The best way I can describe it is by saying that he was so far off
course that nobody would want him as a navigator in any of the Air New Zealand planes. He
mentioned some confidential personal files that had been exposed, and we have asked the
next Opposition speaker to present them or lay them on the table of the House.
The member for Lyttelton quoted extracts from a pamphlet issued by the Labour Party.
I should like also to refer to the pamphlet, which is headed "Election 1978", and is
apparently report No. 19 from the Labour Party. Some questions were asked about the
pamphlet by way of interjection. One member asked where the pamphlet had come from.
Having made some inquiries I can tell the House that the member for Hamilton East gave it
to us, and that it was found in Fox Street in May 1978. Obviously it was considered such a
throw-away pamphlet that it was actually thrown into the gutter in Fox Street.
An Hon. Member: Whose name is on it?
Mr LITHGOW: Well, I had intended to lead into that one. The name "W. E. Rowling"
is printed under the photograph on the back of the pamphlet, with the words, "It is wrong on
four counts." I quote from the pamphlet: "In the long run, the merger will almost certainly
mean that many provincial services will be wiped out or handed on a plate to private
operators. This will inevitably mean a more expensive and less reliable service." The
statement I really want to emphasise is this: "Labour totally disagrees with this merger." I
shall now quote a statement made by the Leader of the Opposition. "If it is practicable,
when we resume office we will look at creating two separate airlines under one board of
management." In other words, the Opposition is trying to back the horse both ways.
Certainly, Labour Party members are not committing themselves. They may pretend that
they want to have two airlines, but they are prepared to say only that they "will look at it".
That is hardly a commitment.
I shall refer now to Air New Zealand services to Palmerston North and elsewhere. I
have followed the progress of the dissolution Bill and the merger of Air New Zealand and
the National Airways Corporation with considerable interest. I had an opportunity, before
the merger took place, of speaking to a group of NAC staff in Palmerston North. I can assure
the House that those senior staff-who, between them, have provided about 200 years in
service-indicated very clearly during the evening's discussion that, although they had some
apprehension about going into the new merged operation, they were doing so with interest
and confidence. They felt that the merging of the two companies would be of benefit to New
Zealand. Naturally, they were a little apprehensive. After the end of November many
Opposition members will be apprehensive about getting new jobs. Anyone who moves into a
new company or organisation is apprehensive about how things will work out.
I have been on two caucus committee tours, one to NAC, and one to Air New Zealand.


## p. 2040 (#302) ###########################################

2040
New Zealand National Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill 21 July
The first visit was to the NAC-now Air New Zealand-technical headquarters in
Christchurch, in which over 1000 people are employed. Training is given in the Friendship
simulator to pilots, many from overseas. Combining the two companies and giving overall
training, not only to New Zealand pilots, but to pilots from Malaysia and Australia, is a
worth-while operation. Stewardesses, too, are receiving training in Christchurch. There is no
doubt about the contribution being made and the overseas funds being put into New
Zealand's coffers. A further caucus committee visit was made to Air New Zealand in
Auckland. Pilots, again from overseas, are being trained in the DC10 simulator. I am sure
the House will be interested to learn that Auckland's Air New Zealand kitchen facilities turn
out about 15 000 meals a day for Air New Zealand and various overseas airlines. Staff
turnover is the lowest for any kitchen in the country; in fact there is a line-up of those
genuinely interested in working in the Air New Zealand kitchen.
Mr Quigley: I still have the same cook after 23 years.
Mr LITHGOW: Yes, and much the same continuity of service applies in Air New
Zealand's kitchen. The staff are pleased with their working conditions and are often able to
obtain positions for their friends.
I should like to spend a little time discussing the amount of freight that has been moved
by Air New Zealand. Through an active marketing programme, Air New Zealand has
dramatically increased overseas and domestic freight movements. The figures for Auckland
for 1974-75 were 9 400 000 kg; for 1975-76, 12 800 000 kg; for 1976-77, 16 600 000 kg, and for
1977-78, 17 900 000 kg. That gives some indication of the incredible increase in freight
movement, and Air New Zealand's ability to service that freight and deliver it overseas on
time, while avoiding pillaging.
Mr O'Brien: What has that to do with it?
Mr LITHGOW: The point is that Air New Zealand, through quick delivery of freight to
overseas points, is earning us overseas funds. Every manufacturer is interested in being able
to get his goods delivered overseas quickly. The increase for Christchurch for the last 3
months is already 31 percent. That gives some idea of the satisfaction with Air New Zealand
and the merger. Delta Plastics has expanded its export business extensively, and much of
that freight is flown to Auckland and transported overseas by Air New Zealand. Glaxo
Laboratories has also extended its freight through Palmerston North considerably. I support
the Bill.
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga): I support the amendment moved by my colleague
the member for Timaru to omit the word "now" and to add at the end of the motion the
words "this day 6 months", in order that Parliament and the people of New Zealand may
have an opportunity to assess any advantages that may follow the merger of National
Airways Corporation with Air New Zealand after the feasibility report at present classified
secret is made public.
Members should consider this matter in all seriousness, because a large number of
questions have yet to be answered. We understand that the Government has refused to
publish a secret report that sets out the reasons for the merger. We have asked for the report
to be made available and for it to be tabled so that every member of Parliament will be able
to determine whether the Government's proposals are reasonable and fair. Until now we
have been left in the dark. On behalf of my colleagues I ask that the secret report containing
recommendations on the merger be tabled. I am sure that that is fair and reasonable. After
all, the National Party, when campaigning at the last election, promised open government,
yet a report that affects many people is not being made available.

TUESDAY, 25 JULY 1978

DEATH OF THE HONOURABLE SIR RONALD ALGIE
Mr SPEAKER: I regret to advise the House of the death of the Hon. Sir Ronald Algie, a
former member of the House of Representatives, in which he represented the electorate of
Remuera from 1943 to 1966. The late Sir Ronald was a Minister of the Crown, holding the
Education portfolio, and was Speaker of the House of Representatives from 1961 until his
retirement in 1966. He died on 23 July 1978. I desire, on behalf of the House, to express our
sense of the loss we have sustained and our sympathy with the relatives of the late former
Speaker. I now ask members to stand with me and observe a period of silence as a mark of
respect to the memory of the late Sir Ronald.
[Honourable members then stood as a mark of respect.]
ACCIDENT COMPENSATION AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That the Accident Compensation
Amendment Bill be introduced. The Accident Compensation Act is a complex piece of
legislation, and when it was considered in 1972 it was foreseen that experience with it would
show a need for amendments from time to time. Substantial amendments were made in
1973, when the scheme was widened to cover the whole population instead of being limited
to accidents to earners and victims of motor vehicle accidents. Further substantial
amendments were made in 1974 and 1975, and one minor amendment in 1976. As I indicated
during the debate on the estimates, both the Government and the Accident Compensation
Commission have undertaken major studies of the Accident Compensation Act, and it is
expected that their working parties will report later this year. It is therefore likely that quite
substantial amendments will be proposed for consideration next year.
In the meantime, however, it has been found necessary to make some amendments,
within the framework of the present legislation, to improve the application and the effect of
the Act, and to correct some of the anomalies that have become apparent. Clause 2
introduces a definition of "New Zealand" for the purposes of the Act. Clause 3 removes an
arithmetical anomaly from section 59. Clause 4 expands section 73 to enable the commission
to pay bonuses and impose penalties on employers and self-employed persons according to
the employer's or self-employed person's accident experience. Clause 5 amends the present
provisions of the Act relating to the delivery of statements of earnings and payment of levies
by self-employed persons. The amendment will enable self-employed persons to file a
combined tax-cum-levy return and pay levies at the same time as terminal tax. Clause 6 gives
the commission power to attach monies owing to an employer or self-employed person who
is in default in respect of payment. Clause 7 rewrites the present section 102C to make it clear
that the cover under the Act enjoyed by visitors to New Zealand is intermittent for visitors
who are accommodated on board ship while touring New Zealand and for foreign seamen
who go on and off their ship while it is in port.
Clause 8 will enable weekly compensation to be paid to those earners who suffer a loss
of earning capacity but who are now precluded from receiving weekly compensation because
continued earnings during the period of incapacity exceed $300 per week. Clause 9 removes
from section 105A references to the territorial sea of New Zealand, which are unnecessary.
Clause 10 adds a new section to provide that the commission shall pay the reasonable costs of
all necessary transport of injured persons by ambulance. Clause 11 enlarges the ambit of
section 126, which relates to payments of compensation made to trustees and guardians of
minors and persons under disability or needing protection. Clause 12 extends the ambit of
section 131, which relates to injured persons who, in addition to having cover under the Act,
have a claim for damages or compensation under the law of any other country. Clause 13
amends section 181 by extending the matters that may be the subject of statutory regulation.

a person who already has an obligation under the Act, but who has defaulted in his payment.
No additional payment is required from any person. It is merely a method of collecting
payment from those who default in payment.
I should like to ask the Minister a question in relation to clause 4, which empowers the
commission to pay bonuses and to impose penalties on employers and self-employed persons
according to their accident history. Does this mean that the commission will be effectively
returning to a scheme similar to the credits and debits used under the previous worker's
compensation scheme? If that is the case, it will be welcomed by those many employers who,
in my opinion, have excellent employment records.
I should like to refer briefly to clause 5, which is an excellent example of the Bill making
procedural rather than substantive changes to the law. That clause relates to the delivery of
statements of earnings and the payment of levies by self-employed people. It is well
recognised that one of the deficiencies of the Accident Compensation Act was the way it
dealt with self-employed people. On behalf of those people I thank the Minister for
including this provision. Because the Bill makes changes only to the procedures surrounding
accident compensation and makes no substantive changes to the law, I support its
introduction and oppose its being referred to a select committee.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): I move, That the Accident Compensation
Amendment Bill be referred to the Labour Committee, and that the proceedings of the
committee during the hearing of evidence be open to accredited representatives of the news
media.
Motion negatived.

Union Rules
2. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Minister of Labour: Can he indicate whether the
Registrar of Unions is required to approve rules for the registration of unions, and, if so, is
there a standard requirement for a union to keep an effective roll of its members, to advise
them of the financial statement for the year, and to notify them of the annual meeting; if not,
has he any proposal to overcome a now apparent problem?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The short answer to the member's various
questions is yes. Section 165 of the Industrial Relations Act 1973 provides that when the
registrar is satisfied that the provisions of the Act have been met he shall register a union and
record its rules. Section 175 requires that provision shall be made in the rules of a union for
the keeping of a register of members and the manner of calling meetings of the union.
Section 186 requires every union, on a request in writing in that behalf, to furnish any
financial member, on demand and without charge, with a copy of the latest annual income
and expenditure account and balance sheet, together with the auditor's report on the
accounts. Although a union is not required to include this provision in its rules, the Act binds
each union. I understand it is common practice for unions to publish such facts in their
various journals and newsletters.
Mr Latter: In the preparation of ballots, have some unions disclosed that they do not
have an effective membership list?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Yes. I cannot comment on one case, because it is sub judice, but
in other instances unions have said that they cannot supply rolls.
Mr. N. P. H. Jones: What was the Minister's reaction to the Federation of Labour's
admission that it did not know how many members there were in some unions?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I think and I have to generalise that the view that came
through in the talks I had last week with the Federation of Labour was that it did not endorse
the action of some unions and their failure to have a membership roll. It was pointed out,
however, that some problems arose in unions with a high membership turnover. The recent
inability of members to get access to a union's annual accounts, and the lack of rolls in some
unions, did not, as I understand, have the blessing of the Federation of Labour.

Medical Benefits
6. Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury), on behalf of Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa), to
the Minister of Health: What increases in medical benefits payable to GPs for treatment of
children and young persons have been approved since 1 January 1976?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): In respect of children and young persons,
benefits have been increased since January 1976 as follows: normal hours and non-urgent
services-surgery consultation from $3 to $4.75, visit to patient from $4 to $6; urgent
services-6 p.m. to 8 a.m., and Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays-surgery
consultation from $6 to $7, visit to patient from $7 to $8. In addition, the benefit payable for
immunising children was increased on 1 October 1977. Before that date, the benefit was
$1.85 if immunisation was carried out by the doctor, and $1.55 if given by his nurse. Now
there is one benefit of $2.25.
Mr Prebble: Will the increase in medical benefits be available to the people in the
Auckland Central electorate who are the patients of that good GP, Dr. C. M. Patel, and, if
not, why not?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Patients in the Auckland Central electorate, whether the patients of
Dr Patel or not, have exactly the same rights to medical benefits as any other patients of any
other doctor in New Zealand.
Mr Prebble: Will the increase in benefits be paid to Dr Patel if, in fact, his patients are
to have the same rights, and, if that is not so, how can the Minister reconcile his answer with
the first one he gave?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Benefits have never been payable to doctors. Doctors have been
allowed, on the production of a schedule of names, to collect benefits on behalf of their
patients. Dr Patel, who had been attending up to 120 patients a day and had been paid
$51,000 in general medical service benefits, has, on the recommendation of the Medical
Association disciplinary committee, now been placed under some restraint, so that instead of
his giving a list of names on which the money will be paid he will give a receipt, and the
people will collect their benefits in the way the law provides.

DSIR-Soil Classifications
10. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson), on behalf of Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua), to the
Minister of Science and Technology: When will details of the new soil classifications being
undertaken by the DSIR, which use a world standard of classifying fertility climate and crop
suitability, be available for individual use?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology): The new soil classification
system is being adopted on current soil surveys carried out by the soil bureau, DSIR, and the
results will become available as these surveys are completed. Complete coverage of the
country using this system will take many years, but in the meantime published soil surveys
are available for many parts of New Zealand and most of these contain information on the
climate of the area, fertility of the various soils, and ratings of them for different land uses,
such as crops, pasture, and forestry. The new classification system has also been applied to
soil surveys carried out in the Pacific Islands-the Cooks, Tonga, and the Lau group-by the
soil bureau, and its use will facilitate the transfer of advanced crop technology from more
developed countries to these areas.

Tax Cuts
13. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Prime Minister: Has he seen the report in the
Marlborough Express of 6 July 1978, in which the member for Mangere, commenting on the
Prime Minister's method of illustrating the tax reduction of more than $1,000 for a married
man with young children, used these words, "He chose to compare the taxation of a person
on an income of $120 in 1975 and a person on $120 in 1978. That was disgraceful."; and, if
so, will he confirm that he has already explained to the member for Mangere that the large
tax saving can be easily illustrated in other ways?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Yes, I have seen the report in question
and I can confirm that on several occasions I have explained the substantial tax savings in the
quoted example in a number of different ways. For example, a married man with a
dependent wife and a child under 5 years earning $6,000 a year would have paid $1,425 a
year or 23.75 percent of his gross income in tax under Labour, whereas he will pay only $338
a year or 5.63 percent of his gross income under the first full year of operation of National's
tax tables-a tax savings of $1,087 a year. For the same man to be paying $338 a year in tax
under Labour, he would not be earning $6,000 a year, or $115 a week as he will under
National, but $3,094 a year or $59.50 a week. The member for Mangere suggested that if an
income of $120 "had moved with the general wage trend it would now be $175". However,
the same married man earning $175 a week would have paid $52.12 a week in tax under
Labour, whereas under National's new tax rate he will pay only $31.18 a week, which
represents an increase in net income of $20.94 a week.
Mr Latter: Would the rate of $52 a week tax be exactly double the taxation of $120.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I cannot give an example, because the other is calculated
on an annual basis. However, it would be about that.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Will the Minister confirm that when speaking in Masterton on this
topic, as reported in the Dominion of 19 July, he said that a man with one child and earning
$6,000 a year, or $120 a week, was paying $1,425 a year tax under the present tax tables, but
would pay only $338.50 a year under the new rates? Could he also confirm that on page 25 of
the tax Bill before the House at present it is stated that the absolute minimum anyone could
pay in those circumstances is $409.76?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The member should know that that statement in the
Dominion was not a correct report of what I had said. The matter was raised in the House the
following day when I said that the report was incorrect. The member for Pahiatua, who was
present on the occasion, also made a statement confirming that that report of what I had said
in Masterton was not correct. It is quite useless for the member to use material that has
already been publicly corrected, to try to prove that it is wrong.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Will the Minister deny that he used the figure of $338.50 a year as
being the tax a person with one dependent child and earning $120 a week would pay?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I simply repeat what I said before; the Dominion report
was not correct. I cannot say any more than that.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Will the Minister confirm that he used the figure of $338.50 in his
reply today?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: That's right.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Will he also confirm that on page 25 of his Income Tax
Amendment Bill it is stated that the lowest tax possible that a man earning $120 a week can
pay is not $338.50 but $409.76 a year?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: In the current year the tables operate for only half a year, a
fact the member seems to have overlooked. As I said in my original answer, the figure is
correct for a man on that income and receiving the young family rebate and single income
rebate for the first full year of the National tax table.

almost from the time of the given Budget in one year and go through a process of nearly a
year before they are finally brought out in the following Budget. During that course of time
many other policy proposals have to be considered, and some get through the net and some
do not. But the question of transport obviously would be taken in conjunction with the new
policy.

LABOUR PARTY'S TAX PROPOSALS-NOTICE UNDER STANDING ORDER 89
Mr SPEAKER: I have to inform the House that I have received a request from the
Deputy Leader of the Opposition to move the adjournment of the House in accordance with
Standing Orders 89 and 90. The request, which was received this morning within the
required time, reads as follows: "Pursuant to Standing Orders 89 and 90, I wish to move the
adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a particular case of recent
occurrence which requires the immediate attention of the House and the Government and
which involves the ministerial responsibility of the Government, namely, the announcement
yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition, the Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling, of the new tax
proposals put forward by the New Zealand Labour Party. This matter requires the
immediate attention of the House and the Government because, at present, legislation is
about to be passed through this House which will tax thousands of people who are earning
less than $3,000 a year, many of whom do not now pay any tax at all. Further, the
announcement last Friday of record unemployment levels in New Zealand highlights the
importance of the need to introduce and pass through the House immediately a tax package
along the lines of the Labour Party's proposals which would have the effect of boosting
production and employment and thereby cutting the amount of money required to be set


## p. 2059 (#321) ###########################################

25 July
2059
Labour Party's Tax Proposals-Notice Under Standing Orders
aside by the Government for unemployment benefits or special assistance projects.
Ministerial responsibility of the Government is involved because, in addition to the
responsibility that all Governments face for providing full employment levels and frequent
adjustment to taxation rates, there is a need to understand fully the proposals being put
forward by the Labour Party and assess them in the light of the legislation at present being
passed through this House."
Standing Order 90 states that the statement of the matter proposed to be discussed on a
motion for the adjournment of the House under the preceding Standing Order shall not be
framed in general terms but shall deal with a particular case of recent occurrence which
requires the immediate attention of the House and the Government, and which involves the
administrative or ministerial responsibility of the Government. While it is beyond doubt that
the Government has responsibility for taxation, it is entirely another matter to suggest that it
has responsibility for taxation proposals announced by the Leader of the Opposition
yesterday. The event that has recently occurred, it seems to me, is the announcement that
was made by the Leader of the Opposition, not by a Minister; and there is no ministerial
responsibility for that. Further, this whole subject can and should be discussed during the
debate on the Income Tax Amendment Bill, which, I understand, is now No. 10 on the
Order Paper. Accordingly, I do not think the matter requires the immediate attention of the
House. For those reasons I rule that the motion is not one contemplated by the Standing
Orders, and the application is therefore declined.

wrap-up Bill leaves pilot litigants up in air". Mr Mazengarb points to some of the difficulties
in the Bill. Mr Tony Black, editor of the New Zealand Law Journal, believed that the merger
was constitutionally illegal. In April 1978 he was reported in the Evening Post as having said:
"We have a Corporation established by a decision of Parliament and functioning under an
Act of Parliament. Whether it should stop carrying out the function with which it has been
charged is not a decision for the Corporation or for the Government. It is a decision for
Parliament." This is another instance of the Government ignoring the wishes of Parliament.
Once again we see secret government by secret caucus. We have not been allowed to read
the report, but are being asked to vote on the results of it, because the Minister has assured
us that the report does not in any way affect the principle of the merger. When the Minister
replies, will he indicate whether he is willing, even at this late stage, to table the report? I
hope the decision will be his and not that of the Prime Minister or of Cabinet. If it is the
latter, he is perfectly entitled to say so.
We are being asked to legalise an illegality 3 months after it was first committed. The
New Zealand National Airways Corporation Act 1945 should have been revoked before any
merger went ahead, because, while it is still law, NAC still legally exists. The matter should
have gone before the Commerce Commission. The following interesting comment appears in
Mr Mazengarb's article: "According to clause 5 of the Bill, Part III of the Commerce Act
1975 is not to apply 'for the avoidance of doubt'". This explicitly indicates that the merger is
not a transaction to which the Examiner of Commercial Practices should have given his
consent, and it leaves the critics with the feeling that, by not obtaining the examiner's
consent, the Government has been in breach of the Act and is now bailing itself out.
Mr Mazengarb goes on to say: "The Bill allows Air New Zealand to apply to the Air

without a public hearing." That is yet another example of the Government's total disregard
for the law, a disregard that it has shown ever since its first Cabinet meeting, when the Prime
Minister stopped the superannuation scheme on the basis of a whim that was later
overturned by a judgment in the Supreme Court. It is another example of the Government
using the law to sidestep other laws that safeguard the rights of the people. In other words,
the Government is riding roughshod over people's rights.
This disregard for the machinery that protects people can be seen in the audit
arrangements for the merged airline. Before the merger the Audit Office was responsible for
auditing the accounts of NAC. Now that NAC and Air New Zealand have been merged into
a limited liability company, the Audit Office will have no involvement whatever in that
company's audit. That means there will be no parliamentary control over the financial
management of the new airline. I should like to ask the Minister a straightforward question.

Let us examine whether there is any need for the merger. Parliament is already aware
that the proposal for such a merger is not new, and that studies for a merger have been
carried out by the airlines for many years. The last study, completed 4 years ago, showed
that a merger was undesirable and would have had very limited benefits for the airlines,
inasmuch as the operations of both were dissimilar, as were the type of aircraft used.
However, the report did make recommendations for some co-operation. Is it not true that,
contrary to expert advice, the Prime Minister last year gave his approval for the merger after
the Secretary for Transport submitted a report? The Secretary for Transport admitted on TV
that he had not consulted NAC, but that his discussions were with Air New Zealand. He said
that he felt it was not necessary to consult NAC. This is an example of a sick partner taking
over a healthy partner without any consultation; and since then this report has become a
secret document. Why is it secret? The public and members of the House should not be
treated with contempt. The airlines are owned by the New Zealand public, and Air New
Zealand is a public corporation. Their representatives should have access to information
before agreeing to any further passage of the Bill. We are entitled to know whether there is
any basis at all for the Minister of Transport's claim that the new airline will save $10 million.
Let us examine the supposed benefits. The Minister of Transport said on TV that
savings would be brought about by a greater intercharge of aircraft. During the introduction
of the Bill it was again said that the new airline would be more flexible, and that the DC8s
and DC10s would be used more frequently on domestic services and vice versa. Indeed, I
have been informed that the position is completely to the contrary. Before the merger, NAC
would charter a DC8 or a DC10 when disruptions occurred. Since the announcement of the
merger the management has refused the use of the DC10 when disruptions occur.

cost of training aircrew will double because of the number of sequential steps involving

MINISTERIAL STATEMENT-COOK ISLANDS
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): With the leave of the House, I wish to
make a ministerial statement. That divisions along party lines have deepened in the Cook
Islands since the general elections in March is, of course, no secret. Events in the Cook
Islands have been fully covered by the news media. In addition, the Government has been
receiving regular reports from its mission in Rarotonga.
All the information available has suggested that the social fabric of the Cook Islands
could well be subjected to strong pressure. The Chief Justice had before him a number of
petitions which challenged the validity of the recent elections. Whether he allowed them, or
whether he did not, there was obviously a possibility that there could be repercussions that
would severely strain the resources of the Cook Islands Police Force. We were, therefore,
not surprised when we received indications recently that the Cook Islands Police Force was
worried that it might be faced with a situation in which it needed more police officers than it
had at its disposal to ensure that law and order were maintained, and was contemplating the
need to recommend to whichever Government was in power after the verdict that it request
reinforcements from the New Zealand Police.
The Cook Islands are a self-governing country. No New Zealand policeman can act in
the Cook Islands unless there has first been a request from the Cook Islands Government for
him to do so, and unless he is seconded to the Cook Islands Police Force. At the same time
New Zealand has traditionally responded to Cook Islands Government requests for
manpower assistance, and we felt that it was in keeping with the co-operative relationship
between the two countries for us to be prepared to respond in this case as helpfully as we
could.


## p. 2082 (#344) ###########################################

2082
25 July
Ministerial Statement-Cook Islands
It was evident that if the Cook Islands police needed reinforcement they were most
likely to do so immediately after the Chief Justice had delivered his verdict. In particular, the
possibility could not be discounted that action might have to be taken to ensure the safety of
the Chief Justice, who is also the representative of the Acting Head of State, whatever the
nature of his verdict. The Cook Islands police were concerned that they could not release the
five men needed to perform this task adequately and also attend to other contingencies
which might arise.
To have made no preparations unless we received a request from the Cook Islands
Government for assistance would have meant that any help would have arrived in the Cooks
many hours after it was required. What was needed, therefore, was a small group of
policemen to be available in case the Cook Islands Government requested assistance of this
kind. For this reason five policemen flew to the Cook Islands today and arrived at Rarotonga
at 4.35 p.m. Cook Islands time.
I emphasise that at this stage the five-man New Zealand police team had no power to act
as police in the Cook Islan 's. They had no standing other than that of ordinary visitors.
Accordingly, they had the strictest instructions to do nothing until the Cook Islands
Government formally requested the New Zealand Government for their help and until they
were sworn in as Cook Islands police. Following the request from Dr Davis, the new Premier
of the Cooks, they were sworn in as temporary members of the Cook Islands Police Force
and were allocated to guard the representative of the Acting Head of State, thereby
releasing members of the Cook Islands Police Force for other tasks.
I should add that a senior New Zealand policeman travelled to the Cooks at the end of
last week. He went as a visitor with his wife, and, until the request from the Cook Islands
Government was received, he had no other status in the Cook Islands. If the Cook Islands
Government requested help, his task was to provide advice and report through the New
Zealand Mission to the Government. He too has been sworn in as a temporary member of
the Cook Islands Police Force at the Cook Islands Government's request.
It would have been unthinkable for us to refuse to respond to a request for assistance
from the Cook Islands Government in a situation in which life might be in danger. We
hoped, of course, that there would be no need for the Cook Islands Government to ask us
for help, but we thought it imperative, without in any way interfering in their affairs, to
arrange to have any reinforcements their police force needed promptly to hand.

## p. 2087 (#349) ###########################################

New Zealand National Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill 2087
The basis of that argument is that Government members, particularly Ministers of the
Crown, cannot say what they regard the law to be and what they consider is legal or illegal;
but Opposition members, and anyone else who seeks to comment on the matter, are entitled
to give their views on the law and on how it applies in a particular situation. I want to make it
clear that everybody has a right to state their views on the law, whether they be judge,
magistrate, practising lawyer, journalist, politician, or whatever. As a politician and a
member of the House, and as a lawyer, I will state my view of the law, and I shall exercise
that right to the full.
As I understand it, five issues arise from the argument relating to legality. The first is
whether, in the National Airways Corporation's empowering statute, the New Zealand
National Airways Act of 1945-
Mr Courtney: Why don't you sing it?
Mr McLAY: Not only will I sing it, but I will put it into verse if the member for Nelson
really wants me to, because that is probably the only way he will understand it. Is there
anything in the NAC empowering Act that prevents the corporation merging its operations
with those of Air New Zealand? One can read through the 1945 statute and find that not one
word prohibits NAC from merging its operations with those of any other airline-let alone
Air New Zealand.
Mr Hunt: Come on. That's only a slick lawyer's argument.
Mr McLAY: I wish the member for New Lynn would be silent for a moment. If he
regards what I am saying as a slick lawyer's argument perhaps he would like to produce an
unşlick lawyer's argument in answer to it. He knows that there is no argument against it, and
nothing in the 1945 Act prevents NAC from merging its operations with those of Air New
Zealand. I refer him to section 13, and I suggest that he reads it. Secondly, is there anything
in the memorandum or articles of association of Air New Zealand to prevent it merging its
operations with NAC? I have a copy of the amended memorandum and articles of
association of Air New Zealand, and not one memorandum or article of association of Air
New Zealand prevents Air New Zealand from merging its operations with those of NAC. If
nothing prohibits either of the two companies from merging operations, then the merger is
legal. We have heard something about licences. Is there anything in the National Airways
Corporation's empowering statute to prevent it from transferring its licences to Air New
Zealand? Again, I have checked the Act. I guess the member for Mangere will be the next
Opposition speaker.
Mr Lange: You're wrong.
Mr McLAY: Well, if the member for Mangere is not to follow me perhaps it is because
he, as the Labour Party's spokesman on justice, does not agree with the legal argument put
forward by the Labour Party in this debate. I emphasise that nothing in NAC's empowering
Act prevents it from transferring its licences to Air New Zealand. Nothing in Air New
Zealand's memorandum and articles of association prevents it from taking over the licences
of the National Airways Corporation. Therefore, because there is no legal prohibition, it is
not illegal.
The final point is whether the Air Services Licensing Authority approved the transfer of
the licences from NAC to Air New Zealand. It is a proven fact and I thank the member for
Mangere for reminding me of it-that, on 31 March 1978, the Air Services Licensing
Authority approved the transfer of every one of NAC's air services licences to Air New
Zealand. That, too, was legal, as was the right of Air New Zealand to receive them. The
member for Mangere knows that, if something is not expressly prohibited by the law, or by a
memorandum in the articles of association of a particular company, then it is legal.
The matter before the House tonight is whether or not we should approve, in principle,
the merger of these two airlines-the member for Rangitikei is trying to interject; suddenly
he is becoming an interjector, and all the standards he was intending to impose on this
Chamber have suddenly disappeared in his desire to take part in the debate. I say again that
the House is being asked to agree, in principle, to the merger of these two airlines, but the
Opposition is endeavouring to obscure the issue by raising arguments of illegality. I suggest
that the five questions I have raised, and the five answers I have given, show categorically
that the merger we are debating tonight is undeniably a legal merger.

Hon. C. C. A. MCLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. As I said in my introductory speech, this Bill is designed to clarify the
provisions determining the appropriate licensing authority for harbour ferry services
operated in the vicinity of a regional district. This will be achieved by the addition of a new
subsection to section 120A of the Transport Act, which will provide that a harbour ferry
service operated between terminals, within or in the vicinity of the boundaries of a regional
district, shall be deemed to be operated within that district. Thus, the Bill will correct an
anomaly that has arisen in respect of the licensing of harbour ferry services in Auckland.
I explained in my introduction speech that in 1971 the Government decided that
passenger service licensing in the district of a regional authority should be dealt with by one
authority, the Regional Transport Licensing Authority. In 1974 the Government of the day
decided that harbour ferry service licensing should also be dealt with by the regional
licensing authority. I think I explained this to the House at the time of the Bill's introduction
As members will be aware, an anomaly has arisen because the territory of the Auckland
Regional Authority extends only to the high-water mark. It has been pointed out that this
means that the Auckland Regional Licensing Authority has no jurisdiction over harbour
ferry services. Indeed, a recent decision by the Transport Licensing Appeal Authority
upheld this point of view. The situation has therefore arisen that every decision taken by the
Auckland Regional Transport Licensing Authority, in respect of harbour ferry services since
October 1974, is now in doubt. This Bill is needed to validate the harbour ferry decisions
taken and the licenses issued in good faith.
I shall now describe the Bill. Clause 1 is the short title. Clause 2 is made up of four
subsections defining a harbour ferry service operated, or intended to be operated, between
terminals all of which are within, or in the close vicinity of, the boundaries of a regional
district. I shall point out that "on or in the near vicinity"-and, as the member for Timaru


## p. 2091 (#353) ###########################################

25 July
2091
Transport Amendment Bill (No. 2)
will remember, this point has previously been raised-refers to the shoreline of a regional
district. It does not mean a depot 10 miles inland. Subsection (2) states, in effect, that every
decision relating to harbour ferry service licensing by a regional transport licensing
authority, prior to the enactment of the Bill, shall be valid and effectual. Subsection (3)
validates retrospectively to 29 October 1974. Subsection (4) provides that where an appeal
authority has, on the grounds of jurisdiction, allowed an appeal against a decision of the
regional transport licensing authority, that appeal shall be heard again.
The effect of the Bill is to put into effect the intention of Parliament that the 1974
amendment should give regional transport licensing authorities the job of harbour ferry
service licensing in regional districts. It was unfortunate that the 1974 amendment
overlooked the fact that the territory of the regional district in question extended only to the
high-water line. If this fact had been picked up and the 1974 amendment properly worded,
this Transport Amendment Bill (No. 2) would not be needed.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): The Opposition agrees with the Bill, and the need
for the measure outlined by the Minister is clearly understood. The circumstances arise from
time to time when more than one Act is involved in an operation, wherever it is. The
transport area is particularly susceptible to this sort of thing. The Transport Amendment Bill
1974, as the Minister points out, conferred jurisdication on the regional transport licensing
authority to deal with the harbour ferry licences that were operated or intended to be
operated within the district of the regional authority, but could not do so when the Auckland
Regional Authority Act 1963 was considered in relation to the Transport Amendment Act
1974. It is difficult to cover every eventuality but if the circumstances outlined had been
considered at the time these difficulties might not have arisen. We on this side of the House
agree there is no alternative but to pass this amending Bill, to ensure that the intention of the
1974 Act can be operated. For that reason, we believe there is no point in carrying the
debate further, except to record that the point is taken, and the need for the legislation is
quite clear. The Opposition supports it.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I rise to thank the honourable
member, and the Opposition, for their co-operation. The sooner this anomaly is put right,
the better. I appreciate the Opposition's concern.
Bill read a second time.
NEW ZEALAND REGISTER OF OSTEOPATHS INCORPORATED BILL
Second Reading

Osteopaths are therapists who use manipulative techniques similar to those employed by
chiropractors. Both forms of treatment flourish in America, and to a lesser extent in Canada,
Britain, and Australia. The Bill provides for a fine, not exceeding $200, for any person
convicted of claiming to be on the register when he is not.

15. Mr LA VARIS (Taupo) to the Minister of Internal Affairs: What maintenance and

Minister of Internal Affairs replies: "For the year ended 31 March 1973, $6,029 was spent on
a wide range of maintenance works that includes jetties, ramps, navigation aids, and weed
clearance. Minor capital works on jetties, etc., totalled $1,132. For the 1974 year, a similar

nature amounted to $3,685. For the year ended 31 March 1976, completion of the marina
involved an expenditure of $16,199, while maintenance work on boating facilities, etc.,
totalled $12,025. For 1977, capital work was concentrated on improvements to the
Motuoapa marina, involving major dredging work on the access channel and also work at the
Taupo Landing Reserve on toilets and underground power reticulation to the total value of
$67,730. General maintenance around the lake amounted to $12,928. For the last financial
year ended 31 March 1978, further work was done at Motuoapa and the Taupo Landing
Reserve totalling $87,375, while maintenance, dredging, together with other general
maintenance, amounted to $21,824."
