URGENT QUESTION
Dr Patel- GMS Benefit
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Health: What is the position of Dr
C. M. Patel's patients now that the doctor has had his social security benefit payments
suspended for 6 months?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The honourable member does not appear to
understand the situation regarding Dr Patel's patients. It would perhaps be helpful if I
summarised the position. This doctor, over a long period of time, had been seeing very large
numbers of patients-up to 120 in 1 day. The Department of Health considered that it was
highly improbable that he could provide a good standard of medical service to such an
excessive number of patients. A GP seeing about 50 patients each week day, all in his
surgery-and this is above the average-25 percent of whom were elderly, 25 percent
children, and 50 percent others-which is the general pattern-would receive by way of
GMS benefits at current rates $32,032 for a 50-week year. His charges to patients would be
additional. If he charged each patient only $1 he would earn an additional $12,500 above the
$32,032 GMS. Dr Patel, in the last financial year, received $55,000 by way of GMS. What he
received as additional payment is not known. In accordance with standard practice, two
independent Auckland medical practitioners of wide experience undertook an informal
inquiry, and, as a result of their findings, recommended that a complaint against Dr Patel
should be lodged with the Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Committee, which is a statutory
committee established under the Medical Practitioners Act. I accepted this advice. The
Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Committee recommended that while Dr Patel's patients
would still be eligible for GMS benefits, the doctor would not be able to claim these benefits
direct from the Department of Health by means of the schedule system for the next 6
months. Instead, the patients could claim these benefits through the refund system. I
accepted the recommendations of the disciplinary committee. Patients of Dr Patel are,
therefore, not being penalised. I do not intend to review my decision in this matter. It is
based on a recommendation of a statutory body of practising and respected doctors and one
lay person, who had heard all the relevant evidence, including the testimony of Dr Patel. If
he was unhappy about the result he could have appealed to the Medical Council. He chose
not to do so.

Inflation
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I move, That this House notes with satisfaction the decline in the
annual rate of inflation as shown by the latest publication of the consumer price index, and
further notes with interest how inflation rose steeply under the Labour Government and has now
been steadily brought back by National as shown by the following figures for the June years
since 1972: 1972, 7.4, National Government; 1973, 7.6, National and Labour; 1974, 10,
Labour; 1975, 14.9, Labour; 1976, 17.7, Labour and National; 1977, 14.1, National; 1978,
12.2, National; and even more signficant is that the last two quarterly figures show an annual
rate of inflation of less than 10 percent, thus confirming the success of National's economic
management.
The debate on this motion must centre around the record of the Labour Government
from 1973 to 1975 and the National Government from 1976 until now. The Labour
Government was a Government of high and rising inflation, which the figures prove.
Mr Hunt: Here come the inaccuracies.
Mr BIRCH: There is nothing inaccurate about the figures, which have been prepared by
the Government Statistician and are well documented in the archives of the House. Inflation
increased from 5 percent in 1972 to 17.7 percent at the time the Labour Government was
thrown out of office.
Mr Wetere: What year was that?
Mr BIRCH: The June 1976 year, and that increase was a major factor in the Labour
Government's defeat in the 1975 election. Those steeply rising figures under Labour
disguised the fact that a large lump of taxpayers' money was hidden in the estimates under
the Stabilisation vote. The figures did not reflect the fact that Post Office, Railways, and
electricity charges were being heavily subsidised. Immediately it took office the National
Government, in terms of its promise to the electors, substantially removed those subsidies,
and despite that, the inflation rate gradually came down-not as fast as we would have
liked-until it was back to 12.2 percent in the 1978 June year. What is even more significant
is that, in the last two quarters, it came back to 2 percent in March and 2.6 percent in June,
which gives the lowest annual inflation rate since 1974.
During those years, when Labour was pushing up inflation, section prices rose by 137
percent, representing an annual increase of 44 percent. Section prices went up each year by
almost a half. They rose from $3,800 to $9,167 on average throughout New Zealand. All that
was bad enough, but compare that record with National's record. After 2 years the increase
in section prices has been 19.7 percent, an annual increase of just over 9 percent, compared
with an annual increase of 44 percent under the Labour Government. In the 3 years of

Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): The claim, based on two quarterly figures, that the

economic management. Nothing could be further from the truth.
In a complex economy, one cannot claim that a minor and doubtful success in one
aspect of it has any real meaning, unless the total economic performance of the Government
will stand up to examination in all areas. It is highly unlikely that the Government will
achieve an inflation rate of less than 11 percent measured over a full year. The Government's
claim of a 1 percent to 2 percent reduction in the inflation rate is, of course, an admission

economic and social cost to far too many people. The marginal success with inflation must be
related to the cost in unemployment, which is still rising and, under our restrictive methods

inflation has come about by throwing a huge number of people out of work. When it
sacrifices that number of people upon the altar of a 1 percent to 2 percent drop in the rate of
inflation, has the Government got its social and economic priorities right?
Another major social cost to society for the Government's endeavours to reduce
inflation has been the denial, to far too many people and families, of the right to decent

the Government's attempts to control inflation. A drop in the inflation rate of between 1
percent and 2 percent has been achieved by denying at least 7000 families the right to own a
home of their own. The question must be asked is: has the Government got its social and
economic priorities right when it sacrifices that number of people on the altar of a mere 1
percent to 2 percent drop in the rate of inflation increase?
It is political claptrap for the Government to claim that a small reduction in the inflation
rate is a measure of the success of its economic management, because a barely measurable
reduction has been achieved by transferring problems elsewhere, not by correcting them.
Under the Government's financial policy it is impossible for the inflation rate to be reduced

The Government claims that a small reduction in inflation shows the success of

Income Tax Reform
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): I move, That this House notes the repeated calls by
the Leader of the Opposition for radical reform of the income tax structure, notes with pleasure
that the Labour Party is soon to announce its policy on income tax reform and agrees that it is
high time that New Zealand had a tax system which provides genuine assistance to those on
low and middle incomes, does not discriminate against families because of the age and number
of their children and provides a real incentive for New Zealanders to work their way out of the
economic doldrums which National's policies have promoted.
The fundamental principle of Labour's new tax policy is that every New Zealander has
the right to earn a basic living income without paying any tax, and, further, has the right to
expect the value of that basic tax-free living income will be maintained and increased to take
account of any movement of inflation or wages. New Zealand taxpayers do not have the
right to live in luxury without paying any taxes. However, they do have the right to a basic
income free of tax. Therefore, Labour's tax plan starts with a basic tax-free living income,
which, together with the extra tax relief for families with children, should make it possible
for the ordinary New Zealand family to have a decent standard of living on one income.
This is how it will be done. The extra relief for families will make it possible for a one-
income family to earn the following amounts without paying any tax: a family with one child,
$100 a week; with two children, $105 a week; and with three children, $110 a week, plus $2
for each additional child. To recap: Labour's policy is based on the belief that every New
Zealander has a right to a basic living income-not a luxury income-before paying tax. I
shall now tell members how that will affect the ordinary New Zealand family. For a start,
more than 400 000 New Zealand taxpayers will be able to forget about taxation.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: Why?
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS: The Deputy Prime Minister asks why. The answer is that under
Labour's plan 400 000 New Zealanders will no longer have to pay income tax. They can
forget the hassle associated with paying income tax, because Labour will free them from the
obligation of any income tax at all. Women who work part time to supplement the family
income, students who work to further their education and New Zealand's future, and
apprentices, the lowest paid full-time workers in the community, and many other groups,
will get a helping hand. Under Labour Government, more than 400 000 New Zealanders
who pay tax today, will pay no tax at all. The National Party objects, but those who object
have forgotten that these 400 000 taxpayers pay less than 3 percent of all personal income
tax, which is a very small amount. The cost to the private sector and the public sector of
collecting this 3 percent is enormous. It might not be far short of the revenue gained by the
Government.
The Labour Party's policy is a just policy, it is fair policy, and it is an equitable policy.
Under that policy, widows with teenage children, earning between $100 and $200, will no
longer be called upon to pay $17 a week, or $884 a year, more tax than a married man with
one child. In fact, a widow who went out to work would have her tax reduced by between
$600 and $1,000 on that income, depending upon the number of her children. Likewise, a
married man with a family of school-age children will no longer have to pay $468 a year more
than a married man with one child below school age. Under Labour's proposals a married
man with children at school will save between $400 and $800 a year, depending upon the


## p. 2106 (#368) ###########################################

2106
26 July

number of children in his family. Also, the fifth birthday of the youngest child would not cost
that family $468 a year, and force the mother out to work, as the Government is doing.

change the superannuation scheme, but its tax proposals would ensure that the genuine
pensioner, the superannuitant with no extra income, got a fair deal. Single superannuitants,
with no extra income, would save $15.70 tax per fortnight. That is a saving of $408 a year-
$408 a year more for the genuine pensioner to spend. Likewise, married superannuitants
would save $339 a year each, if they have no other income. We have the spectacle today of
the Minister of Social Welfare announcing that married superannuitants will get an increase
of 23c a week to offset the 23c increase in taxation imposed by the Government in its Budget.
But, on 4 July, the Prime Minister wrote in an article in Truth that superannuitants would get
a tax reduction. He was wrong then. That was the Prime Minister's mistake number one.
The Prime Minister claimed in the House that a married man on $120 a week would pay
no more than $338.50 in tax under National. He was wrong again. The lowest amount a man
on $120 can pay is $409.76. The Prime Minister was wrong again; that is just two cases. The

thought that hundreds of single-income families would be hundreds of dollars worse off.

under Labour's proposals would be hundreds of dollars worse off, unless its income was in
excess of $20,000 a year. I challenge any member opposite to produce one single-income

would be paid on a $20,000 income. The country needs Labour's tax reduction policies

because they are fair, because they are just, and because people would be treated equally.
Those on the same income and with the same size family would pay the same tax. A married
man on $150, with three children, irrespective of the ages of those children, would pay the
same tax as any other married man with three children.
That is not so today. The difference in taxation could be as much as $728 in any year.
The policy that the Government proposes to force on the country on 1 October is an unjust
policy; it is not fair. It taxes a widow with three teenage children $17 more than it taxes a
widow with one child under the age of five. It taxes a married man with school-age children
$468 more than another married man whose child does not yet go to school. It forces a family
to pay $468 a year in tax the day its youngest child goes to school. The Government's
taxation policy is not just or fair. Labour's policy will change all that. It will restore full
employment, increase production, restore self-reliance, and provide a decent standard of
living for everyone, and a choice for an ordinary family to stand on its own feet. Labour's
policy is based on the principle of providing a tax-free income for all New Zealanders. A
married man with one child, in a single-income family, could earn $100, paying no tax at all.
A working widow with one child could earn $90 and not pay any tax. The two-income family
with one child would be able to earn $130 without paying tax.

Import Reduction
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): On behalf of the
member for Tauranga I move, That this House takes notice of the report from the Department
of Statistics, in the New Zealand Herald of 18 July 1978, that private imports for the year to
November 1978 are estimated to reduce to $2,609 million, a decrease of 14.3 percent; a further
and continuing justification of successful Government economic policy, and a concrete
indication of the responsible reaction of importers and industry, to assist New Zealand to
overcome exchange problems while still maintaining exports.
This motion brings to the attention of the House the success of the Government's
economic and import management policies. The quote from the Department of Statistics
release on 18 July 1978 indicates that private imports for the year ending in November 1978
will be $2,609 million, compared to $3,045 million for the previous year, a reduction of 14.3
percent.
There is no doubt that economic and import policies implemented by the last Labour
Government were disastrous. For the year ended November 1972-the month of the general
election-imports amounted to $1,072 million. When the former Labour Government left
office 3 years later in the year ended November 1975-imports had increased to $2,242
million. The Government Statistician reported an increase in imports of 118 percent.
I shall now take the projection for the year ending 1978, so that we can look at private
imports during the 3-year stewardship of the National Government. According to the
Government Statistician's projection, imports will have increased from $2,242 million for the
year ended November 1975 to $2,609 million for the year ending November 1978, an
increase of 16 percent. I emphasise that during the 3-year term of the former Labour
Government the value of private imports increased by 118 percent, and during the 3-year
term of the National Government, to November 1978, it will increase by 16 percent. That is
an indication of the difference in management between the Labour Government and the
National Government. In 1975 we did not say that we would impose further import controls;
we said we would institute policies of economic management, and the figures I have quoted
testify that those policies have been successful.
I shall now refer to statements made earlier in the year by very prominent members of
the Labour Opposition. I believe that those statements are regarded seriously, and should be
regarded seriously as we near another general election. First, I quote a statement made by
the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, from a speech he made to Petone Rotary Club. In a
press release from his office on 11 April this year he said: "There may be no alternative to
imposing at least some form of import controls." The import controls that operate today are
very similar in content to those the previous National Government had introduced by the

Labour Party's Tax Policy
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): On behalf of the member for Manukau I move,
That this House, noting the increase in direct personal taxation that has taken place in the last
10 years, from 10½ percent to 21 percent of income, also notes the basic injustice of the present
system which taxes a man with teenage children $14 more than a man with a child under 5,
therefore eagerly looks forward to the Leader of the Opposition's proposed announcement of
Labour's tax policy on Monday which promises to restore fairness, simplicity, incentive,
reward, and a basic tax-free living allowance for all New Zealanders. This motion could not
be more timely, because the tax packet announced by the Leader of the Opposition is the
biggest slash in income tax promoted by a political party. Under the present system of
taxation the average man pays 21 percent of his income to the Government as taxation,
which means that the ordinary working man works one day a week for the Government.
Under the Labour Party's scheme the average man will pay only 8.8 percent of his
income as taxation, which means that he will work less than one day a fortnight for the
Government. The Labour Party's scheme will restore the position to that of 10 years ago.
Many people who work overtime and who do not receive any allowance work more than one
day a week for the Government.
The Labour Party's scheme is simple and just. It is also honest, because all the figures
have been released so that people can judge for themselves. More than 80 percent of New
Zealanders will benefit from the Labour Party's bold plan to slash income tax. The scheme
will help the economy by putting money back into people's pockets so that they can afford to
buy. The surcharge on overseas exchange will mean that New Zealanders will buy New
Zealand goods with their extra cash, and, therefore, our economy will get the boost it needs.
For the past 3 years the ordinary man has been steadily screwed down by the
Government's income tax system. The Government has made much of its so-called generous
Budget. However, many people do not realise that despite the generous tax cuts the Minister
of Finance claims he has made, the Government will collect more money from income tax
this financial year than it did last year.
The Government has criticised freezing workers. The country needs the freezing
workers, and there is a need for them to work overtime. Under the scheme announced by
the Labour Party, freezing workers will receive a 40c rebate, payable immediately, if they
work overtime, and a $1 rebate, payable immediately, if they work a shift. The average man
can see the advantage of that. Not only has the Government doubled the amount of income
tax the average person is paying in real terms, but it has also upset the whole economic
balance
I should like to mention the tax savings people can expect under the Labour Party's
scheme. A man earning $140 a week with three teenage children will be $986.96 a year better
off. What is wrong with that? People earning $140 a week, which is the average wage, need
tax relief, and the scheme announced by the Labour Party is over and above everything the

Second Reading
Mr SPEAKER: Before I call the honourable member for Rangiora perhaps I should
point out that the Bill, which establishes a community service scheme, provides in clause 6(2)
for the scheme to be paid out of public money. Therefore it is not competent for the House
to proceed with the second reading in the absence of a message from His Excellency the
Governor-General. Notwithstanding that, the House sometimes permits a second reading
debate, at the conclusion of which the Bill is ruled out of order and struck off the Order
Paper. Is it the pleasure of the House that a debate proceed on this occasion?
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I think you should be
aware that on behalf of the Opposition its Whips have offered the Government Whips a
1-hour debate on this Bill, as has been customary for second readings of private members'
Bills this year. We are quite happy for leave to be granted to the member for Rangiora on
the basis of a 1-hour debate, split equally between the Government and the Opposition.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister): I realise that as the Bill involves an
appropriation it is competent for any member of the House to prevent a debate.
Mr Prebble: Don't you want a debate?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The Opposition states that it is content to have a 1-hour
debate. The only point I want to raise is that there happens to be time to devote the evening
to the second readings of two private members' Bills.
Mr Hunt: An hour each.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The second Bill does not involve an appropriation.
Therefore, the debate could go on as long as members wish to speak. On this occasion we
thought we might devote 1 hours to each measure. I have been in Opposition and have used

the whip hand in the matter, and can prevent a debate. However, I suggest that we should
devote 1 hours to each of the two private members' Bills.

Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. First, I
thank the House for the opportunity to discuss the Community Service Bill on a second
occasion, bearing in mind that of necessity, and by virtue of its drafting, it involves an
appropriation. There has been much interest in the measure. I have received many
constructive comments from many people, and I thank them very much.
There has, of course, been some degree of misunderstanding. I suppose that is not
unreasonable, because of the short time- a mere 2 weeks-that people have had to discuss
it. I have been considering it for at least 18 months, and have had the opportunity to consult
a number of people in New Zealand, and a number of organisations overseas.
The Bill is not designed to overcome youth unemployment, as has been suggested by
some people. What it is designed to do is encourage young people to involve themselves
more closely in their local communities. If I were attempting to do something about youth
unemployment in this measure, I would have introduced a much more comprehensive Bill.
I noticed in today's Evening Post a reference to a submission made yesterday by the
Returned Services Association to the Committee on Violent Offending. I believe it is worth
quoting: "It is our firm belief that the concept of service which, in our time, took the form of
military service and which we now believe should be translated into community service, must
be inculcated into the minds and thinking of our young people, both male and female, from
an early age." I support that concept.
In Denmark, a much more comprehensive system of community service has been
introduced as an alternative to compulsory military training. I have a copy of the legislation
and the draft regulations associated with that legislation in front of me. The object of the
community service in Denmark, which extends over a period of 8 to 11 months, is, first, to
give national servicemen who object to compulsory military training the opportunity to do
in-service training in a camp where they receive instruction that will be useful to them later.
They do the remainder of their service at stations for work in the community or in
institutions where they can take advantage of, and make a contribution to, their own
upbringing and to the common good of the community. It appears that these young Danes
are stationed, for preference, in different kinds of institutions catering for children,
adolescents, elderly people, and handicapped persons, or promoting cultural and
institutional pursuits.
As I said, if I wanted that sort of scheme I would have introduced a different sort of Bill.
The Bill before the House is of much more modest proportions. One of the letters I received
during the last few days was from the National Youth Council of New Zealand, and I was
rather disappointed with this comment: "The provision by the Bill for the teaching of
'knowledge, practical skills, and expertise of use and benefit to himself and his community' is
unrealistic." The words quoted come from clause 3(1). I believe that the scheme I have put
forward would achieve that basic objective. It would introduce young people to community
service, and the type of schemes they would take part in are set out quite clearly in clause 3.


## p. 2121 (#383) ###########################################

26 July
2121
Community Service Bill
For example, programmes and training in civil defence and first aid are suggested, and I
believe that all young people could benefit from such instruction.
The sort of work young people would be asked to do, apart from training programmes,
would be work in public and private hospitals and health centres and in charitable
institutions, work on land owned by local authorities or by the Crown, or work with
voluntary agencies. There are endless opportunities in the community for young people and
older people to participate in such work.
Supervision is important, because by and large we would be dealing with young people
who were either still at school or who had just left school. The Bill provides for supervisors
to be employed and to be paid. There are many people among the thousands of retired New
Zealanders who could work in a supervisory capacity, as carpenters, engineers, or in the 101
other occupations in which they were actively engaged in their previous employment, and
many would be willing to give their services unpaid to help supervise the work envisaged.
Community service workers themselves would be unpaid. One criticism that has been
offered is that because community service workers would not be paid the scheme would be
available only to the children of rich parents. That is absolute nonsense, and the sort of
reaction one would expect in an election year, but not last year or the year before. We are
talking about a period of service of between 100 and 200 hours, and clause 8(2) expresses a
preference for persons who enrol while still at school or shortly after leaving school. The
whole thrust of that provision is to enable young people to work during holidays or the
weekend, so that their service would not interfere with full-time employment, and so that
persons of all socio-economic groups could take advantage of the scheme if it were set up.
I was interested in a matter raised by the Anglican Social Service Council of
Christchurch in response to my sending it a copy of the Bill. It asked me to explain the role of
the director. The director of community services would have overall responsibility for the
scheme, and in certain limited circumstances an opportunity to organise programmes on a
national basis. One national programme that could well be arranged by the director is civil
defence. The responsibility for the administration of schemes in particular areas, however,
would be in the hands of local committees. They would have three representatives, one from
the local authority and one from local voluntary service organisations that had signified their
support for the scheme. Of course, there is room for a third person. General administration
would not fall back on the many youth groups already in the community doing worth-while
work.
I was particularly interested in a comment from the senior pupils of the Hawarden Area
School. I believe it sums up the reason for the introduction of the Bill. They said: "The
community seems very apathetic, so something like this would encourage a better
community spirit." That is the concept behind the Bill; it is an introduction to community
service for young people.

HOSPITALS AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. The Bill
provides an easy and simple remedy for the gross waste of time in dealing with problems that
stem from ill-considered, unmandated, insensitive, or indifferent decisions of hospital
boards. The Bill, if adopted, would give the public the right to object to such decisions and to
make hospital boards more accountable for decisions that seem arbitrary and do not have the
authority of the ballot box. My Bill is aimed not solely at St. Helens Hospital, but at any
hospital that may be subject to any arbitrary judgments and decisions made by hospital
boards, and for which there is no justification, other than that which the boards secretly hold
to themselves and are not prepared to defend publicly.
On the introduction of the Bill I tried to keep off the specific issue of St. Helens,
because I realised that it was an issue that had split society in some ways and on which there
were different viewpoints. The object of my Bill is to bring hospital boards to task when they
make a judgment that is not generally acceptable to the public. All that it asks is that the
hospital board's decision should be subject to protest and objection from the members of the
public most directly concerned. It would provide for adequate public discussion and
objection, but the Government has denied the public the opportunity of that discussion by
refusing to allow the Bill to go to a select committee. In fact, the issue that the Bill should be
referred to a select committee forced the third division in the House this year.
The legislation was not introduced in any political vein; it was not intended to be
political, and it was not anticipated that the House would divide on the issue. I thought we
might have a common sense approach to the matter, but the Government would not allow
the issue to be publicly aired. I am afraid that that judgment by the Government will
seriously embarrass the National candidate for Island Bay, just as the attitude of the Labour
member on the hospital board has embarrassed the former member for Kapiti who has some
aspirations in Island Bay.
I have no reason now to keep off the specific issue of St. Helens. What the Bill-with all
its imperfections in drafting-asks is that the people of the region should be consulted on any
hospital board decision on the closing or restricting, or changing the use of any hospital, and
that the public should have the right of objection. If the Bill was to be enacted, it would
restrain hospital boards throughout the country from arbitrarily closing, or restricting, or
changing the use of any hospital under their charge, but it would not remove any hospital
board rights. My constituents will be disappointed with the Minister's attitude to the Bill.
The Government has slammed the door on the public, except, as the Minister said, for


## p. 2130 (#392) ###########################################

2130
26 July
Hospitals Amendment Bill
representations to him through members of Parliament and through National candidates.
None of that seems to have had even the slightest effect on the position of St. Helens, and
during the election campaign some notice will be taken of that by the public.
The public will be disappointed with the attitude of the Minister, because, in the debate
on the introduction of the Bill, he said that he was anxious to ensure "that this matter is
considered by the public and by everyone concerned". Then he promptly slammed the door
on just that. How can the decision to close the hospital be adequately considered by the
public and by everybody concerned, to use the Minister's phraseology? The answer is simply
that until the introduction of the Bill there was just no way for proper or adequate
consideration to be given by the public to any hospital board action. The only voice for
everybody concerned, again to use the Minister's phraseology, is through the territorial local
authorities in the region, which speak for all aspects of the community and the environment
in which we live and raise our families.
The Minister said earlier that councils had no experience in health work. I never
claimed that they did, apart from their sanitation and drainage functions. The Bill does not
require them to have any experience in health administration; their job would simply be to
use their judgment on what they consider is good for the community. The Minister
misinterprets the Bill as a last-ditch stand to save St. Helens buildings physically as a
maternity hospital. The Bill provides for that only if a case can be soundly and reasonably
made to a local authority that is, by the very nature of its function, constantly considering
and judging community needs and what is good for the community in every sphere of
activity-private, commercial, industrial, and environmental. The Government's suggestion
that local authorities have no capability at all to consider representations about decisions on
hospitals would be quite shallow and really quite farcical, if it was not such an insult to the
common sense of those thousands of people in local government throughout the country
whose constant dedication is to building proper, happy, healthy communities. St. Helens is
an example of the weakness of the Minister's argument.
I think the member for Kapiti mentioned that there was a surplus of maternity beds in
the Wellington Hospital Board region. There seems to be something of an inordinate surfeit
of maternity beds, if we are to believe the figures that have been advanced. Surely that
indicates a startling lack of proper planning by the hospital authorities. Local authorities, in
their planning, would hardly have made such a blunder or created such a mess. The Minister
said that a city council could not deal in health administration; neither, it seems, can health
authorities. In fact, planning authorities take all factors into account-demographic, social,
as well as economic-so it would seem that they can consider planning decisions with some
expertise and experience.
The Minister's argument against the local authorities being the channel through which
objections would be heard is totally invalid. The Government does not want decisions of
hospital boards to be questioned in any way, but wants the boards to make judgments on
financial and managerial bases alone. Maternity care is not a matter that can be quantified in
terms of financial or managerial bases. Having children is not an illness, yet mothers will be
transferred from St. Helens to a hospital treating sickness, not treating health. Giving birth is
a matter of health, not of sickness or illness. Mothers do not want to be in hospitals that treat
illness; they want to be in their own environment, which they have in St. Helens. I wonder
why the Government cannot grasp that essential difference between a maternity hospital like
St. Helens and a public hospital dealing with illness. It is that essential difference that makes
St. Helens, and hospitals similar to it, unique.
St. Helens is a women's hospital, where women minister to the unique creativity of
women, and where mothers can, and do, have confidence in the staff. It seems to me that
throughout this whole affair the person least considered has been the mother. I would like to
quote Dr Jerold Lucey, professor of pediatrics at the University of Vermont, and a past
chairman of the American Academy of Pediatrics. He warns that important accepted
practices in maternity care are not supported by scientific research and are more rooted in
tradition among hospitals and health administrators. He says that a considerable body of
opinion supports this scepticism of his on maternity practices in the United States. He may
justify his scepticism on the grounds that 1 in 35 children born under the system in the United
States will be diagnosed as retarded, and 1 in 17 will be afflicted with some form of minimal
brain malfunction or learning disability. We can justifiably ask if his strictures on the health
administration in the USA might equally apply to New Zealand. We can look at these facts
from Dr Lucey, and I quote from a paper entitled "The cultural warping of child birth". It


## p. 2131 (#393) ###########################################

26 July
2131
Hospitals Amendment Bill
states: "While we are told of the value of eliminating small and medium-sized obstetric
services, we find that a national survey of US obstetric services carried out by the American
College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists reveals that, in general, the larger the obstetric
service, the greater the rate of infant and maternal deaths, and the stronger the affiliation
between the obstetrical service and a medical school, the greater the rate of infant and
maternal deaths. Undoubtedly some of these deaths result from the fact that there is a
greater incidence of high-risk mothers in larger teaching hospitals, for economic reasons, but
it is also possible that the greater tendency to intervene in the normal progress of labour and
birth in these institutions, in order to provide teaching opportunities, contributes to these
statistics and may also result in a disproportionately high incidence of neurologically
damaged children."
The statement by Dr Lucey, a foremost American paediatrician, gives a warning that
what has happened in the United States could happen in New Zealand. What happened
there is very serious and dangerous, and shows a marked lack of administrative knowledge
among the people who have to make the decisions. It shows a complete lack of judgment and
an absence of any understanding of trends of thought overseas. The love for St. Helens of
those who have benefited from its service demonstrates quite forcefully that, over the jumble
of maternal, natal, and infant mortality statistics, the hospital has a unique aura and a
particular atmosphere. I shall speak about that if I have time. Under our medical system the
obstetrician's job ceases with the child's birth. The paediatrician then takes over. The
professional midwives are the persons in charge of St. Helens. The midwives and other staff
at St. Helens are involved in the care of the child, not just with labour and delivery. The
midwife is conscious of the importance of providing individual attention for the mother and
the child both before and after labour. She creates a relationship that is missing in the clinical
set-up that will take over the role of St. Helens.
I recognise that the decision on St. Helens may by now be, regrettably and sadly,
irreversible. The Bill tries to stop ill-considered decisions being made in other parts of the
country. While the physical building may be closed for its present function, the saddest day
will come when the individuality of St. Helens is allowed to disappear. I seriously appeal to
the Minister, who has offhandedly set his hand implacably against the save St. Helens bill, to
do his utmost to transfer the spirit of St. Helens into the new surroundings, or whatever
building is prepared to accommodate the maternity facility. This will require imagination, of
which I hope the Minister is not devoid. It will require courage and self assertion. It means
the retention of the non-hierarchical structure in St. Helens.
In 1929, upon the recognition of a much lower maternal mortality rate in Holland, the
Dutch system of having every woman attended during normal labour by a midwife, without a
medical practitioner present, was adopted at St. Helens. An article in the Evening Post dated
14 August 1929 states: "There is a feeling in many quarters that it would be a definite
advantage if the charge of normal labour were more and more transferred to the midwife."
Is the absence of a hierarchical structure the same feature that distinguishes the St. Helens of
today from other modern maternity units, which lack atmosphere? The answer is yes, if we
compare St. Helens to a base hospital, such as in Wellington. All maternity units in New
Zealand produce similar statistical data. It appears that only those that have not retained a
hierarchical structure can lay claim to having a favourable atmosphere. Further investigation
would probably reveal that all base hospital maternity units do not necessarily lack
atmosphere. To be fair to such excellent maternity units as the Hutt Hospital, it would be
pertinent to assert that such a hierarchical structure is apparent only when the maternity unit
is linked to a clinical school, as is proposed in transferring St. Helens from its present site.
An article in the Evening Post dated 19 March 1977 states: "Dr Shand does not think
that it"-the atmosphere-"can be reproduced in a base hospital where midwives will
compete with medical students." It is difficult to imagine a healthy mental or moral
environment in which women are given unnecessary examinations to enable medical
students to get sufficient practice, but this will happen to people who were looking forward
to having their children at St. Helens, but who are now denied that opportunity. All
registered midwives at St. Helens are referred to as sisters. The matron is known as the
principal nurse. The rates of pay or hours of work do not differ markedly for those in
positions of greater responsibility, and most midwives, regardless of years of service or
qualifications, wear similar uniforms. A midwife is seen as an independent, flexible
operator, responsible for her own decisions and actions. Not only was normal labour
successfully transferred to the midwife, but the administrative functions of St. Helens were

What could be expected to happen under the Bill proposed by the independent member

and this, among other things, would have made doctors indentured civil servants.
Clause 4 proposes to replace two short subsections of section 55 of the Hospitals Act
with seven long and detailed sections. The critics of over-wordy legislation-and I believe
the Labour member for Mangere is one-will have their worst fears realised when they read
the Bill. The clause seems to be based on two beliefs. The first is that hospital boards cannot
be trusted. We heard the member enunciate that view tonight. He said repeatedly that the

representatives of the people, democratically elected triennially to deal with health services

When a board proposes to close an institution under its control it can be held accountable for

The thinking behind clause 4 is that detailed law is needed to keep hospital boards
accountable to the public. The member for Island Bay is advocating a sort of legislative
screwing down, and suggesting that, without the measures specified at tedious length in the
clause, hospital boards would surreptitiously close hospitals. Government members consider

approach to this local matter. Consider, for instance, as a hypothetical case, the position
when, for valid clinical reasons, it was decided to restrict a service of Wellington Hospital,
say the renal dialysis service. Under this clause the Wellington Regional Planning Authority
would hear objections and come to a conclusion. But patients requiring this service, as with
any regional specialist service, do not come from just the immediate area of the hospital.
They come from a widespread area, and the member for Island Bay knows that. Patients for
the renal unit come from as far north as Taranaki and Hawke's Bay and from the northern
end of the South Island. Bearing those factors in mind, why then should the Wellington
Regional Planning Authority-and leaving aside any questions of whether the authority has
the expertise to comment on a clinical matter of this kind-be the forum for public
discussion, when many of the people concerned are people the member espouses a concern
about, and may not live in the Wellington area.

debate. While that may sometimes be so, it is not always so. There have been closures, as I
am sure the member knows, of small, outdated, and little used maternity hospitals when the
public has recognised that, for the welfare of the mother and child, the hospital should be
closed and put to some other use. The hospital board can find this out without being dragged
through all the processes covered in this clause of the Bill.

It was interesting to note that the Labour Opposition is prepared to take legislative

many decades been delegated to elected ad hoc authorities-hospital boards. The member

hospital policy the Wellington Regional Planning Authority can be of no assistance to the
Minister, to the House, or to any other decision-making body. For that reason I believe the
Bill fails completely to achieve its objective.
The Hospitals Advisory Council has been established for the precise purpose of advising
the Minister on questions such as the one that has arisen in this instance-the question of
which hospitals should be closed and which should remain open. It is significant that the
membership of the Hospitals Advisory Council consists of a representative of the Hospital
Boards Association from the North Island-who in this case is the chairman of the
Wellington Hospital Board-a representative of the Hospital Boards Association from the
South Island, the Director-General of Health, the Commissioner of Works and
Development, the Secretary to the Treasury, and a further nominee of the New Zealand
Hospital Boards Association. There is no suggestion that there ought to be a representative
from any planning body or any regional authority. The suggestion that the answer should lie
with a regional planning authority underlines the fact that the Bill was misconceived.
I believe that those members who have expressed concern about the proposal to close
St. Helens Hospital should pin their faith on the Hospitals Advisory Council and make their
views known to that council. The council is not a rubber stamp. On previous occasions it has
reversed the decisions of hospital boards to close an institution. Generally, when there is
doubt about the matter, it sets up a subcommittee to investigate the problem. One of the
factors it traditionally takes into account is the degree of public consultation that has
preceded a decision to close a hospital.

Hospital Board undertook a very adequate series of public consultations. In fact, a public
hearing was held, and submissions were invited from the public. Forty-five detailed

Mr PREBBLE: This point is very important, because it relates to wnether this private

being involved is quite clear. If a Bill involves an appropriation, there must be a Governor-
General's message. There has been no Governor-General's message in relation to the Bill.
The word "appropriation" has already been interpreted quite clearly in Speakers' Rulings at
pages 20, 21, 22, 23, and 24, as also meaning the possibility of liability. Since this matter has
been drawn to my attention, I believe I have an obligation to draw it to your attention. I do
so because I believe the Standing Orders should be followed by all members.
Clause 4 makes it clear that any board may, with the prior consent of the Minister, close
a hospital, and goes on to say that any consent of the Minister given under subsection (1)
shall be so given on the recommendation of the regional authority for the region. Under the
provisions of the Bill it would be possible for a regional authority to decline permission to the
Minister, who would then have to decline permission to the hospital board to close the
hospital. The Minister's power to close a hospital is clearly limited by approval from the
regional authority, which might decline the request. Clearly, that is the main purpose of the
Bill. It is not incidental to it; and the member for Island Bay has obviously recognised that
the regional authority may refuse the request. This would mean that a hospital board would
have to keep the hospital open.
Section 89 of the Hospitals Act 1957, reprinted in 1970 in volume 3, states, on page
1943: "In respect of every financial year there shall be paid to the Board by way of grant, out
of money appropriated by Parliament for the purpose, such sum as the Minister may
determine as being necessary to enable the Board to carry out its functions." Under the
amendment introduced by the member for Island Bay, one of the functions of a hospital
board shall be-by order of the Minister-to keep a hospital open. Under another Act of
Parliament there is clearly an obligation on the Minister and on Parliament to appropriate
some money for that hospital. That being the case, it would appear that central to the Bill is
the strong possibility-in fact I should say probability-that if a regional authority refused
permission to a Minister the hospital board would have to keep the hospital open, which,
under section 89 of the Act, is one of the board's functions.
We, as a Parliament, are obliged to give money under that Act, and, therefore, it would
seem that the Bill does involve an appropriation. That being so, Parliament has no say in the
matter if the Government is not prepared to deliver a Governor-General's message. I
suggest that if the Bill does involve an appropriation, leave should be given to the member
for Island Bay to make a 5-minute reply.

there is nothing in the Bill that would require the Minister of Health to spend public funds to
keep a particular institution operating. If the honourable member goes back to the principal
Act he will find that it gives the power of the purse strings to the Minister; and under the Bill
his discretionary powers remain intact. No obligation is placed upon him in addition to that
imposed by the principal Act, as it stands.
Standing Order 324 and associated Speakers' rulings have established that the measure
will involve an appropriation only if the Crown is fettered as to the manner in which it shall
act, and I suggest that it is not so fettered. There is no suggestion in the Bill that the powers
given to the Minister under the principal Act are in any way trammelled by the Bill. The
Minister is not obliged to keep paying out money to a hospital board in order to keep one or
more of its institutions operating. You have made this point yourself.
I believe the position is as I have set it out. I refer you to Speaker's ruling 21/1, which
reads: "Where a private member's Bill contains an appropriation which is incidental to the
Bill and not the main object, the proper course is to allow the Bill to proceed to its second
reading..." The argument put forward by the Opposition is not whether there is an
appropriation, but whether the debate on the Bill should be allowed to proceed. The
Opposition wants to stop the member for Island Bay.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I should be grateful if the honourable member would come back
to the argument about whether I should rule the Bill out of order on the ground that it
involves an appropriation or otherwise. It is a difficult and fine point. I am sure the
honourable member realises that. I should not like him to stray too far.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: I have set out my argument. I submit that the Bill makes no

appropriation is involved and that the member for Island Bay should be allowed to continue
the debate on the Bill, although I concede that the Opposition's purpose is to stop it.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): May I offer yet a sixth opinion from a legal

Hospitals Amendment Bill
source. I suggest that the significant Speaker's ruling is 95/1, which reads: "An appropriation
clause is not only one that increases the amount, but alters the method of payment or the
persons to whom the money is to be paid. Any alteration in the method of payment or the
conditions under which it is paid out amounts to an appropriation clause, as well as by
increasing the amount or decreasing it." If a hospital within the jurisdiction of a hospital
board is kept open against the Minister's wishes, there must be some significant alteration in
the grant made by the Minister to the hospital board for that year's operations, whether the
quantum remains the same or is altered. The direction of it must necessarily be changed, and
in that respect there must be an appropriation in terms of that ruling.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The last argument from the member for
Henderson is satisfied in ruling 97/4 by Mr Speaker Lang. It reads: "A Bill to reduce the
open hours of hotels, the possible effect of the operation of which on revenue for taxation
cannot be foreseen, is not an appropriation Bill and does not require a message." I suggest
that the argument about expenditure could well be put the other way. The ruling would then
read, "A Bill to reduce the open hours of hospitals or maintain the open hours of hospitals,
the possible effect of the operation on which expenditure for an appropriation cannot be
foreseen, is not an appropriation Bill and does not require a message." The wording is
analogous in that respect, because it asks for an appropriation. Mr Speaker Lang said that a
Bill to reduce open hours does not involve an appropriation where the effect cannot be
foreseen. We cannot be sure, but the Bill may have some effect upon the open hours of a
hospital, and it is not an appropriation Bill.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): I refer to the matter raised by the Deputy Prime Minister in
respect of Speaker's ruling 21/1. It is quite clear that the purpose of the Bill is to achieve the
retention of a hospital unit funded by the hospital board when the Minister does not have the
support of a regional authority. Therefore, his hands are fettered. The Deputy Prime
Minister's argument is not relevant.
I refer to Speakers' rulings 95/3 and 98/3, and to section 89 (1) of the Hospitals Act 1957,
which states: "In respect of every financial year there shall"-and I submit that the word is
not "may" but "shall"-"be paid to the board by way of grant, out of money appropriated
by Parliament for the purpose, such sum as the Minister may determine..." However, his
discretion is modified by the use of the words "as being necessary to enable the board to
carry out its functions". That simply means that there shall be a payment and that the
Minister does have a discretion, although that discretion is limited by his assessment of what
the board needs to carry out its functions.
If the private member's Bill being promoted by the member for Island Bay is passed, the
functions of the board will be clearly defined-to run the hospital, in the absence of consent
from a regional or local authority. The Minister's discretion is at an end, because he might
say, or have an idea, of how much he should give for the running of that hospital. Although
the amount may not be the same amount thought necessary by the board, the argument is
irrefutable-something is required to run that hospital. That is the function of the Bill
promoted by the member for Island Bay. Therefore, because an appropriation is involved, it
clearly falls within the ruling.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I want to develop that a little
further. As a former Minister of Health I had the experience of having to cope not only with
the advice of the Hospitals Advisory Council and the board concerned, which wanted to
close a hospital, but also the continuing opposition of the territorial local body, which was in
favour of keeping it open. The reason for the hospital's closure was the impossibility of
staffing it. It is very clear that the purpose of the Bill is to perpetuate what was an effective
unofficial means of keeping a hospital open, in this case Paparoa Hospital in 1973. The local
authorities were not prepared to take the political consequences of going against loudly
expressed views, even though the hospital board-the authority specifically charged with
providing the hospital service-supported the closure. That is relevant to the Bill, the
purpose of which is to keep a hospital open irrespective of whether or not its need can be
established. Therefore, it must involve an appropriation.
Mr SPEAKER: This is one of those occasions in which the buck goes no further. I am
grateful to the six learned gentlemen, as well as other honourable members, who gave me
the benefit of their advice. I do not believe that the point made by the Deputy Prime
Minister is entirely appropriate, because the appropriation he referred to in Speaker's ruling
21/1 was incidental to a Bill. The appropriation normally envisaged would be that involved in
the printing of a Bill or the sending out of a few letters, and so on, which is only incidental,
and does not really involve an appropriation as such.

The Minister of Justice drew my attention to Speaker's ruling 97/4, which deals with

I have had legal advice from six learned gentlemen, and it appears to me that on the
strict legal interpretation it may be that the Bill does not involve an appropriation per se,
because although the Bill would require the Minister not to close the hospital until certain
procedures had been followed, it does not, on the face of it, require him to do so under the

and require him to provide the finance for keeping the hospital open. That is a rather too
narrow legal interpretation of the law.

common sense, aided by some legal advice and a little instinct, tells me that the effect of the
Bill would be to restrict the power of operation of the Minister. If it does restrict the power
of the Minister to close a hospital for one day, or even from one financial year to the next,
the power of the Minister is restricted in some form. Therefore, I feel bound to rule on the

QUESTIONS-ORAL
Fresh Skim Milk Labelling
1. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Health: Could he release the
findings of the committee set up to investigate the labelling of fresh skim (non-fat) milk, and
state whether the product needs to be labelled with a warning like that applied to powdered
skim milk on unsuitability for children under 2 years of age?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The Food Standards Committee, which advises
me in matters of this kind, has recommended that skim milk is not suitable for infant feeding
because fat soluble vitamins are removed, and the removal of fat makes skim milk
inadequate as an energy source. The committee has further recommended that liquid skim
milk should be easily identifiable and that the warning statement already applicable to skim
milk powder should be attached to the bottle in which liquid skim milk reaches the
consumer. It is proposed to amend the Food and Drug Regulations accordingly.
Hon. F. M. Colman: How soon will the amended regulations be brought into force?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I am afraid I cannot give an estimate. When I wrote to the Food
Standards Committee I asked it to forward a decision as soon as possible. I have now
received the decision, and action is being taken. I should think the time would be 2 or 3
weeks.
Otago Catchment Board
2. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Works and Development: What levels
of expenditure have been committed to North Otago by the Otago Catchment Board in each
of the last 3 years?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): The Minister of Works and
Development replies: "The Otago Catchment Board does not keep its accounting records on
a regional basis. Grant and subsidy expenditure can be assigned by scheme descriptions, but
the expenditure of funds received from other sources, such as the administration rate, cannot
be determined. Expenditure on which a grant or subsidy was paid was: 1975-76, $48,348;
1976-77, $22,357; 1977-78, $43,411."

Union Rolls
9. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Labour: Is it correct that the Bank Officers

## p. 2148 (#410) ###########################################

27 July

requires them to keep such a roll?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): This week I have received a letter from the
general secretary of the New Zealand Bank Officers Union informing me that the union has
written to the Registrar of Industrial Unions stating that it is "impracticable for them to
supply the information required under the Act". Section 175(i) of the Industrial Relations
Act requires that the rules of every union shall provide for the keeping of a register of union
members. However, for the purposes of the ballot the union is required to provide a list of all
persons who are entitled to vote that is, the adult workers bound by the unqualified
preference clause contained in the bank officers' award. Such a list will not necessarily match
the register of union members. Some persons not bound to join the union do so voluntarily.
They would not, however, be entitled to a vote in the ballot. On the other hand, there will
undoubtedly be some persons who are bound by the unqualified preference provision but
who do not in fact belong to the union. Such persons would be entitled to vote in the ballot.

PRIVATE INVESTIGATORS AND SECURITY GUARDS AMENDMENT BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Private Investigators and Security Guards Amendment
Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move,
That the report do lie upon the table. The Bill makes a number of changes to the Private
Investigators and Security Guards Act 1974. Although most of the changes are of a
procedural nature, certain substantive alterations have been made to the definition of a
private investigator and to the scope of a security guard's licence. An amendment has been
made also to the grounds on which a security guard's licence or certificate of approval can be


## p. 2152 (#414) ###########################################

2152
27 July
Private Investigators and Security Guards Amendment Bill
cancelled.
The committee received five submissions, two of which were supported by an
appearance to give evidence. The major submission came from the New Zealand Security
Industry Association, and made three points. First, in relation to clause 11-which adds to
section 58 of the principal Act a further ground for cancelling a security guard's licence on
the basis that he has been convicted of a crime of dishonesty-the association suggested that
the ground should also be one for refusing to grant a licence in the first instance. However, in
addition to the general responsibility of the registrar to approve only those persons who are
fit and proper, the principal Act also gives him power to refuse a licence if an applicant has
been convicted of dishonesty within 10 years of making his application. It is the committee's
view that those rules are adequate, without taking the further step of making a conviction for
dishonesty an absolute bar to obtaining a security guard's licence. Inquiries have revealed
that in this matter, the registrar had no difficulty in applying the provisions of the principal
Act.
The association suggested that some practical problems might arise from clause 15 of the
Bill, which provides that two copies of an application for a certificate of approval shall be
served on the registrar, who, in turn, has the responsibility of delivering a copy of the
application to the Police. Previously, the applicant himself delivered a copy of the
application to the Police, who had no means of knowing whether the application had been
properly filed with the registrar. Under the amendment the registrar himself, by forwarding
the document to the Police, will in effect be certifying that the application has been lodged,
and the Police will be able to act on that information. The committee is satisfied that few, if
any, practical problems will arise from this new procedure.
Under the principal Act a certificate of approval must show not only the name and
photograph of the security guard or private investigator but also the name and address of his
employer. Problems have arisen as a result of employees changing their employment during
the period of the currency of the certificate. The actual nature of the certificate-which is
effectively an identity card encased in plastic-renders it almost proof against alteration.
Clause 17 of the Bill therefore provides that, rather than display the information on the
certificate, the holder should be obliged to give, on demand, the name and address of the
licensee by whom he is employed. The association pointed out that notwithstanding this
procedure-which it appeared to approve-there might be a difficulty in that a certificate of
approval could show the address of an employer for whom the approved employee no longer
worked. This can, however, be overcome by removing altogether from the certificate any
reference to the employer. To ensure that a member of the general public who is dealing
with a security guard or a private investigator knows that he is entitled to the name of the
employer, we recommend that the certificate itself should be amended to state that such
information must be made available on demand.
A number of other matters were raised by the association. It suggested that, when an
employee was dismissed, the employer should be obliged to inform the registrar of the
reasons for dismissal. However, the committee regarded this as an undesirable practice, and
felt it was better for the association itself to act as a watchdog in these matters and to
maintain a list of unsuitable employees. The association also disagreed with the use of the
term "security guard", but the committee can find no more appropriate term. The
association also wanted hotel bouncers brought into the Act, but the committee feels that
their activities are sufficiently covered by the Crimes Act, although there may be some
future need for an amendment to the Sale of Liquor Act. The association also argued that a
licence should be issued on economic as well as other grounds, but the committee rejected
the proposal on the basis that it would result in a "closed shop". For practical and
administrative reasons, the committee did not accept proposals from the association that the
duration of a licence or certificate of approval be extended, and that approval of employees
be on the basis of a schedule or list supplied by the employer.
The select committee also listened with interest to the association's suggestion about the
training of security officers. However, it believes that this is basically the responsibility of the
industry itself and not that of the legislation or the registrar. The security industry is quite at
liberty to provide educational and training programmes for employees and, in the opinion of
the committee, it will be to its credit if it does so.
The other major submission was from Mr D. Cook of Wellington Investigations Ltd.,
who asked that credit bureaus and debt-collecting agencies should be brought under the Act.
The committee believes that while the activities of credit bureaus might require future


## p. 2153 (#415) ###########################################

27 July
2153
Private Investigators and Security Guards Amendment Bill
legislative attention, their commercial nature is so different from that of private investigators
and security guards that it would be inappropriate to include them under the principal Act.
Furthermore, such an extension would be well beyond the scope of the original Bill that was
referred to the select committee.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): Opposition members of the Statutes Revision Committee were
instrumental in bringing about some modest changes to the terms of the Bill; and the
committee reserved its position in particular on that part of the Bill relating to businesses or
people who are exempt from its provisions.
During the committee's perusal of the Bill, reference was made to the reasons for its
coming before the House-that it was, in fact, the culmination of some years of experience
in implementing the Act. Accordingly, it is appropriate that the House, and certainly the
Opposition, should refer to the work of the registrar the late Brian Shenkin, and that I
should express, on behalf of the chairman of the Statutes Revision Committee and those of
us who were his contemporaries and colleagues, our sadness at his tragic death, and our
conviction that he was a person who made the Act work, and who immersed himself in his
responsibilities as a registrar as fully as he immersed himself in other aspects of his
professional and social life. We mourn his passing but are glad that he was able to make
these recommendations to the department, so that we now have the opportunity of giving a
more precise edge to the Bill.
The Opposition is concerned that the Bill exempts debt-collecting agencies and credit
bureaus from legislative control. I accept the view expressed in the Statutes Revision
Committee that such control would be better exercised in a separate Bill dealing with those
particular topics, but I argue here, as I did in the committee, that debt-collecting agencies
and credit bureaus do in fact conduct investigations, do tail people, do investigate the
business and personal lives of those who are being pursued by members of the commercial
community, and can exercise a vigilance over private and commercial conduct, as well as try
to extract information from bankers, solicitors, and others who are privy to the commercial
secrets of the person under investigation.
It is idle to pretend that debt-collecting agencies and credit bureaus are only places of
record. They also actively ferret out the details of people's personal and business lives. The
Opposition is firmly convinced that people should have the assurance that those investigators
will be subject to the legal and ethical controls provided not only in the Act, but also in the
amended Bill now before the House. We believe that when the Bill was first introduced such
people were not meant to be exempt, because it was intended to bring down companion
legislation to control credit bureaus and to provide for the keeping of confidences and for
limitations on the way in which they could solicit information. That legislation has not
surfaced, and the exemption still applies.
It is good that the Bill provides a slight hemming-in or restriction of the scope of
activities of debt collectors and credit bureaus, but there is still insufficient control. We will
advance that argument later. The Opposition agrees with the Bill as reported back, on the
understanding that it should have a second reading.
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I had intended, during the second reading debate, to refer to
the contribution made by the late Brian Shenkin, who ensured that the 1974 legislation was
brought into good and proper effect. At this stage, I merely associate myself entirely with the
remarks made by the member for Mangere about Brian's efforts in this field.
The member for Mangere has drawn attention to the fact that the Bill is directed
towards the activities of credit bureaus, rather than of those who simply style themselves as
such. That represents a significant advance in the degree of control, if such is needed. When
reporting the Bill back to the House, and particuarly when commenting on credit bureaus, I
chose my words very carefully. I said that "while the activities of credit bureaus might
require future legislative attention, their commercial nature is so different from that of
private investigators and security guards that it would be inappropriate to include them
under the principal Act". Those words were taken down verbatim from the comments made
by the member for Roskill during the select committee's deliberations. As most members
know, the member for Roskill has had considerable experience over the years in matters of
credit and dealing with credit bureaus. I confess that I personally respected the judgment he
brought to the select committee. I merely draw it to the attention of the House that although
the matter mentioned by the member for Mangere was considered by the select committee,
the majority-including some members of the Labour Party-considered that it did not
appropriately come within the scope of the Bill.
Motion agreed to.

Further consideration of vote, Justice, $66,660,000; and the amendment proposed
thereto.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) expressed appreciation of his long and satisfying
association with the Department of Justice, both in Government and in Opposition. He had
had a happy association with successive Secretaries of Justice, and Under-Secretaries. He
appreciated the assistance he had received from staff at various levels, and particularly the
assistance given in the past 5 years by senior advisory staff, many of whom had laboured long
and uncomplainingly.
He asked the Minister for his views on staffing the courts with people who fully and
adequately represented the community in terms of sex, age, race, and other characteristics.
He knew that the Minister's views would depend on the recommendations to be made very
shortly by the Royal Commission on the Courts, whose deliberations would be conveyed to
members by the end of August. He had not the slightest doubt that the recommendations
would be far reaching.
He had lost some of his earlier enthusiasm for youthful appointments to the bench. He
was not referring to the distinguished occupants of the bench in New Zealand but based his
conclusions on his observations of events overseas. Having studied numerous judges, both in
person or through their writings, he had come to the conclusion that judges who had been
appointed at a younger age became more conservative as they advanced in years.
A person could spend too much time on the bench. Although he still believed that
young people on the bench had much to commend them, he thought a period of long service
ought to be varied in some way or another. Although judges occasionally presided over royal
commissions or commissions of inquiry, that practice was not favoured by some, including
Chief Justices. However, he believed that judges and magistrates welcomed the opportunity
of relief from what could become a drudgery. Although such persons had to bring humanity
and understanding to their work, it was impossible for any individual not to become
somewhat case hardened, and he hoped the royal commission would suggest an interspersing
of other activities with magisterial or judicial work as a welcome addition to such duties. He
enthusiastically advocated interchange between industry, Government, and academic life.
However, although many members of the bench would shine in academic work and in
business, it would be impossible to replace them with people with similar qualifications from
other sectors.
He believed that young people should more frequently be considered as justices of the
peace. Although he had been brought up in the orthodox tradition that only lawyers were
competent to administer justice and preside in courts of justice, he had later changed that
view as a result of his observations of the valuable work done by justices of the peace in some
of the Auckland courts. He hoped that younger people would be recommended for
appointment, because they could bring to the courts a better understanding of the offences
committed by people between the ages of 17 and 24, and, although they would probably not
be any less severe than older justices, they would be able to communicate with the offenders
more effectively. The sermon from the bench was often a waste of time, and of no value to
the offender, because the gap of age and experience between the person who formulated and


## p. 2155 (#417) ###########################################

27 July
Appropriation Bill-Estimates
2155
articulated the sermon and the person to whom it was addressed was so great that there was
no exchange. If the age gap was not so great there would be better communication.
He would like to think with some pride that he had helped to advance the part that
justices of the peace were now playing in the administration of justice. He had commissioned
the writing of a handbook for their information and education. Although there had been
some delay, the book was now in circulation, and a course was available through the
technical correspondence institutes. He was sure that, as a result, men and women of all
races would make a significant and valuable contribution to the work of the bench and to the
social problems dealt with.
The method of selection of justices of the peace should be looked at more carefully.
Although he had a great regard for the services rendered by the Royal Federation of New

Some registrars could be more active in ensuring a proper representation of the community

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) said that he was certain all members who

great interest, not only in 1978, but also in the decades to come. The magistrates that he had
appointed since he took office at the end of 1975 were probably all aged between 37 and 40,

earlier in some people than in others. The fact that a possible appointee was younger than 40
should not be held against him. The retiring age for magistrates was 68, and for judges 72;

would like younger people to be nominated, and many more women and representatives of
minority groups. Members should ensure that 50 percent of their nominations were women.
Justices of the peace were doing a very good job in helping with preliminary hearings
and minor offences. It was remarkable that they had built up a fund at their own expense,
the revenue from which went into their own self-education. Last year $9,000 had been
provided, and this year $12,000 had been voted to help in the education of justices of the
peace. He had recently presented the first certificate from the institute, which had done first-
class work.
The Government was constantly considering ways of providing punishments that would
fit the nature of the crime. A complete consolidation and revision of the Police Offences Act

the vote by $5 on the grounds that the administration of the Electoral Act had been found
wanting. Any problems in the administration of the Electoral Act would be resolved before

1975, and they were being paid for now.
