Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries
Agriculture and Fisheries (excluding Programmes V and VIII), $261,258,000.
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) said that the estimates provided a sum
of $60 million to be paid out to farmers under the vote for the rural retention scheme. In the
1971 Budget the Prime Minister had stated that no Government could justify the extensive
use of public funds to help farmers who were not in financial difficulties. How many of the
Minister's colleagues were receiving some of the $60 million even though they were not in
financial difficulties? The taxpayers did not mind helping farmers who needed help, but they
resented helping those who did not need it.
In its 1975 manifesto the National Party had stated that a National Government would
give priority to controlling farm costs, but the Government had been increasing those costs
ever since. The fertiliser price had been increased in the 1976 Budget by $10 a tonne and in
the 1977 Budget by $2.50 a tonne, with the result that farmers had been forced to pay an
extra $45 million for fertiliser in the 2 years before election year. The Government had
cancelled the haybarn and grain silo subsidies and the lucerne establishment grants that had
been introduced by the Labour Government. The Christchurch Press of 24 July 1978 had
reported that Mr K. M. Wells, the chairman of the agricultural section of Federated
Farmers, had said that it would have been wiser had the Budget contained some measures to
alleviate the need for further drought relief. Cropping farmers had not participated in the
$60 million handout.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture) said that the Budget had
directed additional resources into the main export sector of agriculture. The Government

Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) said there were two different types of
nematodes, one in the south Auckland area and the other near Christchurch. When
infestation had been discovered in the Pukekohe area the land had been immediately
quarantined, and the ministry had fumigated the area. Growers could not grow potatoes on
that land for 3 years after it had been infected. When the land was found to be clear of
infestation farmers were allowed to grow potatoes but had to use an insecticide type of spray
rather than full fumigation. Should land become reinfested, the farmer concerned would be
responsible. This year about 25 ha had been freed after the 3-year quarantine period.
Nematacide cost about $300 a hectare, while the cost of fumigation was estimated at $850 a
hectare.
Nematodes that grew in peat soil had to be treated differently from those that grew in
mineral soil because the fumigant was not effective in peat soil. The potato growers in
Christchurch would now receive the same type of assistance that had been given to potato
growers in south Auckland. The results of research programmes that had been carried out in
other countries were applied here. The ministry believed that the pest could be controlled,
but it would not be known for some time whether it could be eradicated. People in Pukekohe
had diversified from potato growing and were still able to use the land.

Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei) said that diversity within uniformity was the hallmark of a

architectural forms had been made. Unfortunately the move away from stereotyped
construction had not been matched by a corresponding, across-the-board increase in

had been introduced into school curricula, but in recent years the individual curricula had in

apparent than in social studies, which was vitally important, because it had much to do with
helping children learn the art of living as distinct from the skills required to earn a living.
Considerable concern had been expressed not so long ago about the content of the
textbooks introduced into New Zealand for pilot purposes. Some of the concern had been

based. Of equal concern to him were the schemes and syllabuses, based largely on American
models, that had emanated from the curriculum development unit, and that were about to be
extended downwards into the primary schools. He was concerned about the closely defined
schemes that removed the freedom of choice that had been previously available to both
teachers and pupils, and that had forced them into a philosophical strait-jacket that put
emphasis on similarities between people, and had failed to recognise their differences and
the need for highly varied approaches to meet their differing requirements.

Zealand schemes were based. The Minister should be concerned about that. While there was
no harm in all shades of opinion being examined in social studies syllabuses, it was wrong
that any one political orientation, such as overt socialism, should lie at their base. It was
important that the diversity approach should, in consistency, be extended into the curricula
that had been produced for use in educational institutions. The social science departments of
the universities were so saturated with socialist and Marxist economics that, in a situation in
which the extension of welfare could not be provided from taxation on non-existent
profitability, students totally ill equipped to suggest improvements for social reform were
being poured out of the universities.

to be drained, and when the land was ready for farming it would bring in a considerable
amount of money for the Maori Education Foundation.
People had to be aware of the dangers of public education. They had failed to see the
difference between knowledge and wisdom-they had trained the head and let the heart run
hog wild. Culture and character had been allowed to walk miles apart; the head had been
stuffed with mathematics and languages, while manners and morals had been ignored. The
aim had been to turn out exact scholars rather than exact citizens, but education was a
continuing process.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) said that the Moire Road secondary
school in Massey east was scheduled to open in 1982, but there had been some difficulty in
obtaining a satisfactory site. Negotiations with the landowner had been long, difficult, and
sometimes complex. Planning for the school was under way, and it would have to be ready
by 1982 in order to relieve the Massey High School, which currently had a roll of 1317, that
was expected to increase to 1567 by 1982.
There were three ways in which technical institutes could obtain funds for their libraries.
Over the years, there had been an upgrading of library stock; general grants for libraries in
the past 3 years had increased 20.8 percent in 1976-77, 16 percent in 1977-78, and 10 percent
in the current year, keeping up with inflation; and, in addition, every new course set up in a

technical institute received a grant for the establishment of class books as required.
The Government was committed to the completion of the National Library, which
would be one of New Zealand's great buildings. Obviously, the Government wanted to be
quite certain of all the design requirements, and quite certain that finance was available for
completion.
It was most unlikely that much of the $35,000 allocated to the National Library would be
spent in the present financial year, but provision would be made for up to 6 years of
construction work. Thirty-five thousand dollars would not go far towards importing
prefabricated steel for a building that cost $13 million, but that amount had been placed on
the estimates to ensure that the building would begin in the present financial year. It took a
long time to complete documentation and tenders for a building comparable in size with the
Beehive, and there had been no question of delaying the commencement of building.
In 1969 the Graham report had recommended the establishment of a tertiary institution
to train librarians. That training had now become a joint venture between Victoria
University and Wellington Teachers College, and a supply of trained librarians for civic and
school libraries was ensured.
There was an interesting document on whanau schools that members should see.
Whanau was not only a building, but also an approach to education. The best ways of using
whanau had to be studied, and therefore another one or two whanau schools should be built
in order to get a thorough evaluation.
Five or six weeks ago, he had received a deputation about the Petone Technical
Institute. Gair Island had been suggested as an alternative site, but that would divide the
institute, and would be wrong. There was no need to take any of the Petone recreation
grounds, and he was sure that the technical institute could be accommodated on the ground
available without interfering with the recreation grounds or with housing in the area.
He had no doubt that the decision to close the Beresford Street school had been the
right one, as the Auckland Girls Grammar School would gain extra land and some buildings.
The consolidation of the Napier Street and Beresford Street Schools on one site with new
buildings and the extra ground that had been purchased would provide a good school, had
been a sensible decision.
Superannuation did not come under the Education vote, but on page 320 of the
estimates it would be seen that it came under the Treasury vote for general administration.
The establishment of area schools had been a good move. However, the teachers in
those schools were neither primary nor secondary teachers, but special teachers. The NZEI
and the PPTA looked after their interests and made representations on their behalf at the
appropriate time. The report of the Association of Teachers in Technical Institutes on
conditions of employment and class contact hours had been presented to the Government in
April or May 1977. At that time it had been impossible to implement the recommendations
in the report, because all the provisions for the main estimates had been decided. He had
undertaken to examine recommendations carefully and to implement some of them in
1978-which he had done. With the money available, it had been decided to phase in the
reduction in class contact hours from 916 to 880. About a week after the announcement had
been made, further information had come to hand and had revealed that 880 class contact
hours, the objective of the first stage of the request, had been achieved. Therefore, it would
be possible, after negotiations, to meet more stage 1 requests within the sum of money
available, and no doubt a satisfactory agreement would be reached with the institute tutors.
Dr WALL (Porirua) said that not only the Maori section of the population had been
affected by economic deprivation, but, for various reasons, mostly educational, Maoris
remained in that economic group which the education system was failing so badly. A notable
examination of present problems in tertiary education had been carried out in 1977 by Mr
Dempsey of the Hutt Technical Institute. His proposal was to co-ordinate a group of
teachers to work towards the establishment of a technical institute or community college, in
the meantime making use of existing facilities. Considerable interest and enthusiasm in the
scheme had been evident.
Second-chance education in the Porirua basin was urgently needed-not a second

previously failed to carry out. In its 90 year history Porirua School had never been so badly
staffed in some classes as it was now. This year one class had already had seven different
teachers. Because there was no provision for adequate replacements those children were not
being taught. The worried headmaster had said that conditions at his school would be a little

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That the House do now adjourn. I

saw the Leader of the Opposition express his concern on television this evening-and that is
the apparent withdrawal of the Nigerian team from the Commonwealth Games in
Edmonton. I should report to the House that I took steps to get in touch with the
Commonwealth Secretary-General, Mr Shridath Ramphal, who is in Botswana at present. I
spoke to him by telephone earlier this evening and told him of the concern on both sides of
the New Zealand Parliament about the kind of statements which we are now aware
emanated from New Zealand about New Zealand's attitude to sport with South Africa.
It is clear that those statements came from the organisation known as HART, that they
were incorrect and exaggerated, and that they went through the United Nations Anti-
Apartheid Committee. The Chairman of that committee, Mr Harriman, passed them on at
the meeting of the Organisation for African Unity, and that was the basis for the action by
Nigeria.
Mr Ramphal is perturbed. He is very very distressed, and informed me that he caused to
be issued from the office of the Secretary-General of the Commonwealth in London a
statement that, to his knowledge, every Commonwealth country, including New Zealand,
had adhered to the Gleneagles Agreement. The House should know that.

QUESTIONS-ORAL
Medical Service Benefit-Dr C. M. Patel
1. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Health: Why has Ponsonby
doctor, C. M. Patel, been given a 6 months' suspension of his social security payments; have
any of Dr Patel's patients laid a complaint; and will the Minister review the decision in the
light of the strong support for Dr Patel from the whole community?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): As I said in reply to an urgent question on
Wednesday, 26 July, the honourable member does not appear to understand the situation
regarding general medical services benefits for Dr Patel's patients. After an informal
investigation showed that Dr Patel was seeing an excessive number of patients, which made
it improbable that he could provide a good standard of medical service, an informal inquiry
by two independent Auckland medical practitioners of wide experience investigated the
situation and recommended that I lodge a complaint with the Medical Practitioners
Disciplinary Committee. This committee carried out a full investigation and Dr Patel was
given the opportunity of appearing before it. In its recommendations to me the disciplinary
committee put forward that for a period of 6 months Dr Patel should not be able to claim
general medical services benefits for his patients direct from the Department of Health by
means of the schedule system. Instead, the committee recommended that the patients,
during that period should claim these benefits by way of the refund system. I accepted the
recommendations of the disciplinary committee. Dr Patel chose not to exercise his right to
appeal to the Medical Council against the recommendations of the disciplinary committee. I
have had some complaints from some patients of Dr Patel, but clearly these patients have
misunderstood the position. They are still eligible for general medical services benefits. The
only thing that has changed is that during the 6 months' period they must claim the benefit
instead of Dr Patel claiming the benefit on their behalf. As mentioned in my reply to the
urgent question on Wednesday last, I do not intend to review my decision on this matter.
Mr Prebble: Did the disciplinary committee find that Dr Patel was a competent doctor
who kept adequate records; if so, why are his patients being punished?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The disciplinary committee examines only matters of discipline.
Medical competence is handled by the Medical Council, which registers doctors and issues
working certificates. Over the last few years there have been many complaints that doctors
judging doctors never find doctors to be in the right, as previous Opposition Ministers of
Health, including the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, will confirm. This year, the Medical
Council recommended to me, and I agreed, that a change be made. Now, one layman is on
the committee. In the particular case under discussion, the disciplinary committtee in
disciplining itself made a recommendation that has been agreed to. Medical competence is
entirely another matter.
Hon. M. Rata: Is the Minister suggesting that Dr Patel was interested only in collecting
from the social welfare beneficiary the payment he is responsible for, and that the interest of
his patient was irrelevant?

Cement Industry, Weston, North Otago
4. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Regional Development: What forms of
assistance-regional, export, or otherwise-will be available to New Zealand Cement
Holdings Ltd. for its development of a cement industry at Weston, in North Otago?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development): Under current legislation the
new plant being planned by New Zealand Cement Holdings would qualify for the normal
first-year depreciation allowance of 25 percent, which is available for all new machinery. In
addition, plant directly associated with the cement manufacturing process could qualify for
the regional investment allowance of 20 percent. If cement was to be exported from this
plant the company might qualify for several of the existing export incentives. However, these
incentives are currently under review and the situation could alter by the time the plant is
completed. The type of regional development assistance available under the present
programme was not designed to be applied to a project involving the scale of investment
envisaged by New Zealand Cement Holdings. In addition, the company has carried out an
extensive study to determine the most advantageous location for this plant. In these
circumstances the provision of a locational incentive under the regional development
programme does not seem justified. The Government would expect that a major
development like this should be able to achieve viability without large sums of assistance.
Mr Elworthy: What is the scale of investment involved, and the number of job
opportunities that will be created by this development?
Mr SPEAKER: The Minister may tell the member, but not now. The question relates to
the forms of assistance available. He has answered that question.

Unemployment Benefits-Overstayers
10. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Social Welfare: Is it possible to
estimate how much overstayers are costing the country in terms of additional unemployment
benefits that have to be paid out?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): To qualify for unemployment
benefit on residential grounds the applicant must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and
have resided here for a continuous period of 12 months at any time. The Department of
Social Welfare has no details as to the immigration status of applicants for the benefit. I
should mention that applicants for unemployment benefit are required to register with the
Department of Labour, which is, of course, also responsible for immigration matters.

11. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Labour: Why has he not used the
compulsory conference provisions in the Industrial Relations Act to bring about a
resumption of work on the Mangere Bridge contract?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Section 120 of the Industrial Relations Act
enables me to call a compulsory conference only when I have grounds for believing that a
strike or lockout exists or is threatened. As the honourable member will be aware, there is
no strike on the Mangere Bridge, because the work force has been dismissed. It is, therefore,
not possible for me to call a compulsory conference.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Is the Minister able to give an assurance that the Mangere Bridge
contract has been held up because of industrial trouble only?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The latest action taken by the contractor was to dismiss the work
force, which was demanding a new redundancy agreement beyond the present law. I do not
know whether that is counted as industrial trouble.

Non-Union Labour in Bars
15. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Labour: If an ancillary licence is granted
to a sporting club, can that club employ non-union labour in its bar?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I apologise for the length of the reply. If the
honourable member is referring to staff who are actually employed and paid wages in terms
of an employer-worker relationship, the answer is no. Such workers are covered by the New
Zealand Chartered Clubs Employees award, and pursuant to the unqualified preference
provisions in that award, a worker who is over 18 years of age or is in receipt of not less than
the minimum rate of wages payable to a person of the age of 18 years or upwards, must
become a member of the relevant union. If, however, the honourable member is referring to
volunteer barmen, the answer is yes. Before any award or collective agreement can be
applied, it would be necessary for an employer-worker relationship to exist, and this was
recently supported by a decision of the Arbitration Court. In the case of a volunteer barman,
no such relationship does exist. The 1976 amendment to the Sale of Liquor Act 1962, which
provides for the issue of ancillary licences, does not include any provision requiring the
employment of paid staff. The amendment does, however, provide for the appointment of a
manager or a number of managers to ensure compliance with the duties, responsibilities, and
liabilities outlined in the Act.

Hydro Development, Upper Waitaki
16. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Works and Development: What
proposals does the Government have to take up some of the slack that will occur in
contracting following the nearing of completion of the Upper Waitaki hydro development?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The Upper Waitaki power
development works are programmed for completion in 1983, or soon after. The construction
work force, which includes contractors, will be progressively reduced during this time to
match the work remaining to be done. The downturn in work will not be sudden, and it will
be more than matched by the opportunities offering as the Upper Clutha project proceeds.
Those people who are interested in staying on major construction work will be able to do so.
Having said that, I point out that it must be recognised that the Upper Waitaki works are
plant intensive, involving as they do very significant quantities of earth moving. Earth
moving on this scale is not needed on the works that follow on, and contractors will have
recognised the need for them to move away from large investments in earth-moving plant in
keeping with the changing market.

Road User Distance Tax
18. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Works and Development: Has
he seen the report in the June issue of The Contractor in which it is claimed that the road user
distance tax added approximately 30c an hour to the cost of operating a 13-tonne crane, and
is it proposed to review this tax on this kind of equipment?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I have seen the report
referred to by the honourable member, but can advise that the Government does not
propose to review the road-user charge for crane operations. However, should
representatives of the mobile crane industry approach my department with the request to
adopt distance licences for mobile cranes in lieu of the time licence at present required, this
would receive favourable consideration. Using distance licences, crane operators would be
required to pay only for the actual distance travelled. As a result, some would pay more and
some less than is the case at present. At the moment, in paying a fixed amount, there is no
limit on their operations.
MEAT EXPORT CONTROL AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central): I move, That leave be given to introduce
the Meat Export Control Amendment Bill. The Bill aims at giving the Minister of Finance the
power to authorise the New Zealand Meat Producers Board to give financial assistance to a
fertiliser company or companies involved in the growth of goods and material used for
agricultural purposes. It is a very simple measure, and one that Government members
should support. Quite frankly, to oppose the Bill is to fly in the face of farmer opinion at
present. What the Bill specifically provides is authority for the Minister of Finance to allow
the New Zealand Meat Producers Board to invest its funds in areas that will directly benefit
farmers.
At present the Act allows funds to be invested only in meat. The Meat Export Control


## p. 2181 (#443) ###########################################

28 July
2181
Meat Export Control Amendment Bill
Amendment Act 1959 states that the board, with the prior consent of the Minister of
Finance, may subscribe or otherwise acquire shares in any company incorporated in New
Zealand, or elsewhere, carrying on or proposing to carry on operations relating to the sale,
storage, or transport of meat-I think that is the key word- produced in New Zealand. That
is the Act as it now stands, and that is the Act that has been used to advance money to
fertiliser companies in the past. However, if the Act is read carefully, one finds that it refers
only to meat, and the proposal in the Bill is to extend that.
The amendment will allow the Minister of Finance to grant the Meat Board's request to
lend $6 million to the farmer-backed Ravensdown Fertiliser Co., so that it can get control of
Kempthorne Prosser, or at least its fertiliser division. Ravensdown was initially formed to
oppose the Kempthorne Prosser bid for the Dominion Fertiliser Co., because farmers
believed that the takeover would be against their best interests. They lost that round,
however, and the takeover went ahead. But the farmers involved in Ravensdown were not
prepared to admit defeat. They placed a "first come, first served" offer for shares in
Kempthorne Prosser, and the response showed clearly that shareholders were prepared to
sell their shares in substantial quantities.
Ravensdown has received a tremendous amount of financial support from farmers
throughout the country. I understand that 8000 farmers have contributed to the fund. They
are opposed to a fertiliser monopoly by a company not controlled by farmers. Ravensdown
believes it can supply cheaper fertiliser to farmers. Other co-operative fertiliser works in the
South Island have shown that it is possible to undercut Kempthorne Prosser by more than
$11 a tonne for fertiliser supplied to the farming fraternity. That indicates the efficiency of
co-operative fertiliser companies. The East Coast Fertiliser Co., the Bay of Plenty Fertiliser
Co., and the Southland Fertiliser Co., are co-operatives, which have been assisted by Meat
Board funds and efficient operation. Federated Farmers and the Labour Party support
Ravensdown's endeavours. The co-operative principle has worked brilliantly in the dairy
industry, and for the other fertiliser companies I have mentioned. It would also work
extremely well for the Ravensdown Fertiliser Co.
The Meat Board supports Ravensdown's request to borrow $6 million, and the
Government should give its blessing to the project. The National Party has claimed it
understands the farmers' needs. The Government now has an opportunity to demonstrate its
understanding by voting for the Bill. The farming community wants to know where the
Government stands on the principle of Meat Board funds being used to assist farmers by
providing funds for ventures of the Ravensdown type. Will the first Government speaker say
whether the National Party agrees with the offensive attack launched recently by the
member for Palmerston North on farmer co-operatives? He was reported in the Manawatu
Evening Standard as having said: "The Government should reject the Ravensdown request.
If Ravensdown gained control, then Kempthorne Prosser will be taken over by a lot of
'gumboot directors' who will proceed to run the company into the ground. Farmer co-
operatives just don't work." Government members are quiet. Is that the official view of the
National Party? Where does the Prime Minister stand on this issue? Where does the Deputy
Prime Minister stand? He is well aware that when a proposal was made for a co-operative
works at Seadown he, as the Minister of Agriculture, defeated the farmers. They had
collected more than $400,000, but the National Government denied the Meat Board the
right to advance money to the farmers to form a co-operative. It was the farmers' own
money.
Has the city-based business-account-type National Party taken over the farming
community? Have the farmers on the Government benches lost control to the man from the
city? The silence that followed the comments made by the member for Palmerston North
suggests that is the case. I hope that liberal farmers will once again assert themselves at the
National Party conference, because the country has had enough of the city slicker attitude.
The Bill should be welcomed by members opposite, because it gives the Government the
power to allow the Meat Board to support the Ravensdown bid for control of Kempthorne
Prosser. Approval should be given, because, in the final analysis, the Meat Board's funds
belong to the farmers. They should be entitled to do whatever they want with their money.
Farmers are sick and tired of the Government's procrastination.
An article in today's Dominion states: "At the annual conference of Federated Farmers
in Wellington on Wednesday, a motion was unanimously passed calling on Mr Muldoon to
release the funds before next Monday. This is the date the second extension of the
Ravensdown offer for KP shares expires." The Government has been dilatory in making

QUEEN ELIZABETH THE SECOND ARTS COUNCIL OF NEW ZEALAND

Second Reading
Debate resumed from 18 July 1978
Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori): When the debate was interrupted, I was talking about
the aspirations, aims, and objects of the people who are interested in the traditional forms of
Maori and south Pacific art. I am sure that it is because of this bipartisan approach that the
Bill is now definitely improved. Most of the people who made submissions were concerned
about the use of the word "Traditional", and this concern was brought to the notice of the
Minister when he introduced the Bill. Because the word was felt to be too restrictive, it was
eliminated from the Bill. Although concern was expressed about the restrictive meaning of
the word "Traditional", all art, modern and otherwise, is based upon the traditional, either
in the way it is portrayed or in the inspiration behind it.
It is interesting to note that one of the written submissions referring to the restrictive
application of the word "Traditional" was from Mrs Walker, who represented Pacifica. She
said: "Pacifica also has some misgivings about the use of the word 'traditional' referring to
Maori and Pacific arts. We consider it to be too restrictive. Rigidly interpreted it could mean
that the proposed council would not be able to consider the legitimate developments of art
and the use of new methods, materials, and designs proper for a vital and living art." It
seems to me that, however art is portrayed, it is still inspired by tradition. Another
submission that mentioned the restrictive effect of the word was received from the
committee that organised the New Zealand and South Pacific Polynesian festival about 2
years ago. The committee stated: "Secondly, in relation to clause 2 we feel the definition of
traditional Maori and Polynesian art in subclause (1) would quite probably defeat the
purpose of the legislation." Therefore, in compliance with the wishes expressed in those two
submissions, and also by many other people who felt the term was too restrictive, the
committee deleted the word "Traditional". The committee made further major amendments
to the Bill, including an amendment to the term "Community Arts Council", which now
includes the words "Maori and South Pacific Arts".
The member for Auckland Central paid a special tribute to the Maori members of the
committee. The bipartisan approach by all committee members, not only the four Maori
members, has made the Bill what it now is. The expertise of the Minister of Maori Affairs
was also of great help to the committee.
The Bill provides that the chairman of the council shall be either a Maori or South
Pacific Islander, but it appears that this will restrict the ability of the Minister to appoint the
most suitable chairman. The provision excludes people who have the ability, expertise, and
knowledge, and who would probably be accepted by the Maori and South Pacific Island
members of the council, and who could work effectively and maintain a good relationship
with them. Such a person would be Mr Jock McEwen, who is probably known to all
members of the House. He has a mana that is accepted by both Maoris and Pacific Islanders,
and his knowledge of the subject would make him one of the most suitable persons to fill the
important post of chairman-but the provisions of the Bill exclude his nomination. I am not

The Minister said that the New Zealand Arts and Crafts Institute in Rotorua was the

Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua): I congratulate the Minister, who has displayed an insight
into Maori cultural matters. He has always made a valuable contribution whenever the
subject has arisen in the House. The member for Eastern Maori has correctly told the House
of the high degree of unity in the committee's bipartisan approach to the measure.
The Bill emphasises and highlights the unique and valuable contribution that the
indigenous Maori people of New Zealand and more recent migrants from the Pacific Islands
can make to the history, cultural life, and well-being of the country. That has not always
been appreciated. Indeed, there was a period in New Zealand's history when such a
contribution would have been spoken of in somewhat derogatory terms. I think of my own
early life and childhood, when the teaching of the Maori language in some Maori
communities was frowned on. Often, very strong objections were raised by the Maoris
themselves to the natural bilingual instincts inherent in most Maori communities.
Today there is a new appreciation, a new slant, and a new attitude towards the
contribution that can be made to our cultural life by our indigenous people through the
multicultural links New Zealand is now developing. The country will have to cope and live
with those links for generation after generation. New Zealand be described as a foster
country peopled by persons from other lands. Certainly, the culture of the non-Maori has
been transplanted principally from Britain and from other parts of Europe. We have lived
somewhat paternally, tied to the apron strings of the "mother country". Since the second
world war there has been a rekindling, and awakening of an awareness, of the possibility that
New Zealand is a separate nation and ought to be able to develop its own particular life style,
its own distinctive art forms, and its own exclusive culture. Since that time there has been a
real awakening among the country's population of the possibility of embracing, and placing a
proper emphasis on the value of, the very valid contribution that could be made by the
people indigenous to this country and also the people indigenous to the Pacific Islands who
have arrived here in more recent years. I welcome that attitude, and I know it is welcomed
widely throughout the country.
Other aspects relating to the Bill, and perhaps incorporated in it, are aimed at dealing
with the shift of population within New Zealand. There has been a cultural drift, a
movement of people, particularly Maori people, from their traditional rural environment
into the cities. That change has been forced on them by economic circumstances. For the
Maori people in particular, and also for the Pacific Islanders, that change has placed a strain
on family and traditional ties, and has hastened the erosion of a keen knowledge of
traditional skills that were once a very close and intimate part of their lives.
It is appropriate that encouragement should be given to the preservation of those skills,
traditions, life styles, and values. Certainly since World War II, there has been a quickening
of realisation, almost an excitement, and certainly a new understanding among Maori
people, Pacific Islanders, and New Zealanders, of the contribution that can be made to the
arts, the traditions, and the culture of the country. New Zealanders tend to think in terms of
equality; that is a word used constantly. It is said that some day the Maori might be equal to
the non-Maori. I hasten to suggest that what we are debating today in the Queen Elizabeth
the Second Arts Council of New Zealand Amendment Bill (No. 2) is not equality at all, but a
recognition of the uniqueness of Maori and Pacific Island culture-not an equality of culture
but a uniqueness of culture. That is a bonus that belongs only to this country. It can be
identified as a separate contribution or it can eventually be integrated into the evolving
character of our way of life, our life style, and our artistic values, which will certainly evolve
as time goes by. The Maori people and Pacific Island people can take distinctive pride in the
fact that their life styles, culture, understanding, and values will add greatly to the overall


## p. 2201 (#463) ###########################################

28 July
2201
QE II Arts Council of New Zealand Amendment Bill (No.2)
character of New Zealand culture.
All around the world, great cultural changes have taken place following World War II
and more recent conflicts. Because of their distance from Great Britain, New Zealanders,
almost without realising it and this has happened to other people in the world-have been
searching, probably for the first time, for a reference point within their own country, a
knowledge of something that binds them very closely to the land that has nurtured them.
There is a genuine thirst for knowledge and a growing appetite to tie that reference point to
New Zealand. This emphasises the very valuable contribution to be made by the Maori and
the Pacific Islander. The council will be an important part of that concept, because it will
help in the preservation, understanding, illustration, and illumination of the cultural links
that some day all New Zealanders, if for no reason other than a biological one, will take
pride in.
I have never viewed the council as an expression of tokenism. Very often, when efforts
have been made to assist indigenous people in New Zealand, a certain degree of paternalism
and tokenism has crept in, despite the best intentions. That does not apply here. The select
committee fully considered the constitution of the council to ensure that it would truly
represent Maori and Pacific Island opinion and be adequately qualified to study all
requirements in depth. The chairman must be a Maori or a Pacific Islander, this being a
fundamental necessity if the council is to have the mana required to draw from the people
contributing the specialist and intimate knowledge required without any suggestion of
paternalism or tokenism creeping in. At least four of the eight members of the council must
be Maori, and at least two must be of Pacific Island origin, leaving two more to give balance
to the composition of the council. It may well be necessary to bring in non-Maoris or non-
Pacific Islanders who have some special knowledge or skill or experience that can make the
council more effective.
The functions of the council will be largely advisory. It will evaluate information and
make recommendations to the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council. Not only will it help to
implement policy and put forward ideas and promote special interests, but it will also make
recommendations on financial matters. The Bill represents a practical step necessary to give
effect to what is so often put into words but seldom gets off the ground.

CUSTOMS ORDER CONFIRMATION BILL
Second Reading
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. When I introduced the Bill I explained to the House that it makes provision
merely for confirmation in terms of section 131 of the Customs Act 1966, as amended by
section 5 of the Customs Amendment Act 1973 and section 26 of the Customs Amendment
Act (No. 2) 1977, of an Order in Council made under sections 124, 124A, and 125A of the
Act on or after 1 July of the previous session, but before 1 July during the present session
and laid before Parliament in accordance with the Regulations Act 1936. The Bill confirms
the Customs Tariff Consolidation Amendment Order 1978, this order being made, first, to
translate into the 1978 Customs tariff all current tariff amendment orders which were not
incorporated in that tariff; secondly, to amend the rate of duty on unmanufactured tobaccos;
thirdly, to adjust a number of duty rates that became necessary under the terms of the recent
Australian Preference Agreement, which provides for margins of preference in favour of
Australia to be maintained in certain areas; and, fourthly, to incorporate miscellaneous
amendments of both a typographical and minor technical nature.
Bill read a second time.
POST OFFICE AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill amends the Post Office Act 1959 in four respects. Greater procedural
detail than is contained in the principal Act is necessary to facilitate the introduction of
occupational classification. A new section is inserted to clarify the uses to which the Post
Office may put land and buildings. A further new section is inserted to exclude the Crown
from liability in matters relating to the provision of services, facilities, or equipment in
connection with off-shore oil exploration or production. Imperial weights and measures in
the principal Act are converted to their appropriate metric equivalent.
Clauses 2 to 9 in general provide for occupational classification in the Post Office, in
place of the existing divisional classification system. They have the effect of removing the
present 5-yearly regrading reviews and replacing them with a method of continuous review
by the Director-General. Provision is made for the appointment of classification and grading
committees to consider and make recommendations on applications from permanent officers
for a review of the grading of their positions if they have not been reviewed in the preceding
5 years. If the Director-General does not accept the recommendation of a classification and
grading committee, provision is made to give the applicants recourse to the Post Office
Appeal Board.


## p. 2204 (#466) ###########################################

2204
28 July
Post Office Amendment Bill
Some other minor amendments are also included. The specific details of clauses 2 to 9
and of the provisions that are not purely mechanical or consequential are as follows. Clause 2
introduces a definition of "occupational class" into section 3 of the principal Act.
Occupational classification entails the grouping of officers into separate classes, having
regard to common features of the work required to be performed by officers in each group or
occupational class. Clause 5 amends section 196 (1) (a) of the principal Act to introduce a
right of appeal against a decision of the Director-General that is contrary to a
recommendation of a classification and grading committee on an application from an officer
for the review of the grading of his position. This replaces the present right of appeal against
an officer's grading following a quinquennial regrading. Quinquennial regradings are
replaced by a system of continuous review of grading under clause 6.
Clause 6 amends section 218 of the principal Act to provide that the Director-General
shall, after consultation with the Post Office Association, make determinations prescribing
occupational classes, having regard to the nature of the duty required to be performed by
officers. The amendment provides also for the establishment of subclasses and grading
structures. Procedures relating to the publication and effective dates of occupational class
determinations are set out also. Subsection (5) of the amended section 218 makes provision
for the introduction of a system of continuous review of classification and grading of
positions, which will replace the existing quinquennial regrading system.
Clause 7 introduces three new sections into the principal Act. These sections are
modelled on the provisions of sections 45, 46, and 47 of the State Services Act 1962. The new
section 218A provides an officer with a right to apply to the Director-General for a review of
the grading of his position. If the result of the Director-General's review is not satisfactory to
the officer he will be able to request that his application be referred to a classification and
grading committee, provided that the grading of the position has not been reviewed by such
a committee within the 5 years immediately preceding the application to the Director-
General.
The new section 218B empowers the Postmaster-General to appoint classification and
grading committees, each consisting of three members. The chairman is to be appointed
after consultation with the Post Office Association, and one member on the nomination of
that association. Subsection (9) of the new section provides that if the Director-General's
decision is contrary to the recommendation of a classification and grading committee, the
applicant may within 30 days of the date of notification of the Director-General's decision
avail himself of the right of appeal established under clause 5 of the Bill.
The new section 218c provides that if the Director-General agrees to a change in the
grading of a position as a result of a decision under section 218A or 218B, or if the appeal
board upholds the application of the appellant, the Director-General may declare the
position vacant and fill it in the manner already authorised in the principal Act.
Clause 8 amends section 219A of the principal Act to make provision for the Director-
General to prescribe by determination minimum educational or other qualifications required
for entry into or advancement within certain occupational classes. Clause 10 inserts a new
section 223A in the principal Act to make it clear that land and buildings used for Post Office
purposes include the use thereof for ancillary matters such as training schools, hostels,
accommodation for officers, workshops, garages, recreation, and the welfare of the staff,
which may be undertaken with the consent or approval of the Postmaster-General. The Post
Office Act, in section 12, covers only buildings for handling mail and, in section 14, those
associated with lines.
Clause 11 inserts a new section 245A in the principal Act to exclude the Crown, the
Postmaster-General, or any officer from any liability for any error, default, delay, or
omission in respect of any services provided by the Post Office in relation to off-shore oil
exploration, drilling, or production vessels, rigs, or installations, or in connection with any
petroleum produced therefrom. The present Act provides indemnity for the Crown in
relation to telephone service and telegrams. The proposed amendment is designed to put
beyond any doubt that no claim shall lie against the Crown for any error, omission, default,
or delay in respect of the provision of services generally to off-shore drilling and production
platforms.
Clause 12 converts imperial measurements and weights to their approximate metric
equivalents in sections of the principal Act. In section 17(2), 16 ounces are converted to their
nearest rounded-off equivalent of 500 g. In the Post Office Act this is the minimum weight of
letters not required to be carried in the post. In section 143(b), 66 ft become 20 metres as the

Post Office Amendment Bill
maximum distance from a proposed or existing line that officers may cut and remove all trees
and underwood that might interfere with construction of or work on the line. In section
150(a), 18 ft become 5.5 metres. This relates to the height of a line across a public road. The
height of lines other than across a public road has been changed from 14 ft to 4.25 metres.

QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Drinking-driver Blitz-Hospital Waiting Lists
1. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt Albert) to the Minister of Health: In view of the fact that it
has long been accepted that the treatment of victims of motorcar accidents in public hospitals
has kept other patients on long waiting lists for surgery, how many such operations have
been carried out as a result of the dramatic reduction in accidents through the drinking-
driver blitz?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I am sure that the reduction in accidents
resulting from the drinking-driver blitz will have a significant effect on surgical waiting lists at
major hospitals. Unfortunately, it is not possible to obtain the information that the
honourable member has requested, because statistics of this kind are not quickly available.
When the new computer system of admissions and discharges has been developed to cover
all our public hospitals, such data will be more readily available.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Why did the Minister or his senior officers not communicate with the
main hospital boards to find out just how many people waiting for surgery had been able to
be admitted as a result of the blitz?
Hon. T. F. GILL: One needs a little understanding of the way an emergency system in a
hospital works. Unless one can forecast that next Saturday night, because of the blitz, there
will be so many fewer people being admitted after accidents, it is not possible to bring in
people who need surgery and prepare the cases, and have the theatres on standby. There
needs to be a little bit of experience before the opportunity can be exploited. The answer to
the second part of the question is that people in hospitals have a great deal more to do than
carry out surveys to produce an answer of that kind on the dot.
Trade Union Amalgamation
2. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Labour: Is he aware of the proposal
put forward by the president of the Federation of Labour to amalgamate New Zealand's 294
trade unions into 10 large industrial groups, and does he support the principle involved as
being an effective industrial relations move?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I am aware of the Federation of Labour's
plans to organise the present large number of industrial unions into 10 industrial groups.
Those groups were first proposed at the federation's conference in 1972. Later, details of the
proposed groupings were circulated among affiliates for discussion and comment. While I
certainly support the principle of union amalgamation, I point out that, in the initial stages at
least, the federation's plan does not involve formal amalgamation, but rather the grouping of
individual unions into broad associations; but if that leads to the former, then it is
commendable.
Mr W. R. Austin: In view of the fact that the plan was first mooted in 1972, has the delay
been due to an unco-operative attitude in the 3-year term of the Labour Government?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I cannot say precisely what steps were taken by the Labour

East Coal Mine, Huntly
3. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Energy: Can he confirm that the East
Coal Mine at Huntly is running short of reinforcing steel, and is it a fact that orders for the
steel required were cancelled?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): There is no shortage of reinforcing steel at the

Unemployment, Palmerston North
7. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: Can he confirm that
unemployment is at a record level of about 900 in Palmerston North, and that he will take
urgent steps to reduce this high figure for a city of that size?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): On 14 July 1978 there were 811 persons
registered for employment in the Palmerston North district of my department. This district
includes part of the Wairarapa and Central Hawke's Bay, as well as Horowhenua and
Manawatu. Every possible effort is being made to assist persons seeking work, including the
active use of the Government's five job creation programmes.
Mr Isbey: Can the Minister confirm that the 900 unemployed in Palmerston North are
genuinely unable to find work, and they are not reluctant to take a job, as has been stated by
the member for Palmerston North?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: On 14 July, 515 males and 296 females were unemployed in the
Palmerston North district. Of that number, 50 percent are within the Palmerston North city
region.
Mr Isbey: Are they genuinely unemployed?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: As genuine as when the member was the Under-Secretary to the
Minister of Labour. The department has placed 887 people in work in the same area.
Mr Lithgow: What is the unemployment figure for Palmerston North?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Unemployment in that district is 1.56 percent of the estimated
work force. That compares with the New Zealand average of 2.01 percent, which is one of
the lowest in the Western World. The unemployment figure for Palmerston North, which
includes some of the environs, is 50 percent of 811.

Family Planning Association-Government Subsidy
8. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Health: What is the extent of the

specified, what proportion was allocated to the association's recent circular regarding family
planning procedures?

Family Planning Association (Inc.) has been made in the 1978-79 estimates of expenditure
under vote Health to meet the actual expenditure on the salaries of doctors, nurses-
including the periods of initial training-and health assistants (clinical) employed in
approved clinics. None of the funds provided by the Government are used by the association
for any other purpose. Before 1 April 1976 a subsidy was paid, which included a contribution
towards the cost of educational material. The current basis for the payment of subsidies was
made by the present Government with effect from 1 April 1976.
Mr Wellington: Is the Government's subsidy applied only to personnel, and used for no
other purpose?

nurses, and health assistants.

subsidy is spent by the Family Planning Association on showing films?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I can confirm that the expenditure is for the payment of the salaries of
doctors, nurses, and health assistants. Under the previous arrangement the Government
subsidised a portion of the operating deficit. It contributed towards the cost of educational
material, initial equipment and stores, and up to 50 percent of the salary of the executive
secretary. That is no longer paid.
Mangere Bridge Contract Suspension
9. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson), on behalf of Mr ROGERS (Onehunga), to the Minister of
Works and Development: Before he suspended the Mangere Bridge contract, did he consult
his colleague the Minister of Labour about calling a compulsory conference as provided for
in the Industrial Relations Act, and, if so, what was decided in those consultations?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The Minister of Labour
was consulted and involved in the discussions that led up to the decision to suspend this
contract. A compulsory conference was not considered appropriate, because the matters at
issue concerned an industrial agreement between the Master Builders Federation and the
unions concerned. My action in suspending the contract was, in the circumstances, the
course to follow.
Mr Malcolm: What steps have been taken by the member for Onehunga to assist
industrial relations on this project?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: To the best of my knowledge the member for Onehunga has taken
no steps to assist with the problem, and has clouded the issue by stating that the problems are
not of an industrial nature. He has taken the attention away from industrial relations.
Mr Lange: Has the Minister done anything to encourage a return to work on the bridge
site, rather than standing by and washing his hands of the whole affair by suspending the
contract?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: Suspending the contract was not a matter of washing my hands of
the affair. The contractor was advertising for men, and willing, able and competent men
were turning up to do the job. They were confronted by union officials who would not allow
them on the job. Because of the sense of frustration on both sides and to relieve what might
have been a tense situation, it was desirable that the contractor should no longer have the
responsibility of advertising for men.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In view of the fact that the Minister has just said he has not washed
his hands of the contract, what plans does he or the Government have for completing the
bridge?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: In answering the question I drew attention to the fact that the
problem has been an industrial one. It can be solved only by solving the industrial problems,
which have been a series of frustrating rolling strikes to upset the contractor. The only man
who can handle the problem is the Minister of Labour, and I hope he will have the goodwill
of the people concerned and of the Opposition.

Christchurch-Lyttelton Road Tunnel Authority's Finances
17. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Works and Development: Has
he seen the report in the Christchurch Press of 28 June in which it is stated that the National
Roads Board has not increased its annual grant to the Christchurch-Lyttelton Road Tunnel

meeting some big accounts and some had to be held over for a month because of the need to
pay loan interest charges, and, if so, what plans does the Government have to assist the

Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I have seen the report
referred to by the honourable member. The National Roads Board has since paid its annual
grant of $200,000 to the road tunnel authority and this, together with increased revenue from
tolls, will be more than adequate to meet all expected costs in the current financial year. I
understand from the member for Lyttelton that discussions have been going on for some
time at local level regarding the management and financing of the tunnel, but no firm
proposal has come to the board to assist the road tunnel authority. The operation of the
Lyttelton tunnel is governed by the Christchurch-Lyttelton Road Tunnel Act 1956, and any
proposals would require joint Government and National Roads Board decisions.

and paying the authority's outstanding accounts?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: I thought I made it clear to the honourable member that there are
no outstanding accounts. There have been various discussions between the tunnel authority,
the Lyttelton Harbour Board, the Christchurch City Council, and the Government, and I
can assure the honourable member that, in keeping with an undertaking I gave the member
for Lyttelton earlier, I will do my best to promote a sounder basis of financing for the tunnel.
I would not like to go as far at this stage as saying that the proposal would abolish tolls,
although I would not rule that out.

in office the Post Office ran at a loss of $38 million, which had to be made up by direct
subsidy from the taxpayer; and the Post Office had to borrow $62 million, on which it pays
interest in perpetuity, not for a finite term. It may be of interest to those budding financiers
who sit opposite to know that in the first 10 years the accumulated interest bill on that $62
million will cost $51 million. That is an indication of the finance involved when the debt
burden gets out of hand, as it did under the former Labour Government.
In pointing to the National Government's achievement in securing a record profit of
$37.7 million, Opposition members have accused it of profiteering. That, of course, is based
on a fundamental misunderstanding of the whole basis of Post Office financing. As many
members realise, every dollar earned is a dollar less that has to be borrowed, and a dollar
less that has to be added to the debt burden. It was obvious that, if the trend under the
Labour Government during the 1973 to 1975 period continued, the debt burden would
quickly get out of hand and that, even if the Labour Party had been elected to office in 1975,
it would have needed to take action along the lines we propose.
Opposition members have spoken a great deal about staffing, and both the member for
Manukau and the member for Onehunga made the totally misleading statement that 44 Post
Office employees are being sacked each month. I challenge any Opposition member to cite
an example of one person who has been sacked pursuant to the policy we have adopted.

fact, I have the figures for the Post Office staff levels and ceilings for the period 1972 to 1978.

March 1972, and in addition the staff ceiling has been increased recently by 140. I do not

Opposition members have also referred-without a great degree of understanding-to

divisional classification all kinds of different employees were classified together for purposes
to pay and conditions. Under the new occupational classification they are grouped according
to qualifications and type of work to better facilitate comparisons with similar positions
outside the State services. I do not regard that as a retrograde step.

ADJOURNMENT--FOREIGN AFFAIRS
[With the leave of the House, it was agreed that the speaking time allowed the first two
speakers should be 30 minutes each, and 20 minutes thereafter for each speaker]
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): For the purpose of discussing


## p. 2221 (#483) ###########################################

1 August
2221
Adjournment-Foreign Affairs
foreign affairs, I move That the House do now adjourn. I open the debate this evening with a
very simple proposition: that we in New Zealand are fighting for our economic life. The
outcome of the battles we are fighting overseas will have a fundamental effect on the shape
of our society. That is an inescapable fact. In Europe the fight is essentially defensive, trying
to hold on to what we have got. In the United States and Australia it is defensive, and we are
also on the offensive, retaining existing access arrangements, while seizing new
opportunities.
In South-east Asia, northern Asia, the Middle East, the Pacific and Latin America a
vigorous campaign is under way to seek out and exploit new markets. We are fighting for our
economic life, and, if we understand this, all else follows. In my view, at no time in the short
history of our country has there been more at stake in our conduct of foreign and trade
diplomacy. The comfortable, secure, and mutually beneficial relationships that we have built
up in the past, particularly with Britain, are under serious challenge, and we must look at the
situation with clear eyes; but, if we keep our cool, we shall see that, although the dangers are
high, so too are the opportunities.
My theme tonight is necessarily an economic one, and I propose to start by surveying
briefly and selectively the world economic scene within which New Zealand must work. I
shall give an account of our efforts to preserve the important and continuing elements in our
relationship with the European Community. I shall then look at the new prospects, the
opportunities that are opening to us in new markets and in old, and which must now be the
targets of our political and commercial diplomacy. I couple these terms deliberately. The
political and commercial aspects of foreign policy are inseparable. Each acts on the other,
and they must be treated together, for New Zealand's bargaining power in sheer economic
terms is small-and I think that pretty well every one of us recognises that. It is often only
our political relationships with other nations and our political standing in any particular case
that gives us leverage in economic bargaining. We must, therefore, preserve and develop
every such resource that we have. Prospects for a sustained recovery in world economy
remain uncertain. There is massive unemployment, continued inflation or the fear of
growing inflation, monetary instability, and lagging industrial production; all these still
plague the world economy. In fact, for the fourth time in as many years, the leaders of the
major industrialised nations of the world have met to review the situation, and at the Bonn
summit meeting just concluded commitment to an open and interdependent world trading
system was reaffirmed. A series of measures intended to strengthen and sustain the recovery
of world trade, which has so far remained all too fragile, was announced. I hope that they
succeed in that intention, but we cannot be sure.
The protracted recession, and only partial recovery of the world economy, means that
every government is being pressed by its constituents to protect their jobs by excluding
imports. If governments succumb to these pressures, all trading nations will be involved in a
trade war. This National Government has worked actively in every appropriate forum to
check the tide towards agricultural protectionism; and it has had some success. At the
meeting of OECD Ministers in Paris in June, at which I represented New Zealand, member
governments renewed the trade pledge. It is a trade pledge that was first adopted in 1974,
and, thanks to the efforts of my colleagues, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture,
and the Minister of Energy, all of whom have at some stage been involved in meetings of the
OECD, arguing this case, the pledge now covers trade in agricultural as well as industrial
goods, and it commits all members, including New Zealand, to refrain from additional
protectionist measures and practices.
New Zealand succeeded at this Paris meeting in obtaining explicit recognition for all
participants, including representatives of our major trading partners in pursuit of positive
adjustment policies that agricultural products should be treated on an equal footing with
industrial products. That was one of the most favourable outcomes, and one of the most
forward-looking outcomes, of the OECD meeting for New Zealand. The messages from
Paris and Bonn are that the leaders of the industrialised West have declared themselves for
trade liberalisation, and against increased protection. As a trading country dependent on
access opportunities, these declarations are of real importance to New Zealand; but let me
add that I am the first person to remind myself and the House that these are only
declarations. I see that the member for Mangere looks amused by the fact that they are
declarations, and I invite him to tell me if he would be happier if there were no declarations.
I suggest he would not.
At the GATT and multinational trade negotiations in Geneva, the principal challenge

between our major trading partners. I have every reason, and I am encouraged, to believe
that we are making useful progress. My visit to Geneva has given me hope that agreement
between the major participants is possible, and that from the agreement will flow worth-
while benefits for New Zealand by way of improved access conditions. That, in turn, will go
some way to securing the base we need, so that our diversification efforts can be sustained
and expanded, because that is really the base from which we shall work.
Our basic objectives, of course, in the GATT and the MTN negotiations are fairly
simple. We seek an agreement on dairy products that will provide stability in the
international market and protection of the interests of the countries most dependent on
trade in those products. We seek an international agreement on beef to achieve similar
results. We seek a code or other arrangements on subsidies that would work progressively
and effectively to reduce and eliminate the adverse effects of heavily subsidised dairy
products and meat-dairy products and meat placed on the international market to dispose
of surpluses created by domestic price policies of the producing countries, because those
countries cannot dispose of those products in competition with countries like New Zealand
without subsidising them. Finally, and above all, we seek improved and secure conditions of
access into the major markets for our vitally important butter, cheese, lamb, beef, and fruit
exports-and at the lowest possible tariff levels.
I have spoken at some length about the nature of the battlefront in Geneva. An equally
important theatre to us is that presented by the most important of all our trading partners. I
hope there is no misunderstanding in New Zealand about the nature of our negotiations with
the European Economic Community. The Community is 20 years old, or perhaps I should
say that it is only 20 years old. In 1971 we achieved special arrangements for our butter and
cheese trade with Britain for the years 1973 through to 1977, the first 5 years of British
membership. In 1976 we obtained a 3-year extension of our butter arrangements, until 1980.
Since 1973 we have obtained three price increases for our dairy products.

Protocol 18, negotiated in 1971, was but the first instalment of arrangements governing
our vital trade with Britain, and of course it came after more than 10 years of visits and
representations. The extension of our butter trade for the period 1978 to 1980 was the result
of intensive negotiations for more than 18 months, reinforcing all the work that had been
done earlier to achieve the original protocol. None of the decisions is achieved easily or in
the course of a single visit; it is a continuing process. I believe the pattern of our dairy
negotiations is clear, but now we are also engaged in negotiations concerning lamb. What is
at stake is no less than the viability of the New Zealand sheep industry itself-an industry
which, in one form or another provides more than 40 percent of New Zealand's export
income. We face a movement towards common Community rules for trade in sheepmeat,
both within the Community and as regards third country suppliers, of which, of course, New
Zealand is by far the largest.
Under the Rome Treaty there is to be internal free trade in all products. This is not the
case with lamb, which is treated freely only within the original Six, but not within the Nine.
Sheepmeat regulations, if adopted, would replace the present widely different systems which
still apply. Put simply, our perception of the draft regulation now being proposed is that this
is a beast that, I think Ian Fleming is said to have observed of a horse, "is dangerous at both
ends and decidedly uncomfortable in the middle". After my two visits to Europe to explain
New Zealand's views on the sheepmeat question, Ministers there are well aware of the
importance to us of our lamb trade with Europe. Ministers in every capital have confirmed
that New Zealand lamb exports have presented no problem. I think that point is worth
repeating; Ministers in every capital have confirmed that New Zealand lamb exports have
presented no problem. There is recognition of the importance of this trade to our economy,
and many Ministers endorse the commission's view that any sheepmeats regime should
operate in such a way as not to place New Zealand at a disadvantage. Indeed, Mr

So far, I have stressed the danger and the difficulties we face in an effort to protect our

opportunities? Even if some markets and societies seem to be putting up shutters and

future. Foremost among them, of course, is Japan.
In our campaign to place trading and economic relationships with that great economic
power on a stable and long-lasting basis, we have achieved a significant degree of progress in
the face of very real difficulties. We shall continue to press bilaterally, and in multilateral
forums, for further improvement in access for our farm and forest products in return for our
fish. The trading relationship with Japan is moving towards a more satisfactory basis as our
Governments gain a clearer understanding of the others needs and problems. The two
economies can be largely complementary if their potential strengths are properly utilised,
but I come back to the simple point that it is very much a political question for both parties.
I have spoken of dangers and opportunities. In the fight for economic survival the
United States presents us with a challenging combination of both. Emerging protectionist
sentiments will be encountered, but, if we can organise ourselves to take advantage of them,
there are market opportunities to be exploited. The beef market is a striking example of this.
I welcomed, as did everybody in this country, President Carter's recent decision to increase
beef imports by about $200 million this year. I expect New Zealand's share of the increase
will amount to about $50 million. We appreciate this demonstration of good will by the
United States Administration to its friends and allies in the South Pacific, but, at the same
time, we are well aware of the strength of the protectionist cattle lobby in the United States.
The Bentsen Bill, or its equivalent, doubtless will never be far from the surface, and we shall
take care to ensure that New Zealand's interest is never far from the surface in the mind of
the Administration and the Congress.
Beef is not the only prospect. The market for the lamb we send to the United States is
wide open, much larger than we have yet been able to satisfy, and the market for
manufactured goods is almost limitless. The Government, recognising this, has designated
the West Coast of the United States as a priority market in this Export Year. We are
encouraging and helping New Zealand exporters to look there to sell their goods, and the
response has been much greater than was anticipated.

Since 1973 New Zealand has been under the worst threat it has encountered since World
War II. The oil shock, following the collapse of the Bretton Woods financial system, led to
economic difficulties throughout the world. The New Zealand terms of trade dropped by 43
percent. Agricultural protectionism rose around the world. New Zealand had 3 years of a
Government whose policy was borrow and hope. It ran down the reserves that had been
carefully built up by the National Government and began the massive borrowing that has
been necessary ever since. When the National Government came into office in 1975 there
was no time and no justification for New Zealand to adopt a low profile in foreign affairs.
The Ministers and I placed New Zealand's case firmly, openly, and positively before its
trading partners, and at no time did we adopt the low-profile approach that had been
possible in good times, which, although undesirable, was adopted by Labour during its term
in office.
The policies are working. The Minister of Overseas Trade has done a magnificent job in
Britain and Europe. The most recent problem New Zealand has had to face is the
sheepmeats regime. The Europeans have said that it will not damage New Zealand's lamb
trade, but the Government does not accept that. The Government has stated that the regime
will be fatal to our lamb trade, and, in turn, fatal to our sheep industry and our economy.
Because the Government has made that statement firmly, openly, and strongly, British
public opinion is now marshalling in favour of New Zealand. The feeling is certainly anti the
Common Market. The British housewife wants her weekly joint of New Zealand lamb, and
many groups are now mobilising against the sheepmeats regime. The Government has not
adopted the low profile taken by the Labour Government, which disguised the fact that what
it bought with an increase in price was a reduction in exports.
Visits to China by the Deputy Prime Minister and myself have led to friendly relations
and a growth in trade. The cordial personal relations between the Government of Bahrain
and New Zealand have given New Zealand a preferred agreement and a foothold in the
heart of the Arab world. The positive results have come from positive policy. At the
ASEAN summit last August New Zealand's position in trade in both directions was accepted
by the leaders of the five ASEAN nations. Not one word of criticism was heard. New
Zealand put its case, and had something to say to Japan and to Australia. The ASEAN
nations thanked New Zealand for making its position clear. New Zealand's position was
accepted because the nations were satisfied. New Zealand's relations with ASEAN have
never been better; the countries are in total accord.
Over a year ago I made two frank speeches on New Zealand's concern about the
policies of the new Carter Administration in the United States. The Carter Administration
has responded by taking a much greater interest in New Zealand and the South Pacific. In
spite of the duplicity of the present Leader of the Opposition, the ANZUS pact is again on a
sound footing. He said one thing in private to the Americans and something else in public to
New Zealand. He was found out when the Government changed.
In keeping with the Carter Administration's close interest in the welfare and the future
of the independent nations of the South Pacific, the State Department has, for the first time,
established a special section devoted to South Pacific affairs. The Carter Administration
realises that this part of the hemisphere is important to America's global strategy, and that it
is essential that the economies of countries such as Australia and New Zealand be kept
sound if they are to play their part. That development has come about because New Zealand
did not adopt a low-profile approach. It spoke up and stated that it was worried that the
Carter Administration was looking to Japan and Europe, and not in our direction. The
Carter Administration has assisted in New Zealand's negotiations with Japan, and in the

The press likes to state that Malcolm Fraser and I do not get on. We both have the

have attended three meetings in New Zealand this year. The Ministers get together to talk

Governments have never been closer than they are at present. This is not the result of a low-

working together in the trans-Tasman arena.
Under the National Government the South Pacific Forum has taken on a new lease of
life. The idea of a forum was conceived by the Holyoake Government. The meeting

and Secretary Cyrus Vance, and this is one of the reasons why the Americans are taking a
closer interest in the South Pacific.

the Samoa-Auckland service. The forum has been instrumental-through the South Pacific

to all. First, the Japanese have accepted that our trade with Japan and their access to our fish

they had more than 300 vessels laid up; they are still laid up. Thirdly, it is obvious that unless
we get results in our terms of trade there will be no results in terms of access to our fishing
waters.

disclosed. It is true that Laurie Friis, Chairman of the Dairy Board, said, "I don't know what

acknowledge that each nation is a hard bargainer. You can call the tactics bullying, or
