I want to speak for only a minute or two on the South Pacific. As a result of what we
have achieved in the forum, the Germans have established in New Zealand a regional
embassy for the whole of the South Pacific, and they are taking our advice on their aid
programmes. In addition, in the last week or so democracy and the rule of law have
triumphed in the Cook Islands. I want to make it quite clear that at no time did New Zealand
interfere in that democratic and legal process. Cook Islanders are New Zealand citizens and
have dual citizenship. New Zealand pays $6 million a year into their budget for their
sustenance. Mr Justice Donne and Mr Elliot Khan, the Commissioner of Police, came to
New Zealand and said to our officials-not to Ministers, because we decided that Ministers
should not talk to either of them until the judgment was delivered, lest they should be seen
to be interfering-that they were concerned at the tension, and whether the small police
force could handle that tension if things went wrong. We agreed to send five policemen to
the Cook Islands to act as bodyguards for the Chief Justice if the Cook Islands Government
requested it. The policemen flew to the islands on the day the judgment was delivered. If
they had not been accepted or requested by the Cook Islands Government they would have
flown back to New Zealand that evening. However, they were asked for by the Cook Islands
Government and were sworn in as members of the Cook Islands Police Force. They are still
there, acting as members of that police force. That is the kind of help we shall always give to
the Cook Islands if requested; no interference, just assistance. We provided for it, we did it,
and before too long those policemen will return to New Zealand.
I cannot make any pronouncement on corruption in the Cook Islands; that is for the
court.. I remind the House that the accounts of the Cook Islands Government are audited by
the Controller and Auditor-General of the Cook Islands, who is also controller and Auditor-
General of New Zealand. He reports each year, and during the past year or two has found
little that is wrong. However, there is a suggestion that there is something wrong with
accounts of organisations outside the public accounts. That matter is for the Cook Islands
Government and for the courts, not for the New Zealand Government. I repeat that there
has certainly been nepotism; we know that. The Cook Islands have been referred to as the
Henry family farm. Again, that matter is one for the Cook Islands Government. New
Zealand will give all the help it properly can, but it will not interfere.
This is a tough world, and since 1973 it has been a bit tougher than it was before, which
means that a small country such as New Zealand must approach its foreign policy in a
positive way, and not take whatever is handed out by the big nations and say, "Well, there's
another blow we will just have to suffer." The approach now is to talk in simple terms to our
friends and allies, and to make our case positively and forcefully without beating about the
bush. In the 2 1/2 years of this Government that policy has paid off. It will continue.

place it on a continuing basis. Previously, the offer was for one year and a review if required.

on the basis of the requirements of those countries to which Japan was giving aid. Last year

they will be reminded constantly of its success as we debate this issue in the months and years
to come.
In the matter of beef, the Opposition should know that Japan operates on the basis of a

member States realise the importance of the issue to New Zealand and the reason for its
concern. It is a fact that as a result of the Minister's visit, strong and useful allies have been
enlisted and considerable support has been developed for New Zealand.
I now turn briefly, as the Minister responsible for NAFTA, to what the Prime Minister
said in his speech about the very good relationship that has developed between Australia and
New Zealand at ministerial level, and, I may say, among officials throughout the various
ministries. I take the opportunity to refer particularly to the trade arrangements we have
entered into, and also to reply to some of the baseless charges made from time to time by
Opposition members. During the last 2 years relationships with Australia, at both the
ministerial and official level, have improved considerably, as the recent decision of the two
countries on the formation of a New Zealand - Australia Foundation indicates. As the Prime
Minister said, the Prime Ministers and Ministers have had very frequent discussions.
The prospects for steady and positive progress in joint New Zealand - Australia trade
relationships are very good indeed. The total trade between the two countries passed the
$1,000 million mark last year, and New Zealand's share of that joint trade has been
improving markedly. I am not exaggerating when I claim that, at this point in the trading
history of our two countries, New Zealand has never been in a better position.
In 1966, when the National Government of the day took New Zealand into NAFTA,
the Labour Opposition criticised the decision; and Hansard is full of those criticisms. I took
part in the debates and, as Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the then Minister of Overseas
Trade, Minister of Trade and Industry, and Minister of Customs, I had the honour of taking
part in some of the negotiations. When we entered NAFTA the trade imbalance between
Australia and New Zealand was 1:4 against New Zealand. The National Government
worked hard to improve the ratio and when it went out of office in December 1972 the trade
imbalance against New Zealand had improved from 1:4 to 1:2.3. By December 1975, after
three disastrous years of Labour Government, the trade imbalance had again moved in the
wrong direction, to 1:3 against New Zealand. The member for Mt. Albert, the Labour
Government's Minister responsible for NAFTA, who has already taken part in the debate,
described the agreement as shaky, and in the dying months of the last Labour Government
he was quoted in the press as saying that NAFTA was in danger of shaking to pieces. Since
this National Government has taken office the trade imbalance has steadily improved, from
1:3 against New Zealand under Labour in 1975, to 1:1.79 in 1977, and to 1:1.6 for the year
ended March 1978-the best ratio at any time in the history of trade between Australia and
New Zealand. I emphasise that it has never been better.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: But you are cutting the imports.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: It is clear that the member for Roskill does not
understand. He claims that we are cutting the imports, but I have just told him that last year,
for the first time, our joint trade-that is, exports and imports-broke the $1 billion, or the
$1,000 million, mark. It increased by about $200 million in that year, and it is still increasing.
Although there is still a trade imbalance, New Zealand is getting a much greater share.
In addition, the Minister of Overseas Trade and I succeeded last April, in the NAFTA
talks in Canberra with our officials, in renegotiating and consolidating the arrangements for
several commodities. We are in the process of developing a schedule B arrangement for
whiteware. After the efforts of successive Governments over the years to reach some
agreement about whiteware, we have negotiated a longer-term arrangement that will expire
late in 1980. We have also made an article 3.7 industry arrangement for apparel, footwear,


## p. 2237 (#499) ###########################################

1 August
2237
Adjournment-Foreign Affairs
and textiles, and we are seeking to include in schedule B an arrangement for furniture. We
also agreed that the senior officials of both countries should meet on a regular basis, and the
first meeting of the permanent heads of the Department of Overseas Trade and the
Department of Trade and Industry was held in New Zealand only a month ago.
In terms of the future, NAFTA is now departing from the pattern set in the first decade
and moving beyond the stage where its extension can take place solely on a product by
product basis. We have to look at whole sectors of industry and ensure that the decisions that
both Governments take are co-ordinated to the maximum extent possible, and take into
account the desirability, wherever possible, of industries having a total market of 17 000 000
people. That is the policy of the Government; and in contrast to the shaky position under the
Labour Government, we can now report the success of trade relations during the last 2
years between Australia and New Zealand. I am sure that, although honourable members
opposite will deplore their own poor record, they will be pleased that we have achieved this
success.
Trade with Pacific Island States has been mentioned. The Prime Minister referred to the
work of the forum, and I pay a tribute to him for the very great practical interest he has taken
in the Pacific Island States. I had the opportunity of attending the last 3 days of the regional
heads of Government meeting in Canberra when the Prime Minister had to return to New
Zealand on business. I found, when talking to the Ministers, that they were very appreciative
of the Prime Minister's work in developing the joint interests of New Zealand and these
countries.
In November 1976, the National Government introduced the Pacific Islands industrial
development scheme, designed to provide financial assistance and incentives to encourage
New Zealand companies to establish manufacturing operations in Fiji, Tonga, Western
Samoa, the Cook Islands, and Niue. The objective is to foster economic development and
the growth of employment opportunities in those Island States; and it is likely that the
scheme will be extended to other Island States. Indeed, I recently approved a feasibility
study for an Auckland firm seeking to work, in conjunction with its business, in the Solomon
Islands. Incentives and assistance available for a series of projects include suspensory loans,
small-venture grants, feasibility-study assistance, training assistance, and grants to cover part
of the cost of transferring key staff and equipment to the Islands; and the scheme also
provides special access to the New Zealand market for approved goods, but only after
consultation in New Zealand with the Federation of Labour and the Manufacturers
Federation.
Over 200 manufacturing firms in New Zealand have made inquiries to my department
about the scheme, and I am very pleased to report that, after the expected slow start in the
first year, eight projects are now in operation-three in Tonga, two in Western Samoa, two
in Fiji, and one in the Cook Islands. A further eight are about to commence, and an
additional 11 are approaching that stage. Those projects number 27, and other firms are at
present making representations and having discussions with their counterparts in the Islands,
with the Island Governments, and with my own department. In addition, agricultural
projects have been added to the scheme. Some Island Governments were concerned at the
entry of our producers into their areas, but we are taking them one at a time, and I am
pleased to report that there is a growing interest in New Zealand assisting with agricultural
projects under the scheme.
Much more could be said about the scheme, of course, but I have used it as an
illustration of what the National Government has done to develop practical proposals to
assist in employment opportunities and industry in the Island States. It is a balanced
programme. We want to do better in our relationships with Japan, the EEC, and Australia,
and, as a result of the Government's efforts, we are doing better. With the Island States,
however, it is a matter of helping to develop our joint trade. The Government will certainly
continue to do the best it can to provide employment opportunities and further trade for the
Island States. That represents a positive approach to foreign aid. We are seeking to develop
the skills of people in their own countries. The National Government pioneered this, and
will continue to develop it throughout the Pacific Islands in the years that lie ahead.

I want to comment on our trade negotiations, which are very much an international
affair. The trade negotiations in which we are engaged will be as significant as any
negotiations have ever been. They will help to launch our future for the next 25 years. They
are of critical importance. We have been involved in negotiations with the European
Economic Community to settle conditions of access for our lamb, butter, and cheese. In the
GATT multilateral trade negotiations we are seeking to settle a framework within which our
trading negotiations and future trade patterns will operate with our main trading partners.
Our basic objectives within the multilateral trade negotiations are to seek an agreement
on dairy products that will provide stability in the international market and protect our
interests along with those of other countries most dependent on trade in those products. We
seek an international agreement on beef, to achieve a similar stability. We seek, and I
believe we have hope of obtaining, an agreed schedule of subsidies that will work
progressively and effectively to reduce and eliminate the adverse effects of heavily subsidised
dairy products and meat placed on the international market so as to dispose of surpluses.
Above all, we have the right to seek to improve access to the main markets for our vitally
important agricultural primary products.
From the EEC we seek, and I believe properly so, a right to continue into the future. I
believe we have the right to maintain access into the EEC. It will not be an easy task, but
nevertheless we must seek to accomplish that goal. Over the last few months the Minister of
Foreign Affairs has visited Washington, Paris, and Geneva and, despite the problems, we
shall as a consequence be a stronger and more profitable country.
I believe there is now wide recognition and acceptance at top political levels that we are

at the cost in real terms and in terms of money spent in supporting uneconomic agricultural
production that, through high price policies, has too often led to surpluses and ever more
costly disposal programmes. There is a widely held conviction that the GATT multilateral
trade negotiations are probably the last chance, for at least a decade, of negotiating on a
multilateral basis for liberalism in trading conditions. I believe the pursuance of such a goal is
absolutely vital to stimulate growth and to reduce protectionism.

Adjournment-Foreign Affairs
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui): Earlier this evening the Prime Minister claimed that
what he called the high-profile tactics the Government had employed in its conduct of
foreign affairs had succeeded. That is simply not true. The conduct of foreign affairs by this
country and the Government in the last 3 years has been marked not by success but by
clumsiness, gross insensitivity, and even stupidity, and has brought the reputation of this
country to a level lower than I can remember, and probably lower than it has been for 30 or
40 years. Not even in the days of the former National Government was the reputation of the
country so bad. I know that the Minister of what was he called? - "foreign repairs" has
spent a good deal of his time mending fences.
Has the Minister of Foreign Affairs ever talked to expatriate New Zealanders, to New
Zealanders travelling overseas, or to any of his counterparts in other countries, to find out
how small New Zealand stands in the eyes of the world? I am sure that any Minister with an
ear to listen and a mind to hear must know that New Zealand's standing in the forum of the
world is at an all-time low. Not even in the Holyoake years, in the days of the previous
National Government, which were hardly imaginative, sensitive, or realistic, was as much
harm done to New Zealand's reputation as in the three tragic years of this Government.
Many New Zealanders travelling overseas have been ashamed and embarrassed by New
Zealand's stance on so many issues and I am certain that there are members on the other
side of the House who know that to be true. I am sure that people will have told them the
same sort of things that they have told members on this side of the House.
I want to make it plain that Opposition members have no great quarrel with the way in
which the Minister of Foreign Affairs has gone about his business of selling New Zealand
goods overseas and getting the best possible deal. We have no quarrel with the way in which
he has sought to improve New Zealand's standing overseas, but the single most important
issue in foreign affairs is not the Minister of Foreign Affairs, but the unfortunate person who
sits beside him. The clumsy, arrogant ineptitude of the Prime Minister is the single most
important issue in foreign affairs in this country today. The efforts of his deputy to alleviate
some of that damage have helped a little, but the impression remains that New Zealand is a
joke-and a very sick joke at that-in the forums of the world; and a tragic joke when one
considers the progress we have made.
I remind members opposite of the days of the previous Government, when I cannot
recall any New Zealander ever suggesting that he or she should be ashamed overseas of our
country. Many people remember with pride the days of achievement under the late Norman
Kirk and the present Leader of the Opposition as consecutive Ministers of Foreign Affairs in
the Labour Government. The Labour Government had a high profile-
An Hon. Member: It didn't.
Mr MARSHALL: It had a constructive, responsible, high profile of great value. I heard
somebody say that it did not. I remember the very great response there was around the world
to our protest about French nuclear testing in the Pacific. Many people realised for the first
time not only that there was a country called New Zealand but also that there was a small
country down in the Pacific with a conscience, that was ready to speak up and stand up for
the small nations on the matter of nuclear testing. Many people watched with pride when
New Zealand, the major sporting opponent of South Africa, said in the time of the Labour
Government, "We will not allow our principles about racism to be confused by our love for
rugby." At a great sacrifice, admittedly detrimental to Labour candidates in the last election,
we gave up that contact, which was a considerable sacrifice for the rugby-loving people of
this country.
However, many people recognise that the former Labour Government was one of
principle and conscience. If New Zealanders themselves did not always realise the great
value of what was done during that period, the people of many other parts of the world-
especially Africa and the Third World-realised that, although a little belated, the actions
taken were the right ones. When Norman Kirk first started talking in the 1960s, about the
need to give more in overseas aid, many people recognised that they were hearing a new
voice of conscience. At that time the voice came from the Opposition, but when it came to
power the Labour Government put its money where its mouth had been and treated the
question of overseas aid much more seriously than it had been before or, unfortunately, has
been since. It again gave New Zealand an independent voice in the forums of the world, and
many New Zealanders were proud of their country. We shall do that again, from the end of
November this year.
I remind Government members that in spite of their bold talk about a high profile there

are a few low profiles as well, which they have not mentioned. What about the Common
Fund, for example? New Zealand had such a low profile on that that one could hardly see
where the country was. For a couple of years we hid successfully behind other countries, but
one by one they dropped off and joined in the support for the Common Fund until we were
left, as is said in the nursery rhyme, like the cheese that stands alone. In the end we were

Let us look at another issue-and I am sure the Minister of Foreign Affairs is familiar
with the subject of disarmament. Where is our high profile on disarmament? We have such a
pathetically low profile that it can hardly be seen; and today the Government has disbanded
the consultative committee. I remind the Minister and the Government of the green paper
prepared in advance of the United Nations Special Assembly on Disarmament. The paper is
the Government's own document, dated April 1978. I quote from annex 4 the statement by
the New Zealand representative, Miss Jan Beagle, to the fourth session of the preparatory
committee on 15 February: "At the national level New Zealand non-governmental
organisations play a very useful role in informing the public on disarmament issues generally
and at the present time on the special session in particular." Miss Beagle also said, "We
believe that this informal consultative link between the Government and the non-
governmental sector in disarmament is valuable in maintaining a liaison with a flow of
information to the public on this important subject."
The Government set up the committee, but initially provided it with no funds
whatsoever. However, after pressure from the committee, the Government reluctantly gave
it $1,000. None of the major recommendations made by the committee was accepted by the
Government. The committee was not even given the courtesy of seeing the green paper on
disarmament before it was published, although it had been promised that it would have that
opportunity. The committee requested that it be retained after the special session, and was
told that the matter would be considered at the meeting after the special United Nations
session on disarmament. At that meeting, held this morning, there was no discussion; the
Deputy Secretary of Foreign Affairs simply announced that the committee was to be
disbanded. The Government, in its paper, proclaimed that there was value in having such a
committee, but it has now disbanded it. Well, at least that was an honest action, because it
took no notice of the committee anyway. So much for the so-called high profiles that are so
successful! New Zealand is about the weakest and most timid country in the world today on
matters such as the Common Fund and disarmament.
And what about overseas aid? Certainly we do not have a very high profile there. Year
by year the National Government has steadily reduced the effective vote, especially for
multilateral aid and for aid to Pacific countries.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: The honourable member knows full well that the vote is up.
Mr MARSHALL: Well, let us consider the position carefully. In 1976-77 the vote was
down from 0.58 percent to 0.44 percent; in 1977-78 it was reduced from 0.44 percent to 0.35
percent; and this year it is down to 0.32 percent. The Minister of Foreign Affairs tells us that
the vote is up.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: Is the amount up or down?
Mr MARSHALL: Of course it is up in money terms, but let us not play with words.
Hon. Members: Ha, ha.
Mr MARSHALL: The Minister of Foreign Affairs knows very well that the Government
has virtually halved its grant in overseas aid. For 2 years running the aid vote has been kept
effectively at the same figure, which is a very substantial reduction in view of the
Government's inability to control inflation. In case the member for Awarua-who is trying
to interject and who will not be in the House much longer-does not already know, it is part
of the Labour Party's policy to move towards 1 percent of gross national product. Is it the
policy of the National Government to do that? I very much doubt it.
Talking about high and low profiles, the Government has been taking credit for the
industrial development scheme in the Pacific Islands. Of course the ground work was done
by the Labour Government, but tonight, and on several other occasions, the Minister of
Trade and Industry has proudly boasted that agricultural projects have been added to the
scheme. The Labour Government's original scheme included provision for agricultural

WEDNESDAY, 2 AUGUST 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Poultry Board Regulations
1. Mr WETERE (Western Maori), on behalf of Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch
Central), to the Minister of Trade and Industry: Is he aware of the existing activity of feed-
supply companies in the buying of entitlement licences from egg producers at grossly
exorbitant prices during the period before the proposed regulations relating to the sole
purchases by the New Zealand Poultry Board are promulgated, and the fact that this can
result in "tied supply" sale of those licences to other egg producers, and does he know if the
Examiner of Commercial Practices is looking into this?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The question of
financial arrangements for the purchase of entitlement licences falls under the portfolio of
my colleague the Minister of Agriculture, to whom the member for Christchurch Central has
directed two questions on this matter on today's Order Paper. I understand that the
Examiner of Commercial Practices has received no complaints about the sale of licences at
grossly exorbitant prices or in respect of "tied supply". Any substantive complaint he may
receive indicating a trade practice of this nature that appears to be contrary to the public
interest will be investigated in terms of the Commerce Act.
East Timor-American Intervention
2. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Is he aware of recent
claims that Indonesian troops in East Timor are being supported by American advisers on
the ground, and that American pilots are flying bombing missions over East Timor; does he
have any information that would confirm or deny the accuracy of these statements; and has
he expressed concern to the American authorities about them?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): I am aware of these recent
allegations. Fretilin has not substantiated its claim, and New Zealand has no evidence of an
American presence in Timor. Consequently, there has been no occasion for the Government
to express its concern to the United States.
Mr Prebble: Has the Minister of Foreign Affairs received any evidence or submissions
from the member for Eden to back up his question?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: I do not think it is necessary to receive any evidence. On 12
July Mr Ramos Horta, Fretilin's petitioner in the United Nations, issued a press statement
claiming that American military advisers were alongside troops in East Timor.
Cook Islands New Zealand Police Assistance
3. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) to the Minister of Police: Were arms issued at any time to
any or all of the five policemen sent to the Cook Islands, who are now guarding the Acting
Head of State, and, if so, were they issued before or after the official request for police
assistance was received?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): The policemen who went to the Cook
Islands were not in possession of firearms at any time.
Mr Christie: Would the Minister now answer the second part of the question? Were the
policemen subsequently issued with arms?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY: I shall repeat the answer for the benefit of the member for
Napier, who obviously cannot understand English. The policemen who went to the Cook
Islands were not in possession of firearms at any time.

Questions for Oral Answer
Forestry-Private Plantings, Gisborne-East Coast
4. Mr BELL (Gisborne) to the Minister of Forests: What area of new planting has been
carried out on privately owned land in the Gisborne-East Coast region in the years 1972 to
1978 inclusive, and what proportion of those plantings was made with forestry
encouragement grant assistance?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The areas of new planting on private land in
the Gisborne-East Coast region carried out other than for protection purposes only are as
follows: 1972, 45 ha, of which 39 ha were planted through forestry encouragement grants;
1973, 72 ha, including 60 ha through forestry encouragement grants; 1974, 346 ha, all
through forestry encouragement grants; 1975, 1024 ha, of which 430 ha were through
forestry encouragement grants; 1976, 809 ha, of which 271 ha were through forestry
encouragement grants; and 1977, 1472 ha, of which 524 ha were through forestry
encouragement grants. Final figures are not yet available for 1978.
Mr Bell: Did any of this planting take place in what is described as the critical
headwaters area of this region?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I cannot say exactly where the planting took place, but I think it
would have taken place in areas both inside and outside the "blue line". However, I will
make inquiries to get a more exact answer for the honourable member.
Mr Wetere: What areas were planted in production forestry under the forestry
encouragement grants scheme?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The areas planted under the forestry encouragement grants
scheme were all for production forestry as against conservation forestry that is planted for
joint production and water and soil conservation purposes.
National Library Loan Services
5. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Education: Is it correct that the
National Library director of user services, who has responsibility for most inter-library loans
recently informed libraries that without additional staff she cannot maintain the services
normally provided, and concluded her letter, "But we must ask all librarians to restrict
urgent requests, telephone requests and recreational subject requests to the lowest possible
number", and, if so, does he approve of this reduction of service to public libraries, and can
he state what steps he is taking to provide adequate staff?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The National Library's user-services
division is at present short-staffed because of staff ceiling restrictions and a number of recent
resignations, for which replacements have not yet been appointed. While I am concerned
that all urgent and serious requests for information should be dealt with promptly, it is
nevertheless quite appropriate that the National Library should restrict its service in
response to certain categories of telephone requests and recreational subject requests. A
proposal to increase the National Library staff ceiling is now being considered by the State
Services Commission.
Hon. W. W. Freer: What action is being taken to fill the vacancies that have not been
filled?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: A cutback in services is not entirely a bad thing. Librarians
inside and outside the Wellington district constantly misuse the inter-library loan system by
forwarding to Wellington inquiries that should be dealt with locally. In direct answer to the
member's question, the normal steps are being taken to recruit staff and I have a request to
the State Services Commission and Cabinet for an increase in staff numbers.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In view of the Minister's extraordinary statement that it is not a bad
thing to restrict library facilities, would he be prepared to supply either to myself or to the
House the way in which he believes this restriction should apply?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: As I said, the National Library receives requests that should be
dealt with locally but which, for some reason, are not. Miss Claridge, the director of user
services, believes that these requests should be directed to local areas first, and only
subsequently should they be directed to the National Library for service.

Fertiliser Usage
8. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa) to the Minister of Agriculture: What was the total quantity

Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): For the year ended June 1978,

This represents an increase of 7 percent over the 2 162 000 tonnes delivered for the
corresponding period in 1977.
State House Tenants-Savings Schemes
9. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Housing: Can he confirm that
contributions to the limited tenancy savings scheme are compulsory for virtually all tenants
taking up corporation rental units, and that, since his policy does not allow corporation
tenants to belong to both the tenancy savings scheme and the home ownership savings
scheme at the same time, virtually all new corporation tenants are being deprived of the
benefits the home ownership savings scheme offers?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Tenants do not in fact make any
contribution to the tenancy savings scheme, and compulsion plays no part in the scheme.
The position is that all tenants allocated corporation rental houses from and including 1
October 1976 are entitled to the opportunities available through the tenancy savings scheme,
provided they comply with their obligations as corporation tenants. If the option is not taken
up by the end of 6 years, the benefits under the scheme are forfeited. It is quite incorrect to
assume that new corporation tenants are being deprived of the benefits of the home


## p. 2250 (#512) ###########################################

2250
2 August
Questions for Oral Answer
ownership savings scheme. A tenant can, if he or she so wishes, apply to join the home
ownership savings scheme. The tenancy savings scheme. is an alternative to the home
ownership savings scheme, but no one is entitled to the benefits of both schemes.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: Since the Minister has confirmed that tenants cannot belong to both
schemes, is it not a fact, first, that that discourages savings, and, secondly, that the maximum
benefits under the home ownership savings scheme are very much greater than the benefits
under the tenancy savings scheme?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I can confirm that no one can belong to both schemes.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: Why not?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: Because one is a contributing scheme by which one saves,
and the other is a calculation by which one is given a sum of money that can be applied
towards the purchase of a house, if one is a State house tenant.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: Or get out after 6 years.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: Clearly, a State house tenant must make his choice as to
which scheme he will join. Of course, he does not have to make that choice until the end of 6
years. At that time he has to make the choice whether he takes the benefits of the tenancy
savings scheme-to which he has made no contribution or whether he takes the benefits of
the home ownership savings scheme into which he has put his own savings.
Mr Lithgow: Would the Minister confirm that there has been a significant increase in
both the number of home ownership savings schemes and of tenancy savings schemes over
the last 2 years?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I confirm that there has been a growing degree of interest
and, indeed, a considerable increase in both schemes, and many people are now taking
advantage of one scheme or the other.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: Is it not a fact that, because people are denied the benefits of the
home ownership savings scheme and are faced with a 6-year proposition to buy or get out,
they have no alternative but to be attracted into the virtually compulsory tenancy savings
scheme?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I do not think the honourable member understands what he
is talking about.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: Only from thousands of tenants.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: If the honourable member wants an answer, I suggest he
gives me an opportunity to give it.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: That would be a welcome change.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: Let me explain to the member what the tenancy savings
scheme is. As he knows, a tenant in a State rental house pays a rental. The difference
between the rental he pays and a calculation based on one-sixth of a standard social welfare
benefit is credited to him, and if at any time during the first 6 years of his tenancy he wishes
to purchase that house, or any other house, he may pay as a deposit on that house the
amount that stands in credit to his name. If he wants to join the home ownership savings
scheme he may do so, and get all the benefits of that account.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Can the Minister confirm that this Government reintroduced the
policy of allowing State tenants to buy houses they were renting a scheme that had been
stopped by the Labour Administration, and a scheme that resulted in the tenancy savings
scheme?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I cannot confirm that it was reintroduced by this
Government, but I can confirm that it was introduced by a National Government and was
suspended for a while by the Labour Government, which, when it realised how popular the
scheme was, reintroduced it.
Mr Rogers: The Minister said that there was growing interest in the tenancy savings
scheme. Can he give the number of people who have joined the scheme to date?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: From what the honourable member has said, I think he does
not understand the scheme either. A tenant does not join the scheme, he simply indicates
some time during the 6 years of his tenancy whether he wishes to take advantage of it.
Mr Rogers: How many indications?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: A tenant goes along to the Housing Corporation and says he
wants to withdraw his benefit from the tenancy savings scheme because he is buying a house.
It is at that point that there is an indication. It is not a question of joining the tenancy savings
scheme, it is a question of those who take advantage of it. It is very early days yet, and I
cannot, off the cuff, give the honourable member those figures, but they are available if he
wants them.

Regional Development Programmes
10. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) to the Minister of Regional Development:

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development): As part of its continuing review
of regional development assistance programmes, the Government has recently adjusted the
criteria of the small projects assistance grants scheme. The criteria for eligibility for
companies have been increased from fixed assets of $30,000 to fixed assets of $50,000, and
annual sales of $150,000 rather than the previous maximum of $100,000. The limit for
qualifying investment has been increased from $20,000 to $30,000, with grants being made
up to 50 percent of the qualifying costs. This gives a maximum grant of $15,000. This grant is
unsecured, to leave companies' assets unencumbered should they need to raise commercial
finance for the development. The scheme will still apply to all towns in the 11 regional
development priority areas with a population not exceeding 10 000. In addition, businesses
in Gisborne and Invercargill are also eligible for grants.

Mr MacDonell: It is a new scheme.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: It was announced in the Budget. The question refers to changes made

that the provision can be made from the main estimates, but if not a supplementary provision
will be made.

WRITTEN QUESTIONS
Arapawa Island Goats-DSIR Reports
(13/7/78)
Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) to the Minister of Lands: Are there two DSIR
reports by Dr R. H. Taylor and G. M. Clark and G. W. Asher on the subject of
Arapawa Island wild animals-the first of which recommends more research and
investigation into the ecology of the goats on Arapawa Island and the second of
which advises against "hit or miss" extermination attempts and, if this is the
case, why have the advice and recommendations of these studies been ignored?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: I am aware of the reports
referred to, and advise that these were taken into consideration before the com-
mencement of the control programme. However, because of the continuing heavy
damage to the unique stand of bush in the scenic reserve being caused by the
goats, the Marlborough Sounds Maritime Park Board decided the control pro-
gramme should not be delayed any longer. The studies carried out on the goats
have been inconclusive in determining the historic or scientific importance of
these animals and I feel that the 100 goats that my department is to remove from
the island, plus those that have already been removed by private individual
organisations, will preserve the gene pool. While the intention was to bring the
goats into the Waitangirua block near Wellington for farming, they are now to
be removed to the department's Ngawatu development block near Nelson and will
be available for further scientific study by DSIR and any other scientific groups
that may be appropriate.
2.
Russian Trials Government Concern
(13/7/78)
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Will he join
other Western nations and make representations to the Soviet Government about
the contravention of human rights in the recent "show" trials in which Ida Nudel
and Vladimir Slepak were accused of "malicious hooliganism" because they
wanted to be reunited with their families in Israel?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs)
replied: The Government is not aware of any concerted move by other Western
nations to protest to the Soviet Government over the trials to which the honour-
able member has referred. The question of joining other countries in the way he
has suggested has not, threfore, arisen. Nevertheless, the Government does share
the deep public concern in New Zealand about such trials in the Soviet Union and
the harsh penalties imposed on individuals who, by any reasonable standards, have
merely sought to exercise what we in this country would regard as basic freedoms.
The sentencing of Ida Nudel and V'adimir Slepak to internal exile is an example
of this. Equally troubling is the Soviet authorities' harsh treatment of members
of the so-called Helsinki group, who have endeavoured to monitor the Soviet
Union's implementation of the Final Act to which the Soviet Government sub-
scribed at the Helsinki Conference in 1975. We recall the trial and sentence in
May of Dr Yuri Orlov, and shall follow very closely the forthcoming trials of
Anatoly Shcharansky and Alexander Ginsburg. Many New Zealanders have
expressed their disquiet to the Government over this situation, and the Ministry
of Foreign Affairs was instructed last month to bring this concern to the attention
of the Soviet authorities. At the same time, the Government has to accept that
there are strict limits to what it can say officially about another Government's
treatment of its individual citizens. The correct conduct of relations between States
normally precludes our making specific representations for leniency if New Zealand
citizens are not involved. It remains the Government's hope, however, that the
concern expressed in many countries around the world will not be lost on the
Soviet authorities and that this will cause them to adopt a more humane attitude
to people whose sole crime, it seems, is that of following their own conscience.
New Zealand for its part will continue to press strongly in the United Nations
and other appropriate international bodies for universal observance of the inter-
national human rights covenants. It is unremitting pressure of this general kind,
rather than specific direct representations about individual cases, that is most appro-
priate in our view for us to undertake.

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied. (a) Over the last 5

Geothermal Steam Supply, Kawerau
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: When is it
expected that finality will be reached in the negotiations with the Tasman Pulp
and Paper Co. on the conditions for the future supply of geothermal steam to the
company's mills at Kawerau, and what difficulties are holding up the reaching of
an agreement?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: Negotiations for the continued
supply of geothermal energy to the Tasman Pulp and Paper Co. follow from the
new geothermal pricing policy implemented by the Geothermal Energy Amendment
Act 1977. Agreement has been reached on most of the cost components for the
price of geothermal steam. The main outstanding item is the price the Govern-
ment should pay for Tasman's existing bores and borefield equipment. Negotiations
are proceedings on this aspect. I expect that a proposal on the price of geothermal
steam supply for Tasman will be ready for consideration in the near future.

9.
Common Heritage Fund-Landlocked Countries
(13/7/78)
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What support
does New Zealand lend to the request of Nepal's representative at the United
Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea earlier this year for the establishment of
a common heritage fund to provide to landlocked countries a percentage of net
revenues that would be likely to result from the 200-mile exclusive economic zones
of coastal countries?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied:
New Zealand has not lent support in the Law of the Sea Conference to the pro-
posal referred to by the member for Hutt. As the honourable member is aware,
the negotiations in the conference have reached an advanced stage. There is a
consensus in favour of the great majority of the more than 300 articles comprising
the draft convention and the conference is now concentrating its work on a limited
number of outstanding issues. The Nepalese proposal is new, and represents a
major departure from principles that have drawn broad support in the conference
and are embodied in the draft convention. In New Zealand's view the pursuit of
this new proposal will not help the attainment of consensus in the conference. It
will merely add another contentious issue and delay the achievement of a widely
supported convention.
10.
Development of Fishing Ports-Finance
(13/7/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Finance: Is finance
available at lower than normal rates of interest for the upgrading and development
of ports for fishing, and, if so, could he outline the sources?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: Finance is not
available at lower than normal interest rates for the upgrading and development
of fishing ports. Provided the proposed harbour works have the approval of the
New Zealand Ports Authority, a harbour board wishing to upgrade and develop
a fishing port may apply to the Local Authority Loans Board for sanction to raise
the required loan. In line with the Government's 1975 election manifesto the
Government will provide assistance in raising loan moneys if it is not possible for
a harbour board to raise all the funds on the loan market in the normal way.
Interest rates payable would be those applying to local authority loans generally.

Kindergarten Attendances
(14/7/78)
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) to the Minister of Education: What
percentage of the total population of 3-year-olds to 5-year-olds attended kinder-
gartens or playcentres for each of the years 1972, 1975, and 1978?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: As at 1 July 1972,
43 275, or 36.3 percent of the total 3-year-old and 4-year-old population, attended
a kindergarten or play centre. As at 1 July 1975, 51 128, or 40.6 percent of the
total 3-year-old and 4-year-old population, attended a kindergarten or play centre.
Figures for 1 July 1978 are not yet available. However, it is estimated that 53 400,
or 47.2 percent of the 3-year-olds and 4-year-olds are attending play centres and
kindergartens. The question does not take into account the significant number
of children enrolled in other pre-school services assisted through the Education
vote, such as mobile units, the Correspondence School, and pre-school classes in
schools. Neither does it take account of children below 3 years in play centres or
of children over 5 not mature enough for school admission and still enrolled in
pre-school services. If these figures are included, the total number rises to 67 495
children of the 3-year-old to 5-year-old population enrolled in pre-school services.
(14/7/78)
20.
Photographic Contemporary History Unit
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Internal Affairs:
What action is being taken by the Department of Internal Affairs to ensure a
continuity of photographic records of New Zealand activities for the archives?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) replied: An interdepart-
mental committee has been set up to study the establishment of a photographic
contemporary history unit. This committee has identified the present holdings of
Government agencies, the major ones being the National Archives, the Alexander
Turnbull Library, and the publicity division of the Tourist and Publicity Depart-
ment, although there are several other significant holdings. At its last meeting the
committee decided that the next step required is to compile a national directory
of all existing collections of historical importance. My department is at present
undertaking this task. When it is completed, the committee will be able to formu-
late specific recommendations to the Government.

23.
Wainuiomata Road Tunnel
(18/7/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Works and Develop-
ment: Is a road tunnel the best access solution for Wainuiomata, and, if
not, on what grounds have engineers and the National Roads Board declined to
support completion of the present partly built road tunnel; and, if this partly com-
pleted road tunnel has design or engineering deficiencies, would another tunnel
sited on a different route be a possibility, and how would such a proposal com-
pare in cost and completion time with the upgrading of the hill road and con-
struction of the Gracefield road intersection flyover?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: The
question of whether a road tunnel is the best access solution for Wainuiomata is
one that must be considered on economic grounds, taking into account both
capital and tunnel operating costs, particularly lighting and ventilation costs.
Taking these aspects into consideration the upgrading of the hill route has been
preferred at the present time to the construction of a tunnel. The partly completed
tunnel is some 300 m long and was to have had a completed length of 1000 m at a
grade of 1 in 15. As originally envisaged, the tunnel was not deficient, but if a
tunnel was to be considered at the present time it would be necessary to plan for
a much improved tunnel shape (related to present-day operations of the traffic
flows), a lesser grade, and a change in alignment. Such a proposal has not been
estimated recently, but it is considered that the cost would be not less than $10
million for a two-lane facility together with approaches. The design and con-
struction period would be about 5 years. The present works being undertaken to
upgrade the road are estimated to cost $1.8 million and are at present programmed
for completion in 1980-81. The actual completion date will be dependent on the
progress achieved, as it is recognised that the work must be carried out in such a
way as to minimise disruptions to the community, and any possible acceleration of
the work should be encouraged.

Rail Fare Reductions-Masterton-Maymourn
(18/7/78)
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Railways: In view
of the unemployment situation in the Wairarapa, would he be prepared to reduce
the monthly young persons' rail fares from stations Masterton to Maymourn
inclusive to give those people a chance to compete equally on the Wellington job
market?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: Very considerable
concessions already apply to young commuters from the Wairarapa, and to
increase those concessions would run contrary to the Government's policy since
lifting the freeze on railway charges, which has been to move progressively
towards a closer relationship between fares and rates and the cost of providing
the services. In addition, it must be realised that to grant a further concession
would inevitably lead to similar demands from other areas and the expense
involved would be quite unacceptable.

28.
Labour Department Facilities, Wairoa
(18/7/78)
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) to the Minister of Labour: In view of
the fact that the Wairoa district has the highest seasonal unemployment rate
of any area of New Zealand, does he propose to base a Department of Labour
official in the area?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The office of the Department
of Social Welfare in Wairoa provides facilities for persons seeking help in finding
employment to enable them to register for assistance from the employment and
vocational guidance service of my department. Regular visits are made to the
area by employment officers from my Napier district office, who provide every
possible assistance both to those seeking employment and to employers seeking
workers. At this time the level of unemployment in the area does not justify
an employment officer being permanently stationed in Wairoa. However, in the
event of a deterioration in the local employment situation, existing arrangements
will be reviewed to meet the area's changed requirements.
29.
Employment Situation, Wairoa
(18/7/78)
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) to the Minister of Labour: Does the
department plan to hold meetings, such as the one held in Wairoa, with local
interest groups in other areas of high unemployment?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The purpose of the meeting
held in Wairoa on 27 June 1978 was to discuss the local employment situation
and the introduction of local pre-employment courses under the Government's
special training programme. Such meetings are not planned by my department.
It is normal practice, however, for officers of my department, subject to avail-
ability, to accept invitations to attend meetings of local-interest groups when
matters related to the department's activities are discussed.

Housing Corporation Section Loans
(19/7/78)
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Housing: (a) How many
section loans, in addition to Housing Corporation loans to erect dwellings, were
authorised in the year ended March 1976; (b) what was the average section loan
authorised in that year; (c) what was the average total loan for that financial
year for the erection of homes when the basic Housing Corporation loan to erect
dwellings in high-cost areas, together with low-income supplements and section
loans, are taken into account; (d) what were the criteria of eligibility for the full
package, including a loan to erect a dwelling, low-income supplement, and section
loan in that year; and (e) for a typical case in which an applicant was eligible
for the full package under (d), what interest on loans would have been paid,
what weekly repayments could the applicant have expected on the loans, and
what proportion of total average ingoing house and section costs at the time did
the full package of loans represent?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: The number of section
loans authorised in addition to loans to erect dwellings was: (a) section loans
2 128, Crown and HCNZ sections 444. (b) Average section loan authorised $4,351.
(c) Basic Housing Corporation loan for erection of houses in Auckland and Wel-
lington $14,000, plus average low-income supplement $2,000, plus average family

benefit supplement $1,401, plus average section loan $4,351, a total of $21,752.
(This answers the question, but cannot be regarded as "the average total loan"
for the year ended 31 March 1976.) It would be fallacious to conclude that the
average borrower did receive assistance of this order. The average erect loan was
$15,262 (including supplements) and the average section loan $4,351. For those
applicants who received both types of loan the average amount borrowed through
HCNZ was $19,613. (d) The primary policy for eligibility for a Housing Corpora-
tion loan was assistance for those applicants seeking to build a first home, who
had a need to borrow. That policy provided: (i) a standard average loan of $13,000
($14,000 in Auckland and Wellington); plus (ii) a low-income supplement of
$2,000, depending on income earned or family benefit capitalisation approved;
(iii) a dollar for dollar family benefit supplement of up to $2,000 for those holding
a current family benefit capitalisation certificate; and (iv) the income limits for
the low-income supplement were those applying to eligibility for an interest rebate-
i.e., the higher of the applicant's gross weekly income (based on a 40-hour week)
at the date of application, or the average weekly income earned for the 12 months
immediately preceding the application; in either case, to qualify, the income could
not exceed $85 per week, plus $5 for each dependent child. The income limit for
family benefit capitalisation was $80 per week (excluding overtime) plus $5 per
week for each child after the first with a maximum upper limit of $2,000. On
3 March 1976 the allowable income was changed to include the breadwinner's
taxable income-i.e., including overtime, secondary employment, related earnings,
and allowances. Section loans were available to anyone who was landless, married,
or intending marriage, who irrespective of income demonstrated a need to borrow.
Loan assistance with section purchase (other than Crown and HCNZ sections) was
suspended late in 1975. (e) (i) Interest charged: 3 percent when breadwinner's gross
income within a 40-hour week (excluding overtime) was up to $80 per week,
plus $5 per week for each dependent child; 41 percent $80-$85 per week for each
dependent child; 51 percent over $85 per week plus $5 per week for each depen-
dent child. After 3 March 1976 the breadwinner's gross income included over-
time, and the rate charged was 3 percent up to $80 plus $5 for each dependent
child, 5 percent $80-$85 plus $5 for each dependent child, 7½ percent over $85
per week.

Mangere Bridge Construction

work has not continued since the decision to dismiss staff was made; (b) what
steps he took in the period leading up to the dismissals to keep work on the
bridge continuing at a reasonable pace; and (c) when we can expect his action
to ensure that work on the bridge recommences at the earliest possible date?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: Thirty-six working days
have elapsed since the dismissal of the work force. This particular job has had a
long history of industrial difficulties. A great deal of time has been spent on the
site by members of both the mediation and conciliation services, and for a time

2272
2 August

an officer from my department's Auckland district office was also stationed on the
job. I believe all reasonable steps were taken to ensure that work continued with-

tion. As I understand the position, the contractor is keen to recommence work
and has advertised for men. However, a resumption of work has not been possible
because the job has been declared black by the unions and is being picketed.

Private Imports-Estimated Revenue if Taxed
(20/7/78)
Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Finance: Has the Treasury estimated
the revenue that would be raised by applying a 10 percent tax on all payments for
imports (excluding public sector imports) for the year ended May 1978, and, if
so, would such revenue amount to a figure of $400 million?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: Payments for private
sector imports of goods amounted to $2,855.5 million in the year to May 1978.
A 10 percent tax on such payments would have raised $286 million. This excludes
the payments for imports of services, or invisibles. The private sector paid $1,295.6
million for these in the year to May 1978, and a tax on these would raise an
extra $130 million. A tax on private sector imports of goods and services would
thus raise a total of $415 million, assuming there were no exemptions.

Education-Media Seminar
(21/7/78)
Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Education: Is his department
proposing to stage a major press conference during July, and, if so, what is its
purpose, what media representatives have been invited, what is its estimated cost,
and has any particular factor influenced its timing?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The department has
not arranged a press conference in the usual sense. It has, however, conducted a
media seminar over the last 2 days, 19 and 20 July. Similar seminars were held
in 1976 and 1977, in September and August respectively. The seminar brings
together senior education reporters from many centres, provides them with back-
ground papers on topics of current interest in education, and enables them to
seek any additional information they need in meetings with the senior officers of
the department. The seminar consists of several general sessions, and the oppor-
tunity is also provided for individual interviews to be arranged to meet each
reporter's wishes. The purpose of the seminar is to encourage the flow of infor-
mation on the many aspects of education. It is only part of the total effort to make
this information readily available to the public at large. Twenty-four invitations
were sent to newspapers and radio and television stations. Two of these declined
because of staff shortages. Those represented during all or part of the seminar
were: the Dominion, the Evening Post, Radio New Zealand, National, Regional,
and Current Affairs, Television One, Television Two, New Zealand Press Asso-
ciation, New Zealand Sunday Times, New Zealand Truth, the Listener, New
Zealand Herald, Auckland Star, Waikato Times, Manawatu Evening Standard,
Christchurch Star, the Press, Christchurch, the Otago Daily Times, the Evening
Star, Dunedin, the Tablet, the Southland Times, Radio Windy.
The estimated cost of the seminar is $1,360. The main factor the department
takes into account in the timing for the seminar is that it should be after the
presentation of the Budget so that, if journalists wish, they can question the
department over the whole range of its activities.

Underground Coalmining-Buller Area
(21/7/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What are the
department's plans for the future of the underground coalfields of the Buller area?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The reserves of coal in the
Buller coalfield set aside for underground mining comprise 15.3 percent of the
district's total reserve of 50 900 000 tonnes. The two mines at Denniston-Escarp-
ment and Sullivan-will continue to be worked, but because of its high sulphur
content there is no market available for the balance of the Buller's underground
coal reserves.
67.
Underground Coalmining-Stockton Area
(21/7/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What plans has
he for the underground coal mines in the Stockton area?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The coal reserves in the
Stockton area are predominantly opencast and there are no plans for further
underground mining after the present Mt. William mine is worked out. The
only underground prospects of any size that exist are too high in sulphur to be
acceptable to present customers. There are several small isolated pockets of coal
that could be won by underground methods, but mining conditions would be
difficult and they are regarded as uneconomic.
68. Extraction Rate-Mt. William and Strongmen Coalaines (21/7/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What is the
present extraction rate of coal from the Mt. William and Strongman mines
respectively?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: Over the life of the Mt.
William mine a 72 percent extraction rate has been obtained. In the area at
present being worked, a 90 percent rate has been achieved because of a local
improvement in the roof condition. These high extraction rates have been possible
because the size of the mine and the surface terrain are such that there has been
no need to leave coal barriers underground. The mine is worked by the hydro
system of mining. At Strongman, where scraper loaders and hydro methods are
used for coal winning, the extraction rate is 45 percent. Considerable quantities of
coal are left in barriers for fire seals in this mine.

Waitakere Hospital-Antenatal Facilities
(21/7/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: Why were antenatal
facilities at the Waitakere Hospital closed in September 1975?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: As a first phase to the establish-
ment of full obstetric services at Waitakere Hospital, the Auckland Hospital
Board established antenatal facilities there in October 1974. The board proposed
to finance the limited cost of these initial facilities from its annual grant for growth.
During 1975 the board found that it was unable to continue this service because
of shortage of funds. In December 1975 when this Government took office it was
informed of the financial situation of a number of hospital boards and made
immediate grants to assist the boards in their difficulties. These included a grant
of nearly $313,000 to the Auckland Hospital Board, which was to be applied, in
part, to the reinstatement of services at Waitakere Hospital.
71.
LPG Transportation-Safety Provisions
(21/7/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Internal Affairs: Is he
satisfied that adequate regulations and standards of safety are in force to ensure the
safe transportation and handling of LPG, and that a disaster such as that in San
Carlos de la Rapida in Spain could not occur in this country?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) replied: The standards of
safety associated with the transportation and handling of liquefied petroleum gas
in this country are laid down by the Chief Inspector of Dangerous Goods under
the authority of the Dangerous Goods Act and in the relevant provisions of the
Dangerous Goods Regulations 1958, the Shipping (Dangerous Goods) Rules 1953,
and safety codes applied by the industry. The possibility of an accident arising
from malfunction or human error will always exist, but I am satisfied that the
precautions being taken minimise this possibility to the greatest possible extent.
Nevertheless, the regulations dealing with LPG made under the Dangerous Goods
Act are being revised as a matter of urgency to provide better codification of
safety standards and to enable better enforcement of those standards.

Standard Building Code-Revision
(26/7/78)
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Housing: What progress
has been made since the director of the Standards Association stated that New
Zealand houses were "unnecessarily strong" and that for a modest increase in
funding the association would draw up a standard building code that could save
millions of dollars without a diminution in quality standards?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: An interim report
published by the Standards Association of New Zealand in June 1978 intimated


## p. 2282 (#544) ###########################################

2282
2 August
Questions and Replies
that revisions to the Light Timber Frame Code DZ 3604 still require to be
considered by the project committee and others. Provided no further major amend-
ments were necessary the new code could be available as early as November
1978. It has been established that revision is confined to editorial matters. The
Housing Corporation has already experimented with some of the possible pro-
visions of the code. Housing contracts have been let in both Auckland and
Wellington that included some of the expected provisions to determine their
acceptability as minimum standards. In Wellington the opportunity was extended
to interests of the building industry to view the effects of these possible provisions
as construction progressed. All loan securities are now also being built, in general
conformity with the proposed code. The savings that may result directly from
the introduction of the code are difficult to measure. It must be remembered
that the revision has been brought about not only to effect economies in materials
in non-load-bearing walls but also to meet other inadequacies introduced through
the more extensive use over recent years of materials such as glass and non-
traditional materials in load-bearing walls. It is possible that costs could increase
before savings become apparent, because of the time that will be taken for designers
and builders to become conversant with the new code, and the need for timber
producers to adjust to supplying differently sized timber from that at present used.

Waitangi State Forest
(13/7/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Forests: Are there any plans
for a replanting programme in the Waitangi State Forest on the West Coast using
rimu or other native species?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Yes, there are plans to replant those
areas of Waitangi State Forest that are not naturally regenerating satisfactorily to
rimu forest after logging. Twenty-five thousand rimu seedlings have been lined out in
the Totara Flat nursery in preparation for planting trials on the West Coast

Drug Seizures
(13/7/78)
Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Customs: Has a different system of
measuring seizures of drugs been introduced since 1 April 1977, and has that changed
method been adopted in calculating the figures set out on page 17 of the annual report
of the Customs Department?
Hon. P. I. WİLKINSON (Minister of Customs): I can confirm that a new
system of measuring seized quantities of drugs has been introduced since 1 April 1977
and has been used to calculate the figures shown in the 1978 annual report of the
Customs Department. The Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 came into force on 1 June 1977
and introduced new provisions relating to the evidence of analysis of controlled drugs
in court proceedings. Consequent upon the introduction of these new provisions the
basis of measuring the amount of drugs seized by my department was changed.
Formerly, the figure quoted was the bulk weight of the seized substance, including its
controlled drug content. However, the procedure now adopted is to publish only the
net quantity of controlled drugs seized following analysis of the bulk substance by the
DSIR. I should stress that whatever method of measurement is used to record
seizures of controlled drugs it would be quite wrong to interpret a single statistical
table as evidencing the relative success or failure of my department's overall anti-drug
activities.

Fish-Processing Facilities-Chartered Vessels
(13/7/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Fisheries: Have the three vessels
allowed to fish in New Zealand waters under charter to New Zealand companies, as
reported in the National Business Review of 5 July, any fish-processing facilities on
board?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): Most of the processing aboard the
three charter vessels will be limited to heading, gutting, and freezing. However, some
filleting for experimental purposes will be carried out on board the vessels. The
Sealord Products proposal provides for 50 percent of the catch to be further processed
on shore in New Zealand for export. The New Zealand Economic Zone Exports Ltd.
and Wanganui Trawlers (Wholesale) Ltd. will also process fish ashore, but to a lesser
extent. All projects are experimental and are designed to permit each company to
assess the economics of operating with freezer-type trawlers in New Zealand waters
for processing here and marketing the catch as New Zealand-processed products
internationally.

121.
Drugs-Customs Surveillance
(14/7/78)
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Customs: Is there
evidence that a number of illicit narcotics shipments destined for the New Zealand
market have left the country on the ship in which they arrived solely because of tight
surveillance on the part of the New Zealand Customs Department?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): Containment in Customs anti-
narcotic work is one arm of the total activity. There have been Customs operations in
which narcotics have been discovered on board ships and in which there has been
evidence that quantities undetected left New Zealand on the vessels that brought the
goods here. An example is the vessel Straat Fraser, which in the latter half of 1976 was
the subject of long-term surveillance in its period on the New Zealand coast. In this
period, rummages of the vessel revealed quantities of both cannibas and heroin and
there was every indication that further quantities were present on the vessel.
Subsequent intelligence revealed this to have been so and that the narcotics had
returned from whence they came. In cases of this nature information is, of course,
rather shadowy, and it is detailed evaluation of the evidence that produces the
indication I have given. I have quoted only one specific instance, but this is a
sufficient indication of the success of the Customs procedures-procedures that will
benefit greatly from the additional resources that have been made available for the
department's enforcement activity.

Social Welfare Benefit Payments

payment system of benefits to British pensioners resident in New Zealand, and what
efforts were made to simplify. the procedure for the 15 000 elderly people affected by
these changes?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The payment system for
United Kingdom pensions is, of course, entirely a matter for the United Kingdom
authorities. The head of the overseas branch of the United Kingdom Department of
Health and Social Security visited New Zealand in late 1977 for preliminary
discussions regarding the expressed intention to pay pensions direct from the United
Kingdom. Following his return to the United Kingdom, the New Zealand authorities
were informed that it had been decided to introduce the direct payment system.
Accordingly, in August 1978 the United Kingdom authorities will commence direct
payments by bank draft of all British national insurance pensions in force in New
Zealand. This will bring the payment system for New Zealand into line with that
operating for United Kingdom pensions in all other countries. The Department of
Social Welfare, on behalf of the United Kingdom authorities, has written to each
pensioner involved explaining the new method of payment. An invitation to
pensioners who are having difficulties with the new system of payment to contact
their local Department of Social Welfare office has been extended through the news
media.

141.
Antarctic Treaty-Fish Exploitation
(18/7/78)
Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What
changes does he foresee in the Antarctic Treaty to provide for supervision of the
exploitation of the stock of fish and krill in the region?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): The
Antarctic Treaty countries decided at the ninth consultative meeting in London last
year on the establishment of a regime to control the fishing of living marine resources
in Antarctic waters before the end of 1978. This will not involve any changes in the
Antarctic Treaty. A special meeting of treaty countries was held in Canberra in
March of this year, and a draft convention was drawn up: it will be a new agreement
that makes provision for the establishment of a commission on Antarctic marine
living resources. The commission would be supported by a scientific committee and
would be responsible for setting conservation standards. The special meeting in
Canberra did not complete the draft convention and the meeting was resumed in
Buenos Aires on 17 July-yesterday-for a further 2-week sesson.

Antarctic Treaty-Mineral Resources
(18/7/78)
Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What
proposals, if any, are being considered by the Antarctic Treaty powers to control the
exploration and development of mineral resources in the Antarctic region?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): The
Antarctic Treaty powers, at their most recent consultative meeting held in London in
September 1977, agreed to the following principles: first, that they would continue to
play an active and responsible role in dealing with this issue; secondly, that the
protection of the unique Antarctic environment and its dependent ecosystems should
be a basic consideration; thirdly, that the interests of all mankind in Antarctica
should not be prejudiced; and, fourthly, that the principles embodied in the Antarctic
Treaty should be included in the future regime for mineral resources. This subject
will be on the agenda for the tenth consultative meeting to be held in Washington
later next year, and will also be the subject of a preparatory meeting that will focus on
the legal and political aspects. In the interim, it was agreed that States would refrain
from all exploration and exploitation of mineral resources.

Industrial Accidents-News Media Reports
(18/7/78)
Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora) to the Minister of Labour: How many reports on
industrial accidents has the department published and does it have difficulty in
getting adequate coverage in the media?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): As a general rule, details of
industrial accidents are not published in the news media. This is because most
industrial safety legislation administered by my department contains provisions that
prohibit publishing of specific information obtained by inspectors in the course of
their work. One exception to this is the Agricultural Workers Act 1977, which
authorises the publishing of information on agricultural accidents with my consent.
My department has for some time published general summaries of serious and fatal
accidents in the Labour and Employment Gazette, and this has proved to be very
successful and will continue. I personally strongly support the publication of accident
details as part of a prevention programme, and, as industrial legislation lation is reviewed,
amendments will be included to facilitate the controlled release of accident details to
the news media, including trade journals. Where publication is possible, few
difficulties are experienced by the department in getting adequate media coverage.

Infant Mortality Figures
(18/7/78)
RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton
East) to the Minister of Health: Could he outline the latest available figures of infant
mortality in New Zealand; and how do these compare with the rates over the previous
5 years?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I am pleased to say that there is an
improvement in the latest available mortality rates for infants-that is, children
under 12 months of age. For the year 1971 the rate per 1000 live births was 16.6; for
1972, 15.6; for 1973, 16.2; for 1974, 15.6; for 1975, 16; and for 1976, 14. To improve
the rate further, the Department of Health is at present involved in a national study of
the social and medical factors associated with each post-neonatal death in an attempt
to elicit the cause of death so that appropriate remedial preventive action can be
taken.
