Union Finances
(19/7/78)
Mr LATTER(Marlborough) to the Minister of Labour: Does his department
propose any action in the light of the protest by the Wellington labourers union
members as reported in the Dominion of 14 July 1978, and can remedial action be
taken if the union's rules preclude this democratic right?
Mr Lange: What demonstration?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The interjection was, "What
demonstration?" If the member looks at the Dominion he will see a photograph of it. I
am asking my department to inquire into the protest referred to and to determine its
relevance to the provisions of the Industrial Relations Act. The Act requires that
every union shall, on a request in writing, furnish any financial member, on demand,
without charge, a copy of the latest annual income and expenditure account and
balance sheet; and, further, a copy of all resolutions passed at any annual general
meeting or special general meeting of any union shall be delivered by the union to any
financial member requiring the same on the payment of 50c or such other sum as may
be prescribed. The union's rules in this case also require that every member or
previous member having an interest in the funds may inspect the books and register of
the union on giving the requisite notice. If the situation comes into this category then
it is a domestic matter and one that should be properly disposed of within the
procedures provided for in the union rules.

Armed Services Technicians-Shortage
(19/7/78)
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill), on behalf of Squadron Leader DRAYTON
(St. Albans), to the Minister of Defence: Has he seen the article in the Auckland Star
of 8 July in which a Department of Defence spokesman is reported as saying that a
shortage of middle-ranking technicians is partially responsible for the grounding of a
large proportion of Air Force Iroquois helicopters, and what is he doing to keep this
expensive equipment working by replacing the skilled NCOs who have left the force
during the past year?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of Defence
replies: "I have seen the article in question. The grounding of Iroquois helicopters
was not attributable to a shortage of technical staff. Structural cracks were found in
the underfloor beams of four aircraft, and these were grounded for a period. All are
now back in service. Because of some shortages of middle-level technicians, inspection
and repairs took longer than would otherwise have been the case. The training
programme for technical trades has been streamlined over the last 2 years. Delays
between initial military training and specialist courses have been reduced to a
minimum. More intensive technical courses have resulted in an increase in output of
trained technicians. Also, pay levels will shortly be improved for skill and experience,
but it will be some time before the shortfall is made up. At the present rate of
recruiting it is expected that the shortages will be overcome in the next 2 or 3 years."

Misuse of Drugs Act
(19/7/78)
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead) to the Minister of Health: Is he aware of a decision
delivered in the Christchurch Supreme Court on 12 July 1978 by Mr Justice Casey
dismissing an appeal against conviction by a student charged with possession of a
drug for supply; does this decision indicate any problem with the provisions of the
Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, and is any urgent amendment necessitated by the
decision?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have seen the newspaper report of the
case referred to by the honourable member. The Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 does not,
as the reported statements of the judge indicate, contain any offence of possession of a
class C drug such as cannabis for the purpose of supply to a person of 18 years or over.
There are offences under the Act of simple possession or of possession for purposes of
sale, which should be adequate to deal with similar situations. However, care must be
exercised in the preparation of prosecutions for offences under this legislation to
ensure that persons are appropriately charged.

received by the operator, no further action is taken on the matter.

that the overall quotas of all beef imports into Japan have increased, but that the New
Zealand percentage of these quotas has decreased?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade): Allocations for
Japan's beef imports are made every 6 months. Although the total current allocation,
for April to September 1978, shows an increase over the allocation for the
corresponding period in 1977-48 000 tonnes, in comparison with 40 000 tonnes-it
is less than the total allocation for October 1977 to March 1978 of 52 500 tonnes. New
Zealand's exports of beef to Japan for these 6-monthly periods have been as follows:
794 tonnes for April to September 1977, or 1.98 percent of total imports, and 3278
tonnes for October 1977 to March 1978, or 6.24 percent of total imports. For the
current 6-monthly period, New Zealand's share in the two tenders called so far has
been 6.03 percent and 5.36 percent.

these reports have been considered by local authorities in the district and by the
South Canterbury Planning Council. The choices range from promoting the retention
of a substantial proportion of the town as a holiday and retirement centre to the

being met by the Government. I understand that the consultants' report is shortly to
be considered by the councils who will then make their views known to the
Government.

Broadlands Geothermal Power Project
(21/7/78)
Mr LA VARIS (Taupo) to the Minister of Energy: Is the present time-scale
for implementation of the Broadlands geothermal power project still valid, and, if not,
what are the new dates being set for completion of the first and second stages?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): In 1977 the Power Planning Committee
recommended a commissioning date of October 1983 for the first of three 50 MW
units at Broadlands geothermal power station. The second and third units were to
follow at 6-monthly intervals. Although the Power Planning Committee has not yet
formally revised this programme, it is already clear that some changes will be
necessary. The present intention is to develop Broadlands in two stages. The first
stage in commissioning relates to a development of 80 to 100 MW, and the final stage,
to bring the output up to a nominal 150 MW, would follow about 5 years behind the
first stage, or when adequate field experience had been obtained. The likely
commissioning date for the first unit of stage 1 is about October 1984 that is, about
a year later than shown for the first unit in last year's programme.

## p. 2309 (#571) ###########################################

2309
Questions and Replies
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The Clutha Valley
Commission, in its interim report in March 1974, gave comparative estimates of $300
million for proposal F and $320 million for proposal H. Those estimates were based
on 1973 construction costs. Comparative estimates quoted at various times since that
date have remained basically the same, apart from adjustments made to reflect the
escalating costs of construction and the increasing price of purchasing the installed
plant from overseas. The latest updating of the estimate was made in September 1977
in the Crown's submission to the Otago Catchment Board seeking a water right for
the Clyde Dam. At that time the comparative estimates were $732 million against
$797 million, and were based on early 1977 construction costs. Over the period 1973
to 1977 the difference in cost between the two alternatives therefore increased from
$20 million to $65 million.

218.
Union Rules
(25/7/78)
Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Minister of Labout: Can he indicate
whether the Registrar of Unions is required to approve rules for the registration of
unions, and, if so, is there a standard requirement for a union to keep an effective roll
of its members, to advise them of ths financial statement for the year, and to notify
them of the annual meeting; if not, has he any proposal to overcome a now apparent
problem?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The short answer to the member's
various questions is yes. Section 165 of the Industrial Relations Act 1973 provides
that when the registrar is satisfied that the provisions of the Act have been met he
shall register a union and record its rules. Section 175 requires that provision shall be
made in the rules of a union for the keeping of a register of members and the manner
of calling meetings of the union. Section 186 requires every union, on a requsst in
writing in that behalf, to furnish any financial member, on demand and without
charge, with a copy of the latest annual income and expenditure account and balance
sheet, together with the auditor's report on the accounts. Although a union is not
required to include this provision in its rules, the Act binds each union. I understand
it is common practice for unions to publish such facts in their various journals and
newsletters.

(25/7/78)

of the poor state of the roads in the Hokianga area and the report that TV2 did on
them, in which the school bus driver said he has at times considered that for safety
reasons, and because of the road conditions, he should no longer drive the bus to and
from school; and, if so, what steps has he taken to have the situation remedied, and

improved?

the condition of roads in the Hokianga area, and the television news report on the
matter. The Auckland Education Board and the principal of the Panguru High

Savings Bank Funds
(25/7/78)
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister of
Finance: (a) Does the money necessary for savings banks to invest in slow-starting
mortgage schemes described in the New Zealand Herald of 18 July come from existing
funds that are already invested in Government bonds; or (b) does the growth of the
scheme depend on new money flowing into the savings bank deposits with a reduced
liability for investment in Government funds?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): It is intended that the funds
to be invested by the savings banks in slow-start mortgages should mainly come from
the normal flow of funds available to those institutions for mortgage investments. The
funds would be available from both existing deposits and new deposit growth, as well
as normal return cash flow as mortgages are repaid. However, because investment in
these types of mortgages entails a lower return cash flow in the early years to the
institutions than other types of mortgages, the proposed adjustments to Government
stock ratio obligations have been designed to encourage investment in slow-start
mortgages. The adjustments are therefore intended to compensate the savings banks
for the lower return cash flow, and should also provide some additional funds for
investment. I shall make a full press statement on the scheme shortly.

DSIR-Soil Classifications
(25/7/78)
Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson), on behalf of Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua), to the
Minister of Science and Technology: When will details of the new soil
classifications being undertaken by the DSIR, which use a world standard method of
classifying fertility climate and crop suitability, be available for individual use?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology): The new soil
classification system is being adopted on current soil surveys carried out by the soil
bureau, DSIR, and the results will become available as these surveys are completed.
Complete coverage of the country using this system will take many years, but in the
meantime published soil surveys are available for many parts of New Zealand and
most of these contain information on the climate of the area, fertility of the various
soils, and ratings of them for different land uses, such as crops, pasture, and forestry.
The new classification system has also been applied to soil surveys carried out in the
Pacific Islands-the Cooks, Tonga, and the Lau group-by the soil bureau, and its
use will facilitate the transfer of advanced crop technology from more developed
countries to these areas.

in 1978. That was disgraceful"; and, if so, will he confirm that he has already
explained to the member for Mangere that the large tax saving can be easily
illustrated in other ways?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Yes, I have seen the report in
question and I can confirm that on several occasions I have explained the substantial
tax savings in the quoted example in a number of different ways. For example, a
married man with a dependent wife and a child under 5 years earning $6,000 a year
would have paid $1,425 a year or 23.75 percent of his gross income in tax under
Labour, whereas he will pay only $338 a year or 5.63 percent of his gross income
under the first full year of operation of National's tax tables-a tax savings of $1,087 a
year. For the same man to be paying $338 a year in tax under Labour, he would not
be earning $6,000 a year, or $115 a week as he will under National, but $3,094 a year
or $59.50 a week. The member for Mangere suggested that if an income of $120 "had
moved with the general wage trend it would now be $175". However, the same
married man earning $175 a week would have paid $52.12 a week in tax under
Labour, whereas under National's new tax rate he will pay only $31.18 a week, which
represents an increase in net income of $20.94 a week.

Unemployment Benefit Payments, Palmerston North (26/7/78)
Mr WETERE (Western Maori), on behalf of Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the
Minister of Social Welfare: To what extent is the unemployment benefit being paid
to people in Palmerston North who are reluctant to find jobs, as indicated by the
member for Palmerston North in the Manawatu Evening Standard of 18 July 1978?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Like my colleague from
Palmerston North, I, too, have been advised by many employers from various parts of
New Zealand that they have advertised extensively but unsuccessfully for both skilled
and unskilled staff, and they included the footwear industry, fruit and berry picking,
warehousemen, farm labourers, home help, etc. In other cases advised to me, persons
sent out to jobs by the Department of Labour have returned to the department
claiming they were not acceptable to the employer when in fact they had never
reported to the employer. I have also spoken to others or been shown applications
from others who would accept only a specific job-for example, that of an airline
captain or a lion tamer. However, as far as the Department of Social Welfare is
concerned, before a person can qualify for unemployment benefit he is required to
satisfy that department that he is willing and able to accept any offer of suitable
employment and that he has taken, without success, reasonable steps to obtain
suitable work. He is also required to continue actively to seek work through his own
efforts after a grant of unemployment benefit has been approved. Any person who
fails to take reasonable steps to find work may have his unemployment benefit
withdrawn or postponed for a period of up to 6 weeks in accordance with section
60(3) of the Social Security Act.

URGENT QUESTION
Dr Patel-GMS Benefit
(26/7/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Health: What is the
position of Dr C. M. Patel's patients now that the doctor has had his social security
benefit payments suspended for 6 months?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The honourable member does not
appear to understand the situation regarding Dr Patel's patients. It would perhaps be
helpful if I summarised the position. This doctor, over a long period of time, had been
seeing very large numbers of patients-up to 120 in 1 day. The Department of Health
considered that it was highly improbable that he could provide a good standard of


## p. 2319 (#581) ###########################################

2 August
2319
Questions and Replies
medical service to such an excessive number of patients. A GP seeing about 50
patients each week day, all in his surgery-and this is above the average-25 percent
of whom were elderly, 25 percent children, and 50 percent others-which is the
general pattern-would receive by way of GMS benefits at current rates $32,032 for a
50-week year. His charges to patients would be additional. If he charged each patient
only $1 he would earn an additional $12,500 above the $32,032 GMS. Dr Patel, in the
last financial year, received $55,000 by way of GMS. What he received as additional
payment is not known. In accordance with standard practice, two independent
Auckland medical practitioners of wide experience undertook an informal inquiry,
and, as a result of their findings, recommended that a complaint against Dr Patel
should be lodged with the Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Committee, which is a
statutory committee established under the Medical Practitioners Act. I accepted this
advice. The Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Committee recommended that while
Dr Patel's patients would still be eligible for GMS benefits, the doctor would not be
able to claim these benefits direct from the Department of Health by means of the
schedule system for the next 6 months, Instead, the patients could claim these
benefits through the refund system. I accepted the recommendations of the
disciplinary committee. Patients of Dr Patel are, therefore, not being penalised. I do
not intend to review my decision in this matter. It is based on a recommendation of a
statutory body of practising and respected doctors and one lay person, who had heard
all the relevant evidence, including the testimony of Dr Patel. If he was unhappy
about the result he could have appealed to the Medical Council. He chose not to do
SO.

Adjournment-Discussion of Questions
ADJOURNMENT—DISCUSSION OF QUESTIONS
[The questions and replies referred to in this debate appear on the preceding pages.]
Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga): For the purpose of discussing Ministers' replies to
questions, I move, That the House do now adjourn. I refer to question 188, which the
member for Rangitikei asked the Minister of Health on my behalf. The question asked for
the present cost of a patient in New Zealand public hospitals. The reply was $89 a day.
Everybody should understand that in this figure there is an area of substantially unnecessary
expense, and that is in road accidents. These are causing considerable concern to the
hospitals, the health authorities, and to the Ministry of Transport, apart from the personal
tragedies that we witness every day. Over the last 10 years an average of 11 000 people a year
have been injured to such an extent that they have to be in hospital for an average of 12.6
days each. During the 6 years of World War II, 15 000 New Zealanders were injured, and
yet during the last 10 years, about 11 000 people have been hospitalised each year as a result
of accidents, at an annual cost of more than $12 million on today's figures. That money is
being spent unnecessarily, in that so many of the accidents are avoidable.
I am sure members share with the rest of the country a recognition of the importance of
the present blitz on driving infringements, particularly on drunken driving. I hope that the
action that has been started will be sustained. Results cannot be achieved in a short period.
We must take the longer view; regardless of the cost, the savings will be substantial. I have
been heartened by the results of the last few weeks, which have shown a drop in the number
of accidents, but we should aim to have the accident rate drop still further. The loss of
productivity through injuries, not to mention fatalities, is something the country cannot
afford. No country could afford it. The Accident Compensation Commission is required
continually to pay out large amounts. Hospital treatment, particularly of motor accident
victims, frequently involves intensive care, which is very expensive.
With $12 million a year being spent on people involved in accidents, hospital beds
needed for other purposes are frequently used for accident victims, and this has a serious
effect on other hospital needs. The $12 million would go a long way towards paying for
medical research. We cannot measure in terms of money the personal and family tragedies
that are linked with motor accidents, and so I sincerely hope that the House will support fully

present surroundings, with adequate facilities and job opportunities. We do not want people
from Auckland, Christchurch, or Wellington coming down and bringing uneconomic
industries with them.
The Government's idea of regional development is not the same as the Labour
Government's, which burdened the taxpayers with subsidies on uneconomic industries,
offered underpriced freight subsidies, and gave handouts by creating specialist industries,
such as the Matai toy company on the West Coast, in the wrong places. Successful regional
development is not brought about by moving thousands of people out of Christchurch and
settling them in some democratic socialist Shangri-La called Rolleston. The National
Government's regional development policy in Southland is to adapt and encourage locally
based industries that use local resources. Our policy does not cut across existing industries.
Southland and Invercargill have sufficient industries, all of which are receiving, if they need
it-and at their own initiative-regional development finance to help them develop and
expand.
People in Southland do not need massive Government handouts and do not want
industries established along the lines on which the Labour Government established them,
which run counter to the Southland employment scene. If new industries were brought to
Southland and artificially boosted by uneconomic freight subsidies, they would inevitably
close and leave many people out of work. Invercargill is a well established city that depends
mainly on export processing for its farming industry, and most families depend upon the
ports and the Southland farming industry. My idea of regional development, which
fortunately coincides with the National Government's policy, is to ensure that industries that
want to expand and develop can do so. That is what makes the vitality and the community
spirit of Southland so localised and Southland a good place in which to live. People will not
allow it to be spoilt by new industries that are not indigenous to Southland's resources, but
may be misguidedly directed by what they believe would happen under a Labour
Government. I am not standing with outstretched hands on the outskirts of my city asking
people to come to Southland, but if Southland people feel they can do better by migrating to
New Lynn, I wish them good luck.

straightforward system of exemptions followed by tax levy at a flat rate. National's

RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North): I move, That this House notes yet another

congratulates Metalon Products Ltd. on its initiative and notes the role played by the Business

received one of a number of grants that have been made through the Government's
continuing regional development programme. The firm specialises in the manufacture of
metal frame joinery; it started in Dunedin in 1964, and has expanded its range of production
to compete successfully throughout the South Island. It has expanded so much that it found
its present factory crowded and production has become restricted.
The company called in the Business Development Centre of Otago University, a centre
that has given great service to regional development and the expansion of industrial
development in Otago and elsewhere. With the encouragement of the Otago Regional
Development Council it made a successful application for a suspensory loan-yet another

to the Development Finance Corporation, but became one of the first companies to receive
financial assistance from the Otago Savings Bank, which has made an entry into commercial
lending for regional development; it provides another avenue for local companies to
strengthen their bases. Of course, Metalon is only one of a long list of companies that have
received assistance under both Governments-that is the important thing.

bedroomed houses that were previously built on the fringe of the city.

people. However, closures are few and far between. I believe that the Otago Daily Times put
things in the right perspective on 28 July when it published a small comment about a closure

of H. E. Shacklock Ltd.

mentioned before that Wilson Neill Ltd. received the Governor-General's award for

the South Pacific. It is a matter of considerable interest to New Zealand as to how we can
support and assist our South Pacific island neighbours. We have accepted the challenge, and
have accepted a role in assisting them to develop their fisheries research and to create
management policies for their future 200-mile zones. Sometimes it is overlooked that in
many of their 200-mile zones static fish resources are very limited. There are many
beautifully coloured fish in the reefs around the islands, but very little volume of fish, except
the highly migratory species such as tuna.
There has been considerable difficulty, in international terms, in getting agreement on
the utilisation of the resource, because countries like the United States, have domestic laws
that make it very hard for them to accept or agree to international understanding on the
control of highly migratory species. In the many negotiations that have taken place on this
we have endeavoured to put forward positive views and measures that will support our island
neighbours. The House will recall the meeting of the South Pacific Forum last year attended
by the Prime Minister. It was agreed there that it was desirable to establish a South Pacific
regional fisheries organisation. That objective is proceeding, and I have no doubt it will be
achieved in the near future.
At the recent South Pacific fisheries organisation meeting in Fiji the creation of such an
organisation came a step closer, with officials preparing a draft convention covering the
establishment of the organisation. At this stage, the draft convention has been taken back to
the various Governments involved for study and, we hope, for their approval. New Zealand
has a real hope for a beneficial management regime coming out of the draft convention, if it
derives the necessary support from member states. Until this happens, it is proposed to set
up an organisation in Australia on an interim basis with the intention to relocate it eventually
in the Solomon Islands.
A trust fund has been established to finance the operations of the interim organisation,
and New Zealand has made a commitment to contribute $150,000 over 3 years to assist with
this. New Zealand's is one of the larger contributions, and more than $50,000 of this money
has already been made available. The intention is to demonstrate our real and genuine desire
to assist the small but numerous South Pacific nations to gain the maximum possible benefit
from the fisheries resources around their shores. Other resources on which to base their
economies are limited. We endeavour to give them as much help and support as possible.
When I was at the South Pacific conference in American Samoa last year I met delegates
from all the South Pacific nations. I was impressed by their belief in New Zealand, their
acceptance of her support, and their need of her assistance.

I turn now to the Antarctic. New Zealand is completing its twenty-second year of
continuous participation in the Antarctic. Scott Base, set up in 1957, has been the hub of our
activity in the Ross Dependency, and I am glad to say that it is gradually being rebuilt. That
is a very costly job, but it will be rebuilt so that we can continue our activity in that area for
some considerable time. We have also had activity in the Cape Byrd and Cape Vanda areas.
The unique characteristics of the dry valleys have attracted a large number of visitors. New
Zealand has a first-class world-recognised record of efficient research in all aspects of the
work being carried out in the Antarctic. During the 1957 to 1964 period New Zealand also
maintained a joint base at Cape Hallett in conjunction with the United States of America.
That has been one aspect of a long, sustained relationship with the United States of America
in all facets of Antarctic work.
Our Air Force has flown Hercules aircraft to McMurdo Sound and to the McMurdo ice
cap each year, transporting men and materials. The New Zealand Army has played its part
and provided cargo handlers as part of a joint logistics effort by our two countries. During
the past few years our scientists have been involved in international bilateral and multilateral
projects. Among those, we can recall the Dry Valley drilling project in which the United
States of America, Japan, and New Zealand took part, and the volcanic research that has
taken place at Mt. Erebus, with France. It is also worthy of note that in the near future,
following discussions I have had with the Australian Federal Minister of Science, we will
have much closer co-operation, in the logistics supply to the Antarctic, with the Australian
research effort. We have also been associated with Russia, as well as with the United States,
in geological investigation. New Zealand has a very important task to play in the Antarctic,
politically, in research, and in strategic and environmental matters.

## p. 2352 (#614) ###########################################

activities, but also through the activities of other nations in that part of the world. We are
interested in the occupation, use, and conservation of the Antarctic, because of its
importance to New Zealand.
We began our activity there in 1957, during International Geophysical Year. At about
that time 12 nations sought to establish a regime to control occupation of the Antarctic and,
at the same time, to conserve the very unique characteristics of the continent. The result was
the Antarctic Treaty, to which New Zealand is a signatory. The purpose of that treaty was to
freeze all political ambitions and problems, with a view to establishing vital scientific
research and international co-operation in the process. In that regard the treaty has been,
and still is, a very successful model for an international agreement. Regular meetings of the
treaty powers have been held, and we have participated in them and made our contribution.
Important measures have been taken to protect the Antarctic environment, to preserve the
wildlife, and to prevent pollution; and I am sure many people would be astonished if they
could see how efficiently and carefully those measures have been carried out.
We have also established rules to control tourism. I think the great dangers that could
result from uncontrolled tourism in that continent are not generally realised. The 1959
conference was unable to reach any agreement on the exploitation of resources. Most of the
delegates, at the time-I am talking about 1959-were convinced that the Antarctic was
purely a place for academic interest. It was said, quite rightly, that if any resources are there,
they are covered by ice a mile thick, or even thicker. Members who have been to the
Antarctic will know that the South Pole is covered by ice about 10,000 feet thick-a depth of
ice almost beyond conception. It was thought that the resources would be outside the
possibility of being won at any stage.
Since then, two very important commodities have been considered for exploitation by
nations actively involved in the Antarctic. The first is krill, a small crustacean, hitherto the
main source of food for whales. With fewer whales, the volume of growth has probably
increased substantially. There are large quantities of krill in the Antarctic waters, feeding on
the fertile upwelling nutrients from Antarctic sediments. Biologists claim that we might
harvest several tens of millions of tonnes of krill a year; an enormous quantity of protein.
The second resource, oil and gas, is at present only indicated by several drillings in the Ross
Sea by an American research ship.
Mr Marshall: Social Credit might well be interested.
Eon. L. W. GANDAR: Does the member think it might be a new Alberta? The holes
were drilled by an American research ship in 1973, and indicate the presence of gas and oil.
Although we claim legal sovereignty over the Ross Dependency, for 20 years New Zealand's
policy towards the Antarctic has been based on the view that the continent offers a wide
scope for bold experimentation in international administration. When we became party to
the Antarctic Treaty, we indicated our willingness, if necessary and if others did likewise, to
forsake sovereignty in that area in favour of international co-operation. In addition, after
1956 we played a prominent part in political and scientific matters in the Antarctic. We
would, of course, have certain expectations of any regime designed to control mineral
exploitation, and those which might conserve fish stocks. First the regime must ensure that
any exploitation authorised should be limited and carefully regulated. We would want the
widest possible protection for what is the most fragile environment in the world today.
Secondly, we would hope to ensure that New Zealand benefited under the regime to the
maximum possible from any controlled exploitation of the resources, in our claimed sector at
least. Thirdly, the regime should take account of mounting pressures from countries outside
the treaty, who could participate by way of revenue sharing or other activity, following the
precedence established at the Law of the Sea Conference.
In many ways those are conflicting claims and expectations. In order to arrive at a
satisfactory achievement, persistent, delicate, and constant negotiations will be required.
New Zealand has always sought to be scrupulous in its compliance with the international
Antarctic Treaty. We have taken a lead to bring to the notice of the treaty powers any
contravention of existing activities, at the same time drawing attention to any dangers that
might be inherent in exploiting minerals or other resources in the area. New Zealand's
scientific research programme has, therefore, been aimed at increasing the store of
knowledge of the region-its geology, eco system, environment, capacity to play a part in
global climate, and its influence on communications. By maintaining an internationally
recognised programme of scientific research, we ensure that our views on the wider issues I
have just mentioned-preservation, and possible resource exploitation-are respected and
given weight alongside those of other treaty powers.

The other matter I wish to deal with is the part New Zealand has played in the field of
education in the South Pacific and in South-east Asia. There was a time when New Zealand
provided many trained personnel such as teachers and educational leaders. They were sent
from here to the Pacific, or they came here, and, after a period of training, returned to their
own countries as teachers and educational administrators. There was a time, too, when New
Zealand teachers provided direct leadership in schools and in the teacher training colleges in
Samoa, Tonga, the Cook Islands, and Fiji. Times are changing, and the New Zealand
Government approaches things from a different viewpoint. During the last decade or so we
have been associated with the Islands, seeing how best New Zealand could render assistance
to those countries developing their own systems of education. Probably the changing
relationship is best exemplified by the University of the South Pacific, which New Zealand
helped to set up. It is now flourishing, in its tenth year of operation. Recently, when setting
up a project for the extension of education in the Pacific area, rather than go there ourselves,
we supplied funds and encouragement to the Department of Education and the University of
the South Pacific for that purpose. The Tongan authorities, who asked for this type of
assistance, are receiving it from the South Pacific people themselves. That, I believe, is of
greater significance to people of that region.
Finally, in this short outline, I would mention New Zealand's participation in South-east
Asia. Last year, I was privileged to attend the twelfth annual meeting of the Council of
Ministers of South-east Asia. I was greatly impressed by the genuine interest the Ministers
took in New Zealand, and the very high regard they have for New Zealand's contribution.
We are associated in a working relationship with the regional language institute of
Singapore, and the regional centre for mathematics and science in Malaysia. These are two
activities of SEAMEO. It is important because it enables information and expertise to be
shared by educationists in our country and in South-east Asia. It is important in human
terms, because it enables people of different backgrounds to develop better appreciation of
the others background, and establishes points of view important to New Zealand. It also
builds up a consciousness of New Zealand's participation in South-east Asia, something that
we in New Zealand are proud of, and which should be encouraged.
I believe that those are two areas that are not given full recognition for the part they

great deal; in particular to the South Pacific and to South-east Asia. We can give a great deal
in research activities, with the very high standard of our scientists in the Antarctic, while at
the same time preserving our national identity.

merely because of alternation, to take a second or third call. In such circumstances it has for

OKAINS BAY MAORI AND COLONIAL MUSEUM BILL
Second Reading
Miss DEWE (Lyttelton): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. In February
1976, soon after my election to the House, I became aware that Mr Murray Thacker, of
Okains Bay, Banks Peninsula, possessed a delightful and valuable collection of Maori
artifacts and colonial domestic articles. He was then constructing a colonial village and a
Maori meeting house on his property at Okains Bay in which to house them and exhibit them
to the public. It was his sincere wish to gift the collection to the public of New Zealand in
perpetuity, and the Bill is the fulfilment of that desire.
On 5 February 1977 Mr Thacker transferred by deed of trust to 13 trustees about 1 acre
of land, with all the buildings thereon, as well as his Maori artifacts and colonial antiques, for
them to hold in perpetuity for the public benefit. On the passing of the Bill the trustees will
vest these items in the board that is to be established under the Bill. Under the clauses of the
Bill, all the members of the board must be permanent residents of Canterbury, and clause 4
sets out how the board shall be constituted. The House will note that, under the provisions of
clause 4, Mr Murray Thacker and his wife are to be appointed to the board, which will also
have representatives of the New Zealand Antique Arms Association, the New Zealand
Archaeological Association, one representative from each of the six ridings of the Akaroa
County Council, two Maori appointees, and one appointee from the Canterbury Education
Board. Clause 4 and subsequent clauses contain provisions for appointing successors to the
board as at present listed, and set out the normal powers and procedures for such an
authority.
The purpose of the Bill is most worthy. What it achieves is the total protection of a very
remarkable collection of New Zealand history. I trust the House is conscious of this gesture

2399

and its value to the New Zealand public, and will accord the Bill its full support.
Bill read a second time.

CO-OPERATIVE DAIRY COMPANIES AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Co-operative Dairy
Companies Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill reviews the definition of a co-operative
dairy company, amends certain provisions relating to the Co-operative Dairy Companies
Tribunal, and increases the fines payable for offences under the Co-operative Dairy
Companies Act 1949. The Bill widens the definition of a co-operative dairy company to
include a company, the principal business of which is the sale to another co-operative dairy
company or the New Zealand Dairy Board of the milk, cream, or butterfat supplied to the
company by its shareholders. In addition, the Bill makes it clear that a co-operative dairy
company may carry on its business through the agency of another co-operative dairy


## p. 2400 (#630) ###########################################

2400
4 August
Co-operative Dairy Companies Amendment Bill
company.
These amendments arise from representations by the New Zealand Dairy Board after
last year's decision of the Co-operative Dairy Companies Tribunal that a company had
ceased to be a co-operative dairy company because it did not operate a dairy factory but,
instead, had its shareholders' milk processed and marketed by another co-operative dairy
company. There are about four co-operative dairy companies that, because they have
disposed of their dairy factories or find it uneconomical to operate a dairy factory, and
because they wish to retain their identity, arrange for another co-operative dairy company
either to manufacture their dairy produce, or to purchase their milk, cream, or butterfat.
The intention of these amendments is not to encourage co-operative dairy companies to
divest themselves of their manufacturing capacity, but to recognise any rationalisation of the
dairy industry's manufacturing capacity.
The Bill also proposes to increase the membership of the Co-operative Dairy
Companies Tribunal from three to five, to permit it to state a case for the opinion of the
Supreme Court, to widen the grounds for appealing against a decision of the tribunal, and to
allow it to hear submissions from a wider number of persons when deciding whether a
company has ceased to be a co-operative dairy company. These amendments will bring the
functions of the tribunal up to date with the usual legislative provisions that apply to
administrative tribunals. The Bill also increases the fines for offences under the Co-operative
Dairy Companies Act 1949, which have remained unchanged since that year.
The New Zealand Dairy Board has been consulted on the preparation of the Bill. I do
not propose to refer the Bill to a select committee but, immediately upon its introduction,
shall send a copy to the New Zealand Dairy Board and other interested parties to give them
an opportunity to consider it.

has not been raised before. Indeed, I do not know what benefit would come to the workers,
because a co-operative dairy company pays no dividends.

PENAL INSTITUTIONS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Penal Institutions
Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill is basically a machinery measure required to put pre-
release hostels on a proper legal footing. As I do not propose to send it to a select committee
I shall explain its purpose a little more fully than would be usual on an introduction. The
present pre-release hostels have been established administratively as parts of existing penal
institutions or as separate penal institutions. As a result, all the provisions of the Penal
Institutions Act and regulations apply to the hostels. Not all of the provisions are
appropriate for pre-release hostels, which are designed to bridge the gap between prison and
the return to society. Accordingly, the Bill places the hostels on a separate legal basis from
that for prisons, to provide a less restrictive regime than that prevailing in prisons.
The transition from imprisonment to full liberty on release is still too abrupt in most
cases. After months or years in a sheltered community in which the prisoner is away from
normal community life and its responsibilities, it is in some cases too great an upheaval for
him when he is returned suddenly to the community. By going to a pre-release hostel a
borstal trainee or prison inmate may spend the last few months of his or her sentence
working for a local employer, meeting financial obligations, and preparing for release.
Although the residents are still sentenced prisoners, and may be returned to prison if they
misbehave, the hostels are administered by the probation service. Normally a probation
officer visits the hostel regularly to discuss problems with the warden and residents and help
the latter make realistic release plans. There are three hostels for borstal trainees, four for
adult male prisoners, and one for adult female prisoners. Of course, it is anticipated that the
number will grow as resources permit.
In terms of the release of offenders, pre-release hostels have the following advantages.
First, they provide a more natural environment by spanning the gap between the artificial
prison society and the real world. Residents work at ordinary jobs with workmates who do
not know their backgrounds unless the prisoners themselves disclose them. They receive
normal award wages, from which they have to pay board, buy their own clothing, and meet
all other personal living expenses. At weekends they have the chance to mix socially with
others and to get used to entertaining themselves without breaking the law. Secondly, they
instil a sense of personal responsibility that was not necessarily there during their
incarceration. The normal period spent in a pre-release hostel is 3 to 4 months. It has been
found from experience that a longer period presents problems for the residents. This is
because residents are in effect free, yet deprived of some liberty, which creates tensions that
some are unable to handle for any long period.
The Bill is needed because experience has shown that the concept and operation of
these hostels, as I have outlined them, do not sit easily within the law relating to prisons. As I
have said, they are controlled by the probation service, although technically they are parts of
various penal institutions. This causes difficulties over authorisation by wardens of periods of
temporary release from custody. This must now be done by the superintendent of the
institution of which the hostel is part. I shall explain that by an example. There is a borstal
pre-release hostel in Wellington, but an inmate may well have come from Invercargill and be
responsible to the superintendent in Invercargill. Quite clearly this is inappropriate, and the
Bill authorises wardens to carry out this function.
Another problem is in relation to discipline. Obviously the strict rules necessary in a
prison are not all required for hostel residents. The Bill sets out what constitutes disciplinary
offences in hostels and provides for adjudication by a visiting justice. The current technical
right of prison superintendents to discipline hostel residents will lapse. Under the Bill,
inmates who have been granted release to work privileges by the Secretary for Justice on the
recommendations of the release to work committee, will continue to be eligible for transfer
to a hostel. Transfer is by agreement between a warden and a prison superintendent, subject
to any directions from the Secretary for Justice. This is a safety device allowing the secretary


## p. 2402 (#632) ###########################################

2402
4 August
Penal Institutions Amendment Bill
to direct that a certain inmate or certain type of inmate shall not be eligible for placement in
a hostel. Provision is made in clauses 11 to 13 for the transfer of a hostel resident back to
prison, and includes authority for the secretary to direct the return of a resident who
becomes a risk to the community at large or a threat to the safety of hostel staff or residents.
As I have said, the Bill is basically a machinery measure and I do not intend to refer it to
a select committee. I shall send a copy of the Bill to the Prisoners Aid and Rehabilitation
Society immediately, and I expect it to be warmly in support of the Bill. The Government
has said repeatedly that it is not prepared to tolerate lawlessness or disorder in our
community, and has taken appropriate steps when necessary. Nevertheless, it also
recognises the ultimate benefit to society if offenders are persuaded to desist from further
criminal activity. Pre-release hostels play an important role in this respect and represent a
concrete step by society to ease an offender back into a normal environment, with all its
responsibilities.

would guess not more than about half a dozen. The committee would probably not be

RATES REBATE AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That the Rates Rebate
Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill has two objects, the first being to apply, from 1
April 1979, a limit of $200 to the amount that can be paid to any residential ratepayer as a
rates rebate for any one year. This limit, which may be altered by Order in Council, will,
according to a check of some 6000 cases recorded by the department, affect about 1 percent
of applicants overall, but the proportion affected will vary from local authority to local
authority, according to the level of rating. It will not affect any person whose rates are in a
range up to $350. The average rates rebate is less than half the maximum that the Bill
provides for.
So there will be no misunderstanding of the position, I want to stress that the rates
rebate scheme is meant to apply after an applicant has exercised any rights he has for rates
remission or postponement under the Rating Act and the Valuation of Land Act. There
have been some excessive rebates in the past, ranging up to $1,100 in one instance. Many of


## p. 2406 (#636) ###########################################

2406
4 August
Rates Rebate Amendment Bill
those cases should have been dealt with by the law dealing with rates remission and
postponement. For instance, a residential taxpayer with a home in an industrially zoned
area, whose rates reflect an industrial value, can apply for, and be granted, a postponement
of rates on the additional value. Postponements of this nature are written off after 5 years if
the applicant remains in residence. He can then, each year, apply for a rebate under the
Rates Rebate Act on the rates actually paid. A ratepayer with his own single-unit home in a
high-rise residential area can seek a special valuation reflecting the use of his property as a
single-unit residence. He can obtain an absolute reduction of the rateable value, and thus of
his rates. This should be done before an application for a rates rebate is made.
An applicant suffering financial hardship, who would not qualify under the provisions I
have just mentioned, can be granted remission or postponement of rates under the present
law. The rates rebate scheme is meant to apply after the other forms of relief have been
investigated. That is not clear in the present law, and the result has been that some
applicants have obtained very large rates rebates at the taxpayers' expense, when in fact they
should have been granted a postponement of rates by their local authorities, or have applied
for special rateable values. So the limit of $200 would not detract in any way whatsoever
from the other forms of rating relief available to residential taxpayers. Indeed, it would
encourage local authorities and ratepayers to pay more attention to those concessions, which
in some cases could be better than the rebates. I want to stress again that the limit could be
increased by Order in Council, and undoubtedly it will be increased by the Government if
circumstances justify such action.
Secondly, the Bill provides that, from 1 April 1979, all applications for refunds of rates
paid must be lodged with local authority offices. At present an applicant has the option of
applying to his local authority office for a rebate or of paying his rates in full, and
subsequently claiming a refund from the Department of Internal Affairs. About 15 percent
of applicants have been following the latter course. It is quite clear from a study of the
applications that most of them could have been dealt with quite adequately, and with much
less inconvenience to the applicants, by their local town or county clerk's office. The
department would continue to advise and guide the local body officers on difficult cases. The
change would mean that the department would need fewer staff for rates rebate work. I
should not imagine that any local authorities would face any staffing problems as a result,
because the additonal work that would fall on their officers would be work that, in effect,
was transferred from one central government office to about 250 local authority offices.
There are no other matters of moment in the Bill.

FIRE SERVICE AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That the Fire Service
Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill makes changes to the principal Act found to be
necessary as a result of 2 years' experience with the centralised fire service under the control
of the Fire Service Commission. When analysed, the changes are few, bearing in mind the
innovative nature of the principal Act in the New Zealand scene.
The involvement of defence fire brigades with the New Zealand Fire Service is
recognised. These brigades, which exist in the principal military establishments, have in fact
been working in very close co-operation with the New Zealand Fire Service for many years.
The Bill regularises this association. A consequential effect will be that the members of
defence fire brigades will be eligible for membership of the United Fire Brigades Association
of New Zealand-the volunteer organisation-and be able to participate in activities and
benefits accruing from that membership.
Clause 3 is a consequence of the Reserves Act passed last year, and provides that the
Fire Service Commission is deemed to be a local authority for the purposes of that Act.
Clause 4 clarifies that the commission has the right to occupy land on which brigades are
established, notwithstanding that negotiations for the transfer of the land to the commission
may not yet have been finalised. There is provision in clause 7 for a chief fire officer to hold
any other office in the Fire Service. In effect, this will permit the fire chief to be directed to


## p. 2416 (#646) ###########################################

2416
4 August
Fire Service Amendment Bill
act in that capacity, not only in his own district, but also in a neighbouring one.
Other provisions of some importance that I should mention are contained in clause 12,
which effectively removes the $520 limit on the honoraria that may be received by volunteer
firemen, without placing them under any obligation to join a union. The unauthorised
expenditure that may be incurred by the commission is increased from $1,500 to $3,000 in
one year. Provision is made in clauses 15, 17, and 18 for a more practical approach to the
preparation and submission of estimates, without altering the respective overall liabilities of
the insurance industry and the Government in this regard. Provision is made for the rate of
gratuity paid to a volunteer fireman on his retirement, or to his dependants in the case of his
death, to be varied by Order in Council. At present the rate is $20 for each year of service.
The Minister is enabled to delegate to the Secretary for Internal Affairs his authority to
authorise the disposal of property by the commission, and also certain payments from the
commission's reserve fund.
On the personnel side, the Bill makes it clear that a probationer in the permanent
service, whose appointment is annulled, is not to be deemed to have been dismissed for the
purposes of the appeal provisions of the Act. In other words, a probationer in the permanent
Fire Service, like probationers in most other areas of employment, will not have an
automatic right of appeal against the annulment of his probation.
There are provisions in clause 25 that provide that a chief fire officer can stop
proceedings associated with an allegation of a breach of the code of good conduct if he is
satisfied that there is no need to proceed. The lack of authority to do this is a deficiency in
the present law. This clause also clarifies the right of an alleged offender, if he so wishes, to
elect to have his case dealt with by the Fire Service Commission without a preliminary
inquiry by his chief fire officer. It also empowers the chief himself to refer a case to the
commission for decision after he has made his inquiry. The requirement that the chairman of
the Fire Service Appeal Board be a magistrate has been extended to include a barrister and
solicitor of not less than 7 years' standing, whether or not he holds or has held any judicial
office. Finally, the Bill recognises the practical situation by providing in effect that the
appeal board should be serviced by the tribunals division of the Department of Justice.
This Bill has been prepared in close consultation with the Fire Service Commission, and
appropriate discussions have been held with the United Fire Brigades Association-the
volunteer fire brigadesmen-the New Zealand Executive Fire Officers Society, and the
Government departments involved. All have indicated their concurrence with the matters
affecting them.
Dr WALL (Porirua): There are one or two matters that I should like clarified. The first
applies to clause 3. I understand that the Fire Service Commission is deemed to be a local
authority for the purposes of the Reserves Act, but the explanatory note does not include
reference to other Acts for instance, the Public Finance Act and the Town and Country
Planning Act. I realise that in the past, through its association with local bodies, the Fire
Service has had installations put on reserves. Does the Minister expect this practice to
continue? If it does, reserves all over the country could come under pressure. There is

reserves. All over the country people are concerned that reserves should not be encroached
upon, but that there should be an increase in the number of urban reserves.

not the Reserves Act; the question is purely and simply whether the Fire Service

CUSTOMS ACTS AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Introduction
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That the Customs Acts
Amendment Bill (No. 2) be introduced. The Customs Acts Amendment Bill (No. 2) amends
the Customs Act 1966, the Sales Tax Act 1974, and the Motor Spirits Duty Act 1961. It
contains 16 clauses, 4 of which are purely machinery clauses. The Bill makes a number of
other miscellaneous amendments to the Customs Acts. The Customs Act 1966 is amended
with regard to the use of forms, the period after which a collector may sell unclaimed or
unentered goods, the delivery of goods on sight entry, the transhipment of goods, import
deposits, and the detention and searching of persons suspected of carrying narcotics
internally. The Sales Tax Act is amended to correct a spelling error, to provide authority to
change the status of a taxpayer, to provide for a rate of 40 percent tax on record covers to
correct an anomaly, to alter the method of valuation of goods worked upon by a contractor,
and in regard to sales tax refunds on motor cycles. The Motor Spirits Duty Act 1961 amends
the definition of "motor spirits" to bring it into line with the changes made in nomenclature
in the new customs tariff.
Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central): Clause 4 of the Customs Acts Amendment Bill
(No. 2) amends section 55 of the principal Act, and reduces the period of the holding of
goods from 3 months to 2 months. That means that goods not claimed after a period of 2
months can be sold by the Collector of Customs. There may be a very good reason for an
importer not being able to uplift his goods within the period of 2 months. I wonder what the
thinking is behind that reduction from 3 months to 2 months. It could be unfair to an
importer if he were out of the country when the goods came in.
Can the Minister explain clause 7, which deals with the import deposit scheme? That has
been phased out by the Government, but I see that some amendments have been made.
Does it mean that the Government intends to revitalise the scheme, which was not
particularly successful? When questioned last year at a meeting of the Commerce and
Mining Committee, officers of the Department of Trade and Industry admitted that some
companies had been adversely affected by the scheme, and I understand that one or two
companies went out of business. Does the Minister intend to reintroduce the scheme?
The last point I want to raise relates to body searches. I can assure the Minister that
Opposition members will present no argument against any action the Government may take
in an effort to detect drug offenders. I note that the body searches are to be carried out by a
medical practitioner, and I consider that to be desirable. However, I should like the Minister
to explain why it is provided that "if any officer of Customs or member of the Police has
reasonable cause to suspect that any person has unlawfully secreted about his person or
within his body cavities any dutiable, restricted, uncustomed, or forfeited goods,... he may
use such force as may be reasonably necessary against that person to effect such detention or
search." It may be necessary to use force, but the provision does not specify that it should be
a member of the Police who uses that force; it is provided that "any officer of Customs or
member of the Police may use such force". I do not consider it is the job of Customs
Department officers to use force. If it is necessary to use force, surely that must be the job of
the Police. Will the Minister explain whether, in fact, a Customs officer will be able to use
force against any person suspected of bringing drugs or illegal goods into the country?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): Clause 4 only reduces from 3 months to
2 months the period that must elapse before a collector can sell goods which have not been
entered by the importer. That could happen for a number of reasons. It may be that the
importer cannot afford them; it may be that they have been lost for some reason; or it may
be that the importer has changed his mind and the exporter is not prepared to pay the return
freight. It is a contingency provision to ensure that the cargo is not kept on the wharves more
or less indefinitely. I am sure the member for Dunedin Central and the member for Wigram


## p. 2419 (#649) ###########################################

4 August
2419
Customs Acts Amendment Bill (No. 2)
are well aware that cargo congestion has been a problem.
The member for Dunedin Central mentioned clause 7. I can assure him that it is a
contingency provision only, and does not imply any plan to reintroduce the import deposit
scheme. However, it was felt that the power should be available as a weapon to be used if
necessary. It really brings the provisions of the Customs Act into line with those of the 1948
Economic Stabilisation Act. The short answer is that the provision does not herald the
imminent return of the import deposit scheme.
I am pleased, because I expected that the member for Dunedin Central would give his
full backing to clause 8, which will both tighten and clarify the law on personal searches. In
fact, the existing provision in section 213 of the Act already gives fairly wide powers, but we
felt that as this area is sensitive in terms of civil rights, we should make the position doubly
clear by spelling it out.
The member for Dunedin Central also asked about the provision relating to reasonable
force. It was felt necessary to provide for that, because there could be an occasion when it is
necessary for a Customs officer, in the absence of the Police, to prevent someone from doing
something in that type of situation. I should not like my Customs officers not to have that
power, but obviously they will be accountable for their behaviour, and if that behaviour is
unreasonable or in any way reprehensible, action will be taken. I think the member will just
have to accept my assurance that it is considered desirable for Customs officers to have that
power. I think that that, in essence, answers all the questions raised by the member for
Dunedin Central.
Mr KIRK (Sydenham): I want to comment on the point raised by the member for
Dunedin Central, the Labour Party's spokesman on Customs, about the force Customs
officers will be able to use. Will any type of training be given to Customs officers? The Police
receive training on how to restrain or hold people, and if Customs officers are to be expected
to do that they should be given similar training in the best and safest method.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): The suggestion made by the member
for Sydenham is reasonable, and I shall take it up with my departmental advisers. As the
member is aware, we go to some trouble to ensure that the officers are well equipped, and it
is consistent with that basic approach that, when a member of the Opposition suggests a
practical way in which we can organise their work along more predictable lines and make it
more effective, we are prepared to co-operate. Therefore, as I have said, I shall take that
suggestion up with my departmental advisers.

Trustee Savings Banks-Residential Property Lending
2. Mr FENTON (Hastings) to the Minister of Finance: What are the latest figures on
residential property lending by the trustee savings banks and do they indicate any particular
preference by borrowers, given a free choice between an existing property and the erection
of a new house?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): In the 6 months ended 30 June 1978
trustee savings banks approved mortgages for new housing totalling $12.7 million and
mortgages for existing houses of $79.1 million. This compares with the total for the 6 months
to 31 December 1977 of $16.9 million for new houses and $49.9 million for existing houses
and, for the 6 months to 30 June 1977, of $10.7 million for new houses and $27.7 million for
existing houses. The proportion of total residential mortgages approved for new houses in
the lastest 6-monthly figures was 13.8 percent, compared with a range of 24 to 29 percent
over the previous four June years. The absolute percentage of lending going to the
purchasers of new houses is not a true reflection of the overall preference of the market
because of the emphasis of the Housing Corporation in lending for new homes, but the
recent reduction in the proportion approved for new houses indicates some switch of
preference from new to existing houses.
Mr Fenton: Can the Minister state the margin of trustee savings bank lending on older
houses as a percentage of their valuation?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No, I do not have that information with me, but it certainly
has gone up. The pattern, of course, is dependent on price more than anything else, and
there is no doubt that the price of existing houses has stabilised and, in some ranges, has
gone down, so that the difference in price between a new home and an existing house of a
similar standard has widened quite considerably in favour of the existing house. This is
proving a further difficulty in the Government's attempt to keep builders and the building
industry going. Better value is being obtained by the purchaser of an existing house.

centre. By April of this year, local authorities in the area had contributed $82,260, and other
public contributions totalled $13,000. The New Zealand Rowing Association was expecting
to add $20,000 to the fund from a surcharge on tickets, as well as having provided a
considerable amount of voluntary labour towards the project. Total cost of the centre was
expected to be $250,000. The cost to the Rowing Association of organising and competing in
the world championships is expected to be $285,000, towards which the New Zealand
Lottery Board, of which I am chairman, contributed $100,000 and I approved a grant of
$20,000 plus a guarantee against loss of up to $30,000 from recreation and sport funds.
Mr Wetere: Will those amounts be sufficient to complete the project?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I was informed by the chairman only recently, that although there
is still a little way to go, he is confident that it will be possible to meet commitments by the
time the world championships are held.

Voting Rights Protection Bill
VOTING RIGHTS PROTECTION BILL
Introduction
Dr WALL (Porirua): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Voting Rights
Protection Bill. Although the Bill has 10 clauses, its purpose is simpler than the number of
clauses and their extent indicate. It had to be drawn with a degree of detail and complexity to
cover all the factors that would be involved in what is actually a very simple shift of
responsibility concerning the rights of voters.
As the House will be aware, the present right of a voter to vote depends, I think quite
accidentally, upon his name being on the roll. This appears to have arisen from a situation
that existed before 1893, when there was a variety of rolls, and voters were entitled to vote
for a variety of reasons. It appeared to be reasonable to sort the matter out beforehand and
put voters on the roll, and for judgment as to whether they should or should not vote to be
dependent on the roll. To all intents and purposes, universal adult suffrage has existed since
1893, and there appears to have been no justification since then for the legal entitlement to
vote to depend on whether or not a person's name has been put upon the roll. I am sure the
public, and even most members of the House, if they have not examined the matter, would
have thought that a person's right to vote depended on whether he had fulfilled the legal
requirements that entitled him to be put on the voting roll. I am sure people would wish their
right to vote to be determined, not by the conscientious or less than conscientious-work
of a civil servant, no matter how responsible he might be, but by a decision of this House.
Such a decision should not be interfered with by any person, except on the grounds laid
down by the House.
The provisions of clause 4, therefore, provide for a voter's right to be based on eligibility
rather tharf on the fact that he is enrolled. That is most important, and is one of the two prin-
ciples that have been altered. The other is that a person's vote has to be counted. It is not a
question of whether or not a person casts a vote, because the Act lays down that if anyone
casts a vote, that vote shall be accepted. However, thousands of people-about 44 000 in
1975 and some 36 000 in 1972-cast special votes, which, unknown to them, were not
counted. If they had known, they would not have wasted their time. As those are the only
statistics available, it appears that under present procedures between 30 000 and 50'000
people will vote, and will be wasting their time.
Many people are aware of the difficulty of having their votes counted if they are not on
the roll, but discover that only when they go to vote. That number is still unknown because
no record is kept of how many people cast such votes. Experienced workers in polling booths
tell me that the number of such people equals at least the number who record votes but who
are not counted.
The problem is not a small one. It is very easy for people to say, "You did, we didn't,"
or, "It was your Government's responsibility, not ours", and all that nonsense. The matter is
part of the total responsibility of the House, whatever the reasons for the failure of the
efforts of various Governments, including the last Labour Government, to achieve a more
satisfactory solution for electors.
I have brought forward this Bill to overcome, in a simple and practical way, the problem
of the disfranchisement of many thousands of New Zealanders. Other voting problems are
also covered in the measure. Because of the haste, confusion, and rapidity with which people
often have to work in polling booths, accidental technical errors are made by the staff when
dealing with special votes. We have followed through and dealt with the most common of
those technical errors.
Everyone agrees that although a voter's intentions may be clear and although he may
carry out the procedures laid down under the Act to make sure his vote is genuine, such a
voter can be disfranchised because of technicalities. The Bill corrects that, and also provides
for information given, either when filling out an enrolment card or applying for a special
vote-which is all the information necessary for a person to be enrolled-to be part of the
roll. This allows for the normal checks against dual voting. The returning officer will have
the roll in front of him, plus all the cards and applications for special votes. This will show
those who have voted when not on the roll. The committee was assured by the Chief
Electoral Officer that from that information it would be possible to make proper checks,
which are now carried out, against dual voting.
Mr Latter: How long will it take?
Dr WALL: I hear a member who seems unclear as to how long it will take. It is
erroneous to assume that matters could be delayed because of the procedure. Votes that
might be declared invalid have to be examined in detail, not only to see whether the names
are on the roll, but also to check whether they were on the previous roll and whether the


## p. 2429 (#659) ###########################################

4 August
2429
Voting Rights Protection Bill
person voted on a previous occasion. The vote of a person who voted on a previous occasion
is legally allowed. This procedure must be followed for every vote before the count can be
completed.
Its only effect is to declare a big percentage of votes invalid. So, there will be no great
delay at all in counting the votes and using those procedures, which will ensure a valid vote.
The only difference the Bill will make is that votes now being declared invalid will be
declared valid. The safeguards against dual voting, and the safeguards to ensure that people
vote in the right district, are still there. The looseness of the present law, which is a matter of
major concern to both political parties, to the public, and to the House, will not be increased
in any way by the Bill.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): This is the third private member's Bill
brought in by the Opposition in an attempt to amend the electoral law. I must thank the
