Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Thank you, Mr Speaker. May I then
look forward and tell the member for Porirua that the Government will vote against the
introduction of the Bill. Clauses 4, 5, and 6 of the Bill would reinstate into the electoral law
the discredited subsection (f) of section 99 of the Labour Government's 1975 amendment.
That discredited subsection was removed by the House last year in the amendment Act. That
provision enacted by the Labour Government, which gave the right to vote to all who
claimed on reasonable grounds that they were entitled to be on the roll, was described last
year by the then Labour spokesman, the member for Henderson-and I am quoting from
Hansard, Volume 415, at page 4159-as "an experimental and radical change", which "in
practice,... gave rise to some problems, but they could have been ironed out". The Labour
Government's experimental and radical change proved a failure. Under it the number of
special votes not allowed in 1975 for the reason "not on the roll", increased by nearly 24
percent from the figure in 1972-when the National Government had administered the law
and had agreed with the law-to the figure as a result of the Labour-administered election in
November 1975; and it was totally discredited.
Not content to dabble again in a failed experiment, the Labour proposal now goes
further. Although in its preamble, and particularly in clause 4, the Bill pays lip service to the
reality that one purpose of election rolls is to detect any plural voting, it would now have us


## p. 2431 (#661) ###########################################

4 August
2431
Voting Rights Protection Bill
in effect open the gates wide to the deceitful practice of plural voting. We have been told that
last year a Bill was introduced into the United States House of Representatives to allow,
among other things, an elector to register and vote on the same day. That is quite a
departure from our system, which was not well described by the Labour member who
introduced the Bill. The States of Minnesota and Wisconsin have that system, and it is
reported that its introduction "contributed to a marginal increase in voter turnout of about 1
or 2 percent, but it also encouraged many voters to wait until election day to register.
Moreover, it caused long lines and confusion at many polling places, allowing hundreds of
voters to vote in the wrong place and without adequate identification. There is little evid-
ence that either party gained from election day registration, except in the city of Milwaukee.
The potential for vote fraud, however, was great; the probability of detection was extremely
small, and the discovery of fraud could only occur too long after the election to affect the
outcome."
If Parliament were to adopt the Bill-and it will not, because the Government will vote
against it-it would interfere with a special feature of the New Zealand electoral system-
the speed at which election-night figures are made available. Everybody is interested in
whether the first election results will be broadcast by 8 o'clock at night. I am delighted to say
that at the 1975 election, when the member for New Plymouth was elected, Taranaki
electorate beat the field. The 1975 Electoral Act Committee, under the chairmanship of the
Labour member for New Lynn, noted in its report at pages 8 and 9 that the New Zealand
electoral system should be designed so that the results of the election are speedily obtained.
One important aspect is that special votes, which by and large are not counted on
election night, should be kept to a minimum. Under the Bill being considered today, a
tremendous number of special votes would be cast, because a would-be voter who had not
bothered to register could walk into a polling booth and say, "My name is Bill Smith, and I
am here to vote"-and he would be entitled to do so. Many Bill Smiths would then move
around to innumerable polling places and vote again, calling themselves John Jones and all
sorts of names. The potential for plural voting would be enormous.
Mr Wetere: What have you got against Bill Smith?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: All right; it could be Tapiti Tamihana. What about that?
Under the Bill the potential for irregularities is almost unlimited; they should not be
encouraged. I do not propose to speak at any great length.
Hon. M. Rata: You've had a pretty good go.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I have had an interrupted go, and I appreciate the fact that
no strict letter of the law has been ventured upon me. The procedure for this year's general
election was established by the former Labour Government in 1975. I agree that it has
proved to be deficient-particularly the arrangement for registration to accompany a census
return-but the procedures are now working. I have been advised by the Chief Electoral
Officer that about 2 100 000 names are now on the main roll. Members of the Statutes
Revision Committee, and indeed all members of the House, would know, because the
committee has reported back to the House, that the roll has gone forward for printing and
will be published about the first week in September.
We should make the best use we can of the Labour Government's electoral law,
deficient though it has proved to be and its deficiency was recognised by the member for
Henderson in the debate last year and rest on the proven ability of the Chief Electoral
Officer and the electoral officers appointed by the Post Office to encourage people to check
whether their names are on the main roll, which comes out early in September. If their
names are not on the roll, they should register so that they will appear on the supplementary
roll. If they qualify to vote within a month before polling day they can vote on a declaration
for a special vote. That is the sensible way to maintain an efficient electoral procedure.
Confusion is created every time a Labour member-or an opposition member, such as the
member for Rangitikei-introduces a Bill to amend the electoral law during an election year.
It undermines the people's faith in the electoral law. I say again, as I have said before-and I
know it is the language of the market place-stop mucking about with the electoral law.
Debate interrupted.

State Service Pay Increases
1. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister of State
Services: In view of his statement reported in the New Zealand Herald of 2 August that he
expects the total cost of the State Service pay increases to be $226 million over a full year,
and the increase is backdated to 11 October 1977, can he state: (a) exactly how much will be
paid out this financial year; (b) how much was included in the main estimates; and (c) how
much will need to be included in the supplementary estimates?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): (a) The full cost of the State general
adjustment and ruling rates survey adjustment, including the cost of backdating to 11
October 1977, will be paid out this year. The exact amount that will be paid out is not yet
known, as agreement on the State general adjustment was reached with the Combined State
Service Organisations only last week, so that departments have not yet completed their cost-
ings for the supplementary estimates. (b) In accordance with normal practice, a provision of
$250 million was included in the main estimates to cover additional costs of payments related
to movements in the private sector, such as State wages and salaries and national
superannuation. (c) As I explained in my answer to (a), departments are currently preparing
their wage and salary costings. Once this information is to hand, about mid-August,
supplementary estimates will be prepared for tabling in the House.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Does the Minister believe that the amount to be paid out will exceed
the sum of $250 million set aside in the supplementary estimates?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The answer is yes, obviously it will. As a former Minister of
Finance, the member should know that money guessed at or calculated cannot be included in
the supplementary estimates. The best assessment I can give the member, if he wants
approximate figures-and they must be approximate-is that in the 1978-79 financial year
the general adjustment will be about $241 million; that is, $177 million for the full year cost,
and about $89 million for backdating to 11 October 1977. If the $25 million given as the
interim special allowance last October is taken away, the ruling rates survey would be about
$68 million. The general wage order recently announced is estimated at about $58 million.
Trade Negotiations, Geneva
2. Mr FENTON (Hastings) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: Do the offers made in
the trade negotiations in Geneva give any indication of a real interest on the part of
industrialised countries in expanding trade in agricultural products?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade): As I mentioned in the House
last week, the agreed statement of the major participants in the MTN stresses that a final
outcome is dependent on progress being made in agriculture. In the bilateral discussions I
had in Geneva with representatives of other participants I stressed the need for moves on the
access barriers we face on dairy products, meat, and fruit, and the inequalities of opportunity
that agricultural exporters face in the present world trade situation. I think it is fair enough
to say that there is a much greater general emphasis on agriculture in this MTN round than
there has been with other multilateral trade negotiations that have taken place over the last
30 years.
Mr Fenton: Does this progress give a lead to New Zealand farmers and growers to
maintain stock units and horticultural production for export?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: It is not possible at this stage to identify those offers that will
finally be made and included in the final package. However, as I have indicated, we have
reason-and I have certainly been encouraged to believe-that positive moves will be made
in respect of at least some of our requests.
Mr Prebble: Have the offers made in the Geneva trade negotiations by the industrial

School Patrols
3. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Education: Has he read the Auckland Star
of 26 July, which contained a plea by a Mrs Martin, the mother of the teenage girl who was
attacked by a man with a knife while crossing through the grounds of a south Auckland
school, that school patrols be reintroduced to stop such attacks and prevent vandalism to
schools, and, if so, does he intend to take any action?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I have read the article and I am
concerned that such an incident should have occurred on school grounds. The security
patrols that were operating in the south Auckland area were undertaken through the
initiative of local parents and were not organised by my department. The function of the
security patrols was to protect the school from vandalism and it is purely speculative to claim
that voluntary security patrols would have prevented the assault. I am not aware of any plans
to reintroduce the voluntary patrols, but the Auckland Education Board is soon to meet the
regional superintendent of education in Auckland, principals from the south Auckland area,
and the Police Department, and I will consider any reasonable suggestions to prevent the
problem of vandalism that arise from this meeting.
Mr Isbey: In view of the attack in the school grounds, and, also the renewed vandalism

install caretakers in just one or two of the trouble schools in south Auckland?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: As I have said before, consultation is taking place among the
department, the police, and the local school. But the building of a caretaker's cottage on the
grounds would not give 24-hour control of grounds in any case. However, if there is a strong
recommendation from the Police Department we would certainly give very serious
consideration to it.

Waikato Hospital Cardiology Staff
11. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: Did he criticise the cardiology staff
of the Waikato Hospital Board for not "keeping up with current trends in their specialist
field", as reported in the Waikato Times of 25 July 1978?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): As I made clear in my statement to the Waikato
Times on 25 July 1978, the original report in its 17 July issue did not correctly report what I
said to the reporter. I have never given any guidance to medical staff in medical matters, nor
would I ever presume to criticise them or cast doubts on their professional knowledge or
ability. That is not part of my job as Minister of Health. But I can and do give guidance to
hospital boards on matters about which I have received the advice and recommendations of
advisory or expert bodies such as the Hospitals Advisory Council. This is what I did in the
case of the Waikato board's application to establish a cardiac surgical unit.
Mr Hunt: Was the Minister accurately reported in the same article as saying in his
conversation with the reporter, "Nothing I said to her could be construed by a reasonable
person as reflecting in any way adversely on their professional knowledge or ability", when
referring to these experts?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, that was quite correct. Our discussion took place on the
telephone, and I do not think the reporter quite understood the difference between the
hospital board and the hospital board's staff. I did give guidance to the hospital board based
on advice given to me by the Hospitals Advisory Council, but I did not, and would never
wish to, advise the staff acting in their professional capacity.
Mr Hunt: In the statement he originally made to members of the hospital staff, did the
Minister make it clear that he was expressing not his own personal views but the views of the
council?
Hon. T. F. GILL: In my capacity as Minister I had written to the Hospital Boards
Association in specific terms. In what I wrote I had been guided by the advice I had received
from the Hospitals Advisory Council. I accept responsibility for what I wrote to the board,
and the board accepted it as proper for me to write to it in those terms. The comment that I
had been critical of the medical staff was a false interpretation of the matter.

Hon. T. F. GILL: No, I am not satisfied that there has been enough assistance to meet
the expenses; and I have no intention of recommending that, to meet some of the
association's expenses, any Government money be spent.

Electoral Arrangements for Overseas Voters
16. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) to the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the report on page 3
of the Christchurch Press dated 26 July 1978, wherein the member for Sydenham is reported
as saying that 86 000 New Zealand voters in Australia had 5 days in which to cast their votes
in 3 offices, and, if he has seen the report, (a) is the statement correct, (b) is there any
difference from previous election arrangements for absentee voters, and (c) are there 86 000
New Zealanders voting in Australia this year?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): As to whether the statement is correct,
there are a number of errors in it. Voters in Australia have not 5 days but 3 weeks from the
closure of nominations until the night before polling day in New Zealand to cast their votes.
As to the claim that they cast their votes in three offices, there are voting facilities at
Brisbane, Canberra, Melbourne, Perth, and Sydney-five offices and advice for overseas
voters is contained in a pamphlet that has been distributed extensively to overseas posts,
travel agents, and shipping and airline offices. As to whether the arrangements are any
different from previous election arrangements for absentee voters, the answer is that
arrangements for overseas special voters are standard procedures, and have been so since
the 1956 Act-for 22 years. As to the third question-whether there are 86 000 voters voting
in Australia this year-the answer must be that I would not know what the figure is, but
would be surprised if it were as high as the figure quoted. Of the Australian voting centres,
most votes are usually registered at Sydney, and usually in the range of 4000 to 5000 votes.
Fewer votes are cast at other centres.
Mr Kirk: Can the Minister confirm that up to 70 000 New Zealanders at present living in
Sydney have the right to vote in New Zealand?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No.

Standing Orders 89 and 90 enable the House to debate some particular event of recent
occurrence which demands the immediate attention of the House and the Government. In
this case, the announcement deals with an event of recent occurrence-the weekend
announcement that agreement has been reached in the New Zealand - Japanese fishing
talks. This involves the administrative responsibility of the Government. It seems to me to
require the immediate attention of the House because of the point made by the honourable
member in his letter, that Parliament should have an opportunity to debate the matter
before an agreement is formalised. Accordingly, I am prepared to accept the motion. I
presume more than one member wishes to support the motion.

Earlier this year the Prime Minister properly drew attention to the Japanese being
obdurate about New Zealand's approaches for better access for New Zealand primary
products. He said again, most properly, that, unless the Japanese were prepared to talk
about better access to Japan for New Zealand primary produce, we were not interested in
talking about fishing arrangements in our 200-mile zone. This course that the Prime Minister
set out has been followed. The Japanese have talked about New Zealand's trading
relationships in primary produce. There have been several interesting discussions, including
important discussions with the Japanese Minister of Agriculture when he was in New
Zealand, the result of which was a most interesting new interest by the Japanese in New
Zealand's trading relationships with Japan.
I draw attention to an extract from the Prime Minister's comments on those talks: "The
discussions I have had with Mr Nakagawa and specific agreements we have reached
represent a significant step forward. The Japanese undertaking to consult us in advance on
tenders for butter and milk powder gives practical meaning to the earlier statement that
Japan regards New Zealand as a reliable supplier of dairy products. Likewise, the assurance
that Japan intends to use New Zealand dairy products in its aid programme on a continuing
basis gives much greater value to the offer made by Mr Suzuki in Wellington in February." I
continue briefly: "Mr Nakagawa's statements show clearly that the Japanese Government is
serious in seeking to increase its imports of meat and dairy products from New Zealand."
Then the Prime Minister detailed his observations about other products that had been talked
about in those discussions.
Arising out of this, New Zealand expressed a willingness to talk about a fishing
agreement with Japan, and the Japanese sent a delegation to New Zealand. As a result of
discussions, in which New Zealand was led by that very able public servant, Mr Ian Stewart,
we have an arrangement to be initialled shortly. This arrangement is not a deal about fishing
tonnages; it sets out the terms and conditions under which the fishermen of foreign countries
may fish in New Zealand's 200-mile economic zone. It is important that these conditions be
suitable for New Zealand, because New Zealand is the custodian of the fish resource in this
area, and New Zealand must give first interest in the area to New Zealand's own fishing
efforts, and the efforts of New Zealand fishermen. That is what has been arranged. We have
effected arrangements with South Korea and Russia, and it appears that we are now
completing arrangements with Japan. When the arrangements are consummated, then, and
only then, and on New Zealand's initiative, is the other country, in this case Japan, advised
of the fishing tonnages of the various species available that may be fished by it. The amounts
will be determined and made public in the not too distant future, after the initialling and
signing of the agreement with Japan.

Japanese have certain scientific knowledge about the fishing resources of this area, they have

The point that must be made clear to the House and the people listening to the debate is
that the agreement is not a secret. It is an agreement that has reached the stage in
negotiation at which officials can approach their Governments for agreement at Government
level. There is nothing unusual in that; it happens in the House, and outside it in private
business. Negotiations are started at a certain level, and they are carried on, with advice,
throughout their entirety until a full and proper agreement is reached by all sides. The
conditions of the agreement are then taken away to be read and considered by the principals
to the negotiations. That is exactly what has happened in this case. The terms of the
proposed fishing agreement have been sent to the respective Governments for initialling, so
that they can be confirmed. When full agreement is reached and the agreement is signed, as
any trade agreement must be signed, the terms will become public. If Opposition members
want to exercise their proper role-the role expected of them and the role they must play in
the House-they can then criticise the terms of the agreement. At that time they may know
what they are talking about, but today they do not know what they are talking about, as is
often the case.
No Government, either today or at any other time, can publicise the terms of an
agreement before it is signed; to do so would be to break faith with the other signatories.

break faith. I wonder if the reason for the exhibition by Opposition members of their

ESTATE AND GIFT DUTIES AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be
now read a second time. It is a short Bill, and its main purpose is to give effect to the Budget
proposal to make any personal chattels passing to the surviving spouse of a deceased person
completely exempt from estate duty, and to increase the exemption in respect of other
personal chattels from $4,000 to $6,000. The other amendments are of a minor nature and
deal with such matters as the valuation of shares and debts.
Clause 1 relates to the short title and commencement date. Except for clauses 2 and 5,
the amendment will apply to the estates of people dying on or after 1 January 1979. Clause 2
is a machinery amendment to provide that income tax on refunds from a deceased's wool
income retention account is an allowable debt for estate duty purposes. This amendment will
apply to the estates of people dying on or after 1 June 1978. Clause 3 relates to the valuation
of shares for estate duty purposes. The present section of the principal Act provides that the
commissioner, in valuing shares, is to take no account of restrictions imposed on the trans-
ferability of shares that are contained in the memorandum or articles of association of the
company. This clause extends that concept to cover restrictions contained in any other
document or imposed in any other manner. It also adds a proviso to enable the commissioner
to take restrictions into account if he is satisfied they are reasonable.
Clause 4 relates to the valuation of debts. The present section of the principal Act
provides that certain debts owing to the deceased and repayable at a future date are to be
valued as if they were repayable immediately, unless the commissioner is satisfied the parties
were at arm's length. This clause provides for the same treatment for debts owing to a
company controlled by the deceased. Clause 5 provides that all personal chattels included in
the dutiable estate of a deceased are to be reduced in value by the total value that passes to
the surviving spouse of the deceased, and up to $6,000 in any other case. The term "personal
chattels" for the purposes of the exemption, as was the case previously, includes furniture
and other personal effects, but does not extend to such items as motorcars or boats. Grant-
ing complete exemption for personal chattels passing to a surviving spouse will avoid the
need for a formal valuation, with the distress this can cause to widows and widowers.
I believe the move in the 1978 Budget is important for all New Zealanders. It means
that, with the relief of up to $60,000 for surviving spouses, the exemption for matrimonial
homes introduced by the Government 2 years ago, and the extended personal chattels
exemption, there will be no estate duty imposed on most estates in which the property passes
to the surviving spouse. This amendment will apply to people dying on or after 1 June 1978.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): The Opposition will not
oppose the main points in the Bill. It agrees that, provided the term "personal chattels" is
reasonably limited, the surviving spouse should not have the distress of having personal

motorcars and boats were not included in the definition. Will works of art owned on a
personal basis be included? There is a market for some items, and they gain remarkably in

## p. 2463 (#693) ###########################################

8 August
2463
Income Tax Amendment Bill
When introducing the Income Tax Amendment Bill based on the 1978 recovery Budget
I mentioned that it provided for confidence and expansion in the economy, and was a Bill
that included measures of considerable benefit to most individual taxpayers, employees and
self-employed alike. It also provides assistance to a wide range of business activities,
particularly for export and energy. In this Bill the Government has undertaken the largest
reduction in the rates of income tax in our history, a reduction which, when linked with the 5
percent reduction in February, has significantly reduced pressures on the individual taxpayer
by a total of some $500 million. The Government has also undertaken a major reform of the
tax system so as to remove the impact of the previous steeply progressive system. In
particular this will encourage the earning of additional income from overtime and
promotion, and concentrate tax relief on the full-time wage earner.
In 1976 and 1977 the economic situation militated against any large-scale tax relief, but,
to the extent that it was possible, we showed our concern as a Government for the low-
income and single-income family units, and gave the major part of tax relief to those sectors.
Now, in 1978, because of the success of the sometimes harsh economic measures the
Government has had to take, it has been possible, while continuing to help families, to
spread tax relief over a much wider spectrum of the taxpaying public, without acting in any
way irresponsibly, or undermining the substantial progress we have made so far in restoring
stability to the economy.
For ease of reference, the Bill is divided into three parts. Part I contains the changes in
personal income tax. Part II contains amendments to the increased export incentive scheme,
and introduces a new measure to permit the convertibility of that incentive to a refundable
credit for tax in certain cases. Part III contains miscellaneous amendments, both budgetary
and non-budgetary.
I shall now cover the main points in relation to each clause in these three parts. Clause 1
relates to the short title, and provides that the Bill be read in conjunction with, and be
deemed to be part of, the Income Tax Act 1976. As indicated, Part I relates to the Budget
proposals affecting personal income tax, and covers clauses 2 to 14 inclusive. During the
introduction of the Bill I mentioned that these changes represent the most comprehensive
review of personal income tax rates undertaken in the history of this country. I stand by that
statement, and in support of it mention that the cost of these measures in a full year, as I
have said already, is estimated to be $300 million for the second measure in October, on top
of the February measures of $200 million. These substantial reductions, which it is estimated
will benefit 1 400 000 individual taxpayers out of a total of 1 750 000, coupled, I remind the
House, with the 5 percent rebate in February, mean that in the space of a few months the
Government has effectively slashed income tax to the equivalent of $500 million in a full
year. This is a major achievement at a time of economic difficulty, and heralds a new era of
incentive and reward for increased effort by most workers, self-employed and employers
alike.
Clause 2 is the application clause for Part I, and, unless otherwise stated, the provisions
first apply to the tax on income derived during the year ending 31 March 1979, and in every
subsequent year. Clause 3 has the effect of repealing the personal rebate from 1 October
1978. The rebate for the current income year is reduced from $155 to $77.50, and is repealed
completely from 1 April 1979. This means that resident individuals, other than those to
whom clause 4 relates, will not be liable for income tax on the first $462 of income derived
during the year ending 31 March 1979. There will be no such tax threshold in succeeding
years.
Clause 4 introduces a new tax rebate of $78 for a full year to apply to children under the
age of 15, or those attending primary or secondary schools, or special schools for the
handicapped. The allowable rebate for this current year will be $39, which effectively means
it applies from 1 October 1978. For this income year ending 31 March 1979, the combination
of personal and school children's rebates will mean that those children to whom I referred
will be able to derive income up to $695 without incurring any tax liability. If that income
comprises employment earnings, the allowable amount before the standard deduction will
be $710. In 1980 and subsequent years, those figures will be $538 and $549 respectively. The
purpose of this special rebate is to ensure that primary and secondary school children are not
required to pay tax on small amounts of earnings derived as newspaper boys, milk delivery
assistants, messengers, and so on. It should avoid the need for them to pay in their own tax
deductions to the Inland Revenue Department each month in relation to services as private
domestic workers-for example, lawn and hedge cutting, baby sitting and the like. Members


## p. 2464 (#694) ###########################################

2464
8 August
Income Tax Amendment Bill
will note that it was decided not to include the far wider range of income covered by tertiary
students. However, the Minister of Education announced compensatory tertiary measures
on 2 July.
Clause 5 makes consequential amendments to the principal Act on the repeal of the
personal rebate and introduction of the rebate for school children. Clauses 6 and 7 amend
the rate at which the rebate for a dependent spouse reduces. The present abatement of 30c
for each dollar by which the spouse's income exceeds the allowable figure of $520 is to be
reduced to 25c in the dollar. This means these rebates will not be extinguished until the
spouse's income reaches $1,144 instead of the present $1,040.
Clause 8 makes several important changes to the single-income family rebate. With
effect from the current income year, which commenced on 1 April 1978, the amount of
rebate will be increased from $208 to $260 a year an increase from $4 to $5 a week-and
will apply to a child under the age of 12 years, instead of the present 10 years. In addition,
the allowable income of the spouse is to be increased from $1,040 to $1,114, and the rebate
will reduce by 25c instead of 30c for each additional dollar of the spouse's income over that
figure. This means that the increased rebate will not be extinguished until the spouse's
income reaches $2,184 instead of $1,733 at present.
Clause 9 gives effect to the Budget announcement that payments for pre-school
education at registered private kindergartens and play centres will qualify for the rebate of
50c in the dollar for donations and school fees. This will bring them into line with payments
made to free kindergartens and play centres, which already qualify. Clause 9 also adds the
Christian World Service, the New Zealand Catholic Overseas Aid and Raphael-the Ryder-
Cheshire Foundations of New Zealand-to the list of qualifying organisations whose funds
are applied for charitable purposes overseas. Donations made on or after 1 April 1978 to
these organisations will qualify for the rebate, subject, of course, to the overall maximum
rebate of $175.
Clause 10 covers the Budget announcement to increase the standard deduction for
employment-related expenses from $50 to $52 and extend its application to national
superannuation, pensions for past services, and earnings-related compensation payments.
As also announced, this deduction will be built into the PAYE tables from 1 October 1978.
This is being done for two reasons: first, to give a more immediate benefit to the extended
number of people entitled to it; and secondly, to avoid the necessity for pay period taxpayers
to file returns where their only reason for doing so would be to claim the standard deduction.
Clause 11 increases from $200 to $500 the amount of taxable income from interest,
dividends, and rents, that a taxpayer not in business may derive before being required to pay
provisional tax. This clause does not exempt that income from tax. It simply provides for the
tax on that income to be paid on an end of year assessment-generally by the following 7
March-instead of being paid under the more complicated provisional tax system. The
amendment, which applies from the year commencing 1 April 1979, is aimed at simplifying
tax payment procedures for some 45 000 taxpayers deriving reasonably small amounts of
investment income, including many national superannuitants.
Clause 12 substitutes a new composite scale of tax rates that is to apply to income
derived during the current income year. This scale combines the existing rates with those
proposed in clause 13 of the Bill, as if each had applied for half the year. They will be the
basis for producing the self-calculation tables to be incorporated in the 1979 tax return
forms.
Clause 13 is a key clause. It introduces the new five-tier rate scale announced in the
Budget. This will take full effect from the income year commencing 1 April 1979. It
substitutes for the existing and cumbersome 19-step rate system and will go a long way
towards overcoming objections to overtime earnings being subjected to increased marginal
tax rates. It is a very important clause. I wish to make it perfectly clear, because there has
been misunderstanding, that the new rate scale is still progressive and operates in exactly the
same manner as that which it replaces. For example, a person whose annual income is
$10,000 will not pay tax at the rate of 38c in every dollar of that income, as some people have
written to check. He will pay tax on the first $4,500 at the basic rate of 14.5c in the dollar,
and only the balance of $5,500 will be taxed at the marginal rate of 38c in the dollar.
A similar position, of course, applies for higher incomes. I mention this because of the
many inquiries that have been directed to me and to the department. Many people have
been under a misapprehension that the top or marginal rate in the scale will relate to their
total income. I want to make it clear that that is not the case. A progressive scale will apply


## p. 2465 (#695) ###########################################

8 August
2465
Income Tax Amendment Bill
across the board. I repeat and emphasise this because of the need for understanding. The
new rates are progressive. They will operate in exactly the same manner as present and past
rates. Whether a person's income for the year is $6,000 or $16,000, the first $4,500 will be
taxed at 14.5c in the dollar, the next $5,500 will be taxed at 38c in the dollar, and so on. To
do otherwise would, of course, result in the vast majority of taxpayers being required to pay
substantially more tax than they are at present.
Clause 14 substitutes new PAYE tables to apply to tax deductions from payments made
for any period ending on or after 1 October 1978. The new, tables include the full effect of the
new rates scale, and also incorporate the standard deduction that I referred to earlier. I
mentioned that the new tax rate structure given effect to in clauses 13 and 14 will
substantially overcome past criticisms surrounding the marginal tax rates applicable to
overtime earnings, or to increased earnings through accepting increased responsibilities. It
was with that in mind that each step of the new rates was spread over a wide range of
incomes.
There will still be an occasional case when overtime or promotion earnings do take a
person into a higher tax bracket. That is obvious, but it is expected that the great majority of
employees will be accommodated by this new scale, and their earnings will be taxed at the
marginal rate applicable to their ordinary earnings. That is the objective of it. For example, a
person on a weekly wage of $150, or $7,800 a year, may earn additional income of up to $42 a
week, or $2,200 a year, and still pay the same marginal rate of tax on those earnings-that is
38c in the dollar-as he does on his ordinary weekly earnings. That surely is a major
incentive, and, I believe, a major step forward.
In concluding the summary of Part I of the Bill, I remind the House and the people of
the statement by the Minister of Finance upon presenting his 1978 Budget on 1 June. He said
that even with the new rate scale the 38 percent marginal tax paid over the income range is
still too high. This Government is pledged to continue its efforts to further reduce the rates
of income tax as opportunity offers. The introduction during the past 6 months of tax
concessions equivalent to $500 million in a full year is clear evidence of the National
Government's determination and sincerity in this regard.
In Part II of the Bill, clauses 15, 16, and 17 should be read together. As I mentioned on
the first reading of the Bill, they give effect to the changes announced earlier in the year to
the increased exports incentive allowances. Clause 15 redefines the term "export goods". It
adds a new definition, that of "export merchant". The purpose of the clause is to discontinue
the allowance of the increased export incentive deductions to third parties who are not the
true exporters of the goods. The clause takes effect with respect to export goods sold or
disposed of on or after 1 April this year, irrespective of the taxpayer's accounting year. After
that date, only the manufacturer, producer, or processer of the goods who also exports those
goods, or an export merchant, as defined, will qualify for the incentive allowances. The
clause also clarifies the situation when there is a transfer of a business or an export activity
from one person to another. In such cases, in keeping with the original intention of the
legislation, any incentive allowance will be based on an actual increase in export sales over
the base period sales of the previous exporter.
Clause 16 introduces the new tax credit system for exporters who are in a tax loss
situation. This scheme is a new innovation in the tax system. To the extent the current-year
loss is attributable to the increased export incentive allowances, it allows the value of those
allowances to be converted to a tax refund at the rate of 45c in the dollar. The scheme will
first apply to the 1977-78 income year.
Clause 17 has the effect of validating third party export arrangements up to 31 March
1978. The commissioner may accept these arrangements provided the amount of incentive
deduction claimed by the third party does not exceed the amount to which the true exporter
of the goods would have been entitled, had he continued to export the goods himself. The
commissioner may make an adjustment where the parties may have acted in good faith in the
belief that a greater portion of total export sales qualified for the export incentive deduction.
The measures provided for have a threefold purpose: first, to ensure that increased export
incentive allowances go to the true exporters; secondly, to provide the necessary incentive,
through the new export tax credit system, to further increase exports; and, thirdly, to
provide employment opportunities. I am sure the changes will be welcomed.
Part III of the Bill relates to miscellaneous amendments to the principal Act, both
budgetary and non-budgetary. They cover the fishing industry, hygiene assistance grants,
energy conservation expenditure, certain dealings with suspensory loans, terminating dates
for incentive allowances, and the regional investment allowance for the New Plymouth and


## p. 2466 (#696) ###########################################

2466
8 August
Income Tax Amendment Bill
the Bell Block areas. I will take them clause by clause.
Clause 18 is the application provision for this part of the Bill. It applies to tax on income
derived during the year ending 31 March 1979 and subsequent years. Clause 19 is a
machinery amendment to the section dealing with the retrospective pay rebate. It simply
recognises the new tribunal established under the State Services Conditions of Employment
Act 1977.
Clause 20 makes three amendments to section 61, which exempts certain types of
income from tax. The first amendment exempts stake winnings from greyhound racing. This
brings such stakes into line with horse racing and trotting stakes. The second exempts
income derived by the New Zealand Racing Conference, the New Zealand Trotting
Conference, and the New Zealand Greyhound Racing Association. At present the
Totalisator Agency Board, the New Zealand Racing Authority, and racing or trotting clubs
are exempt from payment of income tax, and these exemptions are a logical extension to
those existing provisions. The final amendment deletes a reference to universal
superannuation, that was abolished following the introduction of national superannuation.
Clause 21 amends section 110 of the principal Act relating to depreciation on motorcars
as a result of the specified cost price being increased last year from $6,000 to $7,000. The
effect of this amendment arises where a taxpayer elects to offset depreciation recovered on a
car sold against the cost price of the replacement car. In such cases the cost price of that
replacement car for depreciation purposes is to be the lesser of its actual cost less
depreciation recovered, or its specified cost-that is, not the specified cost of the car sold.
Clause 22 is to overcome a misinterpretation of the manner in which depreciation is
recovered for tax purposes. This has happened when an asset that has been used both for
business and private purposes has been sold or disposed of at a price exceeding its book
value. The amendment makes it clear that the proportion of profit that represents the excess
depreciation applicable to the business use of the asset is to be included as assessable
income. This has been a long-standing practice.
Clause 23 extends, as announced in the Budget, the existing 40 percent fishing
investment allowance to include new motorised boats purchased after Budget night by rock
oyster or mussel farmers for use in their business. Clause 24 ensures that on-shore processing
plant and machinery for which a special hygiene assistance grant has been received will not
also qualify for any investment allowance. This places the fishing industry in a similar
position to the meat industry in respect of similar grants.
Clause 25 implements Budget announcements. To encourage energy conservation,
several new classes of capital energy conservation expenditure will quality for the immediate
100 percent write-off under section 125 of the main Act. It will encourage the re-refining of
used lubricating oils. The cost of plant that burns such oils is to be excluded from the 100
percent write-off. These measures reflect the Government's recognition of the following two
factors: first the right climate must be set now for expanding the use of products from the
great Maui and Kapuni fields; and, secondly, our oil import bill is still too high; and the
Government wishes to help in this way by encouraging both energy conservation and better
utilisation through tax measures. I want to mention in particular the cost of plant installed
for the co-generation of electricity with process heat, expenditure in refurbishing business
lighting, the cost of converting business vehicles to use LPG, and the gas development
expenditure of gas distribution enterprises. These clauses are very important, and I want to
emphasise the value they should have both for the economy and for the industry.
Clause 26 amends section 166 so that employees taking up shares under an employee
share purchase scheme within 3 years of retirement may retain those shares on retirement.
At present any employee who ceases employment within that period for reasons other than
death, serious injury, illness or redundancy is required to forgo his rights to the shares and
sell them back to the trustees. It is considered that employees whose employment ceases on
reaching normal retirement age should be permitted to retain their shares, even if that age is
attained during the restrictive period. This clause so provides.
Clause 27 deals with the taxation treatment of the new land development
encouragement loans announced in the Budget. The treatment that applies to similar
suspensory loans will apply equally to these loans. If the loans are remitted, the amount
remitted will generally be treated as assessable income equally in the year of remission and
the next two succeeding years.
Clause 28 deals with the taxation aspects of the new suspensory loans for horticultural
trials, as well as irrigation and West Coast drainage schemes. These will be dealt with in the

2467
same manner as regional development suspensory loans, in that at the point the loans are
made they will be regarded as grants. The expenditure to which they relate will be reduced
for tax purposes by the amount of the loans.
Clause 29 closes a loophole that was being availed of by some non-resident companies in
relation to losses incurred by New Zealand subsidiaries that form a part of a specified group
for New Zealand tax purposes. In certain circumstances they were able to obtain an unfair
dual advantage for income tax and non-resident withholding tax in respect of the same loss.
Clause 30 removes an obsolete reference to non-assessable income in section 198 of the
principal Act. Clause 31 amends section 210 to exclude New Zealand residents from the
special basis of assessment for individual insurance underwriters. When this arbitrary basis
was introduced in 1959 there were no resident underwriters operating in this country. It was
not intended to apply to New Zealand residents in business as underwriters. This
amendment ensures that such residents will pay tax on their actual profits at the normal
resident rates of tax.
Clause 32 is a minor drafting correction relating to property syndicates. Clause 33 has
two amendments. It reduces the arbitrary rate of net profit for non-resident film renters from
15 percent to 10 percent of the gross rentals received. When the present section was
originally enacted it was not envisaged that there would be payments by non-resident film
renters to New Zealand resident film producers. The exempting provisions of the section at
present, therefore, do not distinguish between payments made to resident and non-resident
recipients. Such payments made to New Zealand residents are now to be treated as
assessable income.
Clause 34 removes the exemption from excess retention tax of privately controlled
investment companies, whose income is solely from dividends. The present position was
never intended, and is now corrected. Clause 35 authorises the young family rebate to be
taken into account for provisional tax purposes. Clause 36 is an extension of a similar
amendment made last year to the Income Tax Act 1976, confirming that the commissioner
may, under his general delegation of powers, authorise his officers to institute proceedings
for offences under the former Land and Income Tax Act 1954.
Clause 37 authorises publication in the New Zealand Gazette of the names of those
taxpayers convicted either for failing to deduct PAYE tax from employees' earnings, or,
having made deductions, failing to pay them to the commissioner. Clause 38 removes any
doubt that, following the consolidation of the Land and Income Tax Act 1954 into the
Income Tax Act 1976, the commissioner may continue to take proceedings for offences
committed after 31 March 1977 in respect of income years ending up to that date. Clause 39
substitutes a new third schedule to the Act detailing the terminating dates for the various tax
incentive allowances. Clause 40 increases from 5 percent to 15 percent the rate of regional
investment allowance for the New Plymouth urban area and Bell Block for new plant and
machinery purchased after 1 June 1978.
Several matters are still under consideration, and I hope to introduce a Supplementary
Order Paper during the Committee stage to cover, among other things, benefits in lieu of
interest, the farming investment allowance, assets used in relation to the use of LPG as a
substitute energy source, the stock adjustment scheme, the export incentive allowance, and
one or two minor clauses. The Government has made continuing use of a fiscal policy to
boost economic confidence and activity. It has introduced major tax reductions combined
with tax reform to reduce previously steep progressive rates by a five-step approach as the
least inflationary way to lift economic activity. I believe that our tax system is being carefully
prepared as the first step of overall tax reform as envisaged in the Budget. We see it as a
medium-term exercise, which will have to be fitted to the shape of our economy and its
needs. We naturally challenge the capacity of any Opposition to produce a better tax reform
system.

where we want to go.
Looking at the tax scales and the provisions clearly outlined in the Budget, the New
Zealand taxpayer has benefited by $520 million in annual terms. That includes the combined
effect of the February and October tax cuts. The Bill is a major step forward, and offers
relief to nearly all taxpayers. It recognises two things. First, from improved effort will follow
improved reward-in other words we are giving incentives to the people of New Zealand to
work harder, to get more money from their work, and more production for the country, and
yet pay less tax. Secondly, it recognises and this is implemented in the Bill-that in the last
18 years the amount of income tax payable, in relation to total taxation, has reached more
than 75 percent; but, even more important to the wage and salary earner, it has gone from
about 30 percent to 45 percent of total tax. That situation actually discouraged the workers,
and the changes implemented in the Bill were necessary.
The new personal taxation rates are a simplification of existing rates, and their ready
acceptance by the people during the last two months is proof that they are doing the job that
the people want them to do, and that the Government wants them to do. They involve only
five steps. It is pretty simple to work out where a taxpayer fits into any one of the five steps.
Within those individual steps, tax rates remain the same. Each step covers about $5,000 to
$6,000, without changing the tax rate. A worker can work extra overtime, or get extra
earnings that might come his way, without penalty; if he stays on the same tax step he does
not incur a penalty on overtime or any other increment he might work for. Additionally, we
gave a personal tax reduction to the full-time wage earner. That was a deliberate step.
Further, the Government has made marked improvements for the low single-income family
with children. About 1 400 000 taxpayers, with taxable incomes between $3,000 and $27,000
a year will receive tax cuts of up to $382 each year. That is a cash-in-the-hand benefit that
will go towards a better standard of living. Families can calculate the money, count it, and
know what it is about.
It is not like the pie-in-the-sky things offered by the Labour Party. Labour said that tax
cuts would be due later next year, if something happens, or if many things happen. Its
promises are conditional on ifs and buts. Labour's tax cuts are not realistic, because they are
replaced by other forms of tax. One admitted form is the foreign exchange tax. Labour will
introduce new and increased taxes. People will pay more with Labour, not necessarily in
direct income tax, but by other hidden taxes, such as the threatened import exchange tax.
Labour gives with one hand, but ruthlessly grasps with the other hand. It has the cold, mean
heart of socialism. Where is Labour's credibility? It talks about tax cuts, but it plans to
introduce new taxes and increase existing taxes.
National's revised tax plan was outlined in the Budget, and it is now outlined in the Bill.
It can be understood. It is fair and just. It cuts personal taxation, and it is credible. It has
been well received by the people. The tax cuts have been made without crushing new taxes, a
capital gains tax, or other taxes that Labour Party supporters talk about-property tax and
others. The tax cuts have been made without increasing existing tax rates. The measures in
the Bill are a major development of the tax system. The Prime Minister said, in the Budget,
that the measures are only part of a fully revised tax system, which will maintain the State
services, give true incentives for productivity and better personal returns, reward instead of
penalising the personal effort of working New Zealanders, and will not include a cruel
inflationary tax such as Labour's import exchange tax. The country can do without that type
of indirect taxation.
Indirect tax would discourage people from contributing towards their own and the
country's future. It would affect every level of production from the moment goods hit the
wharves. Indirect taxation would affect imported goods, whether raw materials, stock for a
manufacturing industry, processed materials, components for assembly in New Zealand,
finished goods, or machinery to go into a factory. The list is endless. When goods entered

New Zealand they would be subjected to a vicious tax. The tax would be vicious, because it

QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Middlemore Hospital Neonatal Intensive Care Unit
1. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen a report in the New
Zealand Herald of 21 July 1978 that a "new neonatal intensive care unit at Middlemore
Hospital has been idle for more than a year because of difficulties in finding a specialist
doctor to run it", and, if so, will the Government assist the Auckland Hospital Board in
finding a specialist doctor to run this unit?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I am aware of the problems that the Auckland
Hospital Board has had in regard to filling the position at Middlemore. Paediatricians who
have further specialised in neonatal work are scarce. Filling this position is a matter entirely
for the Auckland Hospital Board, which has advertised widely here and overseas. There is
little the Government can do to assist, but if the Auckland Hospital Board were to seek
assistance I am sure the Government would do what was within its power.
Mr Hunt: What is the Minister doing to ensure the use of a unit that cost about $80,000
to establish?
Hon. T. F. GILL: It would depend entirely on the facts laid before us by the hospital
board as to where they had advertised, how they had advertised, and what approaches had
been made. When we ascertained this, if we thought there was some way in which we could
assist or bring our influence to bear, or if we had different channels of communication that
the hospital board had not had, we would help in those areas, but we have to know what the
problem is first.
Papakura Military Camp Expenditure
2. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Defence: What total expenditure
at Papakura military camp has been authorised since November 1975?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence): The total expenditure is $4.7 million.
Mr Wellington: What proportion of that has been spent on capital works development
in the camp?
Hon. ALLAN McCREADY: This figure includes $1.9 million for capital works, $2.8
million for the maintenance and the running of the camp, and $34,000 for materials used by
the Army engineer unit.
St. John Ambulance Services
3. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen a report in the Waikato
Times of 10 July 1978 that "St. John Ambulance services could be reduced and drivers could
face unemployment if the Waikato Hospital Board fails to provide more money this year",
and, if so, what steps is the Government taking to ensure that St. John Ambulance services
receive sufficient funds to carry on their work this year?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The Waikato Hospital Board indicated in a press
statement in the Waikato Times on 1 August 1978 that the hospital board would ensure that
essential ambulance services were maintained.
Mr Hunt: Does the Minister's reply mean that some of the St. John Ambulance services
provided previously have had to be cut back?
Hon. T. F. GILL: There is nothing in my statement from which the member could infer
that. I do not believe there were any services in the Waikato that were not essential. The St.
John Ambulance Association does not work that way. Is the member suggesting it was
running non-essential services? The board has said that essential ambulance services will be
maintained.
Mr Hunt: As the article appeared originally on 10 July, and as there was apparently a

good deal of truth in the statements made by the St. John Ambulance people, has the

Benefit Increases
10. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) to the Minister of Social Welfare: To what

terms?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): During the period November 1975
to August 1978 the married beneficiaries referred to have received an increase of $26.02 a
week, or 50,8 percent. During the same period unmarried beneficiaries without dependants
have received an increase of $15.62 a week, or 50.8 percent. These increases were based on
the movement in the consumer price index from June 1975 to June 1978, and in that period
the index increased by 50.7 percent-proving that all beneficiaries are better off because of
increases under the National Government.
Mr Friedlander: What were the amounts payable to beneficiaries in November 1975,

Hon. H. J. WALKER: In November 1975, married couples received $51.26 a week;
today under National they receive $77.28 a week. In November 1975, unmarried persons
received $30.75 a week; today under National they receive $46.37 a week.
Mr Hunt: If the figures have increased as dramatically as the Minister appears to think
they have, why is it that so many people aged over 60 are convinced that they are
considerably worse off under the National Government?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I have invited Opposition members to quote one case of
someone who is worse off, but no one has yet been able to quote one specific case. On the
contrary, everyone is better off because of the introduction of national superannuation.

Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, they were. I researched this after public statements by the
Leader of the Opposition, criticising the policy. In 1973, 98 students who were coming to
New Zealand signed a certificate that stated, "If accepted for a training award, I undertake
to refrain from engaging in political activity." During 1974, 187 students signed such a

Mr Hunt: Was the document signed at the request of the country from which the

Hon. T. F. GILL: No, it was not.
Mr Hunt: Oh, come now.

Governments. The form is prepared in Sri Lanka by the secretariat of the Colombo Plan, is
forwarded to all countries that wish to send students abroad under the Colombo Plan, is
signed by the student, goes back to Sri Lanka, and is sent out to the countries that might
accept it. All students coming under the Colombo Plan sign this form, but not at the request
of the country of origin.

overseas; if not, why does the arrangement apply particularly to Colombo Plan countries?

Commonwealth countries that are developed to the extent that New Zealand is and have
some surplus university and training capacity offer places to underdeveloped countries. We
are a contributor of places under the Colombo Plan, and do not send our own students
abroad under it.
Mr Prebble: What is the definition of "political activities"? Would a talk given to a

that would not be disorderly in the middle of the day could be disorderly in the middle of the
night. It depends on the time and the place. Each case would have to be treated on its merits.
Normally, one would react to a complaint or to an application for a decision on whether or
not some conduct was disorderly. It would not be disorderly conduct to carry a banner in the
Orongorongo foothills, but it might be disorderly conduct to carry a banner at Wellington
airport at the time a visiting Prime Minister was arriving from overseas. Each case would
have to be judged according to the circumstances at.the time.
VOTING RIGHTS PROTECTION BILL
Introduction
Debate resumed from 4 August 1978
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The debate is on a proposal by the
Labour member for Porirua to introduce yet another amending Bill in respect of enrolment
procedures and duties and citizens' rights in elections. Before the House adjourned on
Friday last I said that in 1975 the Labour Government, then responsible for the
administration of the country, introduced amendments to the electoral law, practically all of
which are extant. The Bill under discussion suggests to me that at least one Labour member,
the member for Porirua, is losing confidence in his colleagues' administrative ability, and in
the Labour Government's amendments for the preparation of rolls, as passed in 1975.
Mr Hunt: That is ridiculous.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Well, it is either that or, considering all the other attempts by
Labour members around the country to induce people to believe in non-existent deficiencies
in the roll, it is a carefully concerted attempt to delude people about the adequacy of
procedures carried out by the National Government, consequent upon the Labour
Government's amended Act. Even editors, who should know better because they have been
told, have said that the rolls will be late. We in the House know that the rolls will be out in
the first week of September, and that is not late. In the publicity the member for Porirua
gave to his Bill before it was introduced we were told that previously about 40,000 people in
each election were not able to exercise a valid vote because of non-enrolment. The member


## p. 2493 (#723) ###########################################

9 August
2493
Voting Rights Protection Bill
now knows that only twice, in 1972 and in 1975, were those figures kept separately. In 1972,
under the administration of a National Government, there were just over 36,000, while
under Labour's new law the number has increased by about 24 percent to nearly 45,000.
The Bill proposes a means of voting that would undoubtedly lead to plural voting, and
to deceit on a wide scale should anybody want to deceive returning officers. The National
Government will not accept this proposal, and will vote against the Bill. As I have said
before, the time to look at the Electoral Act is in the first year of a new Parliament. That is
what we should be doing next year, in a select committee consisting of members from all
parties. Then we could carefully look at the adequacy of the law, but we should not do that
just a few weeks before polling day in an election year.
I hope this Bill will be the last, dealing with electoral law, that we will see. After careful
study in the select committee, we have been told that the Chief Electoral Officer and his

Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): This Bill should be introduced, because the right to vote is
more important than the requirement to enrol. Unfortunately, the reverse applies in the
legislation as it stands. The inefficiencies, the problems, and the uncertainties generated by
the present system for enrolment can actively deny people one of the few political rights that
they have, regardless of the extent and meaninglessness of the situation in which Tweedledee
and Tweedledum dominate. One gets a distinct impression that, under the current
procedures, there is a hindering rather than a helping of the process for enrolment. Far too
many voters' ballots, on the basis of the information I have received, appear to have been
disallowed in the Rangitikei by-election. Minor technicalities, which were apparently the
grounds for disallowance, illustrate the desirability of eligible voters being given the right to
make an enrolment by declaration, and to cast a special vote on the strength of that
declaration. Subsequently, it would not be a difficult task to check the validity of the
declaration. It would involve no more work than does the present system.
As the situation stands many voters who, despite their best efforts, have failed to be
correctly enrolled on either the main or the supplementary rolls, will be confused about their
right to vote-it appears to a greater extent this year than in previous years. This matter
must be cleared up-cleaned up might be a better phrase-and done in a way that gives
every eligible voter unchallengeable voting rights. This Bill would achieve this desirable
result for those who, through no fault of their own could otherwise find themselves
undemocratically disfranchised under the present law. Regular boundary changes,
compounding the problem of electoral roll stability, and voter uncertainty and confusion, lie
at the basis of this whole problem. It is high time that the concept of plural member
constituencies, enabling a much greater degree of electoral roll stability, was seriously
entertained as the long-term solution to the whole problem of voter registration.
The deficiency in this Bill, as far as it has a deficiency, is that it fails to take the logical
step of proceeding that far, if only to lay a framework to operate beyond election year.
Nevertheless, I strongly support the introduction of this Bill as it stands, while hoping to see
the subsequent support of its author, and others, for the further and more important steps
that need to be taken if the democracy they seek to promote is to be fully realised. However
this Bill is important in itself, because the more working people the conservative
establishment can keep off the rolls, through unduly complex and restrictive procedures, the
longer its tenure of office can be enhanced. The greatest condemnation of the Government's
negative attitude to this Bill is that, not so much like Labour's attitude, it is based on political
self-interest. It proceeds from an entirely pragmatic motivation of wanting to retain power
for its own sake, rather than from a willingness to give expression to the democratic common
will, in so far as that can be expressed within the entirely inadequate first-past-the-post
electoral system. I repeat that the right to vote ought to be more important than the
requirement to enrol. I do not believe that the administrative procedures that would be
involved, if this Bill were put into operation before polling day, would be any more complex
than those which operate at present.

election under the present law? The Bill then refers to a special election. What sort of

on the strange concept of regular elections and special elections. The Bill refers to an
electoral officer. The person is known as the electorate officer. Drafting errors like that, and
undefined concepts, make it impossible to adopt the Bill.

the proposal it was realised that it was impossible to have an election without a roll.

more to look at each one of those, and probably a couple of months later we would get the

The member for Onehunga said he wants to improve democracy. They tried that in the
United States. It is very interesting that in the Legislature in Ohio they introduced a measure
for instant election-day registration of voters. The Legislature enacted that system, but a
petition was filed demanding a State-wide vote on its application. The vote, taken on 9
November 1977, was overwhelmingly against the instant registration proposal with some 62
percent voting to prohibit it. So, it was thrown out there-the only place where it was tried.
It is very interesting to look at the Electoral Act, and at the people who qualify for special
votes. We fall over ourselves trying to give people the opportunity to vote. It is well known
that there is an obligation to enrol, but a number of people, of a particular political
persuasion, do not enrol because it serves as a form of political protest. Once you get past
that aspect, many people do not vote on election day, again, as a political measure. They
have contemplated, and their political stance is not to vote. In many instances that is as
justified as a vote itself.
Any person who is qualified to vote at any election, in any district, can vote as a special
voter under section 100 of the Electoral Act, if, on polling day, he is outside New Zealand, if
he will be absent from the district on polling day, if throughout the hours of polling he will be
away, or if his name does not appear on the main roll or any supplementary roll, or has been
wrongly deleted; and there are the lighthouse provisions and the religious provisions. I do
not know how much more the member for Porirua wants to handfeed anybody. I suggest that
he sold the Bill to the members of his caucus by omitting to remind them that they had
rejected the Wellington Central Labour Party's proposals in 1975, and that he was covering
his own problems in 1975-problems given to him by electoral reform under a Labour
Government by the proposed new section 48A in clause 10, "Voting when registered for
wrong electoral district." That type of action speaks for itself.

the Government back benches can be.
Marilyn Waring: You're not noted for your liberality.
Dr WALL: It is not liberality, it is just democracy and fair play that I am interested in

known for a very long time, that the only party in New Zealand politics that is not really
interested in democracy is the National Party; that the only party in New Zealand politics
that wants a tight selective voting list is the National Party; that the only party in New
Zealand politics that wants to make sure that everyone cannot vote is the National Party;
and that the only party in New Zealand politics that says to the electors that if they are good,
and do what they are told, they will be allowed to vote.
Every other political party is keen that New Zealanders who are eligible to be on the roll
and eligible to cast a vote can do so, no matter what. No other political party is frightened of
the public. No other political party is concerned about what the public's opinion would be if
it were expressed. That is what the debate is about. We have heard all sorts of nonsense from
the member for Raglan about a mistake the electoral office made concerning some electors
in my electorate. That is exactly the type of mistake that the Bill will prevent. The
Government-not any particular member of a party, or the electorate officer, or the people
concerned with administration-says that we need the present position, when a clerical error
can deprive New Zealanders of the right to vote for the Government of their choice. It will
happen again and again. The Government will not tell those New Zealanders that it has
deprived them of a vote, every one of whom thought he was entitled to vote. The
Government will not tell them that their vote was not counted or the reason why.
A great deal of play has been made about attempts that the last Labour Government
made to correct that. Regrettably, they were not successful. I am the first to admit, and all
members on this side of the House are prepared to admit, that they were not successful. That
is why the Bill is before the House, to complete and to ensure that what the Government
tried to do last time will be done this time. This Government does not want to ensure that
every New Zealander can vote. We have heard a suggestion that this should be delayed. The
member for Raglan must have read a book somewhere. I doubt if she has had much
experience in counting votes, or anything to do with the voting system, because she told us
about all the delays that would occur under my proposed legislation after the poll had closed.

Voting Rights Protection Bill
Every process she mentioned-the checking of voters against rolls, the checking of voters on
previous rolls-has been followed since 1925, so there will be no change whatever in that.
The only difference is the steps that would be taken before the final result is declared.
Instead of ending up with a vote being declared invalid secretly, that vote will end up being
allowed.
The member for Raglan wants the position to continue when voters, who have cast what
should be a valid vote, will have their vote disallowed and not be told either why or how it
happened. No other political party wants that. Social Credit does not want it. We have no
reason to believe that the Values Party or the Communist Party want it. None of those
parties has given any indication that they want the position to continue. The only party that
says that is the National Party. It will suit the National Party's electoral purposes for that to
remain, because, if it was any other way it would join with us in referring the Bill to a select
committee. It could come back to the House, with any minor drafting notes, within 3 weeks.
It would make no difference whatever to the rolls, or to any procedure in the conduct of the
election, except to make sure that the Government does not disallow the votes of so many
thousands of New Zealanders who will go to the polls in the expectation of being able to vote
for the Government of their choice, only to be denied a vote.
The House divided on the question, That leave be given to introduce the Voting Rights
Protection Bill.

ANIMALS PROTECTION AMENDMENT BILL
Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture
Committee to present the report of the committee on the Animals Protection Amendment
Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move,
That the report do lie upon the table. The only amendment of any significance is to clause 2,
which states: "(1) The principal Act is hereby amended by inserting, after section 16, the
following section: ‘16A. (1) Where the owner of any animal is convicted of an offence
against this Act in respect of that animal, the court may, if it thinks it desirable for the
protection of the animal and in addition to or in substitution for any other penalty, order
that the animal be forfeited to the Crown." The amendment adds the following words:
"or to a society that is established for the prevention of cruelty to animals." The effect of
the amendment is that the court's hands are not tied to consulting the Minister on every
occasion. The court may decide, there and then, the means of disposal of an animal for its
own protection. The amendment should improve the Bill, and make the legislation more
effective. Eleven submissions on the Bill were heard. Some sought to introduce other
areas of interest, but there were no submissions against the Bill.
Motion agreed to.
