DISCUSSION OF MOTIONS
Labour Party's Taxation Proposals
Miss DEWE (Lyttelton): I move, That this House expresses its intense interest in the
statement by the member for Sydenham that the Government should follow the lead of the
New Zealand Labour Party in detailing precisely how lost revenue from tax reductions is to
be obtained, and asks that the New Zealand Labour Party now detail precisely just how the
foreign exchange surcharge will be levied and on which goods; also how much will be saved
from reduced numbers on unemployment benefits, and how many people will be left on the
dole after 12 months and when will unemployment be eliminated entirely under their tax
proposals; and explain how the "psychological effect" of a change of Government will assist
in achieving these goals. I present this motion to the House because of a comment by the
member for Sydenham, and I ask the Labour Party to state precisely how its lost revenue
will compensate for the tax reductions proposed in its alternative budget.
I should like to look at the precise details that the Labour Party is so proud of, and to
raise the question in the House so that we can establish just what is intended. The
Christchurch Star of 6 June 1978 printed the following statement about Labour's plans for
tax reforms in its budget: "In order to achieve tax reductions, Labour proposes a
surcharge on the purchase of foreign exchange. Apart from certain exceptions for export
industries there would be a levy on the use of New Zealand's overseas funds." It was
stated that this would discourage the wasteful spending of our scarcest resource,
encourage New Zealand manufacturers to use local raw materials and energy resources,
and stimulate local production, while cutting back the importation of luxury items and
finished consumer goods. No precise details are given in that statement, or in any
statement made since.
It is time that people knew-they ought to know, and indeed they are demanding to
know-just what these precise details are, how this surcharge is to be implemented, and
on what goods. Labour has promised to slash income tax by $400 million a year, and it has
stated that it would pay for this by the surcharge levy. Let it be made perfectly clear that
the proposal is not a reduction in income tax in any way; it is a transfer of tax from direct
to indirect tax, transferring tax from the direct salary and wages earned and company tax
to an indirect tax which would be a levy on goods coming into New Zealand. The public
must know exactly what goods are being considered for the application of the levy, what
rate will be charged, and what goods will be exempt so that an evaluation can be made of
the total taxation package. Labour's credibility is already suffering, and, frankly, I
consider I am doing Labour Opposition members a service by allowing them to give these
precise details to the public now.
What does the public need to have made available to it? First, what percentage is to be
levied on these goods coming into the country? Will it be a variable percentage, depending
upon the type of goods coming in? The total imports for the year ended 31 March 1978 were
worth $3,067 million, which included invisibles such as Government payments, debt
servicing, emigrants' transfers, and so on, which amounted to $1,584 million. That left net
goods coming into New Zealand of $1,483 million. Let us suppose that $483 million of
imports were directly involved in exporting. We end up with $1,000 million worth of imports
in the year ended 31 March 1978 that could be used domestically, or for goods to be re-
exported.
If the Labour Government is to raise $400 million by this method, it will have to levy 40
percent on $1,000 million worth of imports in order to achieve its $400 million compensation.
The net amount on which the 40 percent could be imposed would be $1,000 million, because
I cannot conceive that the surcharge would be levied on invisibles, including the
Government's imports and transactions. If that is a wrong assumption, we have to be told,
because the concept of 40 percent is inconceivable and frightening. Secondly, will farm
imports be exempted? If so, which? Will the exemption include tractors and spare parts, and
steel that comes in and is processed into fencing wire? Will diesel and petrol used on farms
be exempted, and how? Thirdly, how will the calculation be made on such items as steel and
fuels that are used for both domestic and export production? O. K., no doubt a refund could
be claimed when the goods are re-exported, but what sort of paper work will be involved for
businesses and industry, farmers, and the Civil Service?
What sort of evaluation has been made of the additional number of civil servants who

Post Office Profit
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa): I move, That this House congratulates the
Government and the Postmaster-General for providing a sound financial return on Post Office
activities as evidenced by the record $37 million profit for the 1977-78 financial year and notes
that this profit will enable the Post Office to finance its capital development programme and
upgrade and expand postal, banking, and telecommunications services, and further notes that
because of the last Labour Government's freezing of charges, the Post Office was placed in debt
by $65 million and demand for Post Office services was unusually distorted, further notes that
with a sound fiscal base the Post Office can now speed up its cabling programme and reduce
telephone waiting lists as promised in the National Party's 1975 manifesto.
The record of the last Labour Government is in complete contrast to the main thrust of
the National Government. Government members know that the Opposition believes it can
embarrass the Government over the Post Office's record profit of $37 million. In the last
year of the Labour Administration the Post Office ran at a loss of practically the same
amount, $38.7 million. Had the Labour Government retained office in 1975 that loss would
have climbed to $46 million by 31 March 1976. To subsidise Post Office operations the
Labour Government had to obtain revenue out of the Stabilisation vote; in other words, the
taxpayer was paying through a different channel. In addition, the Labour Administration
borrowed almost $62 million. I intend to analyse these figures, because they are a critical and
integral part of the whole argument. In its final year in office the Labour Government ran
the Post Office at a loss of $38.7 million, had to obtain from the taxpayer an equivalent
amount, and then had to borrow $61.9 million and pay $50 million in interest over 10 years.
The National Government's stated objective is that the Post Office should cover its working
costs and running expenses and find the money for 65 percent of its capital programme for
telecommunications, development, and buildings.
The Government was elected, according to its 1975 manifesto, "to speed up the cabling
programme and reduce the waiting lists for automatic telephone connections". That was a
prime objective enunciated in our 1975 manifesto. The record shows that we have achieved
this through a careful husbanding of resources, because we have adopted the principle of
user-pays, as opposed to the Labour Party's principle of borrowing and subsidising. I remind
members opposite that it means that, for every $1 earned, $1 less has to be borrowed. There
has been a reduction in the number on the waiting lists nationally from 30 288 to 22 629 as at
30 June of this year. It is confidently expected that the number will be reduced by the end of
this year to fewer than 20 000. That is another record. I know that the member for Mangere,
who is trying to interject, would not be in favour of that. By the end of 1978 we will have one
of the shortest waiting lists for many years, and at the same time, because it has achieved a
profit, the Post Office can plough funds back into development and that in turn will mean a
further reduction in the waiting lists. For the first time for years the number on the waiting
lists has dropped.
Secondly, there has been a substantial increase in cabling work, from 300 000 km under

pastures, particularly in Australia, and the difference between the taxation rates in New

an open-door policy for travellers between New Zealand and Australia, and there is no
restriction or limitation on a New Zealander who wants to work or settle in Australia.

themselves and leaving New Zealand.

New Zealand is the difference in tax rates between this country and Australia. An Australian
on a salary of $5,000 pays $582 in tax, but a New Zealander on the same salary pays $1,217-
he is disadvantaged by $635. An Australian on a salary of $8,000 pays tax of $1,580, but a
New Zealander on the same salary pays $2,429-an extra $912. An Australian on $10,000
pays tax of $2,280, but a New Zealander on the same salary pays $1,172 more, or half as
much again as that paid in Australia.

has long been contended that if we are to have an open-door migration policy between the

punishing rates of taxation, even under the Bill, will upset that balance and provide the
incentive for even more people to cross the Tasman and settle in Australia.

years in income tax alone practically the same amount as the total national income at the
time when Labour took office.
If one looks at the so-called tax, relief mentioned in the Budget and shown in the tables,
it will be found that they indicate no real relief. The only relief, in a sense, is that the
taxpayer is relieved all right-he is relieved of $300 million more of his own money. National
members complained when they were in Opposition about the Labour Government's tax
rates, and yet in its 3 years in office the present Government will collect $1.66 in income tax
for every $1 that Labour collected. In all forms of taxation, the Government will collect
$1.73 for every $1 collected by the Labour Government.
Some people will say that inflation has continued and the Government has not done a
very good job of controlling it-but the fact is that it is a higher rate of taxation increase,
even with the high, uncontrolled inflation rate under this Government. In the last 3 years the
labour force has hardly changed, and the total population has increased only slightly. This
means that the average tax paid per worker and the average tax paid per head of population
must have risen, even allowing for inflation and the Government's inability to control it, and
allowing for and taking note of the Government's claim to the contrary.
The Minister of Finance is fond of talking about things being such-and-such a
percentage of the gross national product. If one looks carefully at the figures, one finds that
this year's total tax and income tax will be just as high a proportion of GNP as last year's, and
that that proportion is an all-time record. I bet that is not a graph that the Prime Minister
showed at Blenheim or in the Wairarapa on that travelling road show he has been taking
around. I bet he has no chart showing that total tax and income tax, as a proportion of GNP,
are higher than they have ever been in our history.
This year's Budget states on page 39, "It is certainly the largest single tax cut yet
introduced in New Zealand." But here we are, taking more in tax, and especially in income
tax, than we have ever taken before. Given all the softening-up process that we had
beforehand, I was led to believe that this year there would be a swing away from income tax
as a source of Government revenue. Last year income tax represented 75.3 percent of total
tax. This year, in the Government's great leap backward, it has managed to get from 75.3
percent to 75.2 percent.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Spectacular!
Mr MARSHALL: A spectacular improvement. We were told that this was the year in
which the Government would divert the emphasis in taxation away from income tax as the
primary source of Government revenue. What has the Government done? It has reduced it
by 0.1 of 1 percent, from 75.3 percent to 75.2 percent. What a dramatic switch! It reminds
me of one of the other dramatic improvements it has made. The Government talked about
single-figure inflation, but, despite claims to the contrary, that aim has still not been
achieved. Government members said inflation would be reduced to single figures in their
first year in office. In that period they managed to reduce it from 15.7 percent to 15.6
percent, and then in the second year from 15.6 percent to 15.3 percent.
People should listen very carefully indeed to statements made by Government members
about the National Government's economic performance. They should then look at the
facts, because often the claims made cannot be substantiated by the facts. This year-the
year of the great tax cuts and changes-it is estimated that revenue from income tax will not
decrease, but will increase by 11 percent. If the Government seriously believes in its promise
of single-digit inflation, that means that income tax will again increase in real terms. This will
be the second year in a row-and only the second time ever in the country's history-when
more than $25 of every $100 of income is taken in income tax. Both of those years have been
under the National Government.
So much for the pious claims we have heard about changes and improvements to the
taxation system; so much for the claims that people on low incomes, and especially the low-
income families, are being assisted. This is the Government which, for the first time in New
Zealand's history, has charged taxpayers more than $25 on every $100 of their income. In 3
years under National-and I hope all taxpayers listening to the debate will take notice-
taxes have been raised by $3.20 for every $100 of income.

welfare premises attached, but there was a problem because, under the authority of the
Hospitals Act and the Health Act, there was no power for this to be done. When the
National Government came into office, I took the power to make money available for family
health counselling services. In the meantime, as the member knows, we are about to start
work on a health centre at Manukau City nearby, which will cost more than $1 million. The
member will also know that with a maximum of five doctors in a health centre the area is
spread, and if further doctors are added the people from the periphery must travel too far, so
the solution is to build more than one health centre.

Lawyers' Scale Fees-Increases
3. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau), on behalf of Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon), to the
Minister of Housing: How will the recent increase in lawyers' scale fees affect young New
Zealanders buying a home, and what is the percentage increase on an average home of
$28,000?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Information supplied by the New
Zealand Law Society reveals that the legal fees will increase by a weighted average of 20
percent from 15 August. Fees for low-value properties should be subjected to less than the
20 percent average increase. The fees charged are to be related to the cost of the house and
the number and value of any mortgages. The percentage increase of legal fees on an average
home of $28,000 subject to a Housing Corporation mortgage of $17,500 would be 14.35
percent, and, on a loan of $20,000, 15.35 percent.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: What is the justification for increasing lawyers' scale fees when
they have already increased markedly as a result of inflation?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! That is not a question that can be asked, because it seeks an
opinion from the Minister, and he may not give that.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Will lawyers be entitled to charge additional fees for extra work
involved in a transaction, or is one fee set for the whole transaction?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: My ministerial responsibility does not cover legal fees. Fees
are based on, first, the value of the property, and, secondly, the value of the mortgages. For
example, on a property valued at $28,000 with a Housing Corporation mortgage the increase
is $38.15, $8.82 of which relates to the mortgage, and $29.33 to the dwelling.

Railway Carriages
9. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru), to the Minister of Railways: How many steel

carriages could have been refurbished for further use?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways): Since 1 January 1976 a total of 69
steel-panel carriages have been written off. Although termed steel carriages, these vehicles
in reality have wooden framed bodies sheathed with light steel panels screwed to the frames.

not simply refurbishing. The work just could not be undertaken, having regard to other
much needed work that needs to be carried out in the workshops.

11. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Postmaster-General: Is it correct that over 1000

are more than 1000 applicants awaiting telephone service in the area currently served by the
Papatoetoe exchange. Some 200 of those applicants will be given service in October from the
new transportable exchange now being installed at Wiri, and in addition some existing
Papatoetoe subscribers will be transferred to the Wiri exchange early next year, thus
releasing Papatoetoe capacity for waiting applicants. A major extension to the Papatoetoe
exchange is also proposed for completion in 1981.
Mr Isbey: Rather than waiting for the proposed completion date of 1981, would it not be
preferable to use the enormous profit made by the Post Office to provide a better service at
an earlier date for the people of Papatoetoe?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The member is well aware that a number of determinants
control the speed at which we can spend money in the Post Office, one of them being the
availability of foreign exchange and another being the general level of economic activity that
the Government decides is permissible at the time.
Mr Downie: During what period did the waiting list build up to more than 1000, and why
was it allowed to do so?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Over the past few years the waiting list figures have shown a
fluctuating trend, but it is interesting to note, for example, that in June 1973 there were 361
people on the waiting list-that was when the former Labour Government was elected to
power-and in June 1976, shortly after the National Government took over, the number had
increased to 953. I think that is an indication of a fairly substantial growth in the waiting list
in the Papatoetoe area during the time of the former Labour Government.
Dr Wall: The Minister has said that the waiting list figures have shown a fluctuating
trend. Has he any evidence to show that the increase in the number occurred during a period
of full employment and when there was a rise in the affluence of the community, and that the
fall coincided with a decrease in employment opportunities and a reduction in the affluence
of the community after the National Government was elected to office?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The member should be aware that there are many
determinants. Many factors other than simply the growth in employment must be taken into
account, including the lead times for ordering, the availability of equipment, and that type of
thing. The question is too complex to be answered in just a few words.

Renal Dialysis Patients
21. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Health: How many patients are
there in New Zealand requiring renal dialysis treatment, and how many of these are able to
treat themselves within their own homes?


## p. 2541 (#771) ###########################################

10 August
2541
Questions for Oral Answer
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The exact figures are not obtainable at short
notice. The best information available on this subject is contained in the report of the
Hospital Advisory Council's committee on renal dialysis, which was recently released to
interested parties. The report states that planning should be based on a new patient intake of
30 patients per 1 000 000 population a year. It goes on to estimate "that the New Zealand
experience and present emphasis on home dialysis training could well produce a ratio of one
hospital dialysis patient to three home dialysis patients." These are the targets that are being
aimed for. As at September 1976-and I must admit these figures are rather out of date-
there was a total of 128 patients on dialysis, comprising 73 on hospital dialysis, 8 on home
dialysis training, and 47 on home dialysis.
Mr W. R. Austin: Can I take that there is considerable scope for more patients to
receive dialysis treatment in their own homes if the resources are available?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, we are aiming for a ratio of one in the hospital to three in the
home. The 1976 figures I gave were based on a ratio of five in the hospital to two in the
home. Much more equipment has been ordered. Each case is handled on its merits, and, of
course, there have to be training periods; but we are moving towards that target.
Pureora State Forest-Logging Policies
22. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) to the Minister of Forests: Has he seen the New
Zealand Herald of 4 August, in which a Mr W. Campbell claims that the selective logging in
the Pureora State Forest was causing massive damage to the trees left standing, and that "the
conditions of timber sale agreements were being seriously breached, with excessively wide
forest roads and timber haulage tracks and damage to streams and the forest canopy", and, if
so, are these allegations correct; and, if they are, what measures is the Forest Service taking
to protect the forest that is left?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of
the Minister of Forests. "Yes, I have seen the claims by Mr W. J. Campbell in relation to
logging damage in Pureora Forest. It is possible that, because in the general area being
worked some clear felling had taken place prior to the introduction of selection logging, the
company has been the target of some unfair criticism. The percentage of merchantable
timber to be removed has been set by the Forest Service, and the company is meeting this
specification. A rubber-tyred loader has been introduced to the operation and this has
reduced the size of the loading areas by 75 percent. Roading has been under the control of
the Forest Service since June, and width of main and secondary roads has been reduced to
the minimum consistent with safe working. Regular inspections by Pureora staff indicate that
the standard of logging is now satisfactory."
Liquor Referendum
23. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Justice: Has any consideration
been given to not holding a liquor referendum in conjunction with the 1978 general election,
and can he indicate whether any trends in voting have been apparent over the past 15 years
in this poll?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Government has not given any
consideration to amending the Licensing Act 1908 this year to abolish the triennial liquor
poll. The following trends are discernible from the last five polls. Support for national
continuance has fluctuated between 67.5 percent and 69.2 percent. Support for State
purchase and control peaked at 18.3 percent in 1969 and declined to 14.9 percent in 1975.
Support for prohibition dropped to 13.3 percent in 1969, but rose 2.5 points to 15.8 percent
in 1975. This quite clearly shows overwhelming support for national continuance, a decline
in support for State purchase and control, and a minor increase in the prohibition vote.

FRIDAY, 11 AUGUST 1978
Mr SPEAKER took the chair at 9 a.m.
Prayers.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): The business for next week will be
estimates on Tuesday and Thursday, discussion on questions and private members' notices
of motion on Wednesday afternoon, legislation in the evening, local Bills and estimates on
Thursday, and legislation on Friday.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): I want to ask the Prime
Minister if a recess has been contemplated. I am mindful that the wives said at one of their
earlier meetings that, if there was to be a recess, consideration could perhaps be given to
members' family commitments, and the recess, or at least part of it, might coincide with the
August school holidays. Has the Prime Minister considered that suggestion?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I considered it, and I have replied to the
secretary of the wives' union. The wives failed to realise that, when we take a recess at this
time of the year, it is not so that members can be at home with their families; it is so that they
can be here on committee work. Therefore, little would be achieved under the proposal
made by the wives. They would not have their husbands at home, if that is what they wanted.
Their husbands would be here on committee work, as though it were a normal week.
However, putting that aside, there is no proposal for a break now. The work of the session is
proceeding normally, without the need to work any extra time in the evenings. We have a
light legislative programme, and my feeling is that we can work at a normal pace until the
end of the session. I do not see much necessity for late hours, because there is little
controversial legislation, and I think if we work at a reasonable pace we can finish some time
in October and then go away and have an election.

QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Passports
1. HON. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister of Internal
Affairs: Has he read the leading article in the New Zealand Herald of 5 August entitled
"Protecting the passport", and is he considering adopting any of the suggestions contained in
it, including a study of overseas methods of guarding against such malpractice, to reduce the
possibility of passports being obtained illegally?
Mr COMBER (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Internal Affairs): I
reply on behalf of the Minister of Internal Affairs. "Yes, I have read the article, and yes, I
will study overseas methods to see if we can adopt more effective controls".
Hon. R. J. Tizard: I ask specifically whether the Minister is considering the suggestion
whereby an pplicant, by being required to present only a signed photograph of himself, can
be in a position to vouch for his own authenticity in making the application?
Mr COMBER: That will be one of the factors taken into account. Past discussions with
embassies and consular offices here in Wellington have revealed that from their experience it
has proved somewhat difficult so far, to come up with an alternative method. Honourable
members may not be aware that an applicant for a passport must produce three things:
evidence of New Zealand citizenship, which, in the case of a New Zealand-born person, is a
birth certificate; an identification certificate from someone other than a relative who has
known the person for at least 12 months; and a photograph signed by the person signing the
identification certificate to the effect that the photograph is a true likeness of the applicant.
Of course, connivance on the part of two people could circumvent the necessary checks and
balances in the system. The matter is causing some concern, particularly in view of one
recently highlighted case, but I can assure the honourable members that we are giving the
matter every attention.

Area and Secondary School Teachers' Salaries
11. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Education: Is it a fact that a
non-graduate teacher with secondary classification holding an F4 position (so-called deputy
principal) in an area school, who was in the secondary service prior to 1 February 1971, has a
lower maximum salary than an assistant teacher in a secondary school, and that the same is
also true for F3, F2, and F1 teachers in area schools who were in the secondary service prior
to 1 February 1971; and, if so, in the event of no action being taken by the teachers'
professional organisations, what does he propose to do to rectify this anomalous situation?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): It is correct that those non-graduate
secondary teachers who now qualify in terms of the recent secondary salaries settlement for
translation to the secondary graduate scale will have a higher maximum salary available to
them than non-graduate area school teachers with similar service holding F1, F2, F3, and F4
positions. Area school teachers are a distinguishable category of teachers within the
education service, and their salaries are subject to independent negotiation. There is no need
for me as Minister to intervene in the salary negotiation arrangements set out in the State


## p. 2563 (#793) ###########################################

11 August
2563
Questions for Oral Answer
Services Conditions of Employment Act 1977. The two teacher organisations concerned-
the NZEI and the PPTA-have lodged claims with the Education Service Committee, and I
am advised that the committee would expect to deal with any implications for area school
salaries after these claims have been negotiated.
Mr Prebble: How can the Department of Education justify the fact that it is employing
area school teachers-who do exactly the same job and work the same hours as teachers in a
district secondary school-on a lower salary than district secondary school teachers?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I have explained this to the honourable member on several
occasions. Area school teachers are neither primary nor secondary teachers, but are
expected to teach in any part of the area school, which is both primary and secondary. Any
negotiations between the PPTA and the Government for alterations to secondary teachers'
salary scales or conditions of employment obviously would have some effect on secondary
teachers in area schools, as would similar negotiations on primary teachers' salary scales.
However, negotiations on behalf of area school teachers for relativity are matters to be taken
up by the NZEI and the PPTA combined.
Mr Prebble: In his original answer the Minister said that area schools are different from
secondary and primary schools, and that area school teachers do not have their own
professional organisation. Why does the Minister insist that the professional organisations
for primary and secondary school teachers should represent area school teachers when it is
clear that those professional organisations are not representing area schools adequately
because area school teachers are paid less to do the same job?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I think the honourable member should come and see me, and I
will explain the matter to him step by step. There are only two categories of teachers-
primary school teachers and secondary school teachers. A primary school teacher is not
normally expected to teach in a secondary school and vice versa, but, in an area school,
teachers are expected to teach in every part of the school. If there is a change of salary or
conditions of service for primary or secondary school teachers, which will have implications
for area school teachers, the arrangement is that negotiations will be undertaken by the
combined NZEI and PPTA. There is no organisation for area school teachers, because there
is no such thing as an area school teacher.
Planning Council
12. Mr LATTER (Marlborough), on behalf of Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora) to the Minister
of National Development: What actions have been taken by the Planning Council to meet the
Government's requirement that it take over the work of the Monetary and Economic
Council?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of National Development): The New Zealand Planning
Council was requested by the Government to take over two tasks from the former Monetary
and Economic Council. The first was to complete a report on New Zealand and the EEC on
which the Monetary and Economic Council had already started work. The text of this report
has now been finished. More generally, the Planning Council was asked to assume the role of
monitoring economic policy and development. To this end, an economic monitoring group
has been set up. This is fully independent, and will publish its own report. The group is
chaired by a member of the New Zealand Planning Council and is serviced by the Planning.
Council's secretariat and the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research. The group's first
report is expected shortly. In addition to these functions that were taken over when the
Monetary and Economic Council was disbanded, the Planning Council is continuing to study
and publish reports on many aspects of economic development as part of its own terms of
reference.
Mr Latter: Has the taking over of these functions by the Planning Council meant extra
cost to the Government?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: On the contrary, there have been savings. Mr Graeme Thompson, a
former member of the Monetary and Economic Council staff has been transferred to the
Planning Council staff and now holds a senior post. The best indication of the result may be a
comparison of the cost to the Government of the Monetary and Economic Council in
1977-78, which was $62,500, and the cost to the New Zealand Planning Council in 1978-79
for work directly taken over from the Monetary and Economic Council, which is estimated
at around $30,000, or about half the former cost.

14. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) on behalf of Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of

unemployed statistics collected on the basis of the age groups requested in the question. At

unemployed. That represents 3.4 percent of ths 1976 census population aged 15 and under 21

Overseas Students-Political Activities
17. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Immigration: Have there been any
cases in which political activities by overseas students studying in New Zealand have caused
embarrassment to the New Zealand Government?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): Each year my department receives a
number of applications for permanent residence from overseas students. One of the reasons
put forward by those students who want to remain here is that they fear prosecution on
return to their home countries because of views they have expressed or activities they have
taken part in here. To allow students to remain in New Zealand for that reason would
undermine the aim of the student policy, which is to train students so that they can assist in
the development of their home countries. To save any embarrassment to the Government or
students, it is important from time to time that students be made aware that they should not
become involved in political activities. The previous Government took a similar attitude in
the case of the first South African scholarship holder, when the then Minister of Immigration
obtained from the New Zealand University Students Association on 21 June 1974, a written
undertaking that stated inter alia: "We are aware of your concern regarding the political
acitivities of Mr Isaacs during his period in New Zealand. As we agreed during the interview
with you, the NZUSA will advise Mr Isaacs of your concern and will not encourage him to
take any active political role in this country."
Mr Lange: I understand that the Minister said the restrictions are in the interests of the
home Government as well as of New Zealand. What restriction did the Minister place on the
leader of the minority Conservative Party in the United Kingdom, Mrs Thatcher, when she
came to New Zealand and spoke at political meetings throughout the country?

Electoral Rolls for Overseas Posts
18. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Justice: What arrangements are

supplied with a full set of electoral rolls and later supplementary rolls, even though strictly
speaking there is no need for overseas posts to have them. Special votes are, and have always
been, issued to overseas voters without their enrolments being checked at the overseas post.
All posts likewise have a supply of registration cards (E1) and also of the information
pamphlet (E12B), and stocks are replenished on request. Lists of streets and places in each
electorate are also provided.
Mr Marshall: Will the copies of the rolls be available to all posts at the same time as they
are available in New Zealand?

difference of getting them to the posts. For several elections the practice has been that the
Chief Electoral Officer supplies sets of the main and the supplementary rolls to the Ministry
of Foreign Affairs, which sends them by surface mail to the overseas posts. Usually they do
not arrive before the election, but they are not necessary for the purpose of the election. The
people voting overseas have special votes.

SELECT COMMITTEE PROCEDURE
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I seek your guidance
on the procedure that can be followed by members of a committee when a situation develops
such as that which developed on the consideration of the recommendation that the House
has just received from the Social Services Committee on the petition of Mr Cullen. The
committee made a majority decision, with one member dissenting, that the recommendation
to be reported to the House should have a rider. The chairman then moved, and it was
carried, that the recommendation, as well as the rider, be presented to the House, but only
after the chairman had consulted the Minister. He did so, and then advised committee
members that the Minister did not agree with the rider. The matter was again referred to the
committee.
This concerns me, because I believe that the practice followed by the chairman was
irregular, to say the least. The rider, which was agreed to by all members present with the
exception of one, was that the Government should be requested to consider the possibility of
giving the petitioner an annuity equivalent to a war pension. As I said, only one member-
not the chairman-disagreed. I seek your guidance, because if a committee makes a majority
decision that is tied to a discussion between the Minister concerned and the chairman of the
committee, and the recommendation is recommitted because it displeases the Minister, the
whole committee procedure, certainly in regard to a hearing of a petition and the
recommendation on that petition, is open to considerable question. I have had to bring the
matter up as a point of order, because my inquiries revealed that when a recommendation to
the Government is being reported back no one is entitled to speak to it. I am concerned
about what happened, and would be grateful if, either now or at a future date you may
select, you could give a lead to the House to ensure that this type of situation is not repeated.
If petitions are to be finally influenced by an attitude adopted by the Minister concerned, we
might just as well give away the whole petition procedure.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): The point of order procedure has been
used because the member knows he could not otherwise raise the matter in a debate. I
perceive no point of order whatsoever. The committee was the master of the matters that
were being discussed, and it made a decision. It is as simple as that. It is very obvious that the
member for Mt. Albert raised the matter in this manner so as to publicise the facts. He
knows very well that, time and time again, similar situations have arisen in committees and
have been dealt with in the same fashion. There is nothing on which you can rule, Mr
Speaker. The committee has made a decision, and whether that decision was made at the
suggestion of the Minister or any other member of the committee is beside the point. The
views of the Minister, or any other member of the committee, are taken into account in the
deliberation.
The member for Mt. Albert knows that it is as simple as that. He knows there is no point
of order, and that there is nothing on which you can rule. He has simply taken this clever
opportunity of making the facts public, apparently to gain some political advantage. I have
been quickly informed of the essence of the matter. My first reaction is that the Minister is
correct in his analysis, although I would not wish that to be my last statement on the matter,
which has been properly dealt with by the committee within the Standing Orders. The
committee reports back to the House. I have just been handed the report which is a simple
one, and in order. I submit that there is no point of order about the method by which the
committee came to its decision.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Perhaps I can clear up one point at this stage. The committee, of
course, is master of its own fate. Once a matter has been referred to a select committee by
the House, the House has no further interest in that matter until the committee reports back,
unless the committee directs the chairman to come back to the House for further
instructions, or unless there is a suggestion that improper conduct, or something like that,
has taken place in the committee, in which case it is reasonable that the matter should be
referred back to the House. It is only that question, and not the subject matter of the report,
that I will hear anything on at this stage. The subject matter of the report is quite irrelevant
to the point of order. I am prepared to hear some limited discussion on the question of
whether the procedure followed by the committee was in any way incorrect, but, by and
large, that is a matter that should be referred to the House by the committee itself. However,
now that the member for Mt. Albert has raised it, I am prepared to hear the Leader of the
Opposition.

We must also, of course, face the unemployment problem, which has plagued the
Western World for a number of years. New Zealand is now getting the backlash, and we
cannot ignore it. It is regrettable that revenue from taxation must be used to pay
unemployment benefits, which reminds me that incentives are necessary to stimulate activity
and increase the level of employment. There is no short answer. I suggest that the alternative
taxation scheme put forward by the Labour Party has no credibility in the eyes of the public.
I consider it would be far better to try to stabilise the economy by continuing the work
carried out during the past 3 years, difficult though that might be. Radical taxation changes
at this time cannot possibly be effective. In fact, they would be dangerous, and could only
bring about the type of disaster that occurred as a result of the £100 tax rebate introduced by
a former Labour Government. The consequences of that action are still well remembered.
Now, when tax reductions are promised, people ask themselves whether they will really be
any better off.
Genuine efforts have been made to help families with young children. I am sure every
member agrees that more needs to be done, but again it is necessary to equate the revenue
that comes in with the expenditure that goes out. The problem is as fundamental as that. It is
very important to consider the increases that have occurred in expenditure. Indeed, they
have a sobering effect, and give one some appreciation of the present tax burden. For
example, between 1975 and 1978 the number of people receiving the domestic purposes
benefit increased from about 17,000 to more than 31,000. That is just one of the facts of life,
and no member can pretend that he could solve that problem overnight. It is the
responsibility of everyone to meet the problem, and, likewise, it is everyone's responsibility,
regrettably, to help meet the bill, which has increased from $31 million in 1975 to $107
million in 1978-almost a four-fold increase. I emphasise that that bill has to be paid, and I
wonder whether imaginary savings throug tax reductions to a certain section of the
community would take care of the problem. I find it frightening that the number of domestic
purposes benefits has increased from 17,231 to 31,465 in 1978. I wonder how many will be
paid in another 3 years and how much additional tax will need to be raised to meet the bill?
That is but one example of increasing Government expenditure.
The same type of growth is occurring in health expenditure. In the past 4 years the
health vote has doubled, from some $400 million to $897 million; so another $400 million has
to be found. Could the scheme suggested by the Labour Party provide those extra hundreds
of millions of dollars? The people are no longer prepared to look only at offers and promises.
What looks nice, rosy, and attractive to one section of the community will be considered
carefully not only by that section, but by other sections of the community. I doubt very much

him. The great majority of New Zealanders today are thinking more carefully about the
future. They realise that income tax from all sources is spread fairly widely across the board,

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I want to make a few comments on
these Bills, and I want to make them rather informally, because I do not propose to get
bound up in a consideration of masses of figures. I want to talk mainly about the principle of
Government revenue and expenditure, in respect of which these Bills have been produced.
It is important that there should be some discussion on that now, because so many charges
and counter-charges are being bandied about, and so many wonderful things are being
promised if only the public changes the Government. It is time we got back to some realism.
What we are talking about is the major tax that finances Government spending-
personal income tax. Anyone who has held the position of Minister of Finance knows that
the most difficult task is to try to make any significant change to personal income tax. The
reason is that the amount of revenue involved is so great, and the compression of personal
incomes in this country is so great, that any significant change involves a vast sum of
revenue-hundreds of millions of dollars. The picture in recent years is well known. The
National Government kept the Labour Government's tables until the beginning of this year,
when a 5 percent reduction was brought in for just a couple of months.
That brings me to the other important but widely misunderstood point-the time
element. It is not only a question of how much reduction or increase should be made in
taxation or in Government spending on any particular item; it is also a question of for how
long in a particular revenue year that reduction, that increase, or that amount of spending
should continue. In the expenditure field it is bad management to bring in a policy in, say,
March, or to commence a big building in March, without realising that a commitment is
being made month by month for 12 months of the following expenditure year; in other
words, the expenditure is not only from the current year's Budget, but is a commitment also
on the following year's Budget, and not just for 1 month, but for 12 months. I believe that
principle of time has been totally ignored by the Labour Party in its election promise for this
year.
The National Government brought in a 5 percent tax reduction in February, which
continued for the first half of the current financial year. For the second half of the year, the
tables under these Bills will take over, and will represent a very substantial reduction. Again,
the Labour Party professes not to understand this. Further relief is given to the low-income,
single-income family with young children when it is undesirable that the mother should take
a job. That principle has been incorporated in each of the last three National Budgets. The
Labour Party says that a teenage child costs more to keep. That is not the point. The relief is
given for the family with a young child, so that the mother can stay at home with the child. It
is not a question of whether it costs more to keep that young child. We are endeavouring to
make it easier for the mother to stay at home with that child rather than take a job.
I return to the time element. It comes in for half of this year-the plateau effect-so that
the ordinary worker does not go into a higher tax bracket if his wage increases. This has been

The most important point is that the very substantial amount of revenue loss in these

next year as they hit this year. That point should be made, and it should be understood that
whoever writes next year's Budget-and I have a pretty good idea who it will be-will have
to provide for double the amount by way of revenue loss than was provided for this year,
because this year the tables operate for only half of the year. That is point No. 1 in terms of
the time element.
The Labour Party is also overlooking the fact that national superannuation, which
approaches its peak at the end of this month-80 percent of the average ordinary-time
wage-will this year cost the extra amount for only 7 months. Next year will be a full year.
Again, we have pre-empted the budgeting powers of next year's Minister of Finance,
because that additional national superannuation will apply for 12 months. Those two major
items are not for this year's Budget, but for next year's Budget. There is also the normal
increase in Government spending. Public servants have received some major pay increases
from which, of course, income tax will come, but at lower rates, and they are already in next
year's Budget, and must be.

Transport Fuels-DSIR Discussion Paper
1. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Does he support the
statement of the working party transport fuels DSIR discussion paper No. 1 that "a policy
aimed at self sufficiency in transport fuels for New Zealand will not be successful unless there
is a major extension of the research and development programme of both Government and
industry", and, if this is so, what assistance is to be given to this programme?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): It is likely that the efforts given to research and
development in the field of transport fuels will have to expand. As well as the financial
assistance given to research and development through the New Zealand Energy Research
and Development Committee and the DSIR, it was announced in the Budget that a liquid
fuels trust account is to be established. It is expected that this will have sufficient income to
develop the required programme, the basis for which will be defined in legislation.
Hon. F. M. Colman: As the paper was published after the Budget, is the criticism valid
on that score?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The comment made in the liquid fuels report should be viewed in the
context in which it was presented: namely, if there is to be an important new breakthrough in
the development of liquid fuels it is freely acknowledged that this will require a considerable
research effort. An important first step, however, has been the decision announced in the
Budget to establish a liquid fuels trust account.

Television Licence Fees-Hotels/Motels
3. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) to the Minister of Broadcasting: What is the
justification for charging full and separate licence fees for every television set installed in a


## p. 2589 (#819) ###########################################

15 August
2589
Questions for Oral Answer
hotel or motel room?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): Such licence-charging provisions
are based on the principle that all television receivers should be licensed at the rates laid
down and that the ordinary viewer should not be expected to subsidise business enterprises.
That principle has been adopted by successive Governments. Since accommodation
establishments tend to look upon television as a factor in attracting custom and usually build
the licence fee into their tariff structures, any departure from the present basis into multiple
licensing could, I believe, amount to a substantial subsidy.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is it not a fact that only in recent months have proprietors of
organisations such as hotels and motels been required to pay more than one television
licence fee?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: The member referred to "recent months". My
understanding is that they have always been required to do so. Certainly it has been an issue
ever since I have been the Minister-that is, over the past 3 years.
Mr Kirk: Can the Minister confirm that a person staying in a motel that already has a
licence to operate a television set will be charged a second fee for the use of a set in the motel
room?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I think the member is overlooking the fact that it is the
owner of the licensed set who is responsible for the fee. That is a well established practice,
applying to telephones and other systems.
Mr Comber: Can the Minister confirm that if the present charging did not apply people
on low incomes, for example, would be obliged to pay a greater levy as the result of any
adjustment that might be made in favour of hotel or motel operators?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: A very substantial amount of money-about $300,000-is
involved, and it would be necessary to raise that amount in some other form or from some
other licence holders.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Can the Minister not confirm that the single fee payable by hotel
and motel proprietors continued until it was challenged in legal proceedings, which were
determined against the proprietors only in recent weeks?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am sorry to be at odds with the member, but I do not
follow the point he is making. My understanding is that the moteliers challenged the
principle and lost their case. They have had to pay licence fees for each set, as I understand
it, and one particular motelier challenged that practice.

Tourism Statistics
7. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) to the Minister of Tourism: What are the department's

3 years?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism: For the year ended 31 March 1976 there

projected numbers for the years ending 31 March 1979, 1980, and 1981, which are now being
considered by the Tourism Advisory Council, are 411 000, 444 000, and 484 000, increases

Mr Kirk: Why does the Minister expect an increase in the number of overseas visitors to

coming from Australia, but in the year to 31 May 1978 the number of tourists from the
United Kingdom has increased by 9.1 percent, from western Europe by 16.8 percent, and
from Japan by 14.4 percent, and we have every right to expect the increases predicted.
Mr Kirk: By how much does the 2.8 percent growth rate last year fall short of the
growth rate of 8 percent projected by the Tourist Advisory Council?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: If the member was capable of doing simple arithmetic he could
work it out for himself. I go along with the 8 percent projection by the Tourist Advisory
Council. I have given the figures for the 3 years, 1979, 1980, and 1981, for which the
estimates are 3 percent, 5 percent, and 8 percent.

Accident Compensation-Medical Certificates
17. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Labour: Are he or the Accident
Compensation Commission aware of any widespread activity on the part of the medical
profession that enables workers in some areas of New Zealand to obtain medical certificates
covering alleged sicknesses after the events?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Labour. "It is assumed that when the honourable member refers to 'sickness' he means

widespread issuing of medical certificates referring to past incapacity. It does happen, and in
legitimate circumstances. However, the medical profession has always been concerned about
any demand for retrospective certificates, and in a newsletter to doctors in 1976 the
commission warned 'the practice of writing retrospective certificates can be open to abuse
and doctors are invited to exercise reasonable caution'. The commission will normally
investigate any case of a medical certificate being given for an incapacity that the doctor has
not seen personally. This has happened on a few occasions."

SPEAKER'S RULING-SELECT COMMITTEE PROCEDURE
Mr SPEAKER: This is a convenient time to give a ruling on the point of order raised on
Friday, when the member for Manurewa, on behalf of the Social Services Committee,
reported on the petition of Mr Trevor Cullen. The member for Mt. Albert sought my ruling
on whether the Social Services Committee had acted in accordance with the Standing Orders
when it considered the petition. Standing Order 376 lays down that, if the Standing Orders
or the practice of Parliament do not provide, the proceedings of the select committee should
follow, as nearly as possible, those of the Committee of the Whole House. The keynote for
the proceedings of a select committee has always been-and I think it should be-flexibility
and informality so as to facilitate the full examination of the question before the committee.
The minutes of the Social Services Committee reveal that on 2 August the committee
agreed to two motions: first, that the petition be referred to the Government for most
favourable consideration, together with a rider; and, secondly, that the chairman report the
resolution of the committee to the House, subject to discussing it with the Minister and
possibly having a further meeting. The latter motion was carried unanimously. It could
possibly have been argued that the second motion was in conflict with the first and should
not have been allowed, but it seems to me that the committee wanted to recognise Mr
Cullen's case and also to consult the Minister about some details before reporting to the
House. The chairman was authorised to do that and, if necessary, to bring the petition back
to the committee for further consideration. As the minutes of a meeting held on 9 August
reveal, this is what happened. The chairman reported to the committee that he had discussed
the petition with the Minister, and on that basis he then moved that the petition receive most
favourable consideration-without the rider-and he then reported to the House.
It has been suggested that these proceedings conflict with the practice outlined on page
657 of the nineteenth edition of Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, on which it is stated


## p. 2594 (#824) ###########################################

15 August
Speaker's Ruling-Select Committee Procedure
that, once the committee has agreed to a report, it cannot be further amended. Our own
Standing Orders 120 and 121 prohibit the House, and therefore a committee, from putting
the same question again in the same session unless 7 days' notice is given, or leave is granted.
However, I do not see that the proceedings of the select committee necessarily infringe the
Standing Orders or Erskine May.
If committee members felt there had been some irregularity, they should have raised the
matter then, not later. The normal procedure would be for the chairman or the committee to
seek guidance from the Clerk or a ruling from me, and this should not usually be done in the
House. I believe it is an important principle that, when the House refers a matter to a select
committee, the House does not want to hear any more about it unless the committee needs
further instructions, or until it is ready to report. The House does not want to be bothered
with what select committees are doing, so long as they get on with the job in accordance with
the Standing Orders. I find nothing irregular in the proceedings of the Social Services
Committee, as reported to the House on the matter of the petition of Mr Cullen.

People without any degree of skill often found it hardest to get jobs, and they were the
people for whom something should be done. That was why the Government had created
various job promotional programmes. The skill promotion programme aimed to encourage
employers to train people to meet future skilled requirements. The first job programme
aimed to assist employers to make more jobs available to people seeking their first job. The
additional jobs programme had been designed to reduce the initial cost of labour to
employers who wished to extend their activities.
The farm employment scheme assisted farmers by providing a subsidy on the
employment of skilled or unskilled unemployed persons, and an accelerated maintenance
scheme provided additional work for private contractors. The Government had made a
substantial effort in the areas of considerable need.

totally dissatisfied with the tragedy of unemployment. One living monument to it would be
the situation on the Mangere Bridge project which, seemingly, could not be resolved. The
man-days lost had created an unenviable record, but 56 percent of those figures had been
due to economic circumstances.
He thanked the loyal staff, sitting behind him, who had done so much to make his task
easier and the figure of 73 000 people placed in employment demonstrated how
superlatively they had done their job. As Minister of State Services he had been well and
truly served by the State servants, and deplored the attacks being made upon them, both
inside and outside the Chamber. He also paid tribute to those who had worked with him as
Minister of Transport and as Minister of Railways.
Vote, $72,701,000, agreed to.
Health, $897,840,000.
Department of Health
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) said that, because of penny-pinching attitudes and
putting balance sheets before people, the country's health services were falling slowly apart.
The Wellington Hospital Board had nearly closed the Elderslea Maternity Hospital in Upper
Hutt, but the decision had been revoked when it had been found that the cost per bed was
lower than in any other maternity hospital in the area. Marilyn Bowman and thousands of
people in Upper Hutt had signed a petition to prevent the hospital closing, and were to be
thanked. Now it was to be reduced from a 40-bed hospital to a 22-bed hospital, with other
services being made available, but nothing would happen until funds were available. The
only services provided in Upper Hutt, in the Wellington Hospital Board area, were the
district health nurse and the Elderslea Maternity Hospital. What would happen to Upper
Hutt if flooding or some other disaster cut off the area and it became isolated?
In 1975 the then Labour Minister of Health had agreed in principle to a health centre
being built in Upper Hutt, another in the Silverstream area, and one in the Brown Owl area.
Although the present Minister of Health was one of those who had presented a petition to
Parliament at that time, urging the Labour Government to go ahead with the health centre in
Upper Hutt, after 3 years in office nothing had been done. When would the talking stop, and
when would there be action? Already, room sizes and other plans had been altered. The X-
ray unit to be included in the health centre would now be put in as a private development.
In 1976 the Government had called a halt to the building of health centres, but had
reviewed that decision last year, and had given the go ahead. However, 12 months later
there was no firm proposal to build a health centre in Upper Hutt-only an agreement in
principle. More doctors were needed in Upper Hutt in particular and the country in general,
because last year New Zealand had lost more doctors overseas than it had trained.
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) said that in 1975 he had presented a petition to
Parliament asking the Labour Government to make a decision about a health centre at
Upper Hutt, but nothing had been done. Land had now been purchased for a health centre


## p. 2609 (#839) ###########################################

15 August
2609
Appropriation Bill-Estimates
in Upper Hutt, and building was about to start. Negotiations had been started to purchase
land in Silverstream for the second health centre, but some difficulties had been
experienced. The Government did not want to take the land under the Public Works Act,
and was continuing negotiations. The comments about the decision, make by the Hon. T. M.
McGuigan in 1975, were untrue; he had no authority to approve in principle the construction
of a health centre without first getting the blessing. of Cabinet, which he did not get.
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) said the member for Heretaunga had led a deputation of local
body representatives from the Upper Hutt district to the former Minister of Health, who had
suggested that the deputation should prepare sketch plans so that progress on the health
centre could be made. Specific Cabinet authority was not needed. The present Minister had
taken up the petition during the National Party's 1975 election campaign to try to embarrass
the Labour Government. Now the National Government had delayed a decision on the
health centre until election year.
When could people in Pinehaven expect some progress on the development of a health
centre? He understood that land close to the railway line at Silverstream would be used, but
that there was some conflict over the right to occupy the land. Could the Minister clarify the
status of the land, if indeed it was the Government's intention to proceed with a health
centre for the Pinehaven-Silverstream district? About 40 000 people lived in the Upper Hutt
district, and for years a health centre had been needed. He hoped that by next year the
matter would be finalised, and that the people of Upper Hutt would get a health centre.
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) said that nearly $900 million had been voted for health
this year, but the Government had recognised a need for a more imaginative response to the
funding of the health system. The Government had imposed the alcohol and tobacco levy,
from which funds went back to community services. Over $1 million would be expended on
health centres this year, and there was to be a $1 million subsidy to the New Zealand Plunket
Society. The Government had done more than its predecessor to bring primary medical care
within reach of the people, especially those in the outer and multicultural suburbs of
metropolitan areas, and those in remote rural areas.
Would the Labour Party's health policy, to be announced tomorrow, incorporate the
remit-from the member for New Lynn at the party's annual conference, and reported in the
Evening Post on 12 May-that Labour Party policy should include the socialisation of
private hospitals? That resurrected the spectre of Labour's white paper on health, and the
bureaucratic bogy that all doctors should be indentured civil servants. The article suggested
that a community health development conference would be set up by the Labour
Government to complete the overhaul of the country's health services. The Labour
Government's white paper on health would have destroyed the independent hospital boards
with their local body and local authority representation, and would have destroyed voluntary
organisations, such as the Plunket Society and the New Zealand Red Cross Society, which
the National Government had recognised with its subsidy programme funded from the
alcohol and tobacco levy.
The Government had given health a much stronger front-line role, and had given
greater immediacy, relevance, and emphasis to voluntary care. If there were a slogan to
underscore the policy so successfully put into practice by the present Minister, it would be
that primary medical care had been put on wheels and been made more accessible to the
people.
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) said that local authorities had nothing whatever
to do with health centres. Empowering legislation for health centres had been introduced by
the National Government in 1970, giving hospital boards the right and the responsibility for
drawing up plans and for approaching the Government with propositions. If the
Government agreed with a proposition it would be put in the estimates, and money would be
voted for it. This year money had been voted for the Upper Hutt No. 1 Health Centre, and
for the Upper Hutt No. 2 Health Centre at Silverstream. There was some difficulty with the
purchase of land at Silverstream. The Railways Department owned the land, and had leased
it to a private developer. It was important that a health centre should be built in the right
area, because its success depended on the ability of people to go there. Mrs Julie Cameron,
National Party candidate for Heretaunga in the 1975 election, had made a valiant effort to
get something done about the health centres. She knew what had happened at that time, but
the former Minister of Health had done nothing about the centres.
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) said that in 1975 the Minister of Health had said that
he would not read the Labour Government's white paper on health. Health services in south

Auckland had been set back 3 or 4 years. The National Government had adopted a
deliberate policy of denying the people in south Auckland a hospital. Manukau City had the
largest land area of any city in New Zealand, but it did not have a hospital within its
boundaries. The Labour Government had planned to build a hospital in Manurewa, but the
National Government had put paid to that. The Government had wanted to cut expenditure.
Local members had said they did not want one hospital; they had wanted two or three
hospitals. They had decided to establish one hospital south of Papakura and one off Botany
Road in Pakuranga. The Government was still negotiating for the site at Papakura, which
meant the hospital would not be completed for another 5 or 6 years. The Botany Road site at
Pakuranga was not yet serviced. The people of south Auckland were being denied hospital
beds because of a political decision.
Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) said that the hospital proposed at Wiri had been outdated
while still on the drawing board. It was National policy to take hospital services to the
people. After speaking to hospital boards, it had been learned that large 1000-bed and 800-
bed hospitals were outdated because of serious depersonalising effects on patients and staff.
The hospital at Wiri would not have been opened any sooner than the other two hospitals,
because, in the construction of a large hospital, no beds could be commissioned until the roof
was on the top floor. The provision of smaller hospitals, with 300 or 400 beds, was part of the
Government's policy.
The training of nurses and doctors was geared towards community health. One of the
important achievements of the National Government had been the emphasis placed on
health centres rather than on medical centres, and $17 million had been set aside for such
work. The National Government's committees on health, and the Minister, had worked
together closely and had found out what was needed in the community. The figure of $897
million provided for the Health vote was a huge sum; it could not continue to grow at that
rate. A lot would be achieved by using the ancillary services in medicine and health in the
way proposed.
Mr MALCOLM (Eden) said that when the Labour Party's policy on health was released
it would be a rewrapped white paper on health. The member for Wanganui had said that it
was recorded in Hansard that the present Minister of Health had not read the white paper.
That was not recorded in Hansard in any form; the Minister of Health had read the white
paper on health, and was horrified. The Labour spokesman on health had been reported as
saying that socialisation of medicine was a term preferable to nationalisation of medicine.
Under the National Government the number of registered nurses had increased from 17 000
to about 22 000. Health services had been taken into the community. Many nurses were
married women returning to nursing. The Government supported the concept of mature
nurses, who had perhaps raised families, returning to the profession, even if only on a part-
time basis. The number of district health nurses had increased, and there had been an
increase in the meals-on-wheels service.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) said that before the last election the Minister had
gone around the country criticising the white paper on health introduced by the Labour
Government, and later he had said that he had not read the white paper.
Hon. T. F. Gill said, on a point of order, that he had corrected that misapprehension
earlier. It could be checked that the statement was not printed in Hansard.
The DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: The member for Timaru must accept the word of the
Minister of Health.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR said that the present Minister of Health had gone round the
country before the last election, promising hospitals and health services wherever he went,
and now some of his chickens had come home to roost. What assistance would the
Department of Health give to the Bidwill Hospital in Timaru? That private hospital was
faced with closure because of increased costs. A public trust had been formed, led by
prominent citizens and members of the medical profession in Timaru, to try to prevent the
hospital closing. He had written to the Minister of Health, who had replied that it was
unlikely that a loan for the full amount of $150,000 would be supported, because a significant
proportion of the cost involved appeared to be for maintenance, which was not eligible for
assistance. It was maintenance that would decide whether the hospital would remain open.
The hospital trust deserved Government assistance, because, by its efforts, money had been
saved.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin) said he was very happy to be a member of a Government that was
prepared to support the taking of centralised hospital services into the community. He

For many years people in south and greater Auckland had been concerned about the

Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) said that no assurance had been given that the public health
service would continue. Had the Government recognised the right of all New Zealanders to
a public health system, regardless of their ability to pay? The need for a community health
service had been mentioned, and she acknowledged that the Government had made moves
in that direction. Was the Government committed to providing community health services,
or were the statements made by the Minister just window dressing? How much of the extra
tax imposed on tobacco and liquor had been spent on community health, and how had it
been spent? The Health Centres Advisory Committee had recommended that funds be
allocated to build four health centres each year during the 3 years from 1977. How many had
been built?
Richard Walls: One, at Port Chalmers.
Mrs BATCHELOR said that one had been built at Port Chalmers and another at
Ngatea. How many had been built in Christchurch? As at 30 June 1978 more than 3000
people were on a waiting list for surgery at Christchurch Hospital. The establishment of a
Lyttelton Health Centre had been delayed because of the Government's decision to freeze
the building of health centres. Perhaps, as an election bribe, the Government had promised
to start construction in December. When would construction of the spinal unit in
Christchurch start? The Government had done nothing to help health services in
Christchurch.
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) said that the Government would assist the
Bidwill Hospital Trust, to the tune of $122,150, but the money for maintenance, architects'
fees, and other charges would have to be met by the trust. If private hospitals were allowed
to run down, and were not maintained, it could not be expected that the Government would
pick up the tab.
He had made several promises at the time of the last election. He had promised that the
National Government would exploit and encourage the voluntary services and agencies in a
way that the Labour white paper had not. He had promised a dual system of health-private
and public. That system had developed within New Zealand; it met the country's
requirements, and was far better than the purely national public health system in England
and the purely private system in America. That promise had been kept, and the Labour
Government would not have continued the dual system. He had promised that there would
not be a New Zealand health authority, similar to the broadcasting authority, which was not
responsible to Parliament and about which members of the House could not ask questions.
The Labour white paper had recommended such an authority. He had promised that
hospital boards would continue.
He had promised that there would not be a National Government caucus committee
which would meet in a back room, produce a white paper, and spring it on the people; the
National Government would consult with the people. The National Party had promised to
set up a Board of Health committee to consult and advise on health reorganisation. All the
people on the Northland committee were from Northland, and they were consulting people
to see what sort of medical services would be wanted. The National Party had promised to
take health into the community. He had never promised to build a certain hospital or a
certain health centre, because until he became Minister and had the facts available to him he
did not have the competence to do that.
There was a great deal of good feeling and support for community health. Medical
officers of health, the hospitals boards, Plunket nurses, district nurses, occupational health

nurses, and others all worked together harmoniously, and were in agreement with the
Government about the direction New Zealand should be taking in health services. He was
delighted with the co-operation the Government had received.
He was pleased that the Department of Health, the director-general, the deputy
director-general, the director of nursing, and the top officials all the way down the line, had
had an opportunity to discuss their problems with him. He found people in the department
to be an invigorating group; they wanted to get things done. They wanted to co-operate, and
were not concerned about locking themselves behind doors and discussing matters. The
department members were out in the community, having discussions with the hospital
boards, voluntary agencies, doctors, nurses, and other people concerned about health.
It had been forecast that when the Labour Party announced its health policy tomorrow
it would be a dressed-up white paper. He did not think that would be so. He thought its
policy would be similar to what the Government had stated about health. The Labour Party
had said that when it became the Government it would call a conference. The conference
would last for 3 years. Until the election the Labour Party would say that it had learned the
error of its ways, that it would consult and listen to the people. The member for Porirua
would not be in a back room making decisions with his caucus colleagues. A Labour
Government would socialise medicine. Private hospitals would become a thing of the past.
He expressed thanks to his colleagues on the health committee, and to other colleagues who
had supported him in the debate. They shared his understanding of health. The Department
of Health, the hospital boards, the medical officers of health, and the voluntary
organisations-such as the Crippled Children Society and the Plunket Society-had fine
teams. The Government had kept its promise not to interfere with the voluntary agencies. It
had sought the co-operation of the agencies, but it had not dictated to them. Any questions
about the Karitane hospitals should be addressed to the Royal Society.
Progress reported.
